en: Chapter 19:
The First Chapter of the Brahmagītā in the Upper Section of the Fourth Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa of this Sūtasamhitā.

O Janaka, you have related everything, including both the defects and their opposites. Now we desire to hear the unsurpassed Bhagavadgītā. (1) Since you are the mine of all jewels of knowledge, a great soul, and the very embodiment of the purifying Sun, you alone are our teacher; this is our firm conviction. (2) There is nothing that remains unknown to you; speak the truth. If it pleases you, O Blessed One, you ought to speak here. (3)

Dhruva said: O you who are most proficient in the knowledge of Brahman, listen with faith and with due respect to this unsurpassed *Brahmagītā*, which was spoken by her. (4) In a previous kalpa, all the gods, having deliberated for a very long time, [discovered] the most profound secret of the Vedas. (5) With their minds possessed by doubt, they performed great austerities; then, the gods, being powerless, beheld the Creator, Brahmā. (6)

Salutations to the Lord of the worlds, the omniscient, the bestower of all, the greatly compassionate, the glorious one, who is intent upon the welfare of his devotees through his very name. (7) Salutations to the lotus-feet of the venerable Guru Ānanda, whose sole activity is the eradication of the poison of the great delusion along with its manifestations. (9) Thus, it has been stated that the realization of the oneness of the Self, which is otherwise difficult to attain even for those who have mastered the six systems of philosophy, is the means for the attainment of liberation.

And because this is agreed upon by all schools (*sarvaśālā*), [the author] introduces the question of the sages in order to recount the *Brahmagītā*, which fully expounds the meaning of the Upaniṣads beginning with the *Darvi*, *Aitareya*, and *Taittirīya*: "By you... (1.4). Then, in order to speak of that, he cites an ancient account: "In former times... (5–6). "O Omniscient One, O All-Knowing One!"—one who knows everything in general is "omniscient" (*sarvajña*); one who knows everything even in its specific details is "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*).

When he knows all things, he is "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*). The meaning is that he is one who possesses a body consisting solely of bliss. Indeed, it is Paraśiva of such a nature who, when endowed with the quality of *sattva*, becomes Brahmā for the sake of creating the entire universe. And the scripture declares that Paraśiva has this very form: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9). [From] the Fourth [Part], the Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa, the latter half, the Brahmagītā (Chapter...).

1–12) The first chapter, titled *Brahmagīti*, was presented by the sages: "O Śrī Romaharṣaṇa, you have explained the entire Purāṇa in both its concise and detailed forms. Although we have listened to the Supreme Reality through your words, we still harbor a doubt: is that indeed the sole subject matter propounded by all the Vedāntas? With this inquiry, we now wish to hear the *Brahmagītā*. (1)

"O Great Soul, you are the highly distinguished disciple of the sage Śrī Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the treasury of all branches of knowledge; therefore, nothing remains unknown to you. If you are pleased with us, please graciously recite the Brahmagītā for us. (2-3) Sūta said: "O knowers of Brahman, I shall recite that Gītā for you; listen with faith. (4)

In ancient times, all the gods gathered together and deliberated upon the meaning of the Vedas; however, being unable to reach a definitive conclusion without a teacher who had realized the Truth (*tattva-vettā*), they fell into doubt. They performed severe penance and went to Lord Brahmā to inquire about the meaning of the Vedas without any uncertainty. (5–6) Lord Brahmā knows everything in general as well as in detail.

(What more specifically can be said? O Knower! Although it is possible for you to state everything, nevertheless, we shall begin by first describing infinite objects according to their respective cognitions, which will be considered impossible for the learner to grasp clearly. First, 1.3.
Ya. O performer of action!)

There, in that forest named Brahmavana, which was protected by hundreds of sages, seven hundred *brahmagītās* resounded, sung by those most devoted to the practice of all yogas. It was filled with the sounds of *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *gandharvas*, and *tīrthakaras*, and offered as oblations. (8) It was strewn with various blossoming trees, variegated with diverse minerals, resounding with the songs of birds, and frequented by many holy bathing places (*tīrthas*). (9) It was joined by ten million caves, adorned with mountain peaks, and exceedingly beautiful, abounding in the six flavors beginning with sweet. (10) In that place stood the forest named Brahmavana, which was surrounded by hundreds of sources of origin.

There is a vast forest, extending for many yojanas, well-sprinkled by long ponds; it is filled with various flowers and joined by various birds; it abounds in sweet fruits and is rich in roots and fruits; it is perfumed by the fragrance of swarms of wandering bees; it is stirred by gentle breezes and graced by the soft sunlight; it is illuminated by the rays of the moon—therein stands a great tree, made of gold and resembling the rising sun.

It was provided with nine walls and eighty-four gates, and possessed millions of excellent ramparts endowed with great strength. It was protected by swords, javelins, bows, and other weapons, and was strewn with heaps of flowers and filled with incense. It was adorned with blazing lamps, graced with garlands of pearls, and its millions of walls were resplendent with various wonderful paintings. It was further embellished with strings of gems and canopies made of pearls.

It was joined with sounds that reached the ears, and it issued forth from the eastern archway (toraṇa). It was filled with the weight of songs and other music, and was attended by hosts of celestial singers (Apsaras). It was resounded by various kinds of great musical instruments, as if produced by the gods themselves. It was characterized by the fierce sound of drums in the midst of the assembly, and was accompanied by various types of cymbals (kāhala). It was thoroughly permeated by the resonance of the Vedas, and endowed with the sounds of the Sāmaveda. It was joined with the resonance of the Purāṇas, and possessed the sounds of the Itihāsas. It was filled with the best of all branches of knowledge, and was attended by all the gods.
It was surrounded by an unfathomable expanse of fire, filled with millions of chariots and tens of millions of elephants.

7. They were seated upon the peak of Mount Meru, surrounded by those among the yogis who had attained perfection. Yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, siddhas, and others had gathered on that mountain to attend upon them. 8–9. That place was adorned with various metals such as gold and with jewels; it was hallowed by many sacred fords (tīrthas) and resounded with the warbling of birds.

The caves were filled with wisdom on all sides; Mathurā and other places were overflowing with the essence of rasa, which was streaming forth. (10) On the peak of Mount Meru, there is a Brahmavana forest a hundred yojanas long and as wide, wherein beautiful lakes are situated.

The birds have dispersed, and the roots and tubers are most delicious; it is the best time for digestion. || 2 || These peacocks are crying out upon the flowers of the excellent trees; a gentle breeze is blowing, and the morning mist is light. || 13 || Even the rays of the fourteenth day are still falling softly. In that great forest is a golden city, like the rising sun of Lord Brahmā. || 14 ||

14. It has nine ramparts and eighty gates; strong-bodied gatekeepers remain on guard over them. 15. They stand ready with weapons such as swords, spears, and bows; it remains adorned with heaps of various flowers and fragrant incense. 16. Garlands of flowers beautify that city, and it is made radiant by rows of lamps.

The crores of walls of that city are adorned with variegated paintings. (17) Canopies made of pearls are stretched upon pearl strings; the sounds of *chamve-ṭamve* resound everywhere, and high archways hang suspended. (18) Apsarases who sing and dance reside there, so that the humming of various flutes and rhythmic beats remains constant on all sides. (19)

All kinds of sounds—loud, clear, and high-pitched—are constantly heard, as well as the mischievous voices of the *dāsī-khe* (female celestial attendants). In the City of Brahmā (*brahmapura*), the study of the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas proceeds incessantly; for since omniscient beings dwell there, the essence of all branches of knowledge is heard at every moment. (20–21)

That city extends as far as Pūrvavarta, beyond which it is once again bottomless. On all four sides of the city are ramparts; there are chariots, and even more elephants, horses, and infantry equipped with weapons and missiles—countless in number.

Chapter 9 [The city] was adorned with great Vaiśvadeva sacrifices performed by millions of experts, and it was endowed with those possessed of strength who were skilled in the science of weapons. (1) It was protected by these very best of men, who were like the essence of the gods; it was attainable by the meritorious, but unattainable by those whose deeds are merely physical. (2) In that inner apartment, which was filled with the fragrance of incense, adorned with all auspicious marks, and graced with every ornament, (3) the two [princes], joined in battle and accompanied by their respective armies, shone forth. (4)

Accompanied by the lion-bannered [Indra] and joined by swift-footed horses, [he dwells] where the darkness of ignorance is being gnawed away, and where the circle is pierced by the *ra* and *la* vowels. Together with the Goddess Sarasvatī, whose form consists of the phonemes, he dwells there, the abode of all words, meanings, and sounds. Then the gods, having gone to the Lord of the World, beheld him who was endowed with the splendor of the sun, wondrous, blazing with majesty, adorned with a jeweled crown, and possessing a face that was victorious and beautiful.
Adorned with necklaces and ornaments set with various gems, and wearing a beautiful, well-fashioned crown of great jewels. || 20 ||

[They saw] the Self-born One, eternally meditating upon that which is higher than the highest; his lotus-feet were being praised by the lords of the gods and the best of sages. (24) Having seen Him, the creator of all, the stainless one who is beyond even that, they were filled with the darkness-dispelling light of great joy, their eyes fixed upon His supreme form. (25)

Covered in horripilation from joy, their voices faltering, with tears of bliss welling within their stainless hearts, they cast away all mental afflictions and bowed upon the surface of the earth; placing their joined palms to their heads, all the gods remained there with concentrated minds. (26–27)

For it is impossible for those burdened by sin to enter. 22–24 ||

Moreover, within that palace, in the jeweled pavilion, Brahmā was seated together with Goddess Sarasvatī. Thousands of massive pillars supported that pavilion; it was auspicious and adorned in every way.

Brahmā was adorned with a crown set with various gems and jewels of diverse colors, as well as jeweled earrings, necklaces made of precious stones, armlets of shimmering gems, and fingers decorated with various kinds of rings. (29–30) He wore a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and a beautiful upper garment (*uttarīya*), and a lovely girdle was fastened around his waist.

They were perfumed with *keca*, sandalwood, *agaru*, *karūra*, and other fragrant substances; they wore many garlands of scented flowers; their garments were white, and their own complexion was like gold. (31–233) The Supreme Brahmā, higher than the highest, illuminates everything by his very nature. All the gods, asuras, lords of sages, and others bow down and offer salutations at his feet. 1. [Ca: "by action"].

The gods spoke in the *Brahmagītā*: "Salutations again and again to the one who bestows Brahman, who has dispelled the darkness of ignorance for those desiring liberation, and who has manifested the ocean of the Vedas. (29) Salutations indeed to the witness of all beings, who is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), and who is the cause of deliverance for those suffering in the ocean of worldly existence. (20) Salutations again and again to the supporter of all, the ordainer, and the remover of all distress, who is the witness of all beings in all their various states. (9) Salutations to the Supreme Being, the highest abode, who is beyond all prayer. (1)

Salutations again and again to the one who possesses complete knowledge and who is the refuge of the true nature of the self. (42) Salutations to the lotus-born, the purifier, and the one praised by Padmanābha; salutations to the one worthy of worship with the lotus flower and to the bearer of the lotus. (42) Salutations again and again to the one highly praised, who acts as the protector of the gods beginning with Sūrya, and who bestows happiness upon the gods, demons, humans, and others. (42) Salutations again and again to the one who is encompassed by the Vedas, the eye of the universe, whose form is the knowledge of the Vedas, who is the object of the Vedas, and who is the knower of the end of the Vedas. (45)

Salutations to the one who is beyond the world (*vidhava*), who is free from ritual injunctions (*vidhihīna*), who ordains the words of the sacred law (*vidhivākyavidhāyin*), and who bestows liberation (*viyapradāvin*) upon those whose actions have been cast off through steadfastness in their practice. Salutations again and again to Viriñca, the most distinguished, the remover of the distress of the most eminent, and the one who destroys the ocean of despondency for those who are dejected. Salutations to the one who exists within the golden egg (*hiraṇyagarbha*), who dwells upon the golden mountain, who is attainable through the gift of gold, and who transcends even the golden. Salutations to the one who possesses a hundred joys (*śatānanda*), who is peaceful (*śānta*), and the bestower of knowledge born of the mine of wisdom.

Salutations again and again to the one who bestows knowledge only upon those endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues. (9) Regarding the phrase "as the essence of the Self" (*pratyagātmatayā*): it means for the sake of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) who desire to directly realize Brahman—the ultimate reality, free from the manifold world (*niṣprapañca*), consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), and of the nature of a single undivided flavor—as the very form of the inner Self characterized as described above. (39) Regarding the term "the Witness" (*sākṣin*): it means the illuminator at all times of all objects by means of His own essential consciousness, which does not enter into the state of being an object of proof.

"To the one devoid of latent impressions" (sāśayahīnāya): because there is an absence of even a trace of that which is its effect within the ultimate reality (paramārtha), it is "devoid. [Verse 45] "In every way" (sarvathā) means here: supporting the entire world; the sense is that it is the supreme foundation. "Abiding as the witness in all states" (sarvāvasthāsita): the sense is that it remains as the witnessing consciousness throughout all the states of living beings, such as waking and so forth. [Verse 46] "To the one devoid of the supreme and the inferior" (parāparavihīnāya).

The Great One (mahat) and the rest [of the principles], consisting of the elements and their derivatives, are superior to the body; even superior to that is the Unmanifest (avyakta), which is another synonym for Māyā—the meaning being "one who is devoid of that. 42 || 43 || 44 || "To Viśvanetra" means he who is like the eye that illuminates the entire universe. 45 || "To Vidhirīna" means he for whom there is no other creator (vidhi). 46 || 47 || 48 || "To Śatānanda" means he whose bliss is multiplied by a hundred;
or else, he whose life of a hundred years is lived in happiness. 49–56 ||

O God, you who do not abandon even the most wicked beings, salutations to you who have established this ocean of existence; salutations to you who grant the form of Brahmā to those who desire to behold your true nature. (39) Salutations to you, the witness of all living beings, who rescues these creatures from the ocean of suffering and from worldly existence, and who are the refuge for all who are afflicted by calamities. (40)

I bow again and again to You, who sustain the entire universe, who create all things, who bestow happiness and administer the fourfold punishments, and who remain as the witness of all within every state, such as waking and the rest. (41) Salutations to You, who are free from Māyā, who transcend the cycle of worldly existence, who are the Supreme Being, and who are the very Self of the wise. (42)

Salutations to you who are born from the lotus, who are pure, who are worthy of worship by the very pollen of the lotus, and who hold a lotus in your hand. || 43 || We bow down to you, the foremost among the gods, the one who creates the sun and other deities, and the one who bestows happiness upon those who are distressed. || 44 || Salutations to you, O Brahmā, the illuminator of the entire world, whose nature is knowledge, and who are praised even by the Victorious One (Jina).

45. There is no other physician than you; you are the instructor of the ritual injunctions (*vidhi-vākya*), the one who grants the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-vidyā*) to those who perform the actions prescribed by me with faith. Salutations to you, the master of the *japa* ritual. 46. You are superior to all, the dispeller of intense suffering, and the destroyer of the ten-fold miseries that afflict the miserable. We bow to you, the creator of the universe, whose name is "Viriñci."

47. Obeisance to Hiraṇyagarbha, who is beyond the reach of the qualities of the material world (guṇas), who is attainable through the gift of gold, and whose nature is the supreme Brahman. 48. Obeisance to Prajāpati, who bestows hundreds of times more bliss than that found in the state of Niriṣṭa; who imparts the knowledge of the Self; and who grants wisdom only to those who possess the means of discipline such as tranquility (śama) and the like.
O devotee of Śiva, you who bring about the welfare of embodied beings and possess the knowledge of the Yakṣas.

Chapter 9 Salutations again and again to the enemy of those embodied beings who are devoted to falsehood and are devoid of the virtues born of noble lineage. (50) Salutations to You, the Self-born, the Bestower of liberation; to the Independent Supreme Soul who Himself purifies all sins. (51) Salutations again and again to the Giver of the Self to the wicked-souled one who is intent on evil conduct, and who bestows suffering upon infinite enemies. (52) Salutations to the One who is beyond the forest, the Forest-dweller, the Giver of boons, and the Supreme.

Salutations to the most excellent among the most excellent, who is indeed the speaker of the ancient truths. (59) Salutations always to Him whose fame is most pervasive, the Lord of all beings, who is detached from the progeny of others, and the bestower of liberation. (54) Salutations to the Grandfather, who is free from the cycle of birth beginning with fatherhood, and to the Mountain-dweller whose body cannot be reached even by the gods. (55) Salutations to the Supreme Self, the creator of the world, the protector of the world, and the destroyer of the world; to Him who is devoid of worldly enemies and is the light of the consciousness-ocean. (56)

Salutations to the one who has transcended the universe, to the All-pervading, to the witness devoid of attributes, to the one whose sole measure is Himself, to the perfect Supreme Self. (57) Salutations again and again to the Truth, to the one beyond praise, who in reality is the object of all hymns, and who bestows happiness upon all those who offer praise. (58) Ruta said: Having thus praised Brahmā with great devotion, the Ādityas respectfully inquired about the meaning of the Vedas. Brahmā, the knower of Brahman, being thus extolled by all the gods, [spoke]. (59)

He spoke with profound words concerning the supreme essence of the Vedas. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Upaniṣad of the Brahmagītā," in the latter part of the fourth section, the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa’s Brāhma-saṃhitā. "Self-luminous, having a single means of knowledge": that whose sole means of knowledge (*māna*) is consciousness (*caitanya*) which is self-luminous by its very nature is so described. The meaning is that it shines forth by its own power alone, and is not cognizable through any other means of knowledge. || 57 ||

Regarding the phrase "to one who is always wretched": praise (*stuti*) is indeed the naming of qualities residing in a qualified object (*guṇin*); and since that [praise] cannot exist in reality for one who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), he is "wretched" (*dīna*) because he is being praised. (58) Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the Vedas": the meaning of the Vedas as expounded by the venerable Tārya—what kind of thing is that? This is the sense of their having asked. (59–60)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Song of Brahman" (*Brahmagīti*), within the *Upaniṣads* of the latter portion of the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*, of the *Sūtasaṃhitātātparyadīpikā* composed by Mādhavācārya—the most devoted servant at the feet of the illustrious Śrīmad-Amyaka, who was a performer of the rites of the illustrious Kājīyilāsa and an initiator of the Upaniṣadic tradition. || 1 ||

Salutations to you, the auspicious Brahmā, who are devoid of those things [which bind others]. (50) Salutations to you, the self-existent one, the teacher of the Vedas, the independent Supreme Soul of the virtuous Brahmā. (51) Salutations to you, O Viṣṇu, who bestow yourself upon others and inflict suffering upon such evil-minded ones who are always intent on wicked conduct.

(He who destroys the wicked through the manifestation of this [power]; they say that one who becomes angry with the wicked is "Ha. Such is one name of Brahmā. || 52 || There is no one to be worshipped by you, for you yourself are the one to be worshipped by all; O four-faced one, I bow to you, the bestower of boons upon others and the most excellent among the most excellent. || 52 ||

Salutations always to you, Prāṇapati, who bestows the knowledge of the eightfold stages of detachment even from the state of Prāṇāpati, the protector of all vital breaths. || 54 || We offer salutations to you, the subtle Pitāmaha, whose father and other kin cannot even be imagined, whom neither the gods nor the demons can perceive. || 55 ||

Salutations to You, the Supreme Self, who creates the universe, protects it, and withdraws it; who is untouched by the visible world of the universe, and whose manifest form is pure consciousness alone. || 56 || Salutations to You, the Perfect Supreme Self, who is beyond all, the All, yet devoid of everything; who is the Witness, not an object of any means of knowledge, and who shines as the very nature of reality. || 57 ||

Obeisance to You, the essential reality (tattvabhūta), who are worthy of praise yet cannot be praised because You are in truth devoid of attributes (nirguṇa); who, being the soul of all, are Yourself the very form of praise; and who bestow happiness upon all those who offer hymns of praise. 58.

Sūtajī spoke: O sons of Aditi, none among the gods had previously offered such devoted praise to Brahmā as he did, nor had they ever questioned him regarding the meaning of the Vedas along with their commentaries (rādhās). || 59 || Then, the eminent Brahmā, being highly pleased by all the gods, explained the most excellent meaning of the Vedas to them in a profound voice. || 60 ||

1. "The Self-born is the supreme Veda, the secret; He is the Self-existent," so it is said (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.6.3). 2. Obeisance to the one who bestows [liberation]. 3. Obeisance to the binder. 4. Śāpā of Ṣaḍdarśana. 5. The primary [portion] of the I-brahman. —704— Brahma-gītā, Second Chapter.

Brahmī said: "The meaning of the Vedas is indeed inexpressible in every way to those who possess discursive thought. Nevertheless, I shall speak for the sake of you devotees; listen to me with faith. (1) O believers, at the beginning, this entire universe was only Śiva—the one, the primordial, and eternal Self. There was nothing else whatsoever that could be perceived. Then, through the power of Time, and by virtue of the accumulated karma of living beings and His own inherent power, He, the Beneficent One, beheld the entire world as if it were a dream. (2–3)

Then Brahmā, having been questioned, began to explain the meaning of all the Vedas; first, he stated that the intended meaning of the Vedas—which consists of the nature of the non-dual, attributeless Brahman—cannot be the object of the function of verbal expression (*abhidhā-vṛtti*), saying: "It is inexpressible" (*avācya*). That meaning of the Vedas, characterized by the aforementioned Brahman, cannot indeed be established by words through any mode of verbal expression whatsoever.

Because that [Brahman] is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatvena*), the causes for the application of words—such as genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*)—are absent therein. For this very reason, scripture shows its state of being beyond the range of speech with the words, "from which words turn back. Likewise, the word "even" (*api*) means that although it is not the object of the denotative function (*abhidhāvṛtti*), it will nevertheless be made known through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*). || 1 ||

In this regard, since the Ṛgveda comes first, and because the portion concerning qualities (*saguṇa-bhāga*)—beginning with "This is the path"—is intended to produce one-pointedness of mind and so forth as a means for [understanding] the meaning taught in its Upaniṣads, whereas the portion devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa-bhāga*)—beginning with "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone"—produces the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman, which is fruitful in itself and independent of anything else, [the author] summarizes the meaning of that very portion devoid of qualities by means of the words "That which is called the Self," and so forth.

In this regard, just as transformations of water such as waves and bubbles are not distinct from the nature of their cause, the water, so too the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—which consists of effects produced by modifications of form—is established as non-different from the non-dual Supreme Lord who is its cause; to prove this, the following scriptural passage is cited as an illustration: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever that blinked. He thought: 'Let me create the worlds. He created these worlds... The author explains the meaning of this scripture with the word "Ātman."

Because it pervades the entire universe, both internally and externally, by means of its own effects which have *āpo* (water) as their material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), it is called *Āsā*. For it has been said: "Because it reaches (*āpnoti*), because it takes up (*ādatte*), because it eats (*atti*) objects here, and because its state persists through continuity (*saṃtati*), it is therefore measured as the *Ātman*. And that which is designated as *Ātman* is none other than the Supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda-lakṣaṇa*); it is not the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) or the atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth favored by opponents, for those are insentient and thus lack the nature of the Self.

Since this Śiva is auspicious (*śiva*), he is therefore pure (*śuddha*). He is not impure, because the bondage of *māyā*—which is caused by the connection with *karman*—has already been refuted. For it has been stated: "The supreme Śruti declares the absence of any connection with *karman* in Brahman" (Pūrva 4.47.50). By the qualifying term "of Him" (*tasyāyam*), the exclusion of difference from heterogeneous things (*vijātīya-bheda*) is established. By the word "only" (*eva*), the exclusion of other homogeneous things (*sajātīya-antara*) is established. By the word "one" (*eka*), the exclusion of internal difference (*svagata-bheda*) is established.

The qualification "then" (sat) is used to indicate that even at a time subsequent to the creation of the world—as it was before creation—that Supreme Lord remains of the nature of pure Consciousness (dṛgrūpatva), being free from all modification. Before creation, this entire universe, consisting of name and form as it is about to be described, existed only as that Being characterized by the aforementioned definition; that is to say, it remained latent within His own essential nature in an unmanifest state. || 2 ||

The author establishes the non-interruption [of the causal process] by stating "tataḥ" (from that). The meaning is: from that, which is of the nature of *āsīt* (was), there was not any existing thing whatsoever—distinct from it and appearing as something else. Thus, by demonstrating the existence of the cause, the position that the effect is non-existent (*asad*) is refuted. Now, [one might ask]: even if this is so, what is the purpose of investigating the meaning of the Vedas for one who is indifferent to worldly existence? This is the second chapter, titled "Investigation."

Lord Brahmā said: "The meaning of the *Kalmāṣaveda* is absolutely inexpressible by any conscious being through the medium of objects; nevertheless, because you are a devotee, I shall tell it to you—listen with faith. (O Śiva, the meaning of the Vedas is not an object of verbal denotation (*śabda-śakti*) because it lacks such *pravṛtti-nimittas* as genus and so forth; rather, it can only be understood through convention [*saṃjñā*].)"

In reality, even when there is a primary denotation (*lakṣya*), there can be a possibility of the delimiting factor (*rakyatāvacchedaka*) which may be set aside by the examples of instances of individual indication (*vyakti-lakṣaṇā*). To prevent such a possibility from arising, the teachers have taught that through words, only the exclusion of the non-auspicious (*aśiva-vyāvṛtti*) occurs, while Śiva himself shines forth because He is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*). This same application is also the method for Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*).

It is said in the *Sāhasrī*: "The word 'That' (tat) has the inner Self as its meaning, and the reality denoted by that word exists; thus both [words] exclude the state of being an object and the state of being the non-inner Self. And in this way, the two [negations] 'not this, not this' (neti neti) cause one another to be understood. Thus, even though it is inexpressible, the purpose of the scripture (*śāstra*) is fulfilled. ||1||

In the beginning, before this entire phenomenal world was manifested, there was only Śiva, known as the Self (Ātman)—eternal, singular, and pure. (2) Other than Him, there was no other object, whether insentient or sentient. When the fruits of the previously accumulated karma of living beings began to manifest as pleasure and pain, then [the Lord], though not desiring to assume a body for His own sport, spoke thus to encompass [all things] within Himself: "There was nothing else whatsoever.

That vehicle [the wind] moves these worlds as if they were its own, by its power, in the very same sequence as before, swiftly and without effort. Some desire Him to be Hara; some, the best of men, desire Him to be Viṣṇu; some desire Me alone; some desire the deities such as Indra; and some desire Him to be Pradhāna—the independent, solitary, and insentient [source] composed of the three guṇas.

To address the doubt as to how the vision of the Lord—which consists of the discernment of the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*)—is possible, he says: "But that [vision]... At the time of dissolution, the vital activities (*prāṇakarmāṇi*) appropriate for the past *kalpa* are merged into the nature of Paraśiva along with their cause, Māyā, in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). These [impressions] ripen like grains in a granary and reach a state of extreme intensity characterized by being ready to yield their own respective fruits.

And from that [Unmanifest], which consists of Time, there arises the latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—an intermediate synonym for *apūrva* produced by karma—which has been awakened in the Supreme Lord who desires to create. From that awakened [impression] of Him, the Lord of the state of dissolution, or rather of Śiva, the power of Māyā consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇā*) is activated. Therein, due to the cause of that primordial reality (*ajaṃ tattvam*) which is not yet differentiated by Rajas and Tamas, and by the force of that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the vision (*īkṣaṇa*) whose nature is the desire to create arises; this is the meaning. How did He look? That is stated: "All this which is characterized by name and form."

"May this world have been non-existent for so long; let me now create it"—the word *nu* here expresses deliberation (*vitarka*). "Let me create that worship" means he gazed upon it in the form of a lotus. By saying "the entire world" here, the author indicates that the scriptural statement regarding the creation of the worlds—such as "Let me create the worlds"—intends to include the creation of the elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*). However, since that [creation of the elements] is established by the principle of summary (*upasaṃhāranyāya*), the intention described is that it was not treated separately due to a lack of necessity. || 3 ||

Immediately after this observation, what did he do? To that, [the author] says: "Then again... Those worlds which were enumerated in the Śatarudriya—namely, water (*ambhas*), rays (*marīci*), and the waters of immortality (*amṛta*)—all these, together with their presiding deities, that Supreme Lord, the Master, by his own power, according to the sequence of the Vedic tradition beginning with the text, "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before," [manifested them]. Or rather, by his own power, [he manifested] the three qualities (*triguṇā*) which, as his own related power, undergo a transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of the universe.

The meaning is that [the Lord] has properly drawn forth [the world] by means of His power of *māyā*, as if with a net. Furthermore, the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of "water" (*ambhas*) and the other elements has been set forth in the Śruti itself: "That which is beyond the sky is water; the rays are the atmosphere established above; the earth is the dust below; these are the waters."

The worlds beginning with *Gavarchoka* and ending with *Satyaloka* are denoted by the word "water" (*ambhas*); the atmospheric worlds are the "rays" (*marīci*); and the earthly world (*bhūloka*), consisting of mortals, is "mortal" (*mara*). That which is below its foundation is denoted by the word "heat" (*tāpa*); such is the meaning of its [the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka*] firm statement. Herein, the supreme lordship of the Supreme Self is declared. And that He is so has been determined by the venerable author of the Commentary (Śaṅkara) in the first section of the *Adhikaraṇa* titled "Apprehension from All Sides," based on the subsequent [text].

For instance: having raised the question, "Is the Virāj, the lord of creatures, spoken of here as the Self?"—and having considered that [the passage] "from the Self, space was produced" refers to the great elements such as space being created by the Supreme Lord as their agent; and since in this context, following the creation of the elements, the creation of worlds by the Virāj is specifically mentioned in the words "He created these worlds"; and since there is observed the worldly activity of one who possesses a body, such as "From them he brought forth a cow, from them he brought forth a horse"—it follows that the phrase "one alone" is intended to establish his non-duality.

Furthermore, with reference to the detailed description of the transformation of the dog, it is stated that Virāj alone is mentioned here as the subject of the vision; thus, it is declared [in the text]: "The earth, wind, space, water, and light," and so forth, by which he [the creator] sequentially enumerates the entire collection of effects through the great elements. Since it is heard in the concluding portion that "all this is indeed Brahman," it follows that even at the beginning, the creation of the great elements must be understood. Therefore, the questioner here is indeed the Lord himself, whose scope is the subject of the creation of the elements.

And thus, even the determination of oneness (*ekatva*) is not rendered inconsistent; however, the bringing of the cow and so forth is contradicted here because it serves the purpose of praising the injunction. As it has been said: "In the passage 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent,' [the entity] is either Virāj or the Lord. Through the bringing of the cow and so forth, he becomes Virāj due to the manifestation of the elements (*bhūta*). Due to the withdrawal of the elements, he is the Lord (*īśvara*) from the determination of non-duality (*advaita*). The mention of the cow and so forth is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); what is intended to be expressed is the identity of Brahman. (4)

Having protected the essential nature of the Supreme Lord by establishing it as the support of this world, and since the purpose of the creation of the worlds and so forth—which consists of the sixfold manifestation—is already understood through its unity, there remains nothing further to be said; for [the scripture] says, "He, having pierced this very aperture... and so on. Thus, by burning away ignorance, one attains supreme knowledge. Through the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the power of *māyā* that protects the oneness with Brahman, the door of the power of *māyā* is opened, and thus the second [state] arises.

It is as if Śiva himself has deliberated, "I shall create this entire world" (in reality, since there is no creation, there is no occasion for these questions—what was there previously, and what was the nature of the ripening of karma; for if one accepts it as being of the nature of God's will, then since will is a quality of a conscious being, it would depend upon a cause, leading to infinite regress and other such fallacies).

Now, it is said that even by asserting eternality, these doubts are resolved; however, that is merely for the sake of satisfying those who seek the fruit of logical reasoning. Non-origination (*ajāti*) alone is the true answer. (2) Or rather, the independent Supreme Lord, by His own autonomous power, fashioned all these worlds exactly as they were in the previous cycle. (4)

The Kuṭhas consider this creator of creation to be Hara; the Kuṭas [consider him] Viṣṇu. || 5 || The Kus consider Muñ-Rahmā alone to be the creator of the world, while other devotees accept such a status for deities such as Indra and others. The Kukas, who are discerning thinkers, [accept] the three qualities...

9. That [word] is repeated for the sake of taking up the position again and for the purpose of connection (*sandhi*). 2. The sense is that he did not even think about it. 3. *Śaktavat* (capable). 5. But at the end of a syllable, having taken up another alternative, there is no contradiction with the statement of the one who has established the topic. 706. Some, deluded, desire atoms; some desire sound; some, their minds exhausted, desire consciousness that perishes in an instant. (Brahmagītā 7)
Some gods, utterly deluded, maintain the notion that it is empty; some desire it to be mere sounds, while others, through error, claim it is nothing at all.

In each respective case, various arguments are advanced according to their capacity; it is my conviction that all such disputations are mutually contradictory. When one desires to explain the meaning set forth in a composition of words—such as the Vedic passage beginning with "He entered by the opening of the foot" and "Having split this very aperture, he entered through that door"—regarding the two who have entered [the body] through the opening at the top of the foot and the opening at the crown of the head...

Among the two jewels characterized by the powers of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which one is that [jewel]? Since there is a dispute among various schools of thought arising from doubt as to which it might be, he provides an illustration for that reason, beginning with the words "He who... and so forth. That Self, who has been described as the creator, is not without purpose. Some say it is the "Primal Source" (*pradhāna*).

For, since the world cannot be insentient if it were to have consciousness as its material cause (*upādāna*), they maintain that the material cause of the world is indeed *pradhāna*—insentient and composed of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—and thus assert that this alone is the primordial source. He states the distinction of *māyā* from the *māyā* favored by the Vedāntins: "independent" (*svatantra*). For that [Vedāntic *māyā*] is dependent upon the Supreme Lord, being presided over by Him. (5–6)

"Some [hold that] atoms [are the cause]" means: since we observe the production of earth and other substances from clay particles of minute dimension, the logicians (*tārkika*) maintain that atoms such as those of earth and so forth—possessing unseen merit (*adṛṣṭavat*)—begin the entire universe through the process of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so on. "Some [others]" refers to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), who describe the causality of *Śabda* alone, asserting that the Supreme Brahman, which is *Śabda*, undergoes transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of objects.
For it has been said: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the imperishable essence of sound; it manifests in the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds. (7)

Regarding the view that "the elements desire," this is because the material world is seen to arise precisely from the elements; thus, it is these alone that possess the capacity for creation, and there is no other creator distinct from them—this is the position of some. Others, however, maintain that because the world has never been otherwise, it is the elements themselves that bring about creation.

Likewise, even in the Śruti, the disagreement among disputants regarding the cause of the world has been shown: "Nature, inherent essence, necessity, chance, the elements, the womb, or the Person—these are to be considered. And the Śrutis themselves are contradictory: "He desired, 'May I become many, may I procreate,' and He performed austerity by Himself"; and, "There is nothing else whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya; all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread."

"Under my supervision, Nature (prakṛti) produces the world of moving and non-moving beings"—from such scriptural and traditional texts, since the Supreme Lord is heard to be both the material cause and the efficient cause of the universe, and since the contradictions among disputants regarding this matter are shown to be unauthoritative, it is established that there is no doubt concerning the cause of the world; thus it is asserted that Śiva is known by the name Ātama. || 8 || 9 ||

Some maintain that the independent, insentient *pradhāna* (primordial nature) alone is the creator of the world. Others say that the atom (*aṇu*) is the initiator of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). In the view of some, sound alone is the cause of the manifold universe (*parapañca*). Still others, whose minds are greatly deluded, consider momentary consciousness (*vijñāna*), which perishes at every instant, to be the producer of the world. (6–7)

Other proponents of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavādins*) maintain that there is nothing else to be worshipped—meaning, they hold no other entity to be worthy of devotion. It is not that these proponents accept some specific principle called "emptiness" (*śūnya*); rather, their position is simply this: everything, including consciousness and experience, is false (*mithyā*). For this reason, those who assert emptiness are refuted. This has been clearly explained by Goḍasvāmī in his *Ratnāvalī* (p. 218, Pr. dvā.).

To clarify this very point, the term *anirvācya* (ineffable) has been provided. On the basis of their own logic, those proponents say: "It is neither empty nor non-empty; it is not 'is,' nor is it 'is-not,' nor is it ineffable. This is precisely the meaning of their "freedom from the four alternatives" (*catuṣkoṭivinirmukta*).

Therefore, it cannot be their position that the cause of the world is *śūnya* (emptiness); rather, the intention of the Purāṇas is that, according to their view, there is no real cause for the world. Since they do not regard the world as eternal like the Mīmāṃsakas, it is necessary to mention them separately.

O Mīmāṃsaka, do you maintain that there is no real cause for the world? It is not so; rather, it is because the world is eternal. However, this is not correct. Even the aforementioned proponent accepts that there is no real cause for the world, but only because, in reality, the world was never produced and nothing truly exists.

Therefore, it is appropriate to grant a place to their conception within the context of the cause of the universe. Some other thinkers consider the *mahābhūtas* (great elements) alone to be the cause of the universe. The view of the *Vaiśeṣikas* is that the universe has always existed; creation never occurred. Their intention is that the universe is inherently diverse by its very nature.

(From this, it is also indicated that if origination must indeed be accepted, it should be accepted as being of the nature of transformation (*pariṇāmātmikā*), because the theory of new production (*ārambhavāda*) is untenable due to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of its application to things like horns on a rabbit's head. It is the very nature of the world to be constantly formed in various ways; therefore, there is no necessity to postulate a creator distinct from the world itself.)

Just as milk and other substances cannot be considered to possess the nature of fire or the like, so too those who regard the powers and movements inherent within the world as its cause must be understood to belong to this same category. || 8 || All these disputants exert their full effort in providing corroborative arguments for their respective assertions; however, my conclusion is that all these positions are contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti.
(Therefore, they are unacceptable. || 9 ||

1. Ja. *pratipta*. 2. Dependence (*pāratantrya*) consists in having its existence dependent upon the existence of another. 3. He states the Mīmāṃsaka position with the words "another," etc. 4. Gha. *°nani°*.

But for those beings who are most excellent among creatures, O gods, their own respective desires arise from the very knowledge of the essence of the manifest world (prākṛtasāra). By means of the ripening of time, through faith that is purified, and by virtue of ancient merit and the grace of the deities, after a long period of time, those gods—striving through a gradual succession of steps—attain this primary, eternal Veda-Mārga. Having discerned the strength and weakness [of themselves and others] solely through the knowledge of the essence of the manifest world...

Even those who have fallen away from the Veda become partakers of liberation [only] by resorting to this path of the Veda. Having abandoned this path of the Veda, one who has resorted to another path is like one who discards the lotus stalk in his hand and licks his own elbow. If living beings could attain liberation without the Veda through some other means, then they might reach the balance scale and such things even without darkness. (93–95)

Therefore, O gods, that which has been declared by me is the truth, the absolute truth; an object known through another is not real from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha). O you who dwell in heaven, ultimate reality has been described by me as twofold: one is the direct ultimate reality, which is eternal by its very nature; that is Śiva, characterized by the self-nature of true consciousness and bliss, and infinite. The other is the conceptualized [reality], which is directly superimposed upon Brahman.

Now, one might object: "If the Sāṃkhya and other systems are thus invalid due to their contradiction with Śruti and Smṛti, how is it that the Tīrthakaras (founders of those schools) engage in them? Anticipating this, he states that the cause of their engagement is indeed sin, beginning with the words "Of those most sinful" (*pāpiṣṭhānām*). Regarding the phrase "by way of a ladder" (*sopānakramataḥ*): the meaning is that while [the founders] generally understood the distinction between heaven and hell, the Sāṃkhyas and others relied upon the traditional path of the Upaniṣads, which teaches the opposite of that [distinction]. || 90 || 11 || 12 ||

"Having reflected on the strength and weakness [of their own path]," means: having deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness of their own path and the Vedic path—recognizing the weakness of their own teacher because he was a product of human intellect, yet acknowledging the faultless authority of the Veda due to its non-human origin—those wise men, desiring to establish their own path, abandoned it and took refuge solely in the Vedic path. Therefore, by means of this gradual sequence of steps, even for them, liberation is accomplished in the long run through the Veda-prescribed method; such is the meaning. || 13 ||

"Therefore" means: since the other paths also find their ultimate fulfillment in the Veda, therefore the goal is that which is taught by the faultless Vedic words alone due to their non-human (apauruṣeya) origin, and not by any means other than the Veda—this is the meaning. || 16 ||

Now, one might object: "If the meaning established by the Veda is true, then even this world—which appears as diverse through distinctions such as substance, quality, action, and so forth—must be true, just like the Self. To avoid this objection and to demonstrate that [the world] possesses a merely empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*), he states the twofold nature of the Vedic meaning: "The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)," and so on. For in the Veda, there are indeed two sections (*kāṇḍa*).

In this regard, that reality characterized by truth, non-duality, and so forth, which has been expounded in the *Jñānakāṇḍa*, is the direct object of the Veda (*śrutyartha*). However, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—characterized by heaven, the *apūrva*, deities, and the like—which is expounded in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, is imagined through the *māyā* superimposed upon the Supreme Self, which is characterized by truth, non-duality, and so forth. This distinction between the imagined and the non-imagined objects of these two sections has already been elaborated upon previously: "One portion of the Veda is devoted to the non-imagined [non-dual] reality, while another portion is likewise devoted to the imagined duality. (Verses 17–18)
Only those beings who are submerged in terrible sins develop an inclination toward these doctrines for the sake of worldly gain. [4. Regarding those diseases...

Just as sandalwood on a cool mountain slope eventually reaches the ground after a long time, so too, when the cycle of time changes, one occasionally attains the fruit of liberation. Thereupon, supreme faith and devotion arise; in that state, by the grace of the gods, even such individuals ascend this eternal Vedic path, which is the sole means for the attainment of ultimate well-being.

Just as in the case of Sītī, the superiority of various doctrines can be understood through their proximity to the goal (*gati*), excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*), and freedom from all worldly attachments (*sarvajanasaṅgarahitatva*) and so forth. This is also considered in the aforementioned *Ratnāvalī* passage; indeed, it has already been explained at considerable length in its twentieth chapter. || 11-12 ||

Those people who, having considered the inconsistency of these positions due to factors such as *ūṣā* and the strength of the Vedic doctrine, set out upon the path of their own conclusions, nevertheless attain liberation at the appropriate time. (13) To abandon this Vedic path and travel by another way is just as foolish as spilling milk from one's hand and then licking the corner of one's mouth.

If the plow reaches as far as the elbow while being pulled by a calf, then give the remaining distance to the other hand. (4) ||14|| Those people who believe that liberation is possible through means other than the Vedas might as well expect to see a pot formed from clay without the use of fire! ||15|| Therefore, only that which is declared in the Vedas is true; the assertions of other books are not actual truth. ||16||

Truth (*satya*) is also of two kinds, distinguished as real (*vāstavika*) and imagined (*kalpita*). Real truth is Śiva alone, whose nature is consciousness-bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda-svarūpa*). Imagined truth is that which is superimposed upon Brahman by *māyā*—that which is established through delusion (*bhrama-siddha*). (17–18) Among imagined non-substantial objects, this [universe] is of such a kind.

Therefore, the venerable author of the Vārttika stated: "Alternatively, due to the reasons already mentioned, the authority of Ālīyāyana and others regarding the Śārāṇas would be indisputable for the sake of producing knowledge of the One Time (ekakālya). Even the Buddha, clearly proclaiming the state of all things as being devoid of suffering and impermanence, strives through passion for their cessation, not for his own destruction. (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika 1.4.4708–9) [Notes: 2. *dha* and *ḍa* read *tīrthakārāṇām*; 3. *ḍa* and *ca* read *gagāpivargadi*;
708 *brahmagītā*.]

Among the things perceived, some are established by means of *māyā* as having ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*) within conventional usage (*vyavahāre*), yet they appear otherwise [in the higher sense]. (19) However, some things established within conventional usage do not possess ultimate reality; these include the world, beginning with the ether (*ākāśa*), which I have described as being the power (*śakti*) of Brahman. (20) The Veda speaks of both the conventional truth (*vyāvahārika-tattvārtha*) and the ultimate truth (*tāttvika-tattvārtha*), but the Māyāvādins certainly do not speak in this manner. (21) In states such as dreaming, these [objects] are equal to those that are real according to conventional truth.

Furthermore, O inhabitants of heaven, they declare these paths to be like this: "In the waking state, however, people consider these objects to be real because they perceive them through their own senses; what then need be said regarding those perceived by the mind? (22) Therefore, having been seen by one person, these objects appear to speak the truth; yet they are exhausted by another observer—such is the examination of the world. (23) In comparison with consciousness, the entire objective world, including space and so forth, is unreal;
it is as unreal as the water in a mirage compared to the reality of a jar. (24-25)

If it is argued that, since the Karma-kāṇḍa is thus devoted to imagined duality, there would be no rule that the entire meaning of the Veda must be real, he says: "Of the imagined" (kalpitānām). Even though everything is non-substantial because it is imagined by Māyā, things such as the ether (ākāśa) are imagined as having a conventional reality (vyāvahārika-sattva); however, things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell are [imagined] as being unreal even in worldly transaction. || 19 || 27 ||

He states—using the term *vyāvahārika*—that there is no loss of the truth of the Vedic meaning even by accepting the world as having a conventional (*vyāvahārika*) reality: "The world, while not sublated as long as the knower exists, is conventionally real; whereas Brahman, which is at all times devoid of duality and whose sole essence is bliss, is indeed ultimately real. The Veda propounds both of these; other paths, however, do not do so. (21)

What, then, is established by the path? To this he says, beginning with "svapna" (dream) and so forth: Other paths constructed by the Buddhists establish only things that are like the objects of truth imagined during the state of dreaming, and not the Self which is real in the manner described.

But other paths, such as those of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, establish in the waking state only categories characterized by substance, quality, and action, which are like that which is imagined through ignorance and accepted by the Vedāntins as conventional reality. || 22 ||

Therefore, what talk can there be regarding the paths, which are the fuel for the fire of truth, concerning the ultimate reality? The meaning is that even the possibility of establishing them does not exist. || 23 ||

"Therefore" means this: because only the world of relative truth (*vyāvahārikasatya*) has been explained, while the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikasatya*), which is the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), has not been explained. "By each one" refers to the conventional perspective (*vyāvahārikadṛṣṭi*); "by another view" refers to the ultimate perspective (*pāramārthikadṛṣṭi*). "Exhausted" means that they are deluded because they have persistently grasped the world of relative truth—consisting of space, form, and so forth—as being the ultimate truth. || 24 ||

[Objection: "But surely, the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-satyatva*) is precisely the relative reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*). For it is not the case that a single entity becomes both real and unreal merely through a difference in perspective. To this, he says: "In consciousness (*caitanye*). Since we observe the appearance of effects such as jars when causes such as clay exist, it is well known that the cause alone is real while the effect is unreal.

And likewise, with reference to the Supreme Śiva-consciousness which serves as its cause, that object of cognition—the collection of elements such as ether and the rest—is unreal. Furthermore, with reference to its own causes, such as the clay and so forth that constitute the nature of a jar or a wall, that [element] is real. (25) Thus, while it is considered truly real in common worldly practice, it is also considered unreal even within that same worldly practice.

For the sake of illustration, space and so forth, which appear as both real and illusory within the world, are considered fourteen unrealities. (19–20) The Veda imparts instruction on both truths; however, other texts do not provide knowledge of the ultimate reality, which is consciousness itself. (21) Non-Vedic scriptures, moreover, convey such truths as those that exist in the state of a dream. (22)
Even those who follow the Veda partially teach truths of the same nature as the objects of awakened reality.

Therefore, it is impossible for any work other than the Vedas, or any treatise other than the Vedānta which provides a complete and perfect imitation of the Vedas, to describe the Supreme Truth as consisting of pure consciousness (*ciddhana*). (The seed of this impossibility is its being beyond the reach of the intellect; the subtlest grasp of the intellect comes to an end within the Sāṅkhya system. However, one cannot even conceive of a distinction between oneself and that [Truth] in any way whatsoever.)

23. Therefore, from a certain perspective, those who teach the truth of the Vedānta path are conventional; yet, from other perspectives, they are merely conventional and even mistaken. What need is there to say that, from the ultimate perspective (*pāramārthika-dṛṣṭi*), they are indeed mistaken? || 24 || The entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), such as space and so forth, which is the object of knowledge, is unreal by virtue of its being distinct from consciousness (*caitanya*); although it is indeed real from the perspective of pots, walls, and the like. || 25 ||

Even the six elements and so forth are non-existent (*atattva*) in comparison to space (*ākāśa*) and the like; however, the meaning is this: when even those things appearing as bracelets and such in dreams are seen to be erroneous by means of another conventional distinction, what need is there to mention their lack of reality from the perspective of ultimate truth? This was also stated by the Teacher [Ācārya] himself with great clarity in the *Māṇḍūkya-kārikā* (3.17–18), beginning with the words "evam asadvādasthitānām," etc., for the sake of the intended meaning. 2. Even entities such as jars and walls, when compared to space, are unreal; likewise, that which is real is so only in comparison to the Supreme Reality. (29) The state called "sleeping" is designated only in relation to the states of waking and dreaming; for it is not ultimately real, just as the gods [of the dream] are not real. (27) Nevertheless, the dream-experience of one who has fallen asleep is indeed a manifestation of his own mind; for even a mere word serves to conceal the non-existent object. (28) In the same way, even the ends of the world are [unreal] in comparison to what is declared by the Veda. (29)

Those who are devoted to the meaning [of the Veda] do not become outcasts; they remain as such. Therefore, this other [type of] Ārya must always be avoided. One who is established in the Veda, even if he should ever associate with them, does not become an outcast. Even if one who is established in the Veda should associate with them through delusion, he certainly becomes subject to penance; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. Even if he has conversed with them even once, one who is firmly established in the Veda, fearing sin even through delusion, should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

If, out of delusion, one performs rites such as giving, receiving, or marriage, or the study of the Vedas, while being blinded by the three types of *kāyakṛtya* (bodily misconduct), he does not attain the knowledge of the Dharma and so forth even if he remains established in the Śruti. Therefore, a king desiring his own welfare should never, even out of delusion, associate with them. Those who have strayed from the paths of Vedic discourse and those who are hostile toward them are indeed heretics (*pāṣaṇḍins*), and likewise, those who are protected by them are as well.

Even things such as a pot, a cloth, and so forth, though they are non-existent in comparison to the great elements (mahābhūta) like earth which constitute their own causes, are nevertheless "existent" only while the cognizer exists, because they are sublated only when the cognizer exists—just as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated only while the cognizer exists. || 26 ||

Likewise, although the waking state is unreal in relation to its own cause, it is real for the cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) because it lacks sublation; whereas the dream state, being the opposite of the waking state, is unreal for the cognizing subject because it is sublated. Thus, the meaning is that for a single reality, there is no contradiction between its being real from the perspective of conventional usage and its being unreal from the standpoint of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). || 27 ||

Objection: Since the state of dream is false from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), how can those things seen therein—which are themselves unreal—be the cause for attaining the nature of the supreme Śiva, who is the ultimate truth and the goal of the Vedic path? To address this doubt, he establishes the point with an illustration: "Even so" (*tathāpi*). Although the state of dreaming is false, even so, an object seen in a dream becomes an indicator of a future result that is real.

The indicative nature [of dreams] was also indicated by the Blessed Vyāsa: "For those who know it declare that a dream is indeed indicative. And that Śruti is recited thus: "When one sees in dreams a crow at ritual acts or gold in one's ears, one should know that to be prosperous; such is the teaching regarding dreams. (28)

And just as this is so, even paths that are illusory (*mithyā*) serve as means (*upāya*) for attaining the ultimate reality—the single, indivisible essence of pure existence, consciousness, and bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda*)—by way of a gradual ascent on a ladder; such is the meaning. [Verses 29–35] In what respect are they true?

(Although objects such as a jar and so forth, as well as space and so forth, are established as having an equal degree of existence, nevertheless, O subtle-minded one, the intended meaning is this: it is possible to ascertain that the effect is in reality not distinct from the cause; therefore, by taking the negation of the jar and other such things, the ascertainment that space and so forth are real is in some way possible.)

Furthermore, while the Truth (*satya*) is eternal and objects such as jars are non-eternal, whereas space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are eternal, even from this perspective the discerning may consider those [non-eternal things] to be less real in comparison to it. (26) The state of dreaming is real in relation to the waking state. (27) Nevertheless, the objects perceived in a dream serve as an indicator for the proof of the reality of the objects of the waking state.

In this same way, even when one is exhausted, other paths that explain the meaning declared in the Vedas will indeed serve as aids, whether from afar or nearby. (28-29) Therefore, those paths are not entirely useless; however, one should not even speak with those who are devoted to the Vedas if they are deluded. (20) Even if one follows them out of delusion while being devoted to the Vedas, one should perform expiation for that. (21)

Those who follow other paths (māyāntara-anugantāraḥ) should not share a meal with us; if they do, one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow as an act of atonement. || 32 || If even those [who follow other paths] should perform sacrifices, give gifts, conduct marriages and other such rites, or engage in the study of the Vedas, they must perform three Cāndrāyaṇas for the sake of purification from sin. || 33 ||

It is appropriate that one who stands on the path of the Śrotas and desires what is auspicious should not learn anything from them regarding dharma, adharma, and so forth. (34) Those who follow the path of the Vedavāhanas and those who associate with them—both are heretics. (35) In the Kali age, people are permeated by hypocrisy; they are destroyers of the world, appearing in the form of truth and other virtues. (36)

People corrupted by heresy will not worship with the Veda Śiva, the creator of the world, whose characteristics are truth and the like. (26) People corrupted by heresy will not worship with the Veda Mahādeva, who is established in the Vedas, accompanied by Ambā, and adorned with the crescent moon. (27) People corrupted by heresy will not perform the smearing [of the body] with ashes according to the very path declared in the Vedas, nor with devotion using cow dung and fuel. (28) [They will not perform] the wearing of the sacred thread with devotion according to the very path declared in the Vedas.

People afflicted by heresy will not perform the *moṭana* rite. (29) Day after day, people afflicted by heresy will not worship the God who is eternally served by Śiva and others, according to the Veda. (40) They do not perform rites for the gods, and especially not rites for the ancestors; people afflicted by heresy do not perform the *aupāsana* fire-sacrifice. (41) They do not perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), nor likewise the honoring of guests; people afflicted by heresy do not offer the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. (42)

Following the path of the Vedic vehicle, they worship Janārdana; yet, people afflicted by heresy and struck by delusion revile Śaṅkara. (43) Deluded by the notion of duality, they regard Brahmā and Keśava as distinct; people afflicted by heresy do not know that He is one. (44) People afflicted by heresy perform a Śrāddha rite without looking at the food, without washing their feet, and likewise without offering water for the feet. (45) Especially on the eleventh, the eighth, and the fourth lunar days...

People afflicted by heresy do not observe the fast. (46) People afflicted by heresy do not consecrate the Lord of Gods with the Śatarudriya, the Camakas, and the Puruṣasūktas. (47) People afflicted by heresy do not visit the ancient abodes of Śiva, the Supreme Soul, with great devotion. (48) People afflicted by heresy will not spend a year with faith at the glorious Southern Kailāsa. (49)

People afflicted by heresy will not observe the conduct that bestows devotion and liberation at Śarīradvayāpūra for one year. (50) And people afflicted by heresy will not observe the conduct at other renowned sacred sites of Śiva for one year. (51) Day after day, people afflicted by heresy, being deluded, will not practice the determination of the meaning of the great Mahāvākyas of the Vedānta, nor will they accept renunciation (*sannyāsa*). (52)

People corrupted by heresy will commit blasphemy against Śiva; people corrupted by heresy will not perform those other rites which have indeed been ordained by the Veda. (Verses 52, 54, etc. They will offer prayers to Śiva preceded by the reviling of the Vedas.

Those people will not perform the worship of Lord Śiva—Candramauli and Sāmba Sadāśiva—nor will they apply sacred ash (bhasma) and wear the *tripuṇḍra* mark according to Vedic rites. They will not wear Rudrākṣa beads, and the daily worship of the *liṅga* will not take place among them. They will remain far removed from service to the gods, offerings to the ancestors (*pitṛ-kārya*), and spiritual practice (*upāsanā*). They will be averse to the five great sacrifices (*pañca-yajña*), the honoring of guests, and the offering of oblations to all deities (*viśvedeva-bali*). (36–42)

(Not only will we abandon the Vedas,) but we shall also perform the worship of Janārdana Viṣṇu through rituals external to the Vedas; furthermore, we shall revile Śaṅkara and regard such blasphemy as a means of spiritual practice. (43) The heretics will come to the firm conviction that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are each distinct entities. (44)

Those people will perform this *śrāddha* without bathing and even without washing their feet; neither will the bestowal of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) be given, nor will the fire-ritual (*agnikarma*) be performed. (45) Heretics (*pākhaṇḍins*) will not observe the vows prescribed for the first, eighth, and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight. (46) While reciting the *Chamakādhyāya* and the mantras of the *Puruṣasūkta*, those who have entered the water for ritual ablution will perform their baths in the river. (47)

He will visit the ancient shrines of Śiva with devotion (verse 48). He will not reside for a year at Dakṣiṇakailāsa with faith (verse 49). Nor will he stay even for a single day at Vyāghrapura, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation (verse 50). It will be impossible for him to dwell for a year in other distinguished Śaiva pilgrimage sites (verse 51).

Day after day, they will not listen to the teachings from their gurus. (52) They will not even take up the renunciant order of the Paramahaṃsas, and instead will harbor contempt for it. (53) They will remain indifferent even toward other Vedic rites. (54) Not only the Śrauta, but even the performance of Smārta rituals will no longer proceed from them. (54) [Note:
