Furthermore, whatever actions the best of men have practiced, those very same things people afflicted by heresy will not perform. (55) Afflicted by heresy, people will wear hair-tufts (*ūrṇā*) that are long, curly, and shaped like half-moons out of sheer delusion. (56) Afflicted by heresy, people will even deform their own faces with crooked and protruding teeth out of sheer delusion. (57) And there will be no end to these men, even in terms of their physical appearance.

People will become marked by sectarianism, struck down by the doctrines of others. O gods, what is the use of the Veda as proclaimed in the scriptures? People, afflicted by heresy, will act only out of blind faith. But the wise, the distinguished, those endowed with the majesty of Maheśvara, and the most eminent ones—O gods, for the sake of attaining liberation, they will joyfully practice that which is taught solely in the Veda.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Investigation into the Meaning of the Vedas," in the *Brahma-gītā-tūpaniṣad* within the fourth section (*Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*) of the *Sūta-saṃhitā* of the *Śrī Skanda-purāṇa*.

The Third Chapter. Bhūmi said: "O best of gods, how is it that the Lord, whose name is *Savita*, is indeed the witness (*sākṣin*) through His power (*śakti*)? In the absence of a witness, how does this entire universe shine? Thus ends the second chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Meaning of the Vedas," within the latter portion of the *Yajña-vaibhava-khaṇḍa* of the fourth part of the *Sūtasaṃhitā-tātparyadīpikā*, which contains the *Brahmagītā Upaniṣad*. [Note: The sequence of verse numbers provided in the source text (9, 47–65) appears to be a transcription error; the translation reflects the logical flow of the narrative.]

Having refuted certain objections and the conflicting views of disputants regarding Him, the meaning was established that He is indeed the Self well-known from the Vedas as described. That very same [Self] exists within His own created bodies through the manifestation of His power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), according to the Vedic text: "He reached that Puruṣa by means of His two feet. Likewise, He is situated within the heart through the form of His power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), according to the text: "Having pierced this very aperture, He entered through the door."

Between these two, which is that Self which is to be known as the nature of the Prājña? Is it of the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), or is it the essence of the power of consciousness (cit-śakti)? This is the question set forth in the Śruti; the answer to it is the scriptural passage beginning with, "That by which one smells, or by which one hears," and so forth.

Now, Ālana establishes that [the Self] is the witness of all in order to explain the meaning of that Vedic revelation: "He who exists as the substrate (ālana) in all bodies—this Supreme Lord is the illuminator and witness of the entire insentient phenomenal world; He must be understood as having the very nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra). He states the subverting argument against the contrary position: "In the absence of a witness... etc.

If the witness (*sākṣin*) were not of the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), by what means then would he perceive this world? Therefore, it follows that its manifestation must be accepted as having the form of the witness; this is the meaning. || 9 || Heretics will place a mark upon their foreheads; they will wear a crescent moon as a sectarian emblem. || 56 || They will have the marks of the conch, the discus, the mace, and the thunderbolt branded upon their own bodies. || 57 ||

O men, what man will ever cause the branding of his body with various marks and the like? Such will be the disease of the heretics. (58) O gods, what more need I say? Those diseases will, with great zeal, perform only one task: the subversion of Vedic boundaries. (59) Endowed with patience and speech, those steadfast and distinguished Great Souls will practice only the duties prescribed by the Vedas for the sake of attaining liberation. (60)
The Third Chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Śiva as the Witness" (the first thirty verses of which provide a commentary on the Aitareya Upaniṣad as stated in the preceding chapter).

Brahmā said: Śaṅkara alone is the Self of all and the witness of all. Without a witness, how could there be the manifestation of the world, which is the object of witnessing? (1) The entire world, both moving and unmoving, is distinct from itself...

1. "The witness" is the commentary on the word *sākṣin* in the verse. The particle *eva* (only/alone) serves to exclude other witnesses. By this, the view held by others—that there are many individual-soul witnesses (*jīva-sākṣins*) and a separate Lord-witness (*īśvara-sākṣin*)—is shown to be untenable. Furthermore, the distinction between the witness and the Self is refuted; therefore, according to the logic of the *vyatihāra-adhikaraṇa* (Brahma Sūtra 3.3.23–37), there is a statement of absolute non-difference. 2. [Note: The word *ātman* is indicated by the term *ātma-*. 3. [Note: From the reading *śagadāyādataḥ*. 4. [Note: Ga. reads *°tedataḥ*.
712. *Brahmagītā*

Indeed, this entire world of moving and non-moving things is devoid of self-luminosity; its state of being conscious or unconscious depends upon its being illumined by another. (2) Some assert that manifestation (*bhāna*) arises from consciousness (*vijñāna*). In that case, if it is not distinct from itself, then it is merely inert. For it is universally accepted that jars and other objects are indeed non-distinct from their own insentience. (3) Furthermore, consciousness is not held to be the producer of manifestation. It is not established that consciousness undergoes a transformation into the form of manifestation. (4)

If its modification consists in being unmanifest and unproduced, then, like a parrot or similar [inanimate] things, would cognition not indeed be an object of consciousness? (5) Likewise, cognition is not accepted as a producer [of its own manifestation], because it is admitted by others to be non-substantial due to its lack of parts. (6)

To the question, "Why does the other [the world], like the nature of the witness (sākṣin), not manifest from itself alone? he says: "From itself" (svataḥ). For the world is insentient (jaḍa) and thus devoid of natural luminosity; therefore, in the absence of the witness's luminosity, its manifestation cannot occur by itself—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of a witness, the insentient world is indeed known by the non-insentient Self, which is the substratum of knowledge. To this he says: "Being insentient" (jaḍatvāt).

Both the non-self (anātman) and the self (ātman) must be understood as being characterized by manifestation (*bhāna*) alone within this world. For if the world were an object of manifestation, then its consciousness would be insentient (*ajaḍa*). However, since that [consciousness] is the substratum of such manifestation, it is itself non-insentient; thus, both sentience and insentience are to be defined in dependence upon manifestation. Therefore, one must accept a manifestation in the form of the Witness (*sākṣin*), which is independent of [any other] manifestation. This is the meaning. || 2 ||

[Objection: Let there be manifestation (*bhāna*); however, that [manifestation] is produced in its own locus by a consciousness that is unmanifest and devoid of activity, like the eye and other sense organs—this is the Bhāṭṭa position, which is now raised as an objection. [Response: That is refuted by the words "tat-tan-na" (that is not so). For if manifestation, consisting in the expansion toward the object, were something produced, then, by virtue of being produced—just like a jar produced from clay—it would necessarily be insentient (*jaḍa*). Therefore, since there is no contradiction in manifestation being insentient just like the object itself, its production is impossible; this is the meaning. || 2 ||

Regarding what was stated—that the manifestation of an object is produced by consciousness—that is not tenable; thus he says, "And [the case of] cognition... The proponent who asserts that consciousness is the producer of manifestation must be questioned: does consciousness transform itself into the form of manifestation, or is it the initiator of manifestation? He says "no" with the words, "of cognition," because transformation is observed only in things subject to change, such as milk transforming into the form of curds and so forth; such [transformation] is impossible for cognition, which is devoid of modification.

If knowledge were also subject to modification, then it would be material, just like a cloth and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that as long as it possesses modification, its very nature as knowledge would be lost. || 4 || 5 ||

He also refutes the theory of origination by stating "likewise" (*tathā*). For a substance (*dravya*) is indeed the originator of another substance, as is observed in the case of threads and cloth; however, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not a substance, because [the opponent] admits it to be a quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, an origination by means of consciousness—which, being non-substantial, is itself unoriginated—is not tenable. (6) The Self cannot be manifested without something else.

Therefore, from the manifestation of saṃsāra, both the insentience of saṃsāra and the sentience of that by which it is manifested become known. (2) Some people say that manifestation—that is, knowledge—arises from vijñāna, meaning experience.

Now, their position is incorrect because, if [the cognition] were produced, its manifestation would have to be accepted as insentient (*jaḍa*), just like produced objects such as walls and the like; and in that case, its establishment would have to be sought through another manifestation, which would lead to defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*). It is the view of those proponents that experience arises unmanifested, but it brings about the arising of a cognition regarding itself, by means of which the apprehension of the experience occurs.

However, one cannot escape from infinite regress and other such fallacies unless one accepts that cognition (*dhī*) arises as something that is itself manifest. Therefore, it is proper to admit that experience and cognition are not two distinct things; furthermore, one must regard that [cognition] as self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). (3) Moreover, consciousness (*cit-jñāna*) cannot even be the producer of manifestation. If, adopting the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), you argue that consciousness undergoes transformation into the form of manifestation, then—

Since it would be undergoing transformation (*pariṇāma*), consciousness (*bhāna*) must be regarded as insentient (*jaḍa*), like curd and other such substances. It is unavoidable that one must regard consciousness as being entirely disconnected from any modification free from change (*avikriya-pariṇāma*). Furthermore, the very cognition (*vijñāna*) whose transformation you postulate must also be regarded as insentient, like milk and so forth; consequently, the transformation of an insentient thing would itself be insentient, and the same fault as before would arise. (4-5)

Similarly, it is also not tenable for consciousness (*vijñāna*) to be the originating cause (*ārambhaka-kāraṇa*) of manifestation (*bhāna*). In the view of those who accept an originating cause, it is invariably a substance (*dravya*) that serves as such a cause; yet in their own system, cognition (*jñāna*) is a quality (*guṇa*), not a substance. If those who maintain that experiential cognition (*anubhavātmaka-jñāna*) is the originating cause of manifesting cognition (*bhānātmaka-jñāna*) were to consider both to be qualities, then the impossibility of origination would be evident.

If one considers consciousness (*vijñāna*) to be a substance (*dravya*), it would contradict their own scriptures; there would be no benefit whatsoever toward achieving their desired goal by regarding manifestation (*bhāna*) as a substance—this is the intended meaning. ||6||

Chapter 3 Knowledge cannot be the producer of the sun, for if it were, then even the knowledge of the son of a barren woman would be a producer. (7) If the knowledge of one who is not devoted to Me were to be a producer [of the sun], then there would be no distinction between the sun and other objects, because there is no difference in their being produced. (8) Therefore, the sun never possesses the quality of being produced by knowledge. (9) There is no such thing as the "producedness" of knowledge itself; for those who perceive its production, that perception is merely an illusion according to the logic already stated. (10)

O gods, the manifestation (*bhāna*) of that [reality] is likewise known as *śāti* (peace), which is the supreme state of the wise. O best of beings, because it exists as being and is non-different [from it], this manifestation is eternal. O gods, that manifestation which is the illuminator of the path is eternally manifest by its own nature; that alone is the victorious, pervasive self, designated as *Uṃkara*.

Regarding the phrase "of the non-existent" (*asataḥ*): in the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*), the established position is that an effect is produced from what is already non-existent. Consequently, it is not logical to claim that the cognition of an object in its non-existent form is the cause of its origination. For if even that cognition were to originate [the effect], then the cognition of a barren woman's son would likewise be an originator [of something]. This is because there would be no distinction between [cognitions of] existent things and [cognitions of] defects such as being a barren woman's son. 7.

[Objection: Is it not the case that since origination (*utpatti*) is accepted as the connection with existence (*sattā*) for that which was previously non-existent, how can there be any capacity to originate things such as a son or a sprout, given that they are absolutely non-existent? To this, he says: "of the non-existent [things] being produced. Since absolute non-existence (*atyantāsattva*)—that is, otherness (*parāktva*) and so forth—is a property (*dharma*) consisting of a negation (*abhāva*), it cannot be the locus (*āśraya*) of any property; and if it were such a locus, it would follow that it is itself a positive entity (*bhāvatva*). Therefore, a distinction based on that [non-existence] is not tenable for the non-existent. This is the meaning. Since no mode of producing other than transformation (*pariṇāma*) or aggregation (*ārambha*) can be defined, he concludes that cognition (*vijñāna*) is the producer of the manifestation (*bhāna*): "Therefore... (vv. 8–9).

He extends the stated point elsewhere as well with the words "ānarye" (in the case of non-sublimity). "By the aforementioned reasoning" means: for if cognition were something produced (*janya*), then by this logic it would be insentient (*jaḍa*) like a jar due to its being produced by a cause. Now, one observes that after the contact of the eyes and so forth with objects such as color-form, the cognition of those objects arises; what then is the explanation for this? To this he says: "In the case of being produced. It is the modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which has transformed into the form of the object, that is produced there.

This very non-eternality (janyatva) appears even in the consciousness delimited by that [object], just as redness appears in a crystal; therefore, the perception of non-eternality in cognition is merely illusory. || 10 ||

Regarding the phrase "of manifestation as well": since manifestation—consisting of the cognition of objects such as a jar—is perceived as something produced, its production is established by the fact that it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the knowledge residing in the substrate (*āśraya*). Thus, it is precisely that [manifestation] which is determined to possess the quality of being produced. Having thus established that manifestation is not produced, he proves its permanence with the words "being an entity" (*bhāvatve*). He specifies this by adding "while being an entity," because even though prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is unproduced, it is observed to be impermanent; therefore, [the qualification] is added to exclude that.
The intention is as follows: "The object of dispute is eternal, because, while being an existent, it is unproduced, like the Self.

(11) Thus, having established the eternity of the Light and its non-difference from the Supreme Lord, he concludes that [Light] consists solely of consciousness and pure existence with the words, "That which is the world": That eternal Light which is the illuminator of this aforementioned world shines by its own nature, independent of any other light; that very [Light] is the Witness and Seer of the entire world, the Supreme Lord who abides at all times as the substrate of all things.

Alternatively, although the word *idam* (this) is neuter, the use of the masculine form *saḥ* (he) as a reference to that very [reality] is intended to indicate the subject to be enjoined (*vidheya*). For it has been said: "Pronouns bring about the identity between the object being pointed out and the subject pointing it out; they assume the gender of that which is predominant. Thus, the meaning is that he who is characterized by such a nature is that very Supreme Śiva existing in his own essential form, and not of an insentient nature. || 12 ||

The appearance of that which is non-existent in nature—that is, an appearance of something that does not exist at all—cannot be the originating cognition (*ārambhaka-vijñāna*). For if the non-existent possessed the capacity to produce an effect, then it would have produced everything! || 7 || If it is argued that although both the appearance and the son of a barren woman are equally non-existent, there is still a distinction such that the appearance...

That which did not previously exist becomes equal to the opponent in the debate; that is, it becomes an answer (*uttara*). Since it does not exist at all, it is improper to speak of it as a "debater," for such specific designations as "the debater" cannot apply to that which is non-existent. Therefore, statements such as "that which does not exist at all did not exist previously" are untenable.

[The existence of] that [object] must also be established as the basis for establishing the relationship; how could that which is not even perceived establish a relationship? (One should also consider other defects such as infinite regress. Therefore, it is never possible for cognition to be produced by an object. Just like the object under discussion, cognition also cannot be something that arises [from an external object]. In this regard as well, the same logical arguments should be applied.

The cognition that "knowledge has been produced" arises merely from mental exertion. Just as in the case of [the illusion] "the staff-holder has become naked," where the birth and destruction of the means (upāya) appear due to non-discrimination caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), so too does knowledge appear; for a state devoid of knowledge is subtler than an atom and is not even an object of recollection. || 90 ||

Both knowledge (*jñāna*) and manifestation (*bhāna*) are established merely through conventional cognition (*paratītimātra-siddha*), not through ultimate reality (*vāstavika*). (14) And likewise, the external objects do not shine by themselves; they shine [only] through that [connection]. (15)

O best of gods, consciousness (caitanya) abiding in the instruments such as inference and the rest is the illuminator of even those [instruments] for some; therefore, it is with that [consciousness] as its instrument. It is said to be the illuminator of all; by it, this world is made manifest. For this reason, a person here recites these forms by means of that very [consciousness].

And he establishes the state of being the witness of the entire universe—which consists of the nature of one's own ignorance regarding the essential form of the Self, which is the non-manifestation of its own natural luminosity—by the phrase "due to the relationship fashioned by that. For, according to the scriptural statement, "This Self is indeed unattached and free," it cannot be said that there is any ultimate relationship between the Supreme Śiva, who is of the nature of non-manifestation, and anything else whatsoever.

Therefore, since the connection with the individual soul (*jīva*) is also imagined (*parikalpita*), it exists [only as such]; by virtue of that connection, ignorance (*ajñāna*) appears as the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) within the substrate of reality (*tattvasūpa*), but not through its own inherent luminosity—this is the meaning. "Produced by ignorance" means: the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which consists of the transformation of the qualities of *sattva* and so forth produced by that ignorance, as well as attachment (*rāga*) and other attributes of that [organ]—all these appear solely because of the consciousness connected to the ignorance that is their material cause (*upādāna*), and not by their own nature. (13)

"Prāṇa as well... means that even the vital breath, the sense organs, the body, and so forth, shine not by themselves, but solely through a connection with the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) via the mediation of their being pervaded by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which is colored by consciousness through its relation to the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that serves as their material cause. "And external objects... means that the entire collection of external objects such as jars and the like also shines not by themselves, but solely through a connection with the witness-consciousness via the mediation of their being pervaded by a mental modification in the form of those objects, which is colored by consciousness through its connection with the intellect (*buddhi*)—such as the eye—when it is in contact with them. || 14 || 15 ||

Regarding the phrase "residing in a mental modification (*vṛtti*) such as 'possessing alumāna'": the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes [mental modifications] such as analogy (*upamāna*). That consciousness (*caitanya*) which, according to the previously stated method, resides in a mental modification produced by a reason such as "possessing smoke"—which [in turn] generates an inference—also becomes manifest through an indirect connection with certain objects, such as "possessing fire," which are the pervaders (*vyāpaka*) of the reasons like "possessing smoke" that produce the mental modification constituting its own substrate.

Because the manifestation of the locus of the horse [the mind] occurs within the objects of another's knowledge, there is indeed a state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*), just as there is a state of being covered (*āvṛtatva*). The intention of one who says that "being the object of another's knowledge through inference and so forth constitutes *vyāpyatva* and thus exists" is as follows. He concludes the established omniscience of Paraśiva, whose nature is pure luminosity, with the words "Therefore": thus, it has been demonstrated that Paraśiva—who, in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), is bound by ignorance—possesses the nature of pure witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya-mātra*).

And thus, by the scriptural passage, "Which is that Self?"—which introduces the subject as before—the reply is given that this Self is indeed the witness of all, whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), and not the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This very same point is established through a series of subsequent illustrations. Summarizing the meaning of the scripture, "That by which one hears, or by which one smells odors, or by which one articulates speech, or by which one discerns the savory and the unsavory," [the author] explains it with the words beginning "Therefore, He is without breath," and so forth.

Because of the reasoning already stated, and because of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which says, "By its light all this shines," the Self, in the form of the witness (*sākṣin*), is the illuminator of all existing things. For that reason, by means of this very nature of Paraśiva—the illuminator of all—who abides in the center of the heart as the witness of everything, one perceives forms through the syllable *ciṃ*, [which is] manifested by the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) produced by the eye when it is directed toward form. 16–17. Ignorance is thus perceived.

Ignorance is never perceived independently by itself. (In such forms as "I am ignorant," the experience of ignorance occurs only as something connected to the self; one does not experience ignorance in isolation.)

Therefore, it appears that ignorance alone exists within oneself; for the existence of ignorance within the Self, which is of the nature of knowledge, is possible only through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). The mind arising from ignorance, as well as its operations such as attachment and aversion, do not manifest by themselves, but rather manifest only through consciousness (*caitanya*) associated with ignorance. || 13 ||

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), external objects, as well as the body—these appear only because they are connected to the Self, not by themselves. Even the manifestation of external objects occurs solely through connection with the Self, and not without it. (15) Furthermore, the consciousness residing within inference and other such cognitions also becomes the illuminator of certain objects.

In the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), since the mental faculty (*manas*) has a connection with the object, its relation to the self—which is distinct from that [object]—is logically established; however, what is the connection between the mind and the object in the case of indirect cognition (*parokṣa*)? Without such a connection, the assumption of knowledge would lead to an obvious over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the answer to this is indicated once again in the *Puṇya* [section].

Regarding this subject, the venerable Prakāśātmā states that the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna*) concerning the supreme reality (*para-vastu*) alone can be considered their [the senses'] relation. His statement is: "Objecthood (*viṣayatva*) consists in the cessation of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) with respect to inferable things. The *Tattvadīpana* explains this as: "'Cessation of deep sleep' means the cessation of ignorance regarding that object" (p.

403, Kumbhakonam edition). For this reason, in the *Laghucandrikā*, even the objectivity characterized by form (*ākārāvacchinna-viṣayatā*) is considered the object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*).

By this [organ], one smells fragrances that are pleasant; by this very [organ], a human being always articulates speech; and by this, a human being discerns what is sweet and what is not among tastes.
(18) But how does the cognition of the sense of touch come about through association with the wise? O best of gods, some say here that it is the intellect (*buddhi*) [that acts] as Brahman. (19)

In the same way, by means of this very light of consciousness (cidprakāśa), which is manifested through the mental modification (manovṛtti) produced by the contact with the auditory organ during autumn, one perceives sounds; and it should be applied similarly to the perception of odors and so forth. "Always speech" means that by means of this very light of consciousness, manifested through the mental modification directed toward the objects of sound to be articulated, one engages in verbal expression—the thing to be spoken—through the door of the vocal organ. And this is also an illustration for the other organs of action, such as the hands and feet. "And by this, what is sweet" [is tasted].

By means of this very [consciousness], which is manifested through the mental modification produced by the sweet and other tastes associated with the contact of the tongue and the sense of taste, one knows the distinction between the palatable and the unpalatable. The word "or" (*vā*) found in the text has the sense of "and" (*ca*). This is what is meant: that pervasive luminosity which persists even in the cognitions of form and so forth, produced by distinct instruments such as the eyes and ears, is itself the Self in the form of the Witness (*sākṣin*).

Indeed, this [Self] is to be understood through such scriptural passages as "He sees" and so forth; however, since it is denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the word "sees," which expresses the agent, how can there be a designation with the instrumental case ending as "by this"? There is no fault here. For, by resorting to the distinction imagined through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its modifications (*vṛtti*), it is metaphorically designated as an instrument. It is for this very reason that it is recited even in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "By whom one perceives form, taste, smell, sounds, and touches..."

"By this very [consciousness] one knows; what is there to be deliberated upon here? These are those [powers]," so it is said. But the teachers [hold that] having mounted speech through *prajñā* (consciousness), one perceives all names through speech; and having mounted the eye through *prajñā*, one perceives all forms through the eye. Thus, according to the Kauṣītaki-śruti, for the sake of the internal organ—which is the single object denoted by the term *prajñā*—abiding in the form of various instruments such as speech, the eye, and so forth, and for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which has entered through the two feet of that internal organ, [it is stated]: "That which is *prāṇa* is indeed *prajñā*."

Alternatively, in order to show that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is subordinate to wisdom (*prajñā*)—as indicated by the single term *prāṇa* being used as a means of perception in the phrase "or that which is wisdom is the breath"—the words ending in the instrumental case in the passage beginning with "by which one sees" (*yena vā paśyati*) were interpreted by some as referring to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) divided into its various forms such as the eye and so forth, as in the verse: "That which is this rising mind.

They explained that by the two terms "heart" (*hṛdaya*) and "mind" (*manas*), the internal organ—which consists of resolve and deliberation and is common to all the senses—is presented; thus, they interpreted [the text] with the intention of emphasizing the predominance of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) characterized by the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) produced by the eye and other senses.

Vadha said: "By means of this single internal organ, which has become fivefold, one sees with that which has become the eye, hears with that which has become the ear, speaks with that which has become speech, tastes with that which has become the tongue, and by means of the mind—which is of the nature of mental construction—one wills; and by means of that which is of the form of the heart, one resolves. Therefore, this internal organ is one, though it pervades the objects of the three [senses]. || 18 ||

In this context, however, the heart (*hṛdaya*), mind (*manas*), consciousness (*saṃjñāna*), perception (*vijñāna*), and so forth, are presented as names [of Brahman] because they denote the substrate of the qualities to be superimposed, with the intention of emphasizing those qualities. And these names are recorded thus: "That which is this—mind, thought, consciousness, perception, discernment, insight, intelligence, wisdom, understanding, resolve, memory, will, purpose, intention, desire, and control—all these are names for the breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2). Those who take refuge in that Lord of the Āśrama...

Even without physical contact, the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object become connected simply through the *māyā*—which is like an unconstructed house—which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for the locus of the self’s reflection (*ātma-prativivāśraya*). (Vedāntatattvaviveka, p. 276). Alternatively, since consciousness (*caitanya*) is one and all-pervading, the connection with an imperceptible (*parokṣa*) object can be described as "identity (*tādātmya*) with the consciousness conditioned by the form of that [object]. Furthermore, possessing the form of the object (*tadākāratā*) is not the cause of the object's manifestation.

The teacher Padmapāda stated: "There is no further defect regarding the object of inference (*anumeya*) and so forth; for [the cognition] is not operative toward the reality of the object itself. Rather, it is through the specific nature of the connection between the word and its referent that there arises a cognition of a qualified object. Furthermore, there is no proof for the existence of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) distinct from the arising of the cognition itself. (Brahmasiddhi, pp. 402–403). Therefore, by means of the causal relationship alone, one may assume the "assumption of the form of that" (*tadākāratā*) in cases of indirect perception (*parokṣa*), and thus the aforementioned relation is established.

A doubt may arise as to why, in the case of direct perception (*aparokṣajñāna*), the object (*viṣaya*) is considered the cause. The resolution is this: just as in the case of indirect perception (*parokṣajñāna*), the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth are accepted as the producers [of knowledge], so too in direct perception, the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) with the object is accepted as the producer. Furthermore, since a cause must be a related entity (*sambandhin*) that serves as the basis for the relation, it is logical to accept the object as the producer of direct perception. Otherwise, one would have to posit another producer, which would be difficult to define and involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

If you have the desire to move that which is illusory in nature, then you may also move the "established conclusion" (*iṣṭāpatti*). The essential point is this: even the cognition of objects occurs only through its connection with the Self, and not otherwise. Therefore, Śaṅkara alone is declared to be the illuminator of all; it is by means of Him that this world is perceived. Thus, the human being perceives form through Śaṅkara alone. (16–17)

The sense of hearing perceives sound, grasps it, makes it manifest, and apprehends it as either pleasant or unpleasant. (Although the Self is both the agent of perception and the instrument itself, its twofold nature is nonetheless established through the distinction of limiting adjuncts.)

The Self, as conditioned by that portion of the internal organ called *ahaṃkāra* (ego), is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the enjoyer (*upabhoktṛ*); furthermore, the Self, as conditioned by the active portion of the internal organ known as its *vṛtti* (modification), is the instrument (*sādhana*) of enjoyment; and the Self, as conditioned by the senses aided by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is the instrument of action. (25) That which, having become known through the Vedic injunctions, is expressed by various names—that is called the *vṛtti* consisting of determination (*nirṇaya*). Determination is accepted as being of two kinds: first, that *vṛtti* which, through such means as "this is that," brings about the cognition of an object free from doubt and other [cognitive defects].

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). If one were to say that there is no doubt regarding a certain object, and that when ignorance (*ajñāna*) concerning that object is destroyed, it occurs without the function (*vṛtti*) of the mind, then what need would there be for that function?

O noble one, what is this [state] of yours? It is the Self (ātman) itself, which is the substratum that removes ignorance regarding its own object. For it is the mental modification (manovṛtti) whose substratum is the mind that serves as the remover of that [ignorance]. Just as the Self alone is the agent when there is an effort directed toward its own object, so too, in the production of knowledge regarding its own object, the Self alone is the agent. Thus, the Self alone is the cause of the removal of ignorance regarding its own object.

From this, the doubt that one might remain as a non-embodied soul (*nirāśraya*) during deep sleep is dispelled by the fact that [the self] is the desired object of experience. This is established by such scriptural texts as "In Him he is dissolved" (*tad eva... vilīyate*). What, then, is the meaning of the word *kañcana* (anything) in both types of restrictive [negations]? Others call it the mind (*manas*). || 19 ||

When the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) possesses the modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of doubt, then the Self (*ātman*) conditioned by that [organ] comes to be designated as "doubtful. What is meant by this? When the capacity intended here is the state of being a cognizer (*cetana*), then the individual is indeed a cognizer; however, when the capacity intended is the nature of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then the Self conditioned by that [adjunct] is called "doubtful."

Since that object exists within the mind, while the *saṃnāmanaka* function persists, these very same [functions] such as perception (*darśana*) and so forth remain in their respective individual forms; no one can deny this! As for the explanation that the *oṃkāra* is the "state of being established" (*sthiti-vṛtti*), it is merely the talk of a fool who is devoid of discernment. Even the ignorant call it such; however, it cannot be said that the state of being established is the nature of the object itself. Rather, when that [object] is conditioned by the relationship with another (*īśvara-bhāva*), it receives the name "being known" (*ājñāya*). || 20 ||

(24) Thus, it has been established that the Self is none other than the eternal, self-luminous witnessing-consciousness, which, when conditioned by the modifications of the internal organ, illuminates all objects of existence, such as sound and the rest.

With the intention of showing that this very [Brahman] exists pervasively in every way throughout the entire world—from the moving to the stationary, from the subtle to the gross—both as the individual soul (*jīva*) and as the material cause (*upādāna*), the Scripture establishes its omnipresence in order to dispel the delusion of limitation: "This indeed is Brahman; this is Indra; this is Prajāpati; these are all the gods; and these are the five great elements—earth, wind, space, water, and fire—and these are the various seeds, both those that are planted and those that are not, whether born from eggs, born from wombs, or born from sweat."

"Horses, cattle, and harsh elephants have been pierced; whatever is living—whether moving, such as birds, or stationary—all that is established upon this Person. He summarizes this scriptural passage with the words beginning "This is Brahman," and so forth: "He who was previously described as the self-luminous witness, whose nature is consciousness, this very Self is Brahman."

The meaning is that, being conditioned by the aggregate of the bodies composed of the five unquintuplicated great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their effects, he becomes Brahmā, who has another synonym, Hiraṇyagarbha. Alternatively, there is a word-division as *brahmeti napuṃsakaliṅgatā* (it is neuter gender: "Brahman"). The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman, characterized by bliss, knowledge, and so forth—which, like the reflection of the sun, does not enter into the waves, bubbles, and foam [of the world]—is indeed that very Brahman when it has entered into its own limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and is nothing other than that.

The same method of interpretation applies to what follows as well. Indra is so called because of his possession of supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*). Alternatively, he is Indra because he directly realizes Brahman—which is his own self—as the Witness (*sākṣin*) who stands beyond the sphere of "this-ness," just as the earth and other objects are the locus of the notion of "this. For it is heard in scripture: "I saw this"—therefore his name is Indra; "Indra" is indeed his name, but because he was [originally] not visible (*anindra*), they spoke of him by this indirect term. Or else, *i* means "not" and *dra* means "disease"; thus, he is Indra because he has cast away disease.

(When the body and other faculties are filled with capacity for action, the consciousness endowed with that state is *dhṛti*. According to the view of Kuṣṭha, that is *mati*. (When the mind is agitated by contemplating future objects, the consciousness characterized by that state is *mati*. Others call it *manīṣā*. (The consciousness characterized by the capacity for independent reasoning and deliberation is *manīṣā*. Others have called it *sūti*.

(The mind becoming distressed by disease and so forth—that is, the consciousness characterized by a mental modification (*citta-vṛtti*) that is distressed by disease and so forth—is the meaning of "recollection" (*smṛti*). Although they call it "memory" (*smṛti*) in common parlance, the very same meaning has been expressed in the *Patañjala-bhāṣya*. || 22 || What, then, is called "recollection"? One should understand the negation of the mere object through the heart, and the negation of its particular qualities through the hand; that alone other thinkers call *kāma*. The immobile consists of trees and the like; the mobile is that which is observed to move by means of feet. One should speak thus: "The entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is entirely Brahman. The statement “Prajāpati” is intended to establish that all this is known by Him; for since the entire world is seen to be merely a witness whose activity depends upon the Supreme Lord, it is therefore called the field of the universe (jagatkṣetra). || 27 ||

The Śruti first designates the intellect (*prajñā*) as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) by its predominance, while it is actually subordinate to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), stating, "It is established in the vital breath. This is done so that the fact that pure consciousness alone—which is indicated by the entire world of objects—is the primary object of knowledge may be illuminated. Then, having again designated it as the substratum by its predominance and restated that [prior description], the Śruti establishes its nature as Brahman-Ātman with the words: "Brahman is non-dual, the foundation, and procreation."

To that end, he summarizes [the point] with the words "pratiṣaṭā" (in each hexad). Belonging to the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī*)—because the Supreme Lord himself exists in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*)—this consciousness, which is related to Him, is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) for all things, as previously stated, since it is the locus for the manifestation and persistence of the entire universe imagined through its own ignorance. For this very reason, it is declared in the *Taittirīyaka*: "From which indeed these beings are born."

"From Him all beings are born; into Him they enter when they cease to exist. Thus, that very knowledge—which is the form of the Witness, which always illuminates the entire imagined universe, and which is perceived by the practitioner within the center of the heart—is indeed Śiva, the cause of the world, joined with Śakti and so forth. It is that which is indicated by the word "Self" (Ātman) in the passage: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only."

The meaning is this: just as in the sentence "This lake is Devadatta," one sets aside the temporal relation characterized by mutual contradiction between the words *idam* (this) and *etad* (that), and instead understands the identity of the non-contradictory essence of Devadatta alone; so too here, because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would otherwise be impossible, the word *prajñāna*—which denotes consciousness that is self-luminous and immediate—and the word *brahman*—which denotes the supreme cause of the universe—are [coreferential] with the term denoting the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*).

The true, ultimate nature of Brahman—which is devoid of all adventitious attributes, uniform in essence, and common to both [the individual soul and the world]—is established here in order to dispel the delusion of difference imagined through ignorance. 1.28.

Whether born from a womb, from sweat, or sprouting from the earth—horses, cows, elephants, and all others subject to death; whether stationary or moving, and whatever else exists—that entire world is this auspicious Jambudvīpa, fashioned by the architect of the eye of wisdom. (25–27)

Chapter 3 Only through the realization of the Self does one become immortal; not by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by anything else whatsoever. (29) A human being attains Brahman solely through the knowledge of the Self; regarding this, O powerful one, I swear a solemn oath that there is no doubt. In the *Rutau*, by such passages as “Having departed from this world by means of this self consisting of knowledge (*prajñānātman*)...,” it is established that the realization of the oneness of the Self is the means to immortality; summarizing that, [the author] says, “of such a form. In reality, because the innate ignorance regarding one’s own nature—which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) whose essence is supreme Śiva—is the root of transmigratory existence, and because ignorance is removed solely by knowledge, knowledge alone is the means to liberation characterized by identity with Brahman, and not ritual action (*karman*) or the like.

Because that [ignorance] is characterized by the state of being an obstacle to knowledge, there is an absence of any means for its removal other than that. For this very reason, the Śruti negates ritual action (*karman*) and the like as a means for attaining immortality: "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth. (29) [The phrase] "by means of the knowledge of Brahman alone" [is used].

By the use of the term "only" (*mātra*), the refutation of the view that the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*) is the means to attain immortality is established. Through the mere knowledge of the oneness of the Self, when ignorance is removed, one attains the state of Brahman—which is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss and the object of all desires—simultaneously. By this, the meaning of the scriptural passage, "Having attained all desires, he became immortal," is explained.

It is also recorded elsewhere: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Thus ends the commentary on the Aitareya Śruti. Now begins the commentary on the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad]. Having thus established, through an investigation into the meaning of these Upaniṣads, that the direct realization of the oneness of Brahman—without dependence on ritual action and the like—is the supreme means to liberation, he now commences the exposition by summarizing its meaning, beginning with the words "That which has the injunctions as its object," in order to demonstrate that same state of affairs through an investigation into the meaning of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad as well.

For in the *Taittirīyaka*, with this sentence—"He attains the Supreme Brahman"—which serves as an introductory statement (*upodghāta*) indicating the subject matter to be expounded, the meaning of the aphorism is set forth. This is for the purpose of generating a desire to know that Brahman—which is non-dual bliss free from all impurities—by means of the cessation of ignorance through the mere realization of Brahman on the part of one who has attained the state of a *jīva* due to the connection with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of ignorance and its effects, and who is a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) endowed with the fourfold means. Thus, the meaning is aphorized.

This has been explained through the examples of the *saṃgraha* and the *viśada*. For the sake of easy understanding, the *saṃgraha-vyāpti* (the pervasion of the summary) has been demonstrated by means of an illustrative example. And it is stated thus: “He who knows that Brahman—Being, Consciousness, Infinite—is hidden in the cave of the heart within the highest heaven; he, together with the wise Brahman, attains all desires.”

In this context, since there is no purpose for generating further desire to know among the gods who already possess that desire, [the author], having spoken a word that is both illuminating and a generator of that desire, proceeds to summarize the meaning of that *ṛc* verse by first stating what has been said and what is yet to be said, with the words "That" (*tad*). That Brahman—which is the object of the supreme knowledge that is the means for realizing Truth (*ṛta*) and which is the essence of all—that Brahman is characterized by Truth and other such attributes.

This is because it follows the meaning of the verbal root *vṛhati*. For instance, the root *vṛh* (or *vṛhi*), meaning "to grow," expresses growth; and in this context, since no specific object of pleasure is mentioned, what is intended is simply an excellence of delight.

Furthermore, if there were a limitation by excellence (*viśeṣa*), its nature as being devoid of limitation—such as that of space and so forth—would be destroyed; consequently, it would have to be inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*) as being devoid of limitations created by other substances. This is because, in reality, that which is limited by duality is not distinct from the nature of that very limit. Thus, by the very refutation of limitation created by substance, one should understand that limitation created by space and time is also refuted.

Since space and time, too, are merely imagined and in reality do not transcend that [non-dual] nature, one must understand that non-dual reality—which is devoid of the threefold delimitation consisting in being supported by duality and having limits—is the truth. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of an error without a substratum and a sublation without limits; for if it were unreal even in its own mode of being, it could not function as a substratum or a limit due to its lack of any defining characteristic (*nirupākhyatva*).

And if that arrow were never to appear, it would be invisible and non-existent; therefore, it follows by implication that it must indeed appear. Furthermore, if it were illuminated by another, its own self-luminosity would be lost, because it would be delimited by another entity; thus, there would be a contradiction with the word "Brahman," which denotes absolute perfection and unsurpassed excellence.

Thus, by means of the term *brahman* denoting the unsurpassed (*niratiśaya*) body of bliss (*ānandakāya*), its infinity and other qualities are indicated; explaining the meaning of that term, [the text] says: "Brahman is knowledge and infinite. Furthermore, because this Brahman is established as being the object of knowledge through its non-difference from the Supreme, it follows that for that which is of the nature of bliss, such a status would otherwise be impossible; thus, its nature as consisting of unsurpassed bliss is also established. For this very reason, it is declared in scripture: "He understood Brahman as bliss," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss."

Therefore, this is rightly said: "This [Self] is Being, Consciousness, and Bliss. Now, an objection may be raised: this is merely a secondary characterization (*upalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman; and since words such as "Being" (*sat*) and so forth have as their basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) higher and lower universals (*jāti*) such as "reality" (*satyatva*), how can they denote Brahman, which is non-differentiated, of a single flavor (*ekarasa*), and of the nature described above? This is not a fault. For in Brahman, which is of the single flavor of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), these [universals] are merely imagined.

All categories of objects (padārtha), because they proceed, exist, and dissolve within the three times characterized by past, future, and present—being designated as "unmanifest" (avyākṛta) according to the etymological derivation that it is "not clearly defined"—is denoted by the term *guhā* (the cave) found in the Śruti. Furthermore, because it possesses the power to bring about the knowledge of the true nature of Brahman—which is the cause of the manifestation of the world consisting of various effects difficult to accomplish—it receives the designations of *māyā*, *avidyā*, and so forth.

By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), ignorance (*avidyā*), the power of inertia (*jaḍaśakti*), and so forth are also included. This very [unmanifest] is designated as the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*). For the unmanifest is denoted by the word "ether" (*vyoman*) based on its well-known status in scriptural passages such as: "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the heaven is woven, warp and woof; that which is the space outside a person, and that which is the space inside a person."

Furthermore, it should be understood that this refers to the supreme [space] by comparison with external space. And thus, in the scriptural passage, “In the cave, in the supreme ether” (*guhāyāṃ parame vyoman*), the two words ending in the locative case are in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And thus, the meaning is that [the Self] is placed—that is, situated—within that which has evolved in the form of cause and effect, beginning with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth, consisting of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), and which is unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). This is intended with a specific purpose in mind, because it is impossible for Brahman, who is within all and devoid of distinctions, to have a connection with a specific location.

Thus, within this unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)—which exists in the form of the five sheaths (*kośas*) to be described hereafter, such as the food-sheath (*annamaya*) and the vital-breath-sheath (*prāṇamaya*), and which is composed of the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*—there lies hidden the non-dual Brahman, whose sole essence is Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (*satyajñānānandaikarasa*). He who realizes that [Brahman] directly through a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) in the form of that very Brahman—generated by the means of hearing, reflecting, and so forth upon the Vedāntas, and by virtue of its identity with the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—is [the one referred to]; this is the connection with what follows. || 31 ||

The Lord, who has become the Self of all beings, by means of His perfect knowledge, simultaneously pervades all individual souls—those who have been freed from the defects of suffering and the like—which have become that [Self] through the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss, because ignorance, the cause of delusion, has been uprooted along with its very root. Thus, by stating "by one who has known Brahman," the instrumental case in the Vedic passage "with armor for the wise" (*varmaṇā vipaścite*) is explained not as indicating accompaniment—as in the expression "he came with his son"—but rather as denoting an attribute (*itthambhāve*), similar to the usage in "he saw the king with a white umbrella."

For this very reason, since the scriptures such as "In the beginning, this was indeed one alone" and "The one God is hidden in all beings" establish the self as being ultimately one, and because the perception of multiplicity within various bodies is explained through the postulation of adventitious distinctions—just like the space in a jar or the space in a hut—it is established by scriptural passages such as "Having created that, He entered into it" and "Let me enter with this living self and differentiate names and forms," that the Creator's own self exists in the state of the individual soul (jīva).

Because there are various descriptions of the bodies of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), the non-difference between the individual soul and the Supreme is not established as real. Accordingly, they say: "Are these [the organs] like the elements, subservient to the individual soul? No; he says: 'together,' meaning simultaneously, mounted upon a single moment.
