It has been determined by Sarasvatīsvāmin in his *Tattvaratnākara* (p. 43) that "Brahman itself, possessing power, is the material cause. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Pure Consciousness (*śuddhacit*), when conditioned by the limiting adjunct of ignorance (*avidyā-upādhi*), is the material cause of the world.
And it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "The Lord is of the nature of Consciousness, distinguished from the reflection residing in ignorance. Thus it is said in the *Nyāyaratnāvalī* (p. 275).
*Brahmagītā*, verse 722.

From the primordial time, by the command of Śiva, the sun was produced from the *adusana* [element], and then the five-fold non-quintuplication (*apañcīkaraṇa*) occurred. From wind came fire, from fire came water, and from water came the earth. Having quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛtya*) those elements into the five gross worlds (*bhūtāni*) by the command of Śiva, I, as Brahmā, created this egg of the universe (*brahmāṇḍa*) from them alone. Within the interior of that cosmic egg, various divine abodes were fashioned and established by the command of Śiva. Therein dwell these various gods and demigods, as well as humans, animals, birds, and trees.

By the command of Nivāja, we have proceeded according to our respective desires. The term *vivarta* refers to an appearance that does not obstruct the nature of the cause; therefore, because Brahman is devoid of transformation (*nirvikāratva*), there is no contingency of its being subject to change—this is the meaning. This very point was also established by Bādarāyaṇa: "There is no contingency of modification, nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural texts; this has been determined here. Thus, the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) consisting of the elements and elemental products, which takes the form of Brahman, is superimposed upon the causal substrate. Because it is imagined through the power of *māyā*, it is non-different from the substrate, just as a snake [is non-different] from a rope.

Just as a dirty pot, a jar, a water-pot, or a bowl—whose specific forms such as their bases, bellies, and openings have no existence apart from their causal material, clay—and since these particular forms and the words "pot," "jar," and so forth are merely modifications of speech (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), they are not other than the causal clay itself; in the same way, because the effect of Brahman is non-different from its cause, one should not suspect that Brahman is limited by that [effect]. This is the meaning. (34) "From space," etc.

Because that which has been superimposed is indescribable due to its lack of substantiality, it cannot serve as the substratum for another entity; thus, there is no contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "All this is indeed the Unmanifest (Aśubhaja)," and "From Him are born breath, mind, and all sense-organs, space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe," which negate the entire phenomenal world of duality.

Furthermore, because of the mention of being the source (*yoni*) and the hearing of the word "from" (*āt*), it is intended that Brahman itself—serving as the substrate for the superimposition of its specific effects such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, and conditioned by those adjuncts—is designated as the material cause (*upādāna*) by means of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) in words such as "from" (*āt*). From Brahman, which has assumed the form of space, there arises from its own cause a subtle wind, which is another name for *mahat* (the Great Principle), possessing its own quality of touch along with the quality of sound inherited from its cause.

It has been stated that fire arises from air. In this way, just as a cloth woven from threads possesses the qualities of its own material cause, so too fire, possessing the three qualities through the qualities of its own cause and its own inherent quality, is produced.

And thus, because the *Taittirīyaka* states that fire has air as its material cause in the passage "From air, [fire]," and because the *Chāndogya* states that the existent (sat) is the material cause of fire in the passage "That [Existent] created fire," there is no room for the suspicion that the Śruti is invalid due to contradiction; for even in the *Taittirīyaka*, the status of the Existent (Brahman) as the ultimate material cause is established through the aforementioned method. For this very reason, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa also enunciated this point in the Sūtra: "Fire [arises] from that, and so [do] water [and earth]. "From fire, water."

And from that Brahman which has assumed the form of food (anna), water was produced, possessing four qualities through the three qualities residing in its cause and its own quality of taste. From that very same Brahman which has assumed the form of water, earth was manifested, possessing five qualities through the four qualities residing in its cause and its own quality of smell. || 35 ||

In the Śruti, the creation of the elements beginning with earth is recorded as follows: "From earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, man. He summarizes that [creation] with the words "those [elements]."

This is the statement of Brahmā: "O Lord, by Your command alone, having made the subtle elements such as ether (*viyat*) and the rest gross through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and other things that constitute His body were created by me. For Paraśiva, being conditioned by the subtle elements such as ether which He Himself has created, is designated by such terms as Hiraṇyagarbha, the first embodied one, and Prajāpati; and it is precisely under His authority that the prior elemental creation occurs.

The meaning is: "In the midst of the creation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), I have created all the worlds beginning with the earth, and within them, all objects of enjoyment such as plants, forests, and so forth, for the sake of gods, humans, and others. "O gods" is one form of address; "gods and others" is another. Here, the word "gods" (*deva*) is intended to include [all beings] beginning with Brahmā. [The phrase] "the limited self of others remains within me"—in this way, it is declared that Māyā has assumed a form.

Consequently, it must be abandoned that [the world] exists as something distinct from Being (*sat*). The answer to this is: there is no ignorance other than that which is specifically unknown by the Exalted One (*Raghu*, i.e., Śiva). Likewise, there is no ignorance of the Unmanifest (*kṣiva*) other than that which is unknown by the Exalted One; nor is there *māyā* and so forth. As the venerable Sureśvarācārya states: "Ignorance and that which arises from it are both destroyed for one who has known That" (*Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika* 2.1.174). Ignorance is not distinct from the Self (*ātman*).

It is neither different nor non-different; therefore, there is no defect in its being non-dual. (34) Just as from the ether-like Brahman, air was produced, possessing its own excellent quality—touch—and the cause, the ether, also possessed its quality, sound; and from the fire-like Brahman, air became fire, in which the quality of form increased; and from the water-like Brahman, earth was produced.

In water and earth, the qualities of taste and smell are to be known respectively; they move toward their objects because the qualities of the cause have indeed arrived. These are the five great elements (mahābhūtas). [The subtle elements] do not become objects of the senses; rather, it is their subtlety that [prevents this].

The subtle qualities of the elements (*ākāśa*, etc. belonging to that state do not become objects of the senses; those elements of that state are indeed subtle. (After Brahmā had emerged from Śiva,) he performed their *pañcīkaraṇa*—that is, he made them gross—and from these gross elements, he fashioned this universe (*brahmāṇḍa*). ||-36 || In accordance with the command of Mahādeva, he created specific worlds, and within them, the Ājānadevas and Karmadevas...

1. The theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) is in fact the theory of non-origination (*ajātavāda*); it is merely a figurative expression regarding sound. Since the body that appears as an object of cognition is nothing other than an unreal transformation, it is called the "theory of illusory manifestation. [Note: *vikopa* is likely a scribal error for *vikoṣa* or *vyavahāra*; *kāryam* is likely *kāryam*]. 2. Dh. "Non-sound" (or "without sound"). Chapter 3, Verse 99: The body that appears to embodied beings, consisting of bone, sinew, and so forth, is distinct from the Self, because the Self is composed of consciousness and is internal. 99.

Because they are designated by the term "gods of the gods" (*devānāṃ devāḥ*) in the *Pṛthuvacana*. Regarding the phrase "according to their respective karma": this means that for the sake of experiencing various fruits consisting of diverse pleasures and pains—which have ripened through the merit and demerit performed in those respective [lives]—diverse bodies of experience (*bhogāyatana*) are manifested, distinguished as gods, humans, and so forth. Furthermore, although [this applies] to all living beings, since only the *puruṣa* has the qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*), it is his creation alone that is taught in the *Śruti*. For this very reason, in the *Taittirīyaka*:

The qualification for knowledge is declared for the Self residing within the body transformed into the form of a person (*puruṣa*), as it manifests through specific types of cognition: "In the person alone is the Self more fully manifested; for he, being most endowed with intelligence, knows what is to be known, speaks what is to be spoken, sees what is to be seen, knows what is to come, and desires both the worlds and immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17–19). || 36 || || 37 || || 38 ||

In order to establish that the person who has attained identity with the body composed of food (annamaya) is, in fact, the Brahman that is the innermost of all, the *Śruti*—for the sake of facilitating comprehension by means of an internal and external sequence—presents five sheaths (kośas) known as the food-sheath (annamaya), the vital-breath-sheath (prāṇamaya), the mind-sheath (manomaya), the consciousness-sheath (vijñānamaya), and the bliss-sheath (ānandamaya), beginning with the words "This very person is indeed composed of the essence of food" (*sa vā eṣa puruṣo 'nnarasamayaḥ*). These [sheaths] are summarized by the author with the verse beginning "The bones," and so forth.

In that state, while existing as the individual soul (*jīva*), there are three bodies: the gross, the subtle, and the causal. Among these, the gross body, composed of the transformation of food-essence (*annarasa*) and consisting of the six sheaths (*ṣaṭkauśika*), is the one with which the Self identifies; thus, it becomes the "Self" (*ātman*). This is because the scripture, in the passage "This person indeed consists of the essence of food," refers back to the Self under discussion by means of the word "that" (*tat*) and establishes its nature as being made of food.

In this way, by means of the analogies of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth up to the "joyful" (*moda*), one should understand that the nature of the self (*ātman*) consists of the layers beginning with the "vital-breath-made" (*prāṇamaya*). Furthermore, by teaching that the gross body—which is a transformation of food—is the self, the misconception that things other than one's own body, such as sons, wives, and so on, are the self is removed.

In the midst of that [sheath], there is the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) which has commenced as a state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). That which consists of seventeen parts and is devoid of grossness is the subtle body; and that ignorance (*avidyā*), primarily characterized by the mind, which manifests during deep sleep and serves as the cause for both [the gross and subtle bodies], is its causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*). In this context, the inclusion of the vital-breath (*prāṇamaya*), the mental (*manomaya*), and the cognitive (*vijñānamaya*) sheaths occurs within the sheath of bliss (*ānandamaya*); however, the distinction is that the sheath of bliss is the causal body.

Since the elements are effects of *māyā*, which is characterized by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, they too possess these three qualities. Among them, those five portions of *rajas* present in the elements such as ether (*ākāśa*) constitute the five organs of action—speech, hands, feet, and so forth. Originating from that *rajas*-portion, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the cause of activities such as breathing and is characterized by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), possesses five functions: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and the rest.

Thus, by teaching the Self that is distinct from the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya-kośa*), the Śruti establishes the non-self-nature of this [sheath] through the instruction: "Different from this inner self consisting of food is another inner self, the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). He states this very point with the word "asthi" (bone): one must understand that the Self, characterized by the aforementioned sheath of breath, is indeed distinct from this physical body composed of six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*), which is the effect of food and consists of bone, sinew, and so forth, serving as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the Self.

The meaning is that, for this reason, the self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), which is experienced as existing within the body—inside the skin—is to be understood through discrimination as distinct from the body and its external elements like water. For this very reason, because of the commonality of being an external covering, the body is described as a "sheath" (*kośa*) for the modification [of the self]. In the same way, regarding the subsequent teachings on the selves consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and so forth, one should understand their nature as sheaths by means of the removal of the delusion of identity with each preceding [self], which is distinguished as being external. (39)

The various gods, humans, and the five classes of living beings were fashioned according to the karma of those souls. (37–38) That which is perceived as the physical body of a sentient being—composed of bone, sinew, and so forth—is distinct from the *prāṇamaya* body, for the latter exists within the *annamaya* [body], like the core of a banyan tree.

(Although *tārā* is an adjunct (*upādhi*) of transmigratory existence, nevertheless, the adjunct present within which we have formed the notion of "I" is precisely this aggregate of our body. Therefore, it is necessary to exercise discrimination with respect to that alone. Having analyzed the body into five parts, they are defined as "sheaths" (*kośa*) in the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*. Just as a scabbard encloses a sword, these [five elements] cover the Self from within; therefore, they are called sheaths.)

The physical body, composed of flesh and so forth, which is an object of the senses, is called the *annamaya-kośa* (the sheath consisting of food). The *prāṇamaya-kośa* (the sheath consisting of vital breath), however, consists of the functions of *karma* (action) and *jñāna* (knowledge); its location is strictly within the body. Therefore, this sheath is distinct from the *annamaya*. A distinction can only exist between what is internal and external. Furthermore, the *prāṇamaya* departs even when one leaves the *annamaya*; from this also, their difference is established.

The more one conceals the inner self within these sheaths (kośas), the more that self remains hidden from close proximity; and for this very reason, its separation from the self becomes increasingly difficult. None of the five sheaths is the self—this is the realization. One cannot realize the self by abandoning one sheath for another.

Therefore, the purpose of showing the distinctions among these sheaths (kośa) is to manifest that the Self (ātman) is distinct from these various things; thus, it is established that none of these is the Self. This is the intended meaning in the investigation of the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha). || 39 || As for this sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya)—

1. Gha. Ḍa. °kṣe tvevā? | 2. Gha. vijñānaṃ | 3. Ga. vijñānaṃ | 4. Gha. Ḍa. I. vadyatsa? | 5. Jña. °pādapāyūpasthāni | 6. Gha. tadetadāha! In some manuscripts, there is an additional half-verse before "asthitvādeḥ," namely: "tataścātramayo hyātmā vibhinnaścāntare śvattaḥ. 724. *Brahmagītā*

This self consisting of breath (prāṇamaya), which shines within all embodied beings, is distinct from the self consisting of mind (manomaya), because it is internal to it. || 40 || This self consisting of mind, which shines within all embodied beings, is distinct from the self consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), because it is internal to it. || 41 || The self consisting of consciousness, which shines within all selves, is distinct from the self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), because it is internal to it. || 42 ||

Having thus established, through the instruction on the *prāṇamaya* (the vital-sheath), that the external *annamaya* (the food-sheath) is unreal, the Scripture proceeds to instruct upon the *manomaya* (the mind-sheath) as even more internal than that, in order to demonstrate that the *prāṇamaya* as well is unreal by virtue of its being a mere effect. It says: "Different from this *prāṇamaya* is another, inner Self, the *manomaya*. This is summarized as follows: "This [Self]... The five organs of knowledge, such as hearing and so forth, have their origin in the five elements beginning with ether (*viyat*).

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is a transformation of the aggregate of the *sattva* portion [of primordial matter], undergoes a twofold modification because the *sattva* that serves as its material cause possesses the capacity to manifest the light of pleasure, which is its own inherent nature. Consequently, the internal organ, being its effect, also transforms in two ways: by means of a function (*vṛtti*) that manifests its own essential pleasure, and by means of a function that manifests the light of its own nature. Among these, the function that manifests the light [of pleasure]—being slightly permeated by *rajas*—receives the name "mind" (*manas*) and consists of volition and conceptualization.

Due to its separation from the *saṃsarpa* and *haviḥ*, when there is a lack of impurity (*nemalya*), it becomes fixed in nature and abides in the state of pure consciousness (*buddhatva*). Thus, the sense organs such as the eyes, assisted by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which possesses functions differentiated by the distinction between the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), also become twofold by virtue of generating two kinds of knowledge: that of discernment (*vimarśa*) and that of certainty (*nirṇaya*). Among these, that which is designated by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the internal organ possessing the function known as "mind" (*manas*), which is accompanied by the five sense organs and generates discerning knowledge (*vimarśajñāna*), is called the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*).

And that [sheath], being internal to the sheaths consisting of the aforementioned prāṇa, apāna, and so forth, is distinct. He states the reason for this: "on account of its internality. The meaning is that it is internal because of its difference in essential nature, characterized by its capacity to manifest the consciousness whose own form resides within. However, the *prāṇamaya* [sheath], due to its nature as a transformation of *rajas*, manifests only a slight portion of the light of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) that has been stirred up. For this very reason, even though the function of the *prāṇa* exists during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), no specific manifestation of the consciousness belonging to the waking state is observed.

The one who initiates activities such as inhalation and exhalation performs nothing other than the mere sustaining of this body composed of the elements. Thus says the *Prāṇa-vākya*: "I alone, having divided myself fivefold and having taken hold of this body, sustain it. The point is that because these two possess distinct natures, the mind, which consists of the internal organ (*manomaya*), should be understood as being more internal and distinct from the vital breath (*prāṇamaya*). 40.

Having thus established that the *prāṇamaya* is not the [ultimate] Self because it exists as an external sheath (*kośa*), the Śruti teaches the *vijñānamaya* as being even more internal than that, in order to demonstrate that the *manomaya* is likewise [not the ultimate Self]: "Different from this *manomaya* which consists of mind, there is another inner Self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). This is summarized as: "That which is this *manomaya*..."

According to the manner previously described, the Self, when characterized by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which possesses the function called "intellect" (*buddhi*) and is accompanied by the senses such as the eye and so forth, which produce determinative knowledge—is the "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). It is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it is that by means of which one cognizes; thus, it is "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*), meaning it has that [intellect] as its limiting adjunct. Furthermore, this is distinct from the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) due to its being more internal. Its internality consists in its abiding within, free from contact with the quality of passion (*rajas*), and in its manifestation therein through the specific determination of the inner consciousness in the form of certainty.

Intending to show that only one who possesses the certain knowledge regarding the objects to be performed has the qualification for both knowledge and action, the scripture declares that the self consisting of consciousness is the cause of rituals such as sacrifice: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice, and it also performs the ritual acts. (41)

In order to demonstrate that even the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness) is external and thus not the ultimate Self, the Śruti declares an inner Self beyond this as well—the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss)—in the passage: "Different from this *vijñānamaya* which consists of understanding is another inner Self, which consists of bliss. This is summarized by the phrase "the *vijñānamaya*. Bliss (*ānanda*) is the happiness that is the fruit of knowledge and action; the *ānandamaya* is the Self characterized by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that manifest that bliss. And because it is of the nature of the fruit, it is internal and distinct from the *vijñānamaya*, which is of the nature of the means.

The mind-made sheath (*manomaya-kośa*) is distinct from that which is perceived as the self by embodied beings. This is because it lies within both the food-sheath (*annamaya*) and the vital-breath sheath (*prāṇamaya*); for this reason, the mind-made sheath is separate from those two. When the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) performs its functions consisting of thought and deliberation, but is unable to reach certainty, it is called "mind" (*manas*). The mind, together with the indeterminate organs of knowledge (*jñānendriyas*), constitutes the mind-made sheath.

The meaning of being "inner" is to be proximate to the Self (*ātman*). Being proximate to the Self also means becoming the object of a more firm identification (*tādātmyadhī*). In the *prāṇamaya*, only the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the Self is manifested; in the *manomaya*, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is also manifested. Therefore, the similarity to the Self is greater, and for this very reason, the conclusion that the mind (*manas*) is the Self is even firmer.

When the hands are gone, one does not feel "I am no longer here," but when the mind is led elsewhere, one feels "I was not there. Therefore, because we have a greater sense of identity with it, that sheath is even more internal than the *prāṇamaya*. (20) That which is perceived by everyone as this *manomaya* sheath is also within it; therefore, distinct from that is the *vijñānamaya* sheath.

The internal organ that performs determination is the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, O Knower, the intellect accompanied by the sense organs that produce the act of determination is the "sheath consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya-kośa*). This is what I consider; having made this determination, the intellect merges into Me, who am non-different from it. Thus, this sheath is both external and internal. This alone is the "sheath," for it is the one possessing determination who acts as the agent. || 41 ||

That which is established by the experience of all as consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is distinct from it because of its being internal; this is the *ānandamaya* section. [The term] *ānandamaya* refers to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that manifests bliss. Because it bestows the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), it is the most internal of all. [The state of being an enjoyer...]

The Teacher has indeed established the conclusion of the second section that even in the case of *ānandamaya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). He intends to provide a detailed exposition of this very point immediately following.

Chapter 3, Verse 725: That very Self (Ātman) must be understood through discrimination (*viveka*). However, that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is external (*bahiraṅga*), because it is the means for accomplishing the ritual acts that produce those results; thus, it is not the Ātman. In this way, by discriminating the triad beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), discrimination from even the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) is established. "The five organs of perception, as well as the five organs of action, the five breaths, the intellect (*buddhi*), and the mind (*manas*)—they know these to be the seventeenfold [subtle body]."

Thus, indeed, is the nature of the gross and subtle bodies, since it has been established that this very [Self], which consists of seventeen components, exists in the form of the sheaths (kośas) beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa). Even though the discrimination between the gross and subtle bodies has been accomplished in this way, there must also be a discrimination of that [Self] from the causal body (kāraṇa-deha); for that purpose, this must be considered: Is the Self that is within all merely the sheath of bliss, or is there a Brahman even more internal than that? Is that alone intended to be the Self within all? Or is there...?

[The opponent argues: "It consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and so forth, and is thus merely conditioned. To this we reply: In that context, unlike the statement "There is another inner self consisting of bliss," there is no teaching of an inner self distinct from this [self]. Furthermore, since the suffix *-maya-* is generally used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), its application here is justified by its function as a negation of that [modification]. Moreover, qualities such as having joy as its head are possible in this [self] even as attributes of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Finally, there is the repetition of words denoting bliss, such as "If this bliss did not exist in the ether" and "What is this investigation of bliss? which occurs in the spring... [etc.].

Just as in the injunction, “One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in spring,” the word *jyotis* (light) is understood to refer to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice because that is what it signifies, so too, one might argue that the repeatedly mentioned *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) should be joined with the status of being the innermost Self (*sarvāntara-ātman*). This is not so. Because Brahman—the support of all, including the *ānandamaya*, and the innermost of all—is taught in the passage, “Brahman is the tail, the foundation,” it is Brahman itself that is intended to be expressed as the primary subject.

Having commenced with the fruit-bearing knowledge of Brahman in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and because it is repeated through such statements as, "Brahman is this, consciousness, infinite" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1), and "He who says 'Brahman exists,' let him say so" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), repetition is indeed a sign of emphasis. For it is said: "Commencement and conclusion, repetition, uniqueness, fruit, eulogy, and reasoning—these six are the means for determining the purport [of a text]."

Furthermore, the word *rahas* (the secret) is primarily applied to Brahman, which is most subtle and changeless; it is not, however, [primarily applied] to the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss). Nor should it be thought that this [Brahman] lacks primacy because of the scriptural statement, "Brahman is the tail, the support," which describes it as a limb of the *ānandamaya*. This is because the status of being a limb, which is understood from the sentence consisting of the two words "tail" and "support," is sublated by the direct denotative power (*śruti*) of the word "Brahman. For direct denotation is more authoritative than syntactical connection (*vākya*).

The repetition of the word "bliss" (ānanda) is also primary in the case of Brahman, which is unsurpassed and changeless; for this is well-established by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" and "He understood Brahman to be bliss. If, however, the Self that is within all were merely the one consisting of bliss, then the citation of the verse, "He becomes non-existent, as it were, if he knows 'it is non-existent'" would be inconsistent.

Likewise, the teaching regarding the act of approaching—as in the passage, "He approaches the Self consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*)—would not be tenable [if the *ānandamaya* were not the innermost Self], because there would be no other entity to be approached. Therefore, it must be understood that Brahman alone is indicated as the innermost Self by way of its preeminence. As for the word "tail" (*puccha*), although it primarily denotes a limb, here it indicates the state of being a substratum. In this way, the rule governing the suffix *-maya*, which generally signifies a modification (*vikāra*), is upheld in the term "*ānandamaya*."

Therefore, it is established that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is also characterized by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just like the self consisting of ether (*ātmatmaka*) and so forth. This has been determined in the *Vyadhikaraṇa* [section] under the heading "The one consisting of bliss, because of repetition" (*ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt*). And that adjunct is a mental modification (*vṛtti*)—consisting of the transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in its sattvic state—which brings about the manifestation of the nature of bliss. That [modification] is divided into many forms according to the distinctions of "pleasure," "delight," and so on. For the unsurpassed bliss is the very nature of the Self.

And that [pleasure] is manifested by the various fluctuations of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) designated as "dear," "delightful," and so forth, which arise from the perception and acquisition of desired sons, wives, wealth, and the like, brought about by the performance of virtuous deeds. When it is thus manifested, the world conventionally designates it as "object-pleasure" (*viṣaya-sukha*). The cognition of its momentariness, however, is produced by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the manifesting factors. Furthermore, such fluctuations cease when their own causes are absent, as occurs during deep sleep and the like.

Thus, it is *avidyā*—a synonym for which is *māyā*, consisting of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) and characterized by impure praise—that, abiding as the cause and possessing such a function, is intended as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the *ānandamaya*. And that bliss (*ānanda*) is manifested in a particular modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*). Accordingly, the commentary of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, who states, "In a pure and tranquil internal organ, there is bliss," must also be explained as having the sense that the cause is essentially *sattva*.

However, for those who explain it otherwise, no distinction would have been made from such ignorance and the like. The meaning is that this *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), characterized by such an adjunct (*upādhi*), is to be understood as being internal to the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness) according to the method previously stated. || 42 ||

This knowledge is indeed the very nature of the Self; therefore, the discernment of the Self is so difficult that even the Sāṃkhya philosophy, though skilled in discrimination, has been exhausted by this very inquiry. Only after fully contemplating the Self does one attain peace.

This doubt can also be removed; for it is only upon its removal that the true nature of the Self will be fully understood. Even the notion of distinguishing the Person from the True Self (Satyamātman) could not have arisen [if this doubt were not present]. Therefore, discrimination (*viveka*) is possible only by means of this [doubt]. In reality, however, it is intended that the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*) is excluded by means of the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) doubt.

The sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa) is that very state of ignorance (avidyā) which, characterized by the predominance of impure sattva, becomes dissolved during states such as deep sleep; it is that which manifests happiness. Thus, the distinctness of the Self from the three bodies has been established. (42) This sheath consisting of food (annamaya-kośa) is filled by the sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya-kośa).

1. By Jaimini (3.3.13), in the section on "Subsidiaries" (*śeṣādhyāya*), the weakness of *vākya* was established relative to *śruti* and *liṅga*; and *vākya* is the co-utterance of two things that desire to be connected, lacking a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that expresses their relationship. 2. [The variants] gha and ḍa read *evamā*. 3. [The variants] ja and ña read *°ttikarma*. 4. From the fivefold treasury, the five synonyms beginning with *ātman* are derived through discrimination alone.

In this regard, the author of the Pañcapādikā [Phaṇīśa] holds that, otherwise, it would have to be understood that [the Self] exists separately from the two bodies alone. Therefore, although the Bhāṣya states, "Even though a particular bliss is attributed to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)," and thus establishes the internal organ itself as the object of meditation here, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage should be explained in this way: 5. "The distinction consisting of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of knowledge, action, and their fruits is removed by the word 'consisting of bliss' (*ānandamaya*); it is spoken of here for the sake of ending [the notion of] the agent. (2.6.10)

Thus says the Vārtika: "The fruit of the knowledge of the *su* (bliss) and other [sheaths] is that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which has that as its objective; the consciousness of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is a reflection of pure consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*), is what is expressed here by the term 'consisting of bliss' (*ānandamaya*). Regarding this, Ānandagiri’s commentary states: "He who is full of the *akāra* syllable is filled by the one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*); likewise, he is naturally full of the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*). (43)
Likewise, this mental self (manomaya-ātman) is indeed always filled by the bliss consisting of knowledge; therefore, those who possess supreme knowledge are ever full in every respect. 44.
Likewise, bliss (ānandamaya) is Brahman itself; it is not perceived by any other witness, but rather Brahman is known directly by itself and not by anything else whatsoever. (45)
If, however, due to ignorance regarding the fourfold nature of the tail, one were to say that the essence is always of such a nature [otherwise], then the gods would indeed be non-existent. || 46 ||

(Thus five sections have been explained. Therein, by means of the internal [sheaths] such as the "instrument of the instrument" (*vādya-vādya-svātra*) and so forth, the *śruti* establishes the fullness; thus it is complete. The text summarizes that with the words, "He is indeed of the form of a person" (*puruṣavidha*), by saying "this one" (*ayam*).)

This golden mountain (meru), which has been conceptually constructed with its various parts—such as the summit, the neck, the interior, and the base—for the sake of ease of comprehension, is filled within by the vital air (prāṇamarut) through such conceptually imagined components; just as a mold-shaped image is completely filled on all sides with molten metal poured into it. The same application [of this analogy] should be understood for what follows as well. 43–44.

"Brahman as other than that": although there is no explicit statement here that "there is another inner Self different from the one consisting of bliss," nevertheless, that Brahman—which is characterized by existence, knowledge, and so forth; which is designated as the substratum of the one consisting of bliss by the words "of that, verily, the tail is the support"; which is the witness of all objects within the five sheaths (kośas) that are merely imagined through Māyā in its own self; and which is the ultimate end—is the one [referred to]. And because the selves beginning with the one consisting of bliss are in a state of identity (*tādātmya*) with that Brahman, they are also [designated as] the Self. Therefore, [the text speaks of] that Brahman which is the substrate of all.

Even that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is filled and pervaded by Brahman in the form of the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*); that is, by Brahman and not by anything else. For Brahman, as described, being devoid of the three kinds of limitations (*pariccheda*)—pertaining to space, time, and substance—is non-dual; thus, it is not pervaded by any other entity whatsoever. The meaning is that it exists having itself completely filled everything. || 45 ||

By this much, that which was indicated by the mantra-verse "It is placed in the secret place"—namely, the fact that Brahman is hidden within the secret—is explained. Thus, the five sheaths beginning with the *annamaya* (consisting of food) have been presented as means for the realization of such Brahman, who is the innermost of all; they are not, however, intended for the purpose of meditative worship (*upāsana*). If it be argued: "But from mantra-passages such as 'Those who worship Brahman [as the *annamaya*],' 'those who worship Prāṇa as Brahman,' and so forth, it is understood that the sheaths beginning with the *annamaya* are auxiliary to meditative worship," we say: not so.

This is because, at the conclusion of that section, [the text] cites [the passage] as a corroboration in order to demonstrate the identity of the breath and so forth with the Self, as established by the scriptural statement beginning with "From this, offspring are born" found in the context of meditation in another Vedic school.

If there were an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), then that [meditation] would be mentioned as an object of meditation even in the world; however, no such injunction for meditation is heard. Therefore, the description of the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) has the purpose of mere instruction and not the purpose of meditation. By analogy with that, the same should be accepted here as well. Otherwise, because of the difference in the subject matter to be established—namely, the nature of the instruction for meditation—there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

"And when there is that unity, it is not stated like that [in separate clauses], according to the maxim: 'When multiple meanings are possible within a single sentence, a split of the sentence (vākya-bheda) is not desired. Thus, having taught Brahman as the ultimate reality, this mantra is cited to dispel the doubt that it might be non-existent because it transcends the mind due to its being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*): "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows here 'it is non-existent'; but if he knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existent. In that context, even though Brahman is non-dual and of the nature of non-existence [in terms of attributes], it must nevertheless be known as existing; this is for the sake of instructing the disciple who has been purified by the removal of ignorance.

O, from the *prāṇamaya* has emerged the *manomaya*, and from that, the *vijñānamaya*; and from the *vijñānamaya* has emerged the *ānandamaya*. (Just as a rope can be said to be filled with a snake because the snake is not distinct from the rope, so too each subsequent sheath is described as being filled by the preceding one.)

This [sheath] is full of bliss, just as the sun is full of light; this is the section concerning the *prāṇamaya* sheath (*vārtika*, Śloka 16). Just as the sun is full of radiance, so too is this [sheath] full of bliss. What is its nature? It is consciousness (*caitanya*) qualified by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of ignorance. Upon this very [consciousness], there occurs the superimposition of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*). This same [consciousness] is full of bliss and consists of knowledge (*vijñānamaya*); this is its nature. Furthermore, upon this [consciousness] qualified by the ego, there occurs the superimposition of the mental qualities (*manodharma*) and the vital functions (*prāṇadharmāḥ*).

This is precisely what is meant by saying that the *manomaya* (consisting of mind) is filled by the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness). Agency (*kartṛtva*) is superimposed (*adhyāsa*) only upon that which is qualified [by consciousness]; therefore, the *manomaya* is contained within the *prāṇamaya*. Furthermore, the body is superimposed upon that which is qualified [by the vital breath], because there arises the cognition: "I am the agent; that very same one is the possessor of the body. Therefore, the *prāṇamaya* is filled by the *annamaya* (consisting of food).
The indication of this section has already been given in this chapter [in verse 13, etc.]. [Brahman] is composed of bliss, distinct from itself, and the witness even of that [self].

1. ña. "O best of gods, [the Vārttikakāra], having stated in [Vākyapadīya 2.1.246]: 'Because of the intense heat [of the fire], for the sake of the ritual act of meditation (*upāsanā*) upon the head and other [limbs] imagined as being beyond [the body], they have declared these mental fires'—does not approve of that meditation. Therefore, having considered this very same impossibility (*anupapatti*) which arises from that, he states another position: that the meditation is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established. Thus, the Śruti restates the meditation already attained by him.

"Just as [the scripture] enjoins the abundance [of results] in the case of names and so forth, it enjoins knowledge within the self. However, that [knowledge] which has not yet attained equality with the supreme reality leads to the fruit of liberation; therefore, having referred back to that, knowledge is now declared for the sake of attaining the Supreme. (2.1.249–50) [Note: *vidhiparasvā''la* refers to the fact that the text is devoted to injunction (*vidhi*).]

O best of gods, having directly attained this very eternal Red One (rakta), the embodied soul becomes happy everywhere; it is not otherwise. O gods, who lives, who dies, and who eternally moves about, when [the Self] has become one with the Infinite and has transcended all names? Therefore, Hara, appearing as the Red One within the consciousness of all beings, gladdens the individual soul (jīvātman) even amidst suffering by the power of his compassion. Thus it comes to be.

Is Brahman non-existent alone, or is it existent alone? Likewise, does one who knows that Brahman attain that all-pervading Brahman, or not? If [it is not attained], then on account of that similarity, would even one who knows not attain that Brahman? Or does he attain it? Does anyone go to this world after departing from here as either a knower or a non-knower? Or does some knower, having departed from this world, go to that other world? Regarding this, there is the scriptural text beginning with, "He desired," and so forth. In that context, since Brahman consists of the nature of essence (*rasa*), its existence has been established therein.

That which is designated by the definition "Brahman" is this very Brahman; because it is always tasted directly and without mediation by yogis through the six flavors beginning with sweet, it is called *rasa* (flavor). || 46 ||

He establishes this very point through the words "etameva" (this very one). For, having directly realized within oneself this very Self—which is one's own, eternal, beginningless and endless, and whose nature is *rasa* (flavor/essence) by way of bliss—one becomes happy in all conditions, whether amidst all evils or even amidst all pleasures. However, when there is an appearance of external, non-eternal flavors such as sweetness and the like, apart from this [Self], happiness is merely momentary. Therefore, because it possesses the nature of *rasa*, the existence of Brahman is established as being of the nature of *rasa*. Thus, the meaning is that its existence is proven through its being *rasa*.

Furthermore, for the sake of establishing that very point, it is heard [in scripture]: "Who indeed could inhale and who could exhale? Who could speak? If bliss did not exist in Ākāśa, this [Ātman] would not be blissful; he alone is blissful. This is summarized as: "In the absence of that [bliss]."

If this Self—which is of the nature of unmanifest space within the bodies of living beings, consisting of supreme bliss, and is self-established—does not exist, then what creature would live? Who would maintain their vital breaths? Or who would constantly perform the functions of breathing and so forth? For without the existence of that [Self], the existence of the body cannot be logically established. Therefore, since the existence of the superimposed body cannot be accounted for otherwise, the existence of its cause, Brahman, must be admitted. This is the meaning. || 48 ||

"Therefore" means: because bliss (*ānanda*) exists in this manner, therefore Brahman—which appears within the heart of all living beings—is designated by the term "rasa" (essence/flavor). Why does it have the nature of bliss? To this he says: "It causes bliss. Because it satisfies the soul, which is overwhelmed by the suffering of worldly existence, according to its own specific merit, for that reason it has the nature of bliss.

For this very reason, it is recited elsewhere: "Of this very Bliss, other beings live on only a fraction. [45] It is not filled by anything else; Brahman alone is entirely within it, and there is nothing outside of it. This is not filled by anything [nor is it superimposed]. [45]

That Brahman which is truth, knowledge, and infinite (ananta), is eternally immediate bliss (aparokṣānanda). Even when these [faculties] do not function due to being drawn toward sense objects, that very bliss remains for the yogis. They remain content even without the provision of the means that normally bestow pleasure; this is possible because they have derived their happiness from that Brahman.

The realm of Brahman bestows happiness only when it itself becomes the embodiment of bliss; therefore, it is certain that the Witness alone is bliss. (46) By directly realizing this eternal bliss, everyone becomes happy, and not otherwise.

(Just as the specific modifications (*vṛtti-viśeṣa*) such as cognition are, in reality, the manifest Self (*vyakta-ātman*), so too the pleasure derived from objects is, in truth, the pleasure of the Self itself. || 47 || Without this supreme bliss, which is the nature of one's own and of all immobile beings, no one can live nor can anything exist.

[The self] acquires existence from that [existence] and thus performs activities such as living. By saying "when it exists," one is not referring to any particular state; rather, such a state is impossible, yet one is establishing this by means of its remaining in all states.

For example, it is said for the sake of illustration: "If space were not, where would the earth remain? The meaning of this is not that we are imagining a state in which the earth's existence would be impossible due to the absence of space; for from the perspective of the illustration, since space is eternal, its non-existence cannot even be conceived. Rather, the meaning is that the earth exists within space, and only there.

May you accept this offering of my own mind (verse 48). Therefore, Śiva—who is the very form of bliss manifest within the minds of all living beings—out of his grace makes the living soul happy amidst the suffering of saṃsāra (verse 49). When one hears of this Śiva, whose nature is immovable and so forth...
[728] *Brahmabindūpaniṣad*.

O best of gods, when this person perceives within this very [self] that non-dual oneness characterized by truth and the like, then, O dwellers of heaven, he attains the supreme Brahman—which is his own self, absolute fearlessness, ultimate auspiciousness, and the highest nectar. (50–51) When a man perceives even the slightest difference regarding this, O gods, then for him there shall be rebirth; of this there is no doubt. That Brahman, which is the self of all and is characterized by truth and other such qualities—(52)

The most excellent archers remain indifferent toward one who does not stretch his bow; likewise, O gods, for those whose sole devotion is to *saṃbhastāna*, that very state is the supreme goal, appearing as pure bliss through its own nature (53–54). O best of gods, even for one who has studied the Vedas, that same [state] becomes a cause of fear at that time if it is devoid of reflection (55).

The existence of Brahman is also established in the Śruti by its being the cause of fear: "When he finds no support in this invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and unsupported [Brahman], then he becomes afraid. But when he finds support in it, then he becomes free from fear. When, however, he perceives therein even a slight difference..."

Then, the thought occurs to him: "It exists. He summarizes this with the words "When... and so forth. By the word "adi" (and so forth) in the phrase "invisibility and so forth," there is an inclusion of the qualities mentioned in the scriptures, such as subtlety and the rest. Indeed, when [the meditator] is in this form of Brahman—of what form? Invisible, meaning devoid of the manifest phenomenal world (*prapañca*); "without the gross" (*anālpa*), meaning devoid of the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*), which is called "gross" because it belongs to the self; "undefined" (*anirukta*), meaning devoid of that which is defined as the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), since even though it is subtle, it is nevertheless defined because it is composed of the subtle elements.

For it is heard in scripture: "Neither activity nor instrument is found for him. "In the non-abode" means that which is devoid of the abode—that is, the causal body consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the like, in which the manifold world of effects and forms is established. It is devoid of that.

When Brahman has become thus—devoid of division, free from the illusion of "I" and "another," devoid of distinction, and the ultimate reality beyond all parts—the seeker attains and acquires it through the means of hearing, reflection, and so forth; at that very moment, in that very state, he becomes fearless, because the cause of fear, namely division, has ceased. For division is indeed the cause of fear, as the Śruti says: "From a second [entity], verily, fear arises."

Through the knowledge of the identity of the Self with that Supreme Brahman—which is supremely beautiful because it consists of unsurpassed, changeless bliss; which is the highest and most excellent nectar, never subject to destruction, and is eternal like Mount Meru—he attains it. || 58 || 51 ||

Indeed, when one perceives even a slight internal difference or distinction within this Self during the moment of its realization—thinking "I am one, He is another; I am the transmigrating soul, He is the immortal Brahman"—then, for such a person who sees duality, that Brahman becomes an object of fear and a cause of bondage; this is the meaning. || 52 ||

Since Brahman exists everywhere as the Self and because its manifestation is impossible for one who perceives duality, why would it not be perceived even by those who see difference? To this, he says: "Of all. For all people—both those who perceive difference and those who perceive non-difference—that Brahman characterized by truth and so forth, which is perceived as the Self within the heart, remains indifferent toward the ignorant person. Brahman is indeed indifferent toward those who are ineligible [for inquiry], meaning that it does not manifest itself to them because they are averse to the inquiry into Brahman. || 53 ||

For those who are established in steadfastness, whose desires have ceased, who are free from pride, who have realized the oneness of all, who are devoid of doubt, and who abide solely in the knowledge of the Self—that supreme, most excellent state, which transcends both Māyā and its effects, is that very Brahman alone; it shines forth and becomes manifest through one's own essential nature at the moment of direct realization. Therefore, it is declared elsewhere in the scripture: "This Self is not attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much learning.
Only he whom this Self chooses, by him is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3) || 54 ||

However, it is declared in scripture that for one who, despite being qualified for the truth, does not directly perceive the pillar of reality through the means of reflection (*manana*) and so forth, Brahman becomes a cause of fear because his intellect is impaired: "From that very [Brahman] there is fear for the one who knows but does not reflect. This is summarized as "from that" (*tataḥ*). The meaning is that this very Brahman becomes a cause of fear for one who, even though he has studied the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-veda*), fails to perform the reflection necessary for the direct realization of Brahman. || 55 ||

When this *jīva* realizes its own non-difference from Śiva—that is, when it attains actual oneness—it then reaches the Brahman, which is the supreme nectar-food (*amṛtasūpa*), utterly fearless, auspicious, and most excellent; [and that Brahman is one's very own Self]. 50-51. But when this *jīva* considers itself even slightly different from that Brahman, only then does birth (*bhava*) occur for it, and indeed, death (*kha*) occurs. 52. Although Brahman is everything... 54.
Nevertheless, He does not remain indifferent toward those who possess the vision of duality; He does not manifest as the blissful Self [to them]. (Just like a person born in that state...)

At all times, whatever kind of distinction one perceives through one's vision, that very same nature remains as the object of perception for that individual. Even the Supreme Brahman’s state of indifference is, in reality, our own indifference toward Him. (53) For those who remain established solely in perfect knowledge, that Śiva appears in the form of their own inner self; in this matter, His grace alone is the cause. (54)

Even one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) does not become free from the cause of worldly existence (*bhava*) if he does not practice reflection (*manana*) for the sake of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman; indeed, it is that very Brahman which, when viewed through the lens of dualistic perception (*bhedadṛṣṭi*), becomes the producer of worldly existence. (1) [It is Śiva himself who, when seen through the vision of duality, is the generator of *bhava*.]

It has been observed that the very same person who was the cause of fear for a virtuous wife (*satī*) prior to marriage becomes the cause of her death immediately after the wedding. The reason for this is as follows: previously, she viewed him with a sense of difference (*bheda-dṛṣṭi*), and therefore she was afraid of him; afterwards, however, she views him with a sense of non-difference (*abheda-dṛṣṭi*), and thus there is no occasion for fear. This is how the present context should be understood.

1. *Kaja*. Śiṇa. 2. There is not even a moment’s difference between knowledge (*jñāna*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). In such statements as "the cessation of ignorance occurs from knowledge," the ablative case is used in the sense of an instrumental cause (*prayojaka-pañcamī*). Therefore, when there is knowledge, at that very moment there is the destruction of ignorance; at that very moment, the Self (*ātman*), being free from that [ignorance], is liberated. This should be understood here in the same way as when, immediately after the realization "I am the ten-faced one" (*daśamukho'ham*), there is no delay of even a single moment before the attainment of the fruit. 2. Ḍa. *Kalāhiṣa*.
Chapter—3. 729.

Out of fear of Him the wind blows, out of fear the sun rises; out of fear of Him Agni and Indra, and the fifth, Death, run forth. (96) Even those beginning with Viṣṇu and ending with the post, when they attain supreme bliss, become happy according to the gradation of their respective degrees. (97) The bliss that belongs to one who has renounced those various stations, who is learned in the Vedas, and who is free from pride, shines forth in its true form within his own state. (98) This very bliss is indeed Brahman, and it likewise resides in the heart of the Sun. (99)

And it shines forth of its own accord as the witness within the hearts of others as well. (59) Having stated that Brahman is the cause of fear, he cites another scriptural passage to demonstrate this: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear of Him the sun rises; out of fear of Him Agni, Indra, and Death, as the fifth, run on. He summarizes that here with the word "bhīṣā" (out of fear).

The sense is this: if even the gods—who possess great power and are appointed to carry out the worldly transactions of the entire universe, such as wind and the rest—have Brahman as a cause of fear, what need is there to mention that it is a cause of fear for other living beings? (56) Thus, the existence of Brahman is established by its being both the cause of fear and the cause of fearlessness. [As it is said: "If this bliss did not exist... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).

Regarding the statement, "For this very reason, he is blissful," the Śruti—beginning with "Now follows the inquiry into that bliss" and ending with "That is one measure of the bliss of Brahman"—establishes a continuous flow of bliss, increasing a hundredfold at each successive stage from the sovereign of the whole earth up to Hiraṇyagarbha, in order to substantiate the existence of Brahman by demonstrating its nature as bliss.

He summarizes this with the words "of that very [bliss]": the meaning is that all embodied beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, derive their happiness by attaining a portion of this very unsurpassed bliss which constitutes the nature of Brahman; for they exist in a state of relative gradation—ranging from greater to lesser—due to the contraction of the bliss of their own true nature caused by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that manifest it. || 57 ||

Having introduced the progressive attenuation of bliss beginning with that of the sovereign of the whole earth and so forth in various places in the Śruti, it is stated in those very places: "of one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire. He summarizes the intended meaning of that [passage] with the words "tattad" (that respective...).

Having thoroughly understood that all states, from those of a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) upwards, are impermanent because they possess degrees of excellence relative to one another, the seeker becomes detached. Having abandoned the threefold desire (*eṣaṇā-traya*) and performed the entire collection of means for realization—such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and so forth—the learned knower of Brahman hears of his own nature as the undivided, supreme bliss. Consequently, all worldly bliss, which consists of mere fragments of that [supreme bliss] and exists in varying degrees through distinctions such as that of a universal monarch, is realized by that wise one as being his very own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The meaning is that, just as the expansion of bliss is perceived by universal monarchs and others who are established in that very reality, so too does such bliss manifest for the knower (*vidvān*) spontaneously, without depending on any other means. || 58 ||

By this [passage], it is shown that the various gradations of bliss—beginning with that of the sovereign of the whole earth (*sārvabhauma*) and culminating in that of *Hiraṇyagarbha*—which have been sought after in a state of relative progression like the increasing waves of the ocean, reach a point where they become inexpressible; thus, because there is no further limit to its division, Brahman will exist as the nature of unsurpassed bliss. To establish this, the Scripture dispels the delusion of difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) with the words: "That which is in the person and that which is in the sun, that is one. This is summarized as: "He alone indeed."

This very Supreme Self—which has been described as the cause of ether and so forth, which is being meditated upon by the wise as the nature of the *svarasvaram*, and whose form is unsurpassed bliss—is indeed within the heart of the Sun. For the Śruti declares: "Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sun, divided himself threefold: the Sun as one third, and Vāyu as one third. Thus, He resides in the heart of Hiraṇyagarbha, the first embodied being, conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Māyā, which consists primarily of pure Sattva.

The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) indicates the absence of any intervention; the meaning is that the Lord appears as omniscient because His knowledge is unobstructed. Likewise, this very same [Lord] appears in the hearts of other individual souls (*jīvas*), within the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), as one possessing limited knowledge due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) dominated by impure *sattva*, appearing as the witness (*sākṣin*) to the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). || 59 ||

Out of fear of this Supreme Brahman, the wind blows, the sun rises, and fire, Indra, and Death all perform their respective duties regularly; for they all stand in awe of this Mahādeva. Even by a tiny fraction of the bliss that constitutes His very nature, all living beings, from Viṣṇu down to the smallest insect, find happiness.

Just as we have the conventional usage of "space" being large or small based on a single part of that partless space—such as the space within a jar or a hut—likewise, one obtains all bliss from a single part of partless bliss, namely, the bliss manifested through a mental modification (*vṛtti*).

Just as objects like jars appear large or small depending on their size, so too do all people experience varying degrees of happiness according to the excellence or inferiority of the means that manifest that bliss. || 57 ||

Even one who is detached from various states such as those of the gods becomes tranquil through the realization of Brahman; that bliss, which is his own essential nature, shines forth for him just as it does for the person established in that state.

(Although worldly happiness appears as pleasure only to one who is seated on a throne and intoxicated by sense objects, whereas the knower of Brahman experiences boundless, independent bliss—nevertheless, because the intention here is to establish that the state of liberation is superior to all joys by understanding its nature through illustrative examples, it is said as follows:)

When water has overflowed everywhere, one might raise this doubt: since the use of water for drinking is impossible when "water has overflowed everywhere" (*sarvataḥ samplutodaka*), the purpose of a well (*udapāna*) still remains there; however, according to the intended meaning of the original text, the consistency of the illustration cannot be reconciled, and it should be understood in the same way here as well. (58)
