Having abandoned, through discernment, everything from the body up to Māyā along with its desires, he who realizes the Self as the witness of all—that one truly transcends. || 90 || He who realizes the witness of the "I" (the ego) and so forth, down to the pillar [of the universe], by means of both reasoning and valid cognition (*tarka* and *pramāṇa*)—that one truly transcends. || 91 || Those wise ones who, through such reasoning and valid cognition, have thus realized the Truth, distinguish the Self from this world of suffering by means of the Self. || 92 || [The Self] is illumined by the light of the non-dual, stainless, and pure consciousness.

He approached [the Lord] out of pure faith alone. (62) "O Vāyu, since [all] causes cease to exist due to the absence of any objective basis, how can sound persist in the undifferentiated Śiva? O gods, how does it remain? (63) Thus, he explains the manner in which the identity of these two—the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—which are distinct in their manifested states, is realized: "By means of *māyā*," etc. Here, *māyā* refers to *prakṛti*, which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. It serves as the common substrate for the two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul and the Lord mentioned above.

By the word *atara-tacchabda* (the word "that" which crosses over), the state of being both is intended to be expressed. Thus, having discerned that in both cases [the individual soul and the Supreme] there exists the Self—which is the cause of both, yet characterized by contradictory attributes such as omniscience and limited knowledge, and is therefore non-Self due to its possession of qualities (*sāśrayatva*)—and having abandoned that [non-Self], he who meditates upon the Self as "one alone" through such unity, he indeed becomes Rudra, Nārāyaṇa, and the others. For they are specific manifestations of the Supreme Being, assuming various forms such as those of Kṛṣṇa; and as such, they are, according to the aforementioned method, pure Consciousness (*cinmātra*), acting as witnesses for those [manifestations] and for other living beings (*jīvas*).

And by the power of the mantra, that very knower of Brahman rushes forth. By this, through the removal of the limitations imposed by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the Lord of the world, it is established that the Supreme Reality—whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss—is unlimited, infinite, and consists of the single essence of immeasurable bliss.

Although this [passage] should have been recited at the end—since it is an explanatory commentary on the portion of the mantra, "all desires," which establishes the intended meaning of the subsequent words of the Sūtra—it must nevertheless be understood as having been recited here in the middle for the purpose of supporting the reasoning presented in the statement, "If this Bliss did not exist... Thus, by establishing the existence of Brahman—which is non-dual, characterized by supreme bliss, immutable, and of the single essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss—the doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist has been refuted. || 61 ||

To the objection that even a learned person may not attain [this state], the scripture provides the answer beginning with "He who, knowing thus... and ending with "...he approaches this Self consisting of bliss. He summarizes its meaning as follows: "For one who [knows] thus..."

Indeed, that wise person who possesses the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman, characterized by unsurpassed bliss, in the manner described above—he, being a knower of Brahman, having discerned and distinguished himself from this entire world—which consists of the aggregate of effects and causes seen through the vision of the Seer—and having become free from fear, again relies upon his own inner Self, the Prāṇa, and knowing the unreality of the external world illuminated by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), [he attains liberation].

The practitioner attains that Brahman—which is more internal than even the five sheaths beginning with the physical body, which is the substratum for the conceptualization of the entire universe, and whose singular essence is Being-Consciousness-Bliss Infinite—and which is designated as the support of all in the words, "Brahman is the tail, the foundation"—by the grace of the Supreme Lord who has been propitiated by the offerings of food and other rites performed with the intention of dedicating them to Paraśiva; thus, upon the dawning of knowledge, the cause of duality, namely ignorance, [is destroyed].

The meaning is that, although Brahman is eternally attained due to its omnipresence, one attains it once again—upon the cessation of the delusion of difference caused by ignorance—just as one finds a necklace of gold already around one's own neck. Thus, since it is established that only the knower attains [Brahman], it should be understood that the question of whether or not even a non-knower attains Brahman is also refuted. || 62 || 63 ||

Thus, by demonstrating that Brahman is attained through mere knowledge, the portion of the mantra, "He who knows it attains [it]" (*yo veda so'śnute*), which serves as an explanation of the aphorism "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]," becomes elucidated. Having established this point—that the attainment of Brahman, which is non-dual, supreme bliss, bliss beyond compare, and fearless, is accomplished through knowledge alone—the Śruti cites a certain mantra for corroboration. It is handed down as follows: "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it... (*yato vāco nivartante, aprāpya manasā saha*).

"He who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere"—this [scriptural passage] is summarized by the words "from which. The meaning is that because of Brahman—characterized as described above and absolutely free from conceptual differentiation (nirvikalpaka)—words turn back, being incapable of denoting it. Why is this so? To this he says: "of the grounds for application" (*nimittānām*). The grounds for the application of words are genus (*jāti*) and so forth; the meaning is that these grounds for application do not exist in Brahman.

He establishes this very point: "It is devoid of defects. For, by such scriptural passages as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short... and so forth, Brahman is understood to be free from defects. Therefore, how could a word function through its primary denotative power (*abhidhāvṛtti*) toward that which is devoid of all attributes such as genus (*jāti*) and the like? The meaning is that it is simply not possible for it to function [in that way]. || 64 || What is the consistency here? There is much inconsistency. || 60 ||

That which is designated by the conventional term *samañña*—namely, that Śiva alone is the witness of all beings, including gods such as Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa—is indeed the possessor of *samañña*, based upon reasoning (*tarka*) and valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). || 61 ||

One who has experienced this through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—that is, one whose discriminative intellect (*vivekabuddhi*) has realized the Self as distinct from this entire transmigratory world (the aggregate of the body and so forth, which is considered non-self)—having discarded everything from the *annamaya* sheath onwards, all of which appear only as reflections of the Self, abides solely in the form of Śiva. This occurs only through the grace of Śiva. || 62 ||

Because it lacks the grounds for linguistic application (*pravṛttinimitta*) such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, the word is unable to denote it; it is as if the word stammers and fails to become a signifier. It is certain that this Śiva, who is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), is not the object of words through the operation of their power (*śakti*). In the *Tattvaviveka*, he [the author] stated: "1. That very [Śiva], when characterized by the predominance of the manifestation of pure categories (*śuddhatattva*), is the adjunct (*upādhi*) of Īśvara; 2. when characterized by the predominance of the manifestation of impure categories (*aśuddhatattva*), it is the adjunct of the individual soul (*jīva*)" (vv. 15–17). [Note: 1. *śuddhādi-pañca* refers to the five pure categories.]

Chapter 3 Poison exists by depending upon something else; therefore, this [Self] is considered to be like poison, yet its range is everywhere. (65) Furthermore, O best of men, since the skin, nails, and other such parts, as well as the organs of action and so forth, are pervaded by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they are indeed like poison. (66) But having known through his own nature that Brahman is the eternal, stainless, and true knowledge, he does not enter into anything anywhere. (67)

"Is there no fault in this? [The answer is: In common worldly usage, a word proceeds only by taking up the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which reside in the denotable object (*abhidheya*), as its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Therefore, the meaning is that the application of the word "lotus" (*padma*) to a gem is not stated [as being based on such a ground]. *Sūkṣmam* means "subtle," that which grasps the subtle meaning. Because it acts as a concomitant for all the senses, even the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which perceives all objects, [is included] along with its own functions.

Because it is excluded from—that is, turned away from—the non-conceptual Brahman; for surely that [Brahman], being devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and transcending speech and mind, is not an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of a positive entity.

Would it not be the case here that [the scripture] would be like a mere sprout (*śuṅga*)? This is not a fault, because it possesses the capacity to protect even that which is not yet fully developed. For instance, through the presentation of established truths derived from the knowledge of the Self, the scripture teaches Brahman—which is free from the aforementioned defects—by means of definition (*lakṣaṇā*) in a positive manner; furthermore, by means of the exclusion of all superimpositions, it expresses the distinction from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) through the negation of its difference, thereby defining its nature as being distinct from that difference.

Nor should it be said that, because such a Vedic sentence possesses the quality of being an indicator (*jñāpaka*) and takes the form of an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate in the injunction; for if one were to accept figurative indication in the injunction by abandoning the specific denoted meaning, there would arise doubt due to the multiplicity and lack of restriction of possible meanings. It is with this intention that it is stated that figurative indication is not to be accepted in the injunction.

However, where doubt is dispelled by another means, there figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) does not constitute a fault even in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*). For example: "One should sacrifice with the *ūrjā-dhāman* [verse]. In this way, since there is no doubt regarding multiplicity—because all other [verses] are excluded by the injunction and because they are grasped collectively as being free from any limiting condition (*upādhi*)—[the figurative sense is accepted].

Brahman, while being made manifest through the act of creation, possesses adjuncts (*sopādhika*); yet it does not follow that it is unreal (*avastutva*), because the adjunct, serving merely as a limiting condition (*uparāga*), does not enter into the category of the actual object itself. Thus, even the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the sentence "That art Thou" has Brahman as its object, but as delimited by the exclusion of the adjuncts. This modification, by means of the analogy of the clearing-nut powder (*katakaraja*) in water, removes both the delimiting exclusion and its own self. It is with this very intention that the scripture declares: "This [Self] is to be realized solely through the mind."

Thus, by the manner described above, it is established that the Self—which is devoid of contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and from which all adjuncts have vanished—is infinite, free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), and transcends speech and mind. (65) Regarding the phrase "having external objects as their domain": "external things" (*parāgvastu*) refers to those things such as sound and so forth, which are designated by the word "this" (*idaṃkārāspada*). Those [cognitions] which have these as their objects are so described. And thus it is recited in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "The senses turned outward, he ran away, seeking for the world. (66)

Thus, that Brahman which transcends speech and mind is indeed non-dual, free from heat and free from the distress of the world; for this very reason, it is the sole abode of bliss for all living beings. Having known it as one's own self-nature—surely, how can such knowledge be possible, since it is not an object of the intellect? This is no fault.

For it has been established that [the Self] is capable of being determined by a mind that, through non-proximity, takes as its object that which transcends the body and its attributes (*vyatirikta-avacira*). Thus, one who knows and remains established in the state of bliss—which is free from the manifestation of even the second-order negation—has no fear whatsoever, because there exists no second entity distinct from oneself that could serve as a cause for fear. The word "ca" (and) is used here in the sense of certainty. || 67 || This indicates that whatever specific quality there may be...

(Who could possibly surpass You? No; therefore, You cannot be described through verbal testimony or through the power of [inference]. Even the mind—which reconciles all things and grasps even subtle meanings—cannot make You its object. Nor can the senses of hearing, touch, sight, and so forth, nor the organs of action, for they are directed toward external objects (those that have "this-ness" as their locus).

I alone possess the capacity for comprehension; that Brahman is of the nature of bliss, non-dual, free from sorrow, eternal, and a mass of consciousness. Therefore, like one who has crossed over a river, the knower of Brahman has no fear of anything whatsoever. (65–67) Having heard this desired matter from the instruction of his own guru, he remained composed.

1.3.4. [Adhikaraṇa] 12. Regarding the connection with the *upasadbh* rites, it is known: "The *artha-tvadi* (one who speaks of the purpose) is excluded from the group. In this regard, there is a doubt as to whether the *antar-vedi* (within the altar) is enjoined by way of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), or whether it is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) associated with the *vivadi* (the one who speaks of the non-purpose), such that it excludes the other. Since a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is inappropriate in a primary injunction (*vidhi*), the first alternative—that it is a restrictive rule—is obtained. However, if that were the case, both "half within the altar" and "half outside the altar" would have to be enjoined; and thus, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, the region [of meaning] is understood; since there is the establishment of a single object within that suchness (*tathatva*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is the conclusion established in the third chapter, first section, fourteenth sūtra (*tṛtīya-santame* 6.1.14). Likewise here as well, although there is a syntactical split in the establishment of multiple attributes such as existence (*satyatva*) and so forth, there is no such split when the number of existents (*satvādi-saṃkhyā*) is indicated by the words through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a single individual (*ekavyakti*). Thus, even in the case of the *piṣṭa* [sacrificial cake], the propriety of the hearing is the intended meaning. "It is so" means that very thing is known (*prasiddha*). *Note: The text contains several scribal corruptions and archaic notations (e.g., *tasmād‌*, *deśo*, *tathatva*, *nirmatim*, *piṣve'pi*, *ṭaśṇaucityam*). Thus, when one understands this through the instruction of one's own guru, the Lord never again causes pain to that person who has performed the work of purification. The following has been declared in the Upanishads: "This indeed does not afflict him: 'Why did I not do good? Why did I commit evil? He summarizes its meaning with the word "evam" (thus). One who knows the Self according to the aforementioned method and through the instruction of a Guru—that person, having become Brahman, is not afflicted by unperformed good deeds or by performed evil deeds; this is the sense. For, due to the cessation of primal ignorance (*avidyā*), the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—which consists of action, agents, and results—is also sublated. Indeed, it is the ignorant person who...

In the state of being a human, one who has not performed auspicious deeds such as sacrifice and charity fears those two—the attainment of hell resulting from his own past sins and the attainment of the fruit of suffering resulting from those very sins—by contemplating them with the mind. However, the knower (jñānī) does not suffer because, due to the burning away of the accumulation of karma that brings about future births by the fire of knowledge, there is an absence of future birth; this is the meaning. || 68 ||

He states the meaning of the sentence, "He who knows thus protects these two selves," with the words *tapyatāpaka* (the sufferer and the causer of suffering). The *tapyat* (sufferer) is the world of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-prapañca*), which is the object of the act of suffering; the *tāpakāni* (causers of suffering) are merit and demerit (*puṇya-apuṇya*). Although the entire world exists in this twofold manner, for one who possesses the knowledge of the non-duality of Brahman as the sole reality, it shines forth only as the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*); it does not appear as anything distinct from that [Self]. Therefore, how could he suffer? || 69 ||

This is not said too briefly; for he states [in verses 70–105] with the words "the agent," etc., that the entire phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), characterized by action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), appears to him as nothing other than his own self-nature.

He does not take knowledge of whether this was done well or poorly through karma—[meaning, the knowledge of "why did I not do it well? or "why did I do it so? does not arise in the Jñānī]. For he has already realized that nothing at all has been done. || 68 ||

This essence of saṃsāra, consisting of two forms—the portion of action (*karmabhāga*), as well as the fruit of action and the portion connected to that fruit—is perceived solely as the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) through the knowledge arising from the great Vedāntic statements (*mahāvākya*). (Therefore, there remains no doubt whatsoever regarding the other [the Supreme Self]. || 69 || By the grace of the Supreme Lord, the agent, the instigator, the goal to be attained, the means, the ritual action, and so forth—all appear as nothing but the form of the Self. || 70 ||

Indeed, all these appear solely as the nature of the Self: the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and knowledge itself; the qualified person, the injunction, the means of accomplishment, and the one who issues the injunction; the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, the act of enjoying, and the instruments of enjoyment; the grasper, the grasped object, and the grasping of every object; as well as erroneous cognition, ignorance, and discriminative knowledge.

The cognition of a jar, the cognition of a cloth, the cognition of a wall and so forth; [the objects] such as a jar, a wall, a house, cloth, a vessel, and a mountain; the lower worlds such as Pātāla and the upper worlds such as Satya; this and hundreds of millions of other accepted universes (*brahmāṇḍa*); oceans, ponds, rivers, and all streams (except for the Narmadā, which has a circumference of...); mountains. (Note: The fragmentary text regarding the Narmadā appears to be incomplete.)

(93) He is Śiva, and all these are His manifestations; everything shines as the Self, through the grace of the Lord who is the beginning and the end. (94) The cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, the sky, and the entire circle of the earth—[all shine as the Self]. (95)

Everything shines as the Self, for everything arises from the Lord Ātmeśvara. (96) Vāmadeva, Karṣaṇa, Śatamanyu, and Anirukta—everything shines as the Self, for everything arises from the Lord Ātmeśvara. (97) Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, and Vāmana—all these likewise shine forth by His grace, arising from the Lord Ātmeśvara. (98) The stages of life (āśramas), the castes (varṇas), and various other things as well—all shine as the Self, for everything arises from the Lord Ātmeśvara. (99)

The prohibited and the unprohibited, prohibitions and injunctions as well—all shine as the Self by the grace of that Supreme Lord. (100) The body, the senses, the vital breaths, the mind, the intellect, and the ego—all shine as the Self by the grace of that Supreme Lord. (101) Desire, anger, and all others, as well as delusion and the rest—all shine as the Self by the grace of that Supreme Lord. (102) The individual self and the supreme self, their difference and the differentiator—all shine as the Self by the grace of that Supreme Lord. (103)

The rivers flowing toward the ocean, known as *nada* and *kahāvatī* within this world of transmigration (*saṃsṛti*); the mountains such as Maru and Mandāra; forests, regions abundant with forests, and wild animals; various types of grass—large, medium, and small; the great elements such as space (*ākāśa*) and all material objects; the entire host of beings in the form of subtle elements (*tanmātra*), such as sound and touch; worms, insects, moths, and other small creatures; birds, deer, snakes, and those born from sinful wombs.

Humans, elephants, horses, camels, and donkeys; Vidyādharas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Kiṃnaras, and so forth; Kāmadeva, Devas, Devarājas, Virāṭs, and Svarāṭs; Brahmā, my own majesty, and my embodied devotees; Viṣṇu, his majesty, and his devotees; Rudra, his majesty, and his devotees; Īśvara and his manifestations (vibhūti); and he who is named Sadāśiva. (Note: 9. ḍa. ca. gha. read *snamātrā*.)

734. Although the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) is divided into hundreds of distinctions such as *drahā*, *amitā*, and *jadatī-parā*, it shines as everything through its identity with the Supreme Lord (*Īśvara*), by virtue of being the primordial subject (*grahītṛ*). 735. Even objects that are unmanifest, unperceived, non-existent, or beyond expression shine as everything through their identity with the Supreme Lord, by virtue of being the primordial subject. 736. That which always shines by itself through its own nature is indeed called the Self (*ātman*); yet living beings perceive that very same [Self] through the two words "thou" (*tvam*) and "I" (*aham*).

Those who perceive it as a mere wheel do not know it in its true sense; and those who know it in its true sense do not perceive it as a wheel. Therefore, know this Veda to be eternally stable by its own nature. He remains here naturally, eternally singing this meaning. Just as the dancing of Śiva is for the protection of the world by his very nature, so too this song called "The Play" (Vinoda) is for the benefit of the world.

If all this world is perceived by the knower as being of the nature of the Self, then one might suspect that the Self is easily accessible; to this, it is said: "The Self comes to me. Since it manifests by itself without dependence on any other means, that which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is indeed the Self. However, its true nature is difficult to realize. Now, if the Self is self-luminous in this way, does it manifest equally to both the wise and the ignorant? It is not so; for while the ignorant perceive it through the mental modification (*manovṛtti) directed toward its object—arising from the identification with the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the like—they do not know it as it truly is.

The Knower does not at all perceive that which is non-dual, whose limiting adjuncts such as conflict and attachment have been cast aside, and whose nature is pure consciousness alone; for perception depends upon distinctions such as the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth. (106–107)

He brings about [the realization] through wealth—this is the introduction with the words "so 'yam" (this is that). The meaning is: "Alas! Alas! This world, which was previously occupied by me as the very form of enjoyer and enjoyment, now remains undisturbed because I alone am devoid of the cause for pride, being free from the conceit of 'I'. || 108 ||

He illustrates this with the following example: "Just as... (109). Śiva and his manifestations; the quarters of the sky along with the clouds; the circle of the best of men—Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha; the [incarnations] such as the Fish, Tortoise, Boar, Man-lion, and Dwarf, as well as their devotees; the stages of life (āśramas) such as the householder and others; the social classes (varṇas) such as the Brāhmaṇa and others; and various mixed castes (saṅkara-jātis).

The prohibited and the unprohibited, the negative injunction and the positive injunction; the body of another, the self, the vital breaths, the mind, the intellect, and the ego; evil qualities such as desire and anger, and virtuous qualities such as peace; the individual soul and the Supreme Soul—their difference and non-difference; the insentient power and all its divisions, the sentient power and its divisions: what more need be said? All these are known through this single verse. Indeed, whatever objects are known are realized as being of the nature of the Self through the creative power of the Supreme Lord. (71–105)

The term *ātman* refers to that which always shines by its own nature as the light of knowledge. Although it is distinct from the objects of knowledge such as "this," "you," "I," and so forth, we nevertheless engage in linguistic and cognitive transactions regarding that *ātman* by designating it as "this" and as consisting of consciousness, even though it is devoid of all such attributes.

For there is no one at all who truly knows the Self as being non-dual. (Even when one speaks of "knowing the Self," it is merely a conventional usage; there is no reality [to such knowledge]. In truth, one can only know someone when the knower is distinct from that which is known. Since this is the actual state of affairs, knowing the Self in the ultimate sense is impossible.)

All stages of spiritual practice, beginning with *vraṣāna*, are indeed this very ground; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither "one who remains" nor "the knower of Brahman" (Maṇi 5). || 106 || The person who, through the aforementioned process, realizes the Self as it truly is by means of direct experience—he, being a knower of his own nature, remains forever singing the praises of the Infinite Lord. || 108 ||

Just as Mahādeva’s dance (*āṇandataṇḍava*) is for the purpose of protecting the world, so too this song, which manifests joy born of realization, benefits all beings (by inspiring faith in knowledge and thereby acting as a benefactor). (109)

1. It should be understood that "removal of transformation" (*vikāra-vinoda*) means cessation. 2. And "obscuration-knowledge" (*āvaraṇājñāna*) refers to the state of being covered. 3. The very non-cessation of ignorance is the meaning of the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*); for there is no purpose in postulating anything other than that, as such a hypothesis would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Thus, even in the case of the Veda, the cessation of the ignorance regarding Brahman is the intended meaning; therefore, all is consistent. Chapter 3, Verse 735.

Just as the song of Ādi-Gaurī is for the benefit of the worlds, so too is the song of this Gaurī for the desire of the welfare of the world. (996) The song of the Lord, whose desires are fulfilled, is characterized by the seven musical scales (*svara*); likewise, the song of this virtuous lady is for the sake of helping others. (997) If the Lord shows favor even toward worldly songs, how much more so toward Vedic songs? Therefore, one should take refuge in that [Vedic] song. (998) Even if one is unable to sing it, one should do so with devotion directed toward Śiva. (999)

Or, if one sings even a worldly song without weariness, the knowledge of singing would become a cause for attaining Śiva, the Lord of Gaurī. Through this knowledge of singing, there may arise a union with Him alone, as it were, in an instant. (993) If one who knows singing does not reach the Supreme Lord through yoga, he shall nevertheless become an attendant [of the Lord] due to the destruction of his obstacles. (115) A twice-born man should never perform even a worldly journey out of negligence; if he should become intoxicated by pride, he will fall. (999)

Therefore, one who is intent on destroying the cycle of rebirth through the authority of the Vedas and the path of logic, having attained awakening, should always protect this earth as the son of Śiva. Thus has been declared to you the Upaniṣad, which concerns the reality of the Supreme Truth, which destroys all suffering, and which indeed bestows liberation upon the wise man who seeks his own welfare. 117–118.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Witness-Self," in the *Brahma-gītā* within the latter portion of the fourth section, the *Yajña-vaibhava-khaṇḍa*, of the *Sūta-saṃhitā* in the glorious *Skanda Purāṇa*.

Just as the dance of the Supreme Lord is for the protection of the world, so too is the knowledge of Brahman; thus, having established that it is a means for attaining the supreme reality, he explains this by means of an analogy: "As [the dance] of the Supreme Lord. (1) [This refers to] the Supreme Lord.

The genitive case is used in the sense of the agent; thus, it is a song whose author is he. It is well known that this was composed by the venerable Veṅkaṭanātha as an exposition of the principles of Bharata. By teaching this song, which benefits the world, his own liberation is also rendered meaningful through the grace bestowed upon the universe by the manifestation of the supreme reality. || 518 || 111 || Now, one might object that such instruction is established even from other sentences, and therefore it is improper to claim exclusive authorship; to this, he replies: "In worldly matters... || 152 ||

"Regarding the *vyākhyāgāna*s": the *vyākhyāgāna* consists of prose and verse composed in the refined (*saṃskṛta*) language. The worldly conduct regarding the various local dialects is the discourse concerning the Lord Paramēśvara. (Verses 113–118). "The *śruti* is the *upaniṣad*" (verse 117). This summarizes that which is the contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). By this, the *upaniṣad* has been taught as the means for attaining the supreme reality (*paratattva*). The *upaniṣad* belongs to the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*).

The Upaniṣads bring forth Brahman as the inward tethering-post (pratyagālāna) devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and thereby remove the ignorance (avidyā) that is the cause of the delusion of difference; thus it is said by those who have attained [the truth]: "Having brought this very Self near as Brahman, they destroy from its own nature that ignorance along with its effects; therefore, it is called 'Upaniṣad'. (118)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Sākṣin," in the *Brahmagītā-ūpaniṣads*, within the latter portion of the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*, of the *Ītūtasaṃhitā-tātarvadīpikā*. [Verse 910: The primordial Guru Śiva sang this song as an instruction for the sake of all people, destroying their suffering; likewise, this song of the wonderful wonder of Brahman serves as an instruction for the welfare of the world.

Since Rudra, whose desires are fulfilled, has made the singing of the Supreme Reality his own experience, this singing of the True Guru, who is Brahman, is itself an exposition of that very Reality. (111) Śiva is pleased even by worldly songs; therefore, it is beyond doubt that He is gratified by Vedic songs. Consequently, one should sing [them]—that is, one should sing the Vedic verses that establish the true nature of the Self. (112)

If there is a similarity in singing between a Sanskrit song and a worldly song concerning the Supreme Lord, then one should properly sing that worldly song. (5.3) Indeed, singing is a necessary means for attaining liberation, because through the knowledge of singing, one can practice Yoga and thereby attain perfection. (114)

If a musician, despite practicing separately, is unable to attain the Supreme Lord, then his labor is surely in vain. [115] However, one should never sing songs related to worldly existence; even by mistake, one should not direct one's devotion toward worldly themes. [116]

Therefore, O friend, having attained knowledge through hearing the Upaniṣads and reflecting upon their meaning with logical reasoning, one should wander the earth while constantly singing of that very [Brahman] alone, having brought an end to the cycle of worldly transmigration. 5.117.

This Upanishad, which reveals the ultimate reality beyond all suffering and reaches the further shore, has been imparted by you to one who is a thief! To one with a sinful heart, this teaching is no god; it is a god only for the devotee of the Divine. 118.

**Brahmagītā, Chapter Four** Rahma said: There exists a God, self-established, the witness of all, at all times. He is the direct liberator of the virtuous who are submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. (9) By him alone is the mind of all completely restrained; yet it moves toward its objects, the vital breath (prāṇa) exerts itself, and speech also speaks. (2) The eye casts its gaze, the hand releases the arrow, and the ear likewise resounds with sound. All other senses as well are indeed impelled by him alone. (3)
They proceed incessantly, piercing their own respective objects; and this capacity to cause them to proceed belongs to it through *māyā*, not by its own inherent nature.

Thus, the purport of these [texts] has been established according to the *Taittirīyaka* and the *Svādhyāya*. Now, beginning with the Sāmavedic Upaniṣads, which have as their primary aim the unity of Brahman and the Self, the author first summarizes the meaning of the Maitrāyaṇīya Sāma-śākhā Upaniṣad in four chapters. To illuminate the point that the aforementioned unity of Brahman and the Self is to be understood solely through instruction (*upadeśa*) and not through one's own effort (*tarka*), Brahman is taught by means of questions and answers.

"By whom impelled does the mind fly forth, directed by another? By whom is the first breath joined and sent out? By whom impelled do they speak this speech? Who is the divine one who joins the eye and the ear?"—this is the question. "The ear is the messenger of truth, and the mind is the messenger of the mind; for he indeed made the speech the messenger of speech, and he made the eye the messenger of the breath"—this is the answer.

This [text] summarizes both of these points in substance with the words "The Lord exists," and so forth. By the phrase "established by Himself" (svataḥ siddha), what is intended is His existence which is eternal and ultimately real. By the term "Witness" (sākṣī), there is indicated His nature as the basis for the worldly transactions of both self and others, as well as His state of being eternally established as the substratum for the entire manifold of witnessed objects. Regarding the word "of all": by that Supreme Lord, who is the witness of all and whose nature is self-luminous, the mind is set in motion within the heart of every living being, such that He is to be meditated upon.

Nor should it be said that the aggregate of the *deni* and so forth is itself the impeller of that [mind]; for that would result in the absurdity of rendering the instruction on the well-known means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) useless. Therefore, it is logical to accept that the mind, impelled by some light of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-jyotis*) distinct from those [aggregates], causes its own object to be known. And the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), which consists of the fivefold functions such as inhalation and exhalation, performs the activity of breathing and so forth only when surrounded by that [consciousness].

Likewise, the internal organ (*manas*), which is the cause of all verbal usage and consists of pure consciousness alone, performs its own function—namely, speech—only after being impelled by this [Self]. This same principle should be applied to the eyes and ears as well. (2) "The others" means the sense organs of cognition and the organs of action, distinct from that [internal organ].

Now, one might ask: "How can such agency be possible for that which is indifferent like a spectator, eternally immutable, and comparable to a person in deep sleep, whose nature consists solely of pure consciousness? To this, he says: "The state of being the director" (*paravartakatvam*). "By means of *māyā*"—the meaning is: by virtue of contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), namely the body, senses, and so forth, which are transformations of *māyā* dominated by the quality of *rajas*. || 3-4 ||
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Explanation of the Talavakāra Upaniṣad"

(An inquiry into the Kenopaniṣad is now commenced. The Brahmin spoke: Mahādeva is the eternal witness of all; he rescues everyone who is drowning in the ocean of worldly existence by making them perceive him through direct realization. || 1 || The minds of all are impelled by that very Mahādeva and invariably perform their respective functions. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) and speech (*vāk*) also perform their tasks as granted by him. || 2 ||

It is by His impulsion alone that the eye sees form and the ear hears sound; all other senses likewise perform their respective functions only by becoming His instruments. That they render the senses and other faculties dependent on another—that too is due to *māyā*, not by their own nature. (When Mahādeva, who is essentially the individual soul (*jīva*), undergoes the superimposition of the attributes of the senses upon Himself, then the capacity for action arises in those senses.)

In reality, according to the Upaniṣadic view, that which is the means (*sādhana*) for the attainment [of knowledge] is called an organ (*indriya*). As stated in the *Sūtrabhāṣya*: "Whatever indeed is the means of perception, its very function at other times constitutes its status as an instrument" (2.4.7). It is precisely the means that acts as the organ. The conceit (*abhimāna*) that "I am the possessor of such-and-such a means" is what constitutes the agency (*kartṛtva*). Therefore, Mahādeva, who is the substrate of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), is indeed the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of the organs.

The Ācārya has clarified this point in his *Padabhāṣya*: the intended meaning here is that the activity of the mind and other faculties is established solely by their specific, mutually coordinated efforts, which must belong to some non-composite entity (*asaṃhata*). That non-composite entity is Mahādeva; in reality, he is pure existence (*sattāmātra*) and is also the impeller. This has been made clear with an illustration in the *Vākyabhāṣya*.

Before eating his own meal, the king feeds the *cakora* bird. If there is poison or the like in the food, the *cakora*'s eyes turn red, and then the king does not eat; if they do not turn red, [he eats].
[Note: 1. Mutual superimposition (*itaratarādhyāsa*) is also a product of *māyā*. 2. *ka*: *bharthikasa*;

Chapter 4 O best of men, the contraction of the senses is not considered to be natural, just as the heat of a red-hot iron ball exists through its very nature. (4) The Lord Maheśvara himself, having entered the ear which is superimposed upon the Self, being established in the essence of that [Self], grants the state of being a hearer to the ear; thus Hara is the hearer. (6) The Supreme Lord, having entered the mind which is superimposed upon the Self, being established in the essence of that [Self], grants the state of being the mind to it by means of His own power. (7)
Having attained the state of speech, Hara bestows speech; having prostrated himself, he grants life; and likewise, by means of restraint alone, he grants wealth and cattle.

[Objection: But surely, since the manifest [world] is distinct from that [Self], it follows that there is duality consisting of the mind and so forth. To this he says: "Of the senses... (indriyāṇām). The meaning is this: because the mind and the rest are superimposed upon the Self, by the logic of the heated iron ball, the very existence of the substratum (the Self) appears as a property within the superimposed entities such as the mind; however, their own inherent nature does not exist [independently]. This is the sense.

In this way, although the question—"What is that by which the mind and so forth are perceived through their own respective functions?"—is not explicitly stated, it is to be understood from the context. And he provides the answer to this: "The ear. First of all, the ear, like the rest of the phenomenal world, is superimposed upon Pure Consciousness (sac-cin-mātra), which is its substrate, because it is an object of perception.

And that [organ] is called "hearing" (*śrotra*) by virtue of its etymology as "that by which one hears. Having entered into it as its substrate, Paraśiva, whose nature is self-luminous consciousness, bestows upon that ear the capacity for hearing—that is, the power of the instrument of audition. For it is only through proximity to the light of consciousness, which is self-luminous and the innermost of all, that the ear becomes capable of manifesting sounds that have the elements as their objects.

Therefore, I shall strive; for from the supreme gift of hearing, such a thing occurs—the internal consciousness of the ear is revealed as "Om," as the Śruti declares. This is to be understood similarly in passages such as "the mind in the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3). Regarding the phrase "situated in existence" (sat-stha): it means that the *sattva* which is the cause inherent within the effect, namely the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), possesses the capacity to manifest the light of consciousness, and is delimited by that [capacity].

For the mind (*manas*) is that which is characterized by the capacity for reflection (*manana*); and that capacity is bestowed upon it by Consciousness (*caitanya*) in the manner previously described. Thus, it is taught that the mind is the "mind" of that [Consciousness]. Regarding the phrase "and speech is the speech-ness": having reached the organ of speech (*vāg-indriya*) which is superimposed upon its own seat, it bestows "speech-ness"—the capacity for speaking—upon it through its own presence. This is the meaning.

Likewise, it bestows upon the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is superimposed upon its own self, the state of being "breath" (*prāṇatva*)—that is, the capacity for the activities of breathing and so forth. For this very reason, it is recorded elsewhere in scripture: "He sends the *prāṇa* upward and casts the *apāna* backward; the All-Gods worship him as the dwarf seated in the middle. [The phrase] "the state of being sight by means of sight" means that just as the ear is the hearing of the ear, so too is it the seeing of the eye. || 8 ||

O bird, you who are free from food, poison, and the like, the king is eating his meal. In the king’s act of eating, the *cakora* bird becomes a cause merely by its presence; it does not say "Eat! or "Do not eat!"; it makes no effort whatsoever, nor does it even inform the king. In this same way, the Self becomes the impeller of the mind and other faculties simply by its existence.

The meaning of the statement that the mind and other faculties are transformed by the mere will of the Self is that the Self exerts no effort toward the activity of the mind and so forth; it does not imply that the Self forms a volition.

There, the commentator has stated: "By the phrase 'merely by the will,' the absence of effort is maintained, not the non-existence of desire, because the state of being changeless (*nirvikāratva*) is intended. This also makes it clear that both the *Vākyabhāṣya* and the *Bhāṣya* maintain that the ears, following the Self, attain their own form according to their own capacity. The very manifestation of sound is the nature of the ear. An insentient sense organ cannot manifest [sound]. Therefore, it is possible for the ear to obtain its own specific nature through its conformity with the Self.

As it has been said by me: "In this matter, the ear possesses the capacity to illuminate [objects] only through the power of the Self (*ātman*), not independently, nor by its own nature" (*Kenopaniṣad-bhāṣya*, p. 38, Ma.a.saṃ.). This entire point is indicated by the word *māyayā* ("by means of Māyā") in the Purāṇa. || 3-4 || There is no independent power belonging to the sense-faculties; rather, they are endowed with existence only through the existence of Śiva, just as heated iron becomes hot only through the heat of fire. || 5 || The ear is an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the Self (*ātman*).

The Supreme Lord Himself, who is self-luminous, enters into the mind; having entered, He brings about the manifestation of that mind. (The meaning of "having entered" is clear according to the previously cited commentaries. || 7 ||

Only through entry does speech become the lord of speech, the vital breath become the lord of breath, and the eye become the lord of sight; indeed, it is by this alone that the other senses also attain their true nature.

738. O best of those who have attained perfection, among all other perfected ones, he alone is the supreme; having reached that state, he bestows [liberation] according to his rule. (9) There, speech, mind, and all other senses do not reach that self-luminous Supreme Self, which is their own true nature. (10) That God is different from what is known, and likewise from what is unknown; He cannot be reached by speech, nor by the mind, nor by the eye, (11) nor even by the ear, O gods, nor by any other superior means whatsoever. (12)

It is not possible for anyone to perceive it; rather, it is the very being that rejoices. That which is eternally its unobstructed field of perception, appearing as if possessing form like the sun—that alone, know ye, is the supreme, eternal Brahman. 92–93.

Because the purpose here is to indicate what is not mentioned [in the text], the phrase "of others" is used to exclude those who hold different views. In this way, the instruction regarding Brahman as the innermost essence and of a single flavor—taught through the imagined sequence of the ear and so forth, and by means of those very [senses] imagined for the purpose of perceiving [the Self]—is established. || 9 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Why is such a thing not clearly perceived through direct experience, as is the case with objects like a jar? To dispel this doubt, the scripture declares: "Neither the eye goes there, nor speech, nor the mind. This is summarized by the word "others" (*itare*). By the phrase "and speech," both the sense organ that manifests sound—the ear—and the sound manifested by it are intended here by the term "speech. Therefore, these [senses] beginning with the eye are incapable of reaching Brahman, because they are superimposed upon It through *māyā*.

Therefore, how could there be any activity of those [senses] toward Brahman, which is self-established? This is because the relationship between object and subject depends upon duality. To establish that it is not an object, he says: "Self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotiḥ*). The intention is that since it is of the nature of self-manifesting consciousness, the innermost witness of the eyes and other instruments, it is impossible for it to be an object of them. 110.

And having raised the doubt as to how even the *Āgama* (scriptural tradition) could make known the nature of Paraśiva, which is thus beyond the scope of all means of valid cognition such as perception and the rest, [the author] maintains that it can indeed be made known by delimiting it through the distinction between the known and the unknown; with this intention, the *Śruti* declares: "That is indeed other than the known, and furthermore, other than the unknown. He summarizes that [point] with the words: "sa devaḥ" (that God).

The meaning is as follows: that which is the innermost witness (*sākṣin*), the luminous one, and the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)—which bestows the capacity for hearing and so forth as indicated by the passage beginning with "the seer of hearing" (*ratasya dhotṛ*)—is distinct from and of a different character than the object (*viṣaya*) which is pervaded by the fruits of actions such as knowing and the like; likewise, it is distinct even from the unknown (*avidita*), because it is self-luminous. Thus, it can be understood through the authority of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*) by its difference from both the known and the unknown.

Even though it has been taught in this manner through the method of elimination (*apohana*), immediately thereafter, the following is recited in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) for the purpose of removing the notion that anything else is to be worshipped: "That which one does not perceive with the mind, but by which the mind is perceived—that alone know thou to be Brahman; do not think that it is this which people here worship. That which one does not see with the eye, but by which the eye is seen—that alone know thou to be Brahman; do not think that it is this which people here worship. That which one does not hear with the ear, but by which the ear is heard—"

"Know that very Brahman; do not know this which they worship here—[that] by which one does not breathe, but by which the breath is led forth. That very Brahman you should know; do not know this which they worship here. Thus he summarizes it with the words "and [the one] in the wind."

That which cannot be made an object [of perception] by the senses such as speech and the rest, which is indicated as being neither known nor unknown, whose nature is that of self-luminous direct intuition (*svaprakāśa-sākṣāt-kāra*), and by the cessation of whose entire activity the world—along with speech, mind, and the rest—is illumined like the form of the sun and set in motion in its own functions; know that very interior Brahman. The meaning of the negative particle (*na*) is that there is nothing other than this which serves as the locus of fear. (11–13)

I am indeed Maheśvara, the Giver. || 8 || The eyes, speech, mind, and other senses cannot make that Self-born, self-natured Supreme Soul an object of perception. (Just as no one can illuminate the sun, for it shines by its own radiance, so too no sense-organ can make the Self, which has attained its true nature, an object. || 90 || That Mahādeva is distinct from both the knowable and the unknowable.

Because it is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), that which is to be known is indeed such; yet, because it is eternally self-luminous, it is distinct from that which is unknown. Speech, mind, eye, ear, breath (*prāṇa*), and others cannot make it an object for anyone. Just as the sun becomes the object of sight, so too this eternal Supreme Brahman is the constant object of perception for all these senses. It is the Sanātana Parama Brahma.

Know this for certain: (*The meaning of "eternal" is "during its own time of existence"; that is, as long as it remains, its object remains known.*) ||13|| That which is established by the intellect through reasoning and valid means of knowledge...

Chapter 739 Those wise ones who thus know [Brahman] through reasoning (*tarka*), through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), through the weight of their teacher’s instruction, and through their own direct experience—they indeed stand at the forefront. (12) If you are swift and think, "I have known Brahman," then consider this: how could that which is the witness of even this very thought be Brahman? (15) For one by whom Brahman is known as one's own self, without being an object of action—that is indeed the state of being free from agency and knowledge. (16)

Thus, having taught the knowledge of the nature of Brahman regarding the inner self (pratyagātman)—the witness of those [faculties] which is distinct from the senses and so forth—the scripture declares its fruit: "Having become liberated, the wise, through transcendence, become immortal from this world. To explain the meaning of that, he says: "Thus," etc. "The wise" (dhīrāḥ) means the intelligent ones who possess knowledge.

The meaning is this: having distinguished the body, senses, and so forth from the Self in the manner described above, and having understood from the mouth of the Guru that "that which is thus distinguished" is Brahman—which is without beginning or end—those who know it through their own innate nature at the moment of indubitable direct realization produced by reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), attain liberation characterized by immortality. 5.14.

Thus, at the time of the realization of Brahman as taught by the Guru, in order to demonstrate that the appearance of difference—characterized by the relationship of object and agent in the thought "I know myself as Brahman"—is devoid of reality, and in order to make known the true nature of Brahman as an undivided single essence free from such difference through its own essential form, the Śruti speaks by way of the words uttered by the Guru: "If one thinks 'I have well known [Brahman] with the mind,' that is surely but a small thing."

"You know the Brahman along with its essence"—this is the statement of the Guru. "I do not think 'I know it well,' nor do I think 'I do not know it'; yet I know it"—this is the statement of the disciple, which takes the form of a reply to that [Guru's] thought. Having grasped this very meaning intended by both [the Guru and the disciple], Brahmā instructs the gods, saying: "It is well known."

O gods, if you know that this Brahman—which has become the object of your austerity—has been made an object of our own limited intellect through a state of non-enlightenment, then you must understand that it is merely the Supreme, whose nature is undivided, appearing as such due to the limitation of the fluctuations of the intellect. And thus, this knowledge has for its object the reality itself; however, the form [of Brahman] perceived through such a fluctuation of the intellect is not its unconditioned (nirupādhika) form. This is the meaning of the "knowability" of the Reality. || 15 ||

Indeed, for him by whom that Brahman has been known as the witness-form itself—not merely through its own nature, but even without being a partaker of the fruits produced by the act of knowing—it shines forth solely as the manifestation of its own essential nature; and since that mode [of being] is eternal, even agency does not exist for him. For that knower, Brahman becomes known as unconditioned and devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 16 ||

Those who, in accordance with the words of the Guru, meditate upon the ever-fresh Mahādeva as distinct from the *saṃdhātṛ* (the synthesizer), become immortal. || 14 || O gods! If you should think that you have known Brahman, then your intention would imply that Brahman is limited (*paricchinna*), for [in your view] perfect discernment (*pariccheda*) alone constitutes knowledge (*vitti*). But Brahman is the Witness; how could He, being the Witness, be an object of perception (*sākṣya*), a Veda, or an action? || 15 ||

Even when it ceases [from its modification], it does not lose its nature as Brahman; rather, it remains Brahman in its own essential form (*svarūpa*). It cannot be said that Brahman is the agent of the act of knowing. Indeed, the moment one enters [into that state], one becomes Brahman. (Regarding the phrase "the knower of Brahman," one may say that this occurs through identity with the mental mode (*vṛtti-tādātmya*). This knowledge of Brahman is that which possesses such identity with the mental mode.)

Therefore, how can one who possesses this knowledge claim, "I am a knower"? This is a contradiction, just as it would be for a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) who falsely claims to have a wife; likewise, it is a contradiction to say, "I am a knower. Similarly, for one who has realized that Brahman is not an object, to say "Brahman is known by me"—that is, "Brahman is the object of my knowledge"—is also contradictory.

Just as one cannot say, "Having known that space has no color, the color of space has been understood," so too should this [case] be understood. A doubt arises: if this is so, why do scriptural statements such as "I was Manu" and "I have attained the eternal" exist? The answer is: these were spoken by the learned for the sake of making the supreme secret understood, even though they themselves did not [actually] experience that state.

Because cessation (*nirodha*) remains [as the ultimate], it is therefore also clarifying the state of being indescribable in other contexts such as *prakṛti* and so forth. For instance, Svāmī Ānandagiri has reflected upon this in his commentary on the *Nyāyaratnadīpāvalī*: "Since the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is not an object of cognition, can anything be known regarding the Supreme Self or not? If it can be known, then [the following options arise]...
[Note: The manuscript fragment reads *taddhāna*]. (Brahmagītā, 740)
He for whom there is no thought has truly understood; he who thinks he has understood does not know it. That which is unknown to the wise is known, while that which is known to them remains unknown.
O believers, do not entertain even the slightest notion regarding cognition, the cognition of objects, or the cognition of the self; let there be only the pure consciousness that is Brahman. 18.
O best of gods, that which appears as the agent is the Brahman; since it is the agent, therefore that [Brahman] is indeed considered its [the world's] cause. 19.

The Śruti confirms the meaning determined through the dialogue with the teacher: "He by whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; he who thinks he knows it does not know it. That which is known belongs to those who understand; that which is not known belongs to those who do not understand. He summarizes this [verse] with the words "of whom... (yasya).

The meaning is as follows: for that practitioner (*sādhaka*) by whom Brahman—which is his very self—has been made an object of the mental mode (*manovṛtti*), yet remains unmanifested [as an external object], as if unknown due to its subtle nature; for the attainment of the mental mode is desired in some cases. As it is said in scripture: "When one has made the mind perfectly steady, free from dissolution and distraction, when there is the state of being like a child, then that is the supreme state" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8); and "The mind should be restrained within the heart until it reaches destruction"; and "This is knowledge," and so forth. (Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad).

And according to the Smṛti passage, "He awakens from the non-born to the born" (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 3.33), even the pervasion of mental states (*vṛtti*) is not required; rather, when it is revealed exactly as heard—merely by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*)—then that Brahman becomes "known" (*mata*), meaning realized. However, he for whom that Brahman is "known" (*mata*) only as an object of the mind does not truly know it.

Therefore, for those who know [Brahman] through the medium of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is characterized by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), that Brahman remains as if unknown; however, for those who know it through the transcendence of the intellect, it becomes manifest in its own true nature. Now, one might object: "How can that which is known by one person be the same as the doctrine of another, given their mutual contradiction? Anticipating this doubt and in order to establish that the doctrines expressed by the six teachers are consistent with the intended meaning, the scripture declares: "The doctrine is known through awakening" (*prativodhaviditaṃ matam*).

The cognitions, which are the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi*), abide in all their modifications as the illuminator of that [intellect], being pervasive and self-luminous; because they do not deviate from being self-illuminating, they are inherently pure. Thus, for this reason, he summarizes the meaning by saying "Brahman."

Among all these forms of functional knowledge (*vṛttijñāna*)—namely, the knowledge whose object is Brahman devoid of all adventitious attributes (*upādhi*), produced by means such as hearing and reflection; the knowledge whose object is empirical reality such as earth and so forth, produced by the contact of the eyes and other senses; and the erroneous knowledge whose object is illusory silver and the like, produced by the sense of sight—all these, Brahman does not become either an agent or an object, because it is changeless, partless, and its own self, consisting solely of consciousness. Rather, it is [the witness] of that...
The meaning is that, by virtue of being the witness of everything, there would remain only self-luminous knowledge as the illuminator. || 18-19 ||

Thus, that which was said to be "beyond the scope" (aviṣaya) has itself become an object of description; and so, there is a contradiction. If my own movement [of speech] were possible, then it would be futile to say that the Supreme Self is beyond the scope, for one could not negate its status as an object. This dilemma is resolved as follows: just as the injunction for Vedic study (svādhyāyavidhi) prescribes the study of other sentences while simultaneously prescribing its own study—this being accepted in the Mīmāṃsā—so too is this case.

In this same way, by stating that [the Self] is not an object of cognition (*aviṣaya*), just as one demonstrates the non-objectivity of other things, one simultaneously demonstrates its own non-objectivity. Otherwise, if the statement "it is not an object" were to result in it becoming an object itself, the term "non-object" would be meaningless. Similarly, by speaking in a manner that appears contradictory to the statements of the Śruti and Smṛti, [the author] has established precisely that which is non-contradictory.

Since all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are unreal, the means for attaining the realization of Truth must itself be unreal; this has indeed been stated by Hari and others. (1.16) The seeker does not perceive Brahman as an object (*viṣaya-rūpeṇa*); rather, it is manifested solely through its own self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*). That is the true knowledge of Brahman. He who understands Brahman merely as an object does not know it at all.

Brahman remains unknown to those who possess knowledge regarding it; those by whom it is known do not possess knowledge of it. (17) In the case of the knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of a pot, or the knowledge of an illusion, Brahman does not become the agent, the object, the locus, or the subject of any of them. It remains as pure consciousness alone—mere knowledge. (18) The author of the *Śrutipadīrasī* does not accept that Brahman, though non-agent (*akartā*), is [perceived] as an agent.
Chapter 4, verse 741.
O best of gods, for one to whom the activity of Brahman appears as mere action, Brahman remains unknown; for only he whose action is understood as such has truly understood it.
But he who knows Brahman—which is directly manifest as the object of non-action and by its own very self, yet devoid of any perceived movement—he truly knows. (21)

Even the knowledge of the practice of yoga would belong only to the nature of the object; how then could he who perceives it as such be a knower of Brahman and the Self? (22) Even if one knows the science of Brahman, one becomes like a jar [limited] by the Vedas; one would become Brahman itself only through the complete cessation of all attachment. (23) Even though bound by the knots of ignorance, one may become free from them; therefore, one should know the supreme, stainless Brahman and shine forth as the Self. (24)

Brahman must exist either as a substratum or as an object; otherwise, how could Brahman be Brahman there? (25) If it were devoid of the nature of Brahman, then, O gods, it would be impossible to know it as Brahman; who indeed could realize the Self that is Brahman? (26)

This very point establishes that Brahman is devoid of the status of agent and object—by means of the phrase "connected with Brahman" (*brahmasambandha*). To begin with, it is impossible for Brahman, which is changeless and unattached, to be either the substratum or the object of knowledge. For if [Brahman] were characterized by such attributes, its all-pervasive nature would be delimited; consequently, it would lose its designation as being denoted by the term *śabda* (the Word), which establishes an unlimited reality.

Therefore, since no ultimate connection can be established for that which is not delimited by anything, one must accept that knowledge is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of connection with Brahman. And if it is of such a nature, then in that case, Brahman cannot be known through that knowledge.

Because Brahman is not an object of knowledge (*avedyatva*), it cannot possibly be the recipient of the fruit of an action produced by an injunction, nor is such a thing of any use; for indeed, what utility could there be for knowledge regarding that which is ultimately free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), self-luminous, and incapable of having any excellence added to it—such that, by being the recipient of a fruit produced by that [knowledge], it might become an object of knowledge? In that case, since it is thus not an object of knowledge, who indeed would seek to know the Brahman-Self?

Because of the doctrine that [the individual soul] is distinct from Brahman due to its connection with the attributes of being an agent of even a fragment of karma and its preservation of dharma, the knower—by means of the exclusion of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—perceives Brahman as it truly is: independent, transcending speech and mind, self-luminous, and solely Brahman alone; the meaning is that he does not perceive himself as "not-Brahman" (*abrahmavit*). || 26 ||

If it is argued that when [the self] becomes an object of cognition, there is in reality no knowledge of the self because it is regarded as the agent [of that cognition]—just as one who knows the form of a person is not called a knower of that person, so too the self, by being the substratum of knowledge, is not a knower of itself—[we reply: even that [notion of the self as an object] is merely a matter of verbal convention regarding Brahman, which is in fact beyond the scope of objects; this too is established by scripture. ||19-20||

That which is neither an agent nor an object, and whose nature is pure bliss, is known by its own self-luminosity alone, not through tarka (logic) or other means of valid cognition; such a one is truly wise. || 21 ||

Since that which is truly the witness of the undivided mental mode (*akhaṇḍākāravṛtti*)—which is Brahman—is itself perceived only through the sphere of the visible (*dṛśyapakṣa*), how then can anyone become a knower of Brahman? (A person becomes a knower only when Brahman is the object of his knowledge; since Brahman never becomes an object, no one can be its knower.)

One may become *brahman* through the cessation of ignorance, but one does not become a knower of *brahman*. (22) It must be admitted that the knowledge of *brahman* (*brahmajñāna*) is itself known; for knowledge that is unknown is unauthoritative, impossible, and fruitless. Therefore, like a house, the knowledge of *brahman* is certainly perceptible (*vedya*). If *brahman* is related to that [knowledge], then *brahman* too will become perceptible. (23)

When there is a relationship with an object of knowledge, such as the speaker being related to the act of speaking, then for one who possesses that knowledge, there must necessarily be some object of cognition. However, Brahman is devoid of distinctions; therefore, the Self in the form of Brahman [is not an agent].
742. *Brahmagītā*: "If it is argued that the manifestation of Māyā and so forth is superimposed upon Brahman, we say no; for Māyā cannot exist apart from something else. (27)

The inner self (pratyagātman) is pure light; Māyā is indeed the greatest darkness. This being so, how could an illusion born of ignorance exist within the inner self? Therefore, through reasoning, scripture, and one’s own direct experience, Māyā does not exist in the Supreme Self, which is the singular consciousness that is self-luminous. This [notion of Māyā] is merely conventional, arising from ignorance and not otherwise; for according to the ultimate reality, only the Absolute Reality exists as it truly is.

Thus, although it is impossible for Brahman to produce illumination through its own nature due to the absence of such a capacity, it is nonetheless established that [the scriptures] have that as their purport by means of producing the cessation of ignorance, which constitutes the veil over its true nature.

"O Nirāśvatitṛṣṇaka. The meaning is that when the absolute Brahman, which is beyond desire (*nirāśaya*), has been directly realized as the inner self (*pratyaktvena sākṣātkṛte*), there is no possibility for the appearance of the world consisting of *māyā* and its effects; therefore, since ignorance has ceased, this [state] is not fit to be deliberated upon. (27) He establishes this very point with the words "the inner self" (*pratyak*). Even well-known luminaries such as the sun possess their power of illumination only by virtue of being connected to the light of consciousness (*cidprakāśa*); thus, the Self, which is the knower of such a light of the sun, is the supreme light (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*).

For it is heard in scripture: "By whose light the sun shines, kindled with splendor," "Everything shines after Him as He shines; by His light all this world is illumined," and "Having reached the highest light, he emerges in his own form. Because it veils like dense darkness and brings about the appearance of the non-existent manifold of names and forms, Māyā is indeed a darkness characterized by illusion. And how could that [Māyā], which possesses the aforementioned characteristics, not be the cause of the manifestation of the Lord?

The meaning is that the nocturnal darkness of sorrow does not pervade—that is, does not take as its object—the one who is shining [with knowledge]. (28–29) Now, an objection is raised: "According to the manner stated above, knowledge is of no avail regarding the nature of Brahman. Yet, there are scriptural passages such as 'The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme,' 'He who knows the Śrīra becomes Brahman itself,' and 'Then, indeed, he reaches that Imperishable. Therefore, the teaching that knowledge is the means for attaining the true nature of Brahman is contradictory. To this, he replies: "Vyāvahārika... (conventional).

Since all means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, have indeed proceeded on the basis of the conventional reality (vyavahāra) imagined by me, even the Veda, being included therein, teaches that knowledge is a means to the cessation of ignorance only from the perspective of conventional reality. Therefore, both of these [the world and the Veda] exist only from the perspective of conventional reality. From the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), however, there exists only the non-dual, self-luminous Brahman. || 30 ||

The knower of the knower—that which is the self-knower—is impossible here [in this world]. (24) Brahman can never be of another kind—that is, it cannot be of the nature of being dependent on duality nor of the nature of being an object. If it were of two kinds, how could it still be Brahman? [The infinite and undifferentiated Brahman cannot possess finitude or differentiation. (25)

If you say that there is no relationship between inquiry and Brahman (and therefore that the knowledge of Brahman is possible without inquiring into Brahman), then in reality it must be admitted that Brahman cannot be known through inquiry.

(Only an object that is related [to the subject] can be known through knowledge; otherwise, there would be a clear case of over-extension. This being the case, who could be a knower of Brahman? (That is to say, no one at all could be said to know Brahman. Once this insistence—that knowledge must have an object—is removed, the state of pure consciousness can be attained.)

The knower (*jñātṛ*), the act of knowing (*jñāna*), and its object—through this triad (*tripuṭī*), one attains identity with Brahman; this alone is the knowledge of Brahman, which is not [merely] the knowledge of Brahman. (26) Nor can it be said that knowledge removes ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like superimposed upon Brahman, because in reality, there is no *māyā* at all within the inner self (*pratyagātman*). (27) The inner self is supreme light, whereas *māyā* is supreme darkness.

In such a state, how could Māyā possibly affect the Pratyagātman (the inner self)? || 28 || Therefore, it is certain through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), reasoning (*tarka*), and the experience of the wise (*vidvadanubhava*) that there is no Māyā in the Supreme Self, who is established as the mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*) by His own self-luminosity alone and is free from doubt. || 29 || Both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) exist from the perspective of empirical reality (*vyāvahārika*). [Note: *ghra. ḍa. ca* and *niravadya* are manuscript variants]. Since the relationship of being the locus and the object for both darkness (*tamas*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) is natural to Him who possesses self-luminosity, it is He alone who is made the object [of ignorance]. || 30 ||

Chapter 4: Because it is never non-deviant from the nature of the one who brings about [liberation] and so forth, it is indeed always of that very nature. (21) And the expression "it is not to be taken" is also due to its non-deviation from that nature; therefore, silence is indeed always maintained. (39) By means of the pramāṇas such as perception and so forth, by logical reasoning, and likewise by sacred tradition, and by the staff of one's own teacher, [one attains] Śiva. (43) Even within the heart, by the ripening of time, [there is] the state of bliss for those seeking peace. (44)

O Jaka, this great purpose shines forth for a person of noble character (puruṣaska). For him by whom this most exalted purpose has been directly revealed, there is no further need for all ascetic practices, since he knows [the truth] through his state of divine realization.

Thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because Brahman is unattached and lacks any connection with objects of knowledge, the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) illuminates all mental modifications (*vṛtti*)—whether they have Brahman or anything other than it as their object.

Concluding the meaning of the scriptural passage—"Because it is the object of that [perception], it is with form, and because it is not an object of that [perception], it is without a second; thus it is known through realization"—he states: "From the empirical perspective... From the perspective of a person engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is indeed of the nature of the means of differentiation between self and other, which is pervasive and unchanging, by virtue of its capacity as the illuminator within all mental modifications (*manovṛtti*) directed toward objects such as pots and cloths, since it is invariably present as the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*).

Therefore, it is established that because the manifold world of appearances—which is subject to deviation—is merely imagined within the non-deviating, variegated Brahman, like the snake or the streak of water upon a rope, Brahman is indeed revealed as being devoid of difference. This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "By the word 'undivided' (*advitam*), Brahman is understood as characterized by the negation of duality; how then is the establishment of a featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) Brahman possible? To this, he says: "Undivided" (*advitam*).

The meaning is as follows: even the statement of negation (*adatukti*) is understood through the single means of the non-deviating light (*avyabhicāri-cit-sākṣāt-karaṇa*), because it is never separate from that manifestation (*prakāśa*). Thus, "manifestation alone is eternal. Since any negation of duality other than the nature of manifestation itself is insubstantial—being like a mere word—it is sublated by its own very nature; consequently, only the pure form of consciousness (*cid-ākāra*), free from all negation, remains.

And since that [Brahman] is devoid of any distinction from its own manifestation, it is non-manifest; such is the meaning of the word *tattvamasi*. Thus, when Brahman—which is without distinctions and whose nature is pure existence—is made an object of both word and mind, the wise person’s only means for attaining realization is to remain silent, free from the association with the various limiting adjuncts (*upādhis*). He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*): the senses, including speech and so forth, together with the mind, having turned away from their respective objects and being inward-turned, [should remain] liberated from the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of distraction.

The intention is that when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is purified, Brahman—which is of the nature of the pure essence of the witness-consciousness that illuminates it—shines forth by itself. By this much, the meaning of the Vedic statement, "He whose [Brahman] is not known is known," is properly established. Now, one might object: if the instruction regarding Brahman consists merely in silence, and since that is easily attained by everyone, there would be no need for such an effort. To this, he says: "Because of the supreme mystery" (*parokṣādīti*). || 33 ||

The meaning is that this subject matter, being exceedingly profound, shines forth as a great secret only to a certain person seeking liberation (mumukṣu) who—having propitiated the Supreme Lord through devotion to the duties of their caste and stage of life throughout a succession of births, and having attained the fourfold means (sādhana-catuṣṭaya)—possesses a complete realization of those [means], and not to anyone else. || 24 ||

By the passage beginning with "For one finds immortality" (*amṛtatvaṃ hi vindate*), the fact that the aforementioned knowledge—being independent of other means—is established as the means for attaining immortality, is explained by elucidating its intended meaning through the words beginning with "yasmin... [and so on].
