The phrase "because of non-duality" (*advayatvāt*) means that because there is no appearance of any other entity serving as a means for knowledge and action—which are themselves born from the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the non-dual Self—the knower who abides in the state of the non-dual Brahman has no further obligation (*anadhikāra*) toward those [means]. || 25 ||

Indeed, from that perspective, these two rivers are one and the same supreme reality. Even the *kalā-puruṣa* (the individual soul as a limited manifestation) is indeed the Supreme Reality (*prakāśa*), because it remains inseparable (*avyabhicarita*) from its source of illumination. It is always non-different from Him, just as fire is non-different from wood. (The term *avyabhicarita* implies that deviation is impossible; this is illustrated by examples such as the imagined snake, a streak of water, or a garland within the sphere of "this-ness" [the phenomenal world]).

Since non-deviation (*avyabhicārin*) is indeed [a property] within knowledge, and since all [properties] are imagined therein, it is always non-giving (*adatta*), because that which is imagined cannot give the real. (21) This statement "non-giving" (*adatta*) is also imagined as its own kind within the category of non-deviation, because it would otherwise be deviant; therefore, it is eternally of one kind.

Consequently, silence is appropriate; for whatever [else] one might do would be inconstant, and therefore, being merely conceptual, it would not be so. Thus, silence is fitting. For this very reason, in Paramaśiva, there are no such things as the right-hand path (*dakṣiṇāmārga*), the upward path (*ūrdhvamārga*), the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*), or the secret path (*guhyamārga*). Nor can it be argued that silence, too, is equivalent to speaking because it is inconstant; for the statement "silence is fitting" means simply that "speaking is not fitting," and thus there is no fault in its not being an injunction for silence.
— *Brahmagītā*, 744.

This great reality, which is self-manifested, is neither that individual soul (jīva), nor Brahman, nor anything else whatsoever. This great reality, which is self-manifested, has no castes (varṇas) for it, and likewise no stages of life (āśramas). This great reality, which is self-manifested, has neither dharma nor adharma for it, neither prohibition nor injunction.

My mind is firmly resolved that he who has attained this great goal through the grace of Śambhu is indeed Śambhu himself and none other. (29) I am truly unable to describe the majesty of him who has attained this great goal through the grace of Śambhu; this is what I have spoken as the truth. (40) Even Viṣṇu is not able to express the full extent of the majesty of him who has attained this great goal through the grace of Śambhu. (41)

O believers, even one who has attained this great reality through the grace of Śambhu is not able to describe its true majesty. (32) He states, by means of the verses beginning with "This matter is great," that not only is it so, but no worldly transaction whatsoever can occur for him by relying upon duality. (36–40) Indeed, the supreme essence is such that "from which words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4). (32)

This great and auspicious human goal manifests for a person when, in the course of time, his accumulated merit bears fruit and favorable conditions such as an apt intellect arise; when his doubts have been resolved through the instruction of a Guru; when he has determined the meaning of the Upanishads; and when their consistency with logic and other means of valid knowledge has been firmly established. (33-34)

For one for whom this most significant matter has become firmly established, there is neither action nor knowledge. (35) That in which this human goal (pumartha) has manifested by itself is neither the individual soul (jīva), nor Brahman, nor anything else. (Brahman, too, is ultimately but a name; how could that which is devoid of attributes possess even such a name? Nor should one understand the attainment of the state of emptiness as being something other than this.)

This is merely the conclusion of a conventional discourse. (36) In this reality, there is no caste, no stage of life, no merit, no demerit, no injunction, and no prohibition. (37–38) Whoever has correctly understood the meaning of these words through the grace of Śambhu, he is Śambhu himself; none other than him—this is my firm conviction. (39)

The glory of that one who is established in Brahman cannot be described. (40) Even Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Vedas cannot express its greatness; for being infinite, how can its full majesty ever be told? (41–42) If, while this body still remains, one realizes the aforementioned great meaning of the Mahāvākya, then immediate, true, absolute liberation is attained. (44)

If time were spent in the opposite manner, there would be no effort toward the attainment of the designation "actor" (*naṭī*), and a great calamity would arise; an upward course will not be attained. It has been established in the *Rekhikādhikaraṇa* (3.4.16.51) that the practice of the means of knowledge (*vidyā*) is beneficial even in another birth. However, it is determined in the subsequent section that knowledge itself yields its fruit without delay.

Chapter 745: O Noble One, he who has attained this great purpose through Your instruction—neither the Vedas nor the learned believers are able to describe His glory. (432) If this great meaning spoken by the Puruṣa is realized in this very body, then that human being attains the non-dual reality (*advaita-tattva*) and reaches liberation (*nirvāṇa*). (44) If this great meaning spoken by the Supreme is not understood in this body, then there is only great ruin for him; indeed, there is no higher goal for him. (45)

Having firmly realized that [Self] as equal within one's own body and in the bodies of others, the wise indeed never again fall under the sway of delusion at the end. (46) The statement, "One who possesses intelligence attains power" (*āsanā vindate vīryam*), has established that the wise person attains the power capable of overcoming the effects of ignorance through the very form of the Self purified by the Vedic injunctions. This is further clarified by the phrase, "His majesty" (*vaibhavam tasya*). "Majesty" (*vaibhavam*) means greatness.

Because of the impossibility of greatness in that which is subject to decay, by means of that greatness, an unsurpassed heroism (*vīrya*)—which is its own cause—is intended. Heroism produced by means such as wealth, grain, and medicinal herbs is perishable; since it is produced by [external] things, it is merely a means for a fruit other than immortality (*amṛtatva*). Even if one were to assume that the heroism produced by the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) is not of such a nature, it is still impossible to say so—that is the meaning. || 41–43 ||

And this knowledge, which is the means for attaining immortality, having been obtained through the power of one's good deeds (*sukṛta*), must be diligently acquired by those desiring to know while the body still exists. For even when that [knowledge] is present, if it is not attained due to attachment to it, there is only endless transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) for the person; thus the Śruti addresses the qualified seeker: "If one has known here, then there is truth; if one has not known here, there is great ruin. The meaning of the word *iha* (here) in this Śruti is "in this [life]."

When this very meaning—consisting of the previously mentioned dissolution of the body—is realized while one still possesses a human or other physical body subject to the jurisdiction of the senses, then, through that realization, one attains the reality of the Self which is distinct from the intellect, free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), characterized by the non-dual Brahman, and identical with liberation itself. (44) He establishes the aforementioned point by means of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "If not," etc.

If, for one who is qualified for knowledge, the previously mentioned [liberation] were not realized due to the impairment of the door of truth (satya-dvāra) and the consequent failure to perform the means such as the meditation on the Śaraṇa-forest, then indeed there would be a loss for him of the supreme human goal characterized by the attainment of unsurpassed bliss. Thus, for that ignorant person, there is only a falling into the continuous flow of saṃsāra; the meaning is that there is never at any time the attainment of liberation. || 45 ||

Having thus established the presence and absence [of the self] in the body and having described its fragrance, the fruit thereof is declared in scripture: "The wise, having discriminated the self from the elements, become immortal, departing from this world. He explains this with the words: "In the body..."

Those wise ones who—through hearing, reflection, and other means—have directly realized the reality of Brahman, which is established as identical in nature to the moon even within their own bodies, in other bodies, in the stages of life such as childhood and old age, and in the states of jar-like decay; who are courageous, energetic, and firm in resolve, and are thus freed from the cycle of worldly existence—they are not born again after the fall of this body, because ignorance, the root cause of the entire mass of transmigratory existence, has been completely eradicated by their wisdom.

Moreover, sometimes even those who lack horses and chariots become successful. Therefore, one should strive for the attainment of knowledge in this very birth until death. If, while making such effort, the body should perish, that exertion will not have been in vain. The intended meaning is that under all circumstances, one should turn away from worldly gains and the like, and instead employ the means for attaining the Lord.

45. When a wise person attains the firm conviction that Brahman alone exists as the witness within all bodies—both one's own and those of others—he is never born again; he becomes immortal. 46. It is Brahman alone that appears manifold through various distinctions such as the enlightened, the liberated, the great scholar, the ignorant, and so forth.

Elsewhere Vyāsa says: "This body has been purchased by the great merchants of merit with the price of piety; as long as it does not perish, one should cross the ocean of suffering. [Thinking thus... [Da. "Bound, liberated, etc."]—according to the Bhārata, there are distinctions such as "Brahmā is bound, Mukunda is liberated, and Mahāviṣṇu is unborn," and so forth.

Just as a carpenter fashions wooden posts with his axe, so does the Friend [the Self] fashion the bodies. || 47 || Therefore, O gods, the knower of the Self knows that by His own liberation alone, there is the liberation of others as well. || 48 ||
He knows the nature of his own self through the sacred revelation (śruti), as well as the essence of the Āśvalāyanas and their ritual practice (gṛhya).
[He knows this] by means of the half-verse beginning with the characteristics of Maṅśara and so forth.
One who knows the supreme state of the embodied soul as being like the tip of a hair-tip possesses liberation.
The awakening of consciousness destroys the cycle of existence that has been fashioned by beginningless ignorance.

We ourselves appear as many in our dreams. (47) Therefore, one who has fallen away from the knowledge of the Self recognizes this [multiplicity] as such; for by the very experience of enjoyment, there is also the perception of other selves appearing as serpents. (Upon investigating this, one realizes that no one possesses true existence; even while performing these actions, one perceives that other living beings still exist, like lamps placed within a house.)

[Aside] Have you ever seen such a thing? While conducting himself as if he were a king, he thinks, "This grain is mine," and thus he performs the ritual of offering it to the deity presiding over his own body. Even while living, he acts as if he were dead; he performs the funeral rites for his own life-force (*jīvatvābhimāna*) so that [the ego] may depart. (48)

As long as one continues to cause the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) for oneself through the notion of "I," one considers the Self to be a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). In this same way, one attains liberation (*mokṣa*) by realizing it for oneself; only then is one liberated.
(49) As long as residual karma (*prārabdha-karma*) remains, the knower of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-vid*) never perceives distinctions such as the world, the individual soul (*jīva*), or the like.

Even great karma exists [only as long as it has not been exhausted]. 59. Just as the world appears to exist, so too everything that is perceived is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the Supreme Self.

747. Until the exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma*, the knower of the Supreme Self sometimes perceives the body and so forth, and sometimes he does not perceive them at all. 40. O best of men, the knower of reality (*tattvavit*), by his very nature, sometimes knows the manifested Brahman and sometimes he does not know it at all. 59.

When Brahman shines forth in the form of the world, the individual soul (*jīva*), and so forth, then even the experience of suffering and the like appears as a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*). (52) But when everything shines forth by its own nature as the Self that is Brahman, then this experience of suffering and the like, though appearing, does not truly appear [as real]. (53) Even while perceiving the world in the form of the individual soul and so on, the knower of the Supreme Self does not fall away from it; he perceives only the reality that is Brahman. (54)

Now, one might object: "In this way, let the appearance of the world exist for the ignorant due to the power of their own ignorance; however, for the wise, since ignorance has been sublated, the appearance of the world—which is its effect—is untenable. To this, he says: "pāravaśyāt" (due to the power of another). Actions (*karma*) are indeed of two kinds: 1) those whose fruits have already begun (*ārabdhaphala*), and those whose fruits have not yet begun (*anārabdhaphala*).

Because those [karmas] whose fruits have already begun do not possess the quality of being removable by knowledge—unlike those whose fruits have not yet begun—and must therefore be exhausted solely through experience, until that point, even when at times experiencing the fruit, he knows the world which serves as its means, consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed; however, at other times, during the experience of the realization of the non-dual Brahman, he does not know that world at all—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Does the perception of the world not exist for the knower just as it does for the ignorant?"

To the question, "What is the distinction regarding his consciousness? he says: "At times, he realizes the Supreme. The meaning is this: when the wise man knows that very Brahman which is his own Self, he realizes that the entire world—which exists as superimposed upon Brahman, the innermost Self of all—is non-different from its substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). Since that which is superimposed is not distinct from its substratum, at the time of such realization, the knower realizes [the world] solely through the nature of the substratum, Brahman.

Sometimes, during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), because the superimposed world is dissolved through the knowledge of the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is Brahman, the wise person does not perceive the world at all due to its very nature of being devoid of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Therefore, for the knower, the appearance of the world occurs only occasionally by way of superimposition; it is not real in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) and is not constant, as it is for the ignorant—this is the meaning. (Verse 51) [The phrase] "the world, the individual soul, etc."...

And when, for one who knows thus, during the state of distraction (*vikṣepa-samādhi*), Brahman appears in the form of the world consisting of the sublater, the enjoyer, and the objects of enjoyment, then even the experience of pleasure caused by that [world] appears for the knower as having the nature of a mere appearance, just like its means. But when, at the time of *samādhi*, the entire perceived world shines forth as non-different from Brahman—the Self which is the ultimate limit of all sublation—then [there is no experience] of the means of suffering.

The meaning is this: because the world does not appear [to him], the cause of it—the suffering of saṃsāra—is likewise not perceived by him at all. (53) Now, one might object: "Just like the ignorant person, the wise man also experiences the entire world as something distinct [from himself]; how then can the world have the nature of a mere appearance for him? To this, he says: "The world... (verse 54). Even though the world is superimposed, he perceives it through the very self of Brahman, which is the substratum and the ultimate reality, and not as having the nature of name and form. This is the meaning. (54)

O friend, this world is like a mirage; when the world does not appear, then the mirage does not appear. (51) Just as the ninefold Brahman, the world, the individual soul, and so forth, appear [as real], so too suffering and the rest—the experiences of *prārabdha* karma—are experienced merely through appearance; they become manifest simply by appearing. (52)

When all defects such as *samādhi* and the like are suppressed and remain unperceived, and Brahman alone shines forth by its own nature, then even the previously mentioned appearances of suffering and so forth are no longer perceived. || 53 || Although the knower of the Supreme Self perceives the various distinctions appearing in the form of the world, the individual soul (*jīva*), and so on, he does not fix his gaze upon them; rather, he keeps his vision fixed solely upon the reality of Brahman established within that very state. || 54 ||

Other than Brahman, there is in reality no appearance of objects whatsoever. 748. That which is other than Brahman never exists, whether it be real or unreal; likewise, how can one who knows the truth perceive anything other than Śiva? 55. Whether as the form of Brahman, or as a tree, a mountain, a forest, or a desert—just as an object appears before the witness, so does it shine forth. 56. Just as this manifestation appears by its very own nature, so too does the continuous contemplation of the yogi become the realization of his own Self. 57.
O bulls among the gods, if Mahādeva is not the Lord even in terms of actual reality, then what does he know and what does he speak? (58)

This very point establishes for the knower the non-existence of anything other than Brahman, as stated in the verse beginning with "of Brahman. In reality (*vastutaḥ*), there is nothing distinct from Brahman, according to such scriptural texts as, "There is not even the slightest diversity here. Even on the level of appearance (*avastutaḥ*), it does not exist at all; for since the entire world is unreal in its true nature, it is necessarily non-existent within that [Brahman]. Thus, the meaning is: how could the knower perceive anything distinct from the Supreme Reality? || 55 ||

He concludes that for the wise person, there is always an appearance as if of Brahman itself by stating, "by one who is equal to Brahman. The connection is as follows: whether by means of the substrate-Brahman (*adhiṣṭhāna-brahma*) or by means of the appearance of the superimposed world of objects and subjects (*āropita-tad-bhogyabhoktṛ-prapañca*), in whatever manner the manifestation, intuition, or knowledge of the wise person occurs, in that very same way, Brahman itself appears directly to him. || 56 || He concludes that even the appearance of the entire universe to the wise person is not distinct from the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi-avasthāna*) according to the method described, by stating, "as before" (*yathāpūrvam*). || 57 ||
Even upon reflection on the meaning of the words of Mahādeva, nothing whatsoever remains to be rejected or accepted by the wise; thus [the author] says "iti" (thus). 58. †

That which is unreal is not [the truth], such as leprosy; therefore, what else could be known other than Śiva? || 55 || Whether as the manifest Brahman, as the void of the universe, or in the form of the individual soul—however it may appear, that which appears is indeed Brahman alone. (Just as a snake, a garland, or anything else may appear, that which appears is indeed the rope. || 56 || By its very nature, it is exactly as it is.

He experiences [all things] by relying upon that [state], constantly maintaining the contemplation of the knowledge of his own Self; (that is to say, for the knower of reality, the state remains the same during both samādhi and vyutthāna). 1.57 ||

Even from the perspective of various other purposes, if Mahādeva alone exists, what could a knower of Brahman abandon and what could he accept? (The intention is that since nothing exists apart from Śiva, this distinction cannot be maintained. In reality, since there is neither a means nor a perceiver apart from Śiva, even acceptance does not occur. || 58 ||

If anything other than Śaṅkara were to be accepted or rejected, then the greatness—whether as excellence or as inherent nature—of Śaṅkara could not be diminished; therefore, this distinction does not exist. (59) Greatness is not a property of Śaṅkara, for it is not distinct from Śiva.

If there were a difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) in that [relation], then by accepting such a difference, the substratum would become non-existent (*atat*), which is the intended meaning. Therefore, there is difference, non-difference, and both difference and non-difference.

Chapter 749 If one knows [the truth], that which is to be grasped is other than [mere] confusion, or else that which is to be abandoned; yet its greatness would be lost, though its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not destroyed. (59) Greatness is not at all a property (*dharma*) of this Supreme Self (*parātman*), because there is no differentiation (*bheda*). Indeed, the discourse of "property" and "possessor of property" exists only when differentiation is present. (60) Differentiation arises from non-differentiation, and likewise, the unity of differentiation and non-differentiation exists directly as the Supreme Self. Apart from its own self, it does not exist; it exists by itself alone at all times. (61)

Brahman alone exists, whether manifest or unmanifest, real or even unreal. This being so, what does the knower of Śiva grasp, and what does he abandon? (62) Some, deluded, maintain that everything exists as Māyā; yet apart from the supreme form of Śiva, how could Māyā exist? (63) O best of gods, if anything other than Śiva were manifested through Māyā, then the supreme greatness of Śiva would be directly diminished. (64) [The phrase] "His is greatness" refers to this.

For its greatness consists precisely in being devoid of the three kinds of concealment (*paracchada*). And that [greatness] would be destroyed if that which is the inner self of all were to be perceived as something other than the Self, even for a moment. He refutes the objection that this is an acceptable consequence by stating: "The nature [of things] is such that it excludes [what is contrary]. That greatness is the very essence (*svarūpa*) of the Supreme Lord. Nor is it logical to deny that, for it would entail the non-existence of the Lord Himself. This is the meaning. || 59 ||

One might object: "Is it not the case that greatness (*mahattva*) is not the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the Supreme Lord, but rather His attribute (*dharma*), and thus the aforementioned fault does not arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because there is no difference" (*bhedābhāvāt*). The meaning is that since the Śruti has established—through such passages as "The Self is one alone, without a second"—the exclusion of internal, homogeneous, and heterogeneous differences for the Supreme Self; and because it was already demonstrated in the previous section that the means of valid cognition, such as perception and so forth, lack the capacity to apprehend difference. [He further states: "Between attribute and substratum" (*dharmadharmiṇoḥ*).

For indeed, a thing cannot be its own substratum (dharmin) by itself; thus, the relationship between property and substratum (dharmadharmibhāva) is not a matter of necessity. The meaning is that because the pervader (vyāpaka), namely difference, is absent even in the case of fire and fuel, the pervaded relationship of property and substratum is also impossible. Now, one might object: "If there is no difference whatsoever between fire and fuel, then non-difference in the form of identity with the manifest world (prapañca) would follow, and thus Brahman would be subject to the fault of transformation (pariṇāmadoṣa). Anticipating this, he says: "Difference... [and so on].

The meaning is that since even difference and non-difference are merely superimposed, there is no existence of the world-appearance apart from the nature of Being (sadrūpa). || 61 || He concludes that the knower is free from the appearance of distinctions between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted with the words "in solitude" (raha eva). The meaning is: since the superimposed phenomenal world, being distinct from the nature of Being, lacks both reality and unreality, it does not exist separately from its substratum, Brahman; therefore, since only the non-dual Brahman shines forth everywhere, what could the knower abandon and what could he accept? || 62 ||

"It does not exist for me": the meaning is that since even *māyā*, which is postulated as the cause of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), is distinct from both existence and non-existence, the statement "the world exists as *māyā*" is a contradictory assertion. (63) "By means of *māyā*": if one were to accept the reality of *māyā* and thereby assert that the world composed of it exists, then the previously mentioned "greatness" (*mahattva*) of Paraśiva—characterized by being devoid of the threefold limitations (*pariccheda*)—would be compromised. (64)

All three are not real apart from the Self; the only reality is the one Supreme Self alone. (Difference is therefore not real, for that which is different from "Being" is "non-being," and thus it must necessarily perish! Non-difference, too, is spoken of only in relation to correlates; since the correlates themselves would have to be distinct, difference being unestablished, non-difference cannot be established either.)

(Thus, difference-in-identity is not established by itself. || 61 || Therefore, in reality and in appearance, there is only Brahman. In this state, what portion of Śiva-nānī (the Mother of Śiva) would be accepted and what portion rejected? || 62 || The foolish disputants argue that the entire world exists through the power of Māyā; however, the truth is this: apart from Śiva, Māyā does not exist even as a subtle atom. || 63 ||

If even Māyā were something other than Śiva, then the greatness of Śiva would be compromised; indeed, it would be defeated. To establish the truth of this matter, one must simply say that there is no restriction whatsoever regarding what belongs to Śiva. [64] To state the actual fact clearly, it must be said that there is no limitation at all concerning anything that is not Śiva.

There is no contraction of the Great Self (Mahānvasya) in the *Brahmagītā* when it is fully established; if one were to say otherwise, it would be invalid, and therefore this [text] speaks of that [truth]. Therefore, Mahādeva alone is directly the Sun, whose nature is bliss; there is nothing else whatsoever beyond him. This indeed is the supreme limit of the Tarka-śāstras, O best of the twice-born; it is the most excellent teaching of the Vedāntas, which are the ultimate atoms of all other systems such as Pūrva-mīmāṃsā. It is likewise the conclusion of the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and the Mahābhārata.

O best of theists, among all the sciences following the Vedas and all other scriptures—including those not spoken by the Ṛṣis—among all the Buddhist scriptures as well as the scriptures of the Arhats, and even the scriptures fabricated by Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and others, for which mortal man could there exist the supreme non-dual realization? Or for which god? Indeed, it is established only for Śiva. (68–71)
O best of the faithful, the supreme non-dual consciousness of Śiva, who possesses immeasurable splendor, as well as that of the goddess Śivā, is established by their very nature. (72)

"If it exists... [If it were so]. If the greatness of Paraśiva, like that of space (*ākāśa*) and other such things, were merely relative, then the scripture which establishes his freedom from all three kinds of limitation—stating "Brahman is infinite" and "one only, without a second"—would be rendered invalid; this is the meaning of the verse. (65) He concludes the point already established with the words "Therefore... (66–72). If this were the case, one would have to regard as non-authoritative the scripture that reveals the truth, which is an untenable position. (65)

Therefore, it must be accepted that the Lord Mahādeva alone—who is immediate, self-luminous, a mass of bliss, and all-pervading—is the reality, and there is nothing other than Him. This is established even upon the final examination; both direct perception and other means of valid cognition, as well as the Vedānta, demonstrate this very point. || 66-67 ||

O Purāṇa, if one were to thoroughly investigate and analyze the Smṛtis, the Mahābhārata, the Vedas, the Śaivāgamas, the Vaiṣṇavāgamas, the Brāhmāgamas, the Bauddhāgamas, the Jaināgamas, and all the Āgamas composed by Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and others, their intended meaning would consistently converge upon this very Śiva. (68–70)

This ultimate non-dual knowledge belongs neither to any human nor to any deity (for they do not exist as such), but belongs only to Śiva (for he alone is one). || 71 || Śiva and Umā possess this supreme non-dual knowledge by their very nature. || 72 || By their grace alone [it is attained] by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Virāṭ.

1. [Śrīkaṇṭha] Prabhācārya says: Having stated that Śiva alone transmigrates and is liberated, and having reconciled the conventional distinction [between them], he speaks [of the Supreme]. 2. [Objection]: But might not the scriptural texts concerning Brahman also be merely figurative, like the scriptural texts concerning the eternity of space? [Reply]: He says: Why would the scriptural text concerning the eternity of space declare its non-eternity? [Objection]: Because it contradicts the scriptural text, "Space was produced. [Reply]: Then you have entered upon the very path [we advocate].

It is an established principle that the authority of Śruti is negated by another means of knowledge (mānāntara) only when there is a contradiction, and not otherwise. Since Śruti concerning the *rahasya* (secret portion) does not contradict other means of knowledge—because those [other means] do not apply (*aprasara*) to that domain—it is not on the same footing as [ordinary Śruti].

"O Śiva, eat from me directly, and likewise, O Viṣṇu, grant me the supreme non-dual realization (advaita-vijñāna) yourself. (73) The knowledge of the Lord known as Virāṭ, of Svarāṭ, of Atyanta, and of Saṃrāṭ, as well as that of others, comes only through direct perception. (74) For all of you as well, the supreme non-dual realization of the Self (paramātman), which is Śiva, comes only through direct perception and not otherwise. (75)

Even the lords of the yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, siddhas, and others, as well as all humans, including those beginning with Brahmā—only through the grace of the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin) do they attain the supreme knowledge of non-duality (paramādaitavijñāna). Whether one is an insect, a bird, a human, a celestial being, or even a dānava, provided that [the means such as] sacred hearing (śruta) exist, one attains the highest knowledge. Indeed, he alone bestows supreme knowledge upon living beings.

"Indeed, there is no one other than Viṣṇu; this which I have spoken is the truth. Likewise, in both taking and giving, the great Hari is not independent; so too am I, O best of gods—this which I have spoken is the truth. (79–80)

Beginning to explain the meaning of the Śruti passage starting with "Brahmā indeed conquered for the gods," [the author] demonstrates, by way of providing a supporting argument, that the knowledge of that [Brahman] is obtainable through the grace of Umāmaheśvara, using the words "prasādādeva" (only through grace) and so forth. || 73–78 ||

Who is the self-sovereign (*svarāj*), who is the universal sovereign (*samrāj*), and who else is that knowledge? Even for you all, non-dual realization (*advaitaniṣṭhā*) can be attained solely through the grace of Śiva. Yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, siddhas, and others also attain it only by His power. Even for Luṣya and all five classes of beings, non-dual knowledge arises only through the favor of the Lord.

Upon receiving Śiva’s grace, worms, insects, humans, gods, and even demons—all obtain this supreme knowledge (732–78). Śiva alone is the bestower of the supreme non-dual knowledge to living beings; neither Viṣṇu, nor Brahmā, nor anyone else is so (79). Hari and Brahmā have no independent authority in its reception or bestowal; Śiva alone is sovereign in these matters.
Without his grace (kapā), no one can bring about the liberation of anyone else. || 80-81 || Without Mahādeva, who is the abode of compassion, even Viṣṇu cannot grant liberation to anyone.
|| 82 || [Note: Variant reading for verse 82 is "parijñānaṃ"].

The Brahmagītā states: "This Śiva alone is independent; for he is the liberator from the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). Without him, O Gaṇas, no one can attain bliss. Even by Viṣṇu and by the Supreme [Brahmā], O best of beings, it is not possible to exist without Mahādeva, the abode of prostrations. Indeed, O gods, neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu himself possesses independence. [Know] the true nature and the majesty of that God of gods."

Who indeed knows? There is no one who knows by himself, or does he not? (84) Even for the great embodied beings, Mahādeva is like the sun; without his grace, the gods [are powerless]—this is truly what I have declared. (85) In ancient times, among all the wicked-souled demons, a delusion difficult to ward off arose through great infatuation. (86) The gods were oppressed by the Asuras and became exceedingly distressed; then the Blessed Lord, the omniscient source of compassion, [appeared]. (87)

He granted victory to the gods and defeat to the Asuras; by that, the gods were quickly overcome by their enemies. (88) In order to demonstrate that the Supreme Reality, whose characteristics have been described, is difficult to know because it is utterly tranquil, and that it is inaccessible to the great gods such as Indra and others, but is attainable through the grace of the Lord, there is recorded in the tradition a narrative in the form of a story beginning with: "Brahman indeed won a victory for the gods. Likewise, that which is unthought and even inconceivable—the world-effect—becomes thought and conceived through meditation upon Him; and likewise, that which is unknown and even uncertain becomes known and certain as non-different from Him through the knowledge that ascertains His sphere. Since non-existence (*asat*)—in the form of absolute destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*)—is devoid of any essential nature (*svarūpa*), it cannot possess properties characterized by a relationship with a substratum (*āśraya*). Consequently, because such a property does not exist, the action of "arising" (*janikriyā*) relative to it is also non-existent; thus, it is illogical for it to have a temporal dimension (*kāla*). This is the meaning. || 14 ||

If, because it is difficult to accept that the effect is existent, you say that the effect is non-existent (and distinct from the cause), then that effect could never come into being at all; for the non-existent, such as the son of a barren woman, can never be the effect of anything. 13.

Can it be argued that the non-existence of an effect is observed in the case of the destruction of a non-existent thing; therefore, is the non-production of the son of a barren woman and the like not also caused by its non-existence? The answer is that even destruction is not an effect, because its origination and so forth are impossible.

Because it is devoid of properties (*nirdharmaka*) like space (*śūnya*), it cannot be related to causal factors (*kāraka*); otherwise, it would become a positive entity (*bhāva*) rather than a non-entity (*abhāva*). Since there is no connection with causal factors, the production of destruction does not occur. Therefore, being a non-product (*akāryatva*) is the logical reason (*prayojaka*) [for its permanence], and there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this regard.

It should be understood that all worldly entities, whether existent or non-existent, are established merely as appearances (*pratītimātrasiddha*); they are neither effects nor causes. Therefore, it is certain that since destruction is a non-entity (*abhāva*), it cannot be an effect. Nevertheless, it is observed that the blow of a stick is the cause of the destruction of a jar; thus, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) "this is its effect" occurs.

It appears exactly as if a son were born from a mother; therefore, the conventional usage of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇavyavahāra*) occurs for one who does not know [the truth] (*avidāvajña*). In reality, however, there is neither effect nor cause. By accepting an effect that is illusory (*māyāmaya*), the loss of one's own position (*pratijñāhāni*) and the establishment of the opponent's thesis (*siddhāntasiddhi*) would follow. Even though something is non-existent (*asat*), an effect can still arise, as in the case of the son of a barren woman (*vandhyāsuta*) and so forth. Therefore, the question arises: what is the difference [between these cases]? If it is argued that the difference is this: an effect enters into a relationship with its causal factors (*kāraka*), whereas the son of a barren woman and such do not—this argument is incorrect. For a relationship with causal factors is observed even in those things that possess no specific distinction whatsoever.

Therefore, the relation of a *kāraka* (grammatical factor) can only exist when there is a qualification (*viśeṣatā*). There is no qualification whatsoever in that which is non-existent (*asat*). If one were to assume that the relation of a *kāraka* constitutes the qualification of the non-existent, it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*): the relation of a *kāraka* would depend upon the existence of a qualification, and yet the existence of the relation of a *kāraka* is required for that qualification to exist; thus, the relation of a *kāraka* becomes impossible. He concludes the demonstration that there can be no causal relationship with a non-existent thing by saying "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is: since, according to the aforementioned reasoning, a specific causal relation is difficult to establish for a non-existent thing—such as a human horn—and since it is equally non-existent, it is not logical for it to possess causality in the same way [as the existent]. He refutes the third alternative—that the effect is both existent and non-existent—by stating "the state of being both existent and non-existent."

Thus, since an effect distinct from its cause cannot be determined through the alternatives of being existent, non-existent, and so forth, one must accept that the effect is indeed non-different from its cause; he concludes this with the words "Therefore, the effect... He states the reason for this with the words "of difference...": the meaning is that because the cognition of difference depends upon the determination of the locus and the counter-correlate, and because it is consequently beset by defects such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), it is impossible to determine difference in an ultimate sense anywhere at all. [Verse 19] "Difference and non-difference... [etc.]

The meaning is that the position of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) is even more untenable, because it is impossible to conjoin existence and non-existence in a single locus, and because it entails the same defects as the positions of absolute difference and absolute non-difference. Now, one might ask: "If the effect is non-different from the cause, what is the status of the perception of difference? To this, he says: "From the cause" (*kāraṇāt*). The meaning is that although, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), the effect is non-different from the cause, the appearance of difference between cause and effect and so forth is established through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). (Verses 20–22)

Consequently, [terms such as] "jar" and so forth are merely names. Always—that is, at all times, even during the period of its existence just as during the state of its destruction—only the mere state of being the cause remains for the effect. (23) 4

23 || All modifications (*vikāra*) are unreal because they consist of forms established through the cognition of others (*paratīti*). Only their underlying causal form (*anugata-kāraṇākāra*) is itself real. (In the ultimate sense, the causal form possesses only empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattā*); in reality, that which is the cause is the limited consciousness (*avacchinna-caitanya*), and since it is consciousness, it is substantially real. || 24 ||

That which is different from the cause in its nature as a real entity (*sadrūpa*) is indeed true; that effect is nothing other than the cause itself. (The effect is the cause). As a real entity, the cause is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and in its nature as the Supreme Self, it is eternally true. To conceive of or speak of anything distinct from that as a separate effect is false—just like the horns of a donkey. || 25 ||

For this reason, it is correct that everything is known as the One; this matter is clearly established, and there is no doubt about it. 26. The cause of the world is one alone—it is neither different (possessing distinction) nor both different and non-different. (It is not different, meaning there is no cause other than the One; nor is it both different and non-different, meaning there is no cause that could be perceived as both one and many. For even though difference is perceived everywhere, it is indeed illusory because...

Chapter 5 767. That cause is indeed one; it is neither divided nor of a dual nature. Difference is everywhere false, because the substratum and so forth cannot be established [as distinct]. (27) For when difference is known, there is the cognition of the division of the substratum and so forth; and when the substratum is fully understood, there is the cognition of difference. (28) Precisely because difference cannot be defined, the coexistence of difference and non-difference is not tenable. Therefore, this Lord is eternally and solely one as the Cause. (29) And even if a division were perceived like that of the parts of a whole, such as the earth, [it would be illusory].

Because they are insentient, the potter and others are required for jars and the like; however, in this case [of Brahman], the cause is indeed sentience alone. Therefore, it does not require any other cause that is sentient by nature. Even though this cause is itself sentient, unlike a potter, it does not require a non-conscious material cause such as clay. (vv. 20–22)

[Objection: But even if the knowledge of the effect arises from the knowledge of the cause, it is impossible to know that which belongs to the same genus as the cause by means of that [knowledge]; therefore, how can there be "the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one"? To this he says: "And that" (tacceti). And that single cause of the world is indeed non-dual; it is neither different nor both different and non-different. The meaning is that since difference has never been perceived anywhere, it is impossible even to conceive of it in the cause.

[Objection: But surely the difference—that the pot is different from the self—is indeed experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To this he says: "Difference is conceptual" (*bhedah saṃvṛti*). For the manifestation of difference is dependent for its determination upon the knowledge of the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Since the status of being a substratum and a counter-correlate belongs only to those things already known as distinct, there is a mutual dependence in their determination; thus, because the appearance of difference is impossible at any time [prior to such knowledge], the meaning is that the perceived difference is merely illusory (*mithyābhūta*). "And therefore" (*ataśca*): because the object of cognition...

Because difference does not exist, even the appearance of objects as distinct is not ultimately real. For this reason, since there is no contact with difference characterized by division, it is established that the cause is eternal; and because there is an absence of internal difference of a similar kind, it is established that it is one and non-dual—this is the meaning. (29) Now, an objection: in the world, both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*) are seen to be distinct in the case of causes such as a jar.

Likewise, one might object that for a non-dual existent reality (*sad-vastu*), an effect cannot be produced without material cause (*nirupādāna*), and if it were to have such a cause, it would follow that it lacks an instrumental cause (*nirnimitta*). Anticipating this doubt, the author states its compatibility with both [conditions] through the passage beginning with "of clay, etc. (*mṛd-ādeḥ*). For clay and the like, being insentient, require a sentient potter distinct from themselves; however, the material cause of the universe, being itself sentient, does not require another sentient agent here. Furthermore, even though it is sentient, it has no requirement for a material cause in the form of something other than the power of the potter.

Because it is the very nature of the appropriation of the efficient cause (*nimitta*). For it is heard in this very context: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. From this, it is understood that the non-dual reality of *Sat* (Being) possesses both the state of being the efficient cause through its volition (*īkṣaṇa*) and the state of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) through becoming manifold. Therefore, the meaning is that the world has itself as both its efficient cause and its material cause. (30–32)

It cannot be stated what difference remains, or whose difference remains, and so forth. (27) First there must be knowledge of difference; only then can it exist, and only then can its classification be made. Furthermore, knowledge of difference occurs only when one knows that "this is that" and "that is this. Therefore, the definition of difference is impossible.

We proceed by accepting this very distinction based on a blind tradition. (To illustrate this clearly: only that which is "non-pot"—that which is not a pot—can have the distinction of being a "pot. That which is a non-pot is what possesses the distinction of being a pot. Thus, the situation is such that a distinction can only exist between that which is distinct and within that very thing itself.)

Two types of difference are recognized: one is that which exists when [the substratum] is present, and the other is that which remains [even when it is absent]. The first is also called "possessing difference" (*bhedavān*) because it is itself a difference.

1. And so it is said: "Therefore, indeed. 2. In reality, however, the word "also" (*api*) is used here to indicate that even in the case of a jar and the like, the potter possesses the status of the material cause (*upādāna*) through a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) directed toward the form of the shards; as stated in the *Nyāyaratnākara* (p. 330, first edition): "In whatever effect a person is the agent, he alone is the material cause. 3. The meaning of "if that [cause] were to be exclusively the material cause" is as follows. 4. [The reading is] *gha. ṇiktapi*.

768. O Brahmins, by means of dependence alone, there exists a power that is formless and composed of darkness; it is the one who brings about the destruction of all things through various manifestations. 22. O you who perform difficult deeds, it is joined with that very nature; the cause of all things is to be seen as such by all believers. 324. And because it is always free from defects, O best of gods, its existence as the threefold form is indeed logical for the believers at that time. 25.

[Objection: But how can such causality be possible for Brahman, who is changeless, unattached, and of the nature of pure Being? If you say it is "by means of Māyā," then [the fault of] mutual dependence arises. To this, he says: "By way of appearance" (*pratītyā*). This means established by mere appearance alone—just as a mirage or a city in the sky. Because it veils the self-luminous nature of Brahman, it is "darkness" (*tamas*); though it cannot be defined even by those capable of defining it, it is nevertheless "inexpressible" (*anirvacanīyā*) in all ways, such as being existent, non-existent, or both. || 332 ||

In this manner, although Brahman is changeless, its state as the creator of the six classes of beings and so forth is established through the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas belonging to that [Māyā], which is superimposed upon the real nature of Māyā. Nor does this result in the fallacy of duality; for since Māyā is indeterminable (anirvacanīya), there is no other "being" (sat) apart from it. (24) Having thus established non-duality, he now establishes its nature as Being (sat): "And that is always existent," etc. For, according to such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," Brahman, the cause of the world, is indeed of the nature of Being.

And thus, the intended meaning is as follows: "The subject of dispute is real, because it has the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpatva); for that which is real but lacks the nature of consciousness is not of the nature of consciousness, just like a snake [imagined] in a rope. He establishes the pervasion (vyāpti) with the words "of that which has the nature of consciousness": since Brahman, the substrate of that [world], exists at all times as the witness to both the perception and the sublation of the insentient phenomenal world (jaḍa-prapañca), it is indeed logical that its nature as consciousness is eternally real. || 35 ||

If it does not exist, it would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā). To consider both as one results in the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya). Furthermore, difference (bheda) must reside in a distinct entity; however, the term "difference" is never perceived independently. One perceives "the difference of X in Y," or "X is different from Y"—it is only in this manner that its cognition occurs.

Consequently, the distinction between "whose" and "in whom" is problematic; it must be understood that these two are separate. Even if one attempts to reconcile them as one, no difference will be established. Thus, the distinction between "the physician" (*bhisakam*) and "of the physician" (*bhisakasya*)—only when this knowledge of their distinctness exists can their differentiation be realized. In this way, circular reasoning (*ātmāśraya*) is clearly evident.

Even if one were to dispel the distress caused by the notion of origination by regarding difference as eternal, it would still be impossible to truly know [the object], for even if one considers it eternal, one cannot accept it as such because difference exists by its very nature (*nisarga*). If the entity is impermanent, then the difference residing within it must also necessarily be impermanent; therefore, difference is established merely through conceptual error (*bhrānti-mātra*). || 28 ||

Since the definition of difference is impossible, it follows naturally that even "difference-in-identity" (bhedābheda) is unacceptable. Therefore, Śiva alone—the one, non-dual, and eternal—is the cause of the universe. (29) Although on the level of empirical reality, the material cause (upādānakāraṇa), such as clay, and the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa), such as the potter's wheel, appear distinct, nevertheless, these do not exist separately within the cause of the world: Śiva alone is both the material and the instrumental cause.

Since [the world] arises from *māyā* and so forth, the weaver and others are merely instrumental causes; in reality, pure consciousness alone is the cause. Therefore, there is no need for any other conscious being. (30–31) Even though Śiva is himself conscious, he is not a cause like a potter, for he has no need to take up any materials external to himself in order to create the world.

A potter, however, requires ink [as a tool], but Śiva does not require even an insentient cause. (32) [Objection: A sentient being takes steps; how could an inert thing do so? Furthermore, how can there be the production of an effect from that which is inactive? The well-known answer is: "Through *māyā*. But for you, what is this *māyā* in relation to Śiva—is it real or unreal? To this, [the author replies]: "And by His own power" (*ca sva-śaktyā*). [The meaning is: by the existence of time and space. (32)† † [Note: The commentary clarifies that the effect arises through the power of time and space.]

Chapter 769: The gods consider that which is without holes and subtle to be the Self; therefore, they hold that its cause is the one, eternal Lord himself. (29) This entire world, including the gods, the Ākītas, and the Suras, is both existent and non-existent; thus say the bulls among the gods regarding its end. (27)

Since it might be asked, "How is it that the world does not possess the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa)? he says: "Because it is unreal" (avidyamānatvāt). This means [it is like] a snake or a rope-snake. For falsity (mithyātva) is observed to be pervaded by the nature of being unreal; and since that [unreality] is excluded from the conscious cause of the world, it excludes its own pervaded [property], namely falsity—this is the intended meaning. To establish this point, he applies the scriptural text: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 36 ||

Since, according to the manner stated, the cause of the world is the non-dual *Sat* (Being) alone, therefore this perceived effect consisting of name and form—the world itself—existed as *Sat* prior to its manifestation; it exists only as identical with the cause that is *Sat*, and not as something characterized by name and form. Thus, having introduced the theory of an unreal cause (*asatkāraṇapakṣa*) favored by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādins*) for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of that [unreal] cause, its rejection has been carried out.

By the passage beginning with "On this point, some say... and ending with "...how could the existent be born from the non-existent?", [the author] reveals the intended meaning of that scriptural statement through the words "It was non-existent in the beginning," and so forth. For indeed, since sprouts and the like arise from seeds and the like only after they have perished, there is no appearance [of an effect] without having destroyed the cause; thus, in that case, non-existence itself is the cause.

Thus, O nihilists (asad-vādins) ending with the Śūnyavādins, you who claim that even the root cause of the world is likewise of an unreal nature! [Your view is] erroneous, because it is impossible for a cause that has perished—like the power to produce a son in a corpse of Devadatta—to possess the capacity to generate an effect; and furthermore, because at the time of the effect such as a sprout, the specific configurations and constituent parts of the cause, such as the seed, persist. Therefore, it is not logical for the non-existent to be a cause. Thus, their position is deluded. 37.

(They say: Through the unconscious form of ignorance, the power of *māyā* exists merely as a mental appearance; therefore, it is not a real entity. Even the learned cannot describe Śaṅkara’s inert power (*jaḍa-śakti*) in any way, because first of all it does not exist, and secondly, it cannot be described as it truly is. || 23 ||

Śiva alone, who is connected in an undifferentiated manner with that power of *māyā* which makes even that which is impossible to obtain appear as if obtained, is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of all.

Māyā is related to Śiva in such a way that it cannot be conceived as being entirely separate from Him; therefore, His relationship with it is even more intimate. Likewise, we and our capacity are joined in such a way that "it is impossible to conceive of the two as separate, for there is no cognition [of them] apart."

Alternatively, just as the redness of a ruby becomes connected with a crystal when it is placed near it—that is, superimposed upon it—such that it appears as if the crystal were red or as if there were a unity between them; in the same way, Māyā is superimposed upon Śiva, so that He appears as if He were "possessed of Māyā" (māyī). It is the one possessed of Māyā alone who performs creation and so forth, as stated in the *Vedāntasūtra* (2.1.14): "The possessor of Māyā creates."

Due to the imbalance of the qualities (*guṇa-vaiṣamya*) superimposed upon Māyā, the differentiation of activities such as creation and so forth appears. Just as, despite all worldly transactions occurring—such as "the world was created," "the world exists," or "the world has ended"—the world is not actually created and so on, but is eternal; likewise, although there are various designations such as Śiva, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu, and consequently the appearance of creation and so forth, this is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*).

The cause of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) must itself be empirical, not non-empirical. Therefore, both *māyā* and Śiva, who is connected to it, are indeed empirical. The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, is Śiva alone. Thus, there is no inconsistency in the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*). (34) That Śiva is eternally existent because he is consciousness. Whatever is devoid of consciousness is necessarily non-existent.

Furthermore, since that which is insentient (*acit*) lacks a witness, it is unauthoritative and cannot be experienced. Moreover, only insentient things such as forest-serpents and the like are observed to be non-existent. Therefore, it is certain that whatever is non-existent is insentient. Consequently, because it is sentient and not insentient, the Self (*chiva*) is indeed existent, eternal, and non-dual.

(That which is real cannot be sublated at any time, and it is consciousness—that is, self-luminous knowledge. || 35-36 || This entire world existed as "Being" (Sat) with unmanifest name and form prior to its manifestation. What deluded person would say that the world was non-existent (Asat) before its origin? || 37 || However, when one reflects upon the reality, it becomes clear that the causal state cannot possess a different nature [from the effect]; otherwise, even the son of a barren woman could be the cause of all things.

770. In the *Brahmagītā*, it is stated that a non-existent cause is illogical when defining the true nature of reality; for even the son of a barren woman would [absurdly] become the cause of all things by his own nature. (28) If it is argued that this [causality] occurs through their own power (*svaśakti*), [we reply: there is no power in what is non-existent, because we observe that a seed must be existent. (29) Indeed, the power to produce a sprout and so forth is observed only in an existing substance; it does not exist in a non-existent thing, because such a power is never observed therein. (40)

He establishes that very point with the words "the non-existent is not a cause," and so forth. First of all, it is not logical for the non-existent to possess causality; for that which is in every respect indefinable (*nirupākhyam*) cannot possibly be a substratum for a property characterized by causality. And if it were such a substratum, then since there would be no difference from the son of a barren woman in terms of their total non-existence, it would follow as a consequence that [the non-existent] is the cause of everything—this is the meaning. || 38 ||

[The opponent] restates [the objection] in order to refute it, suggesting that even for a non-existent cause of the world, causality is established by virtue of its own power, using the words "by its own power" (*svaśaktitayā*). He refutes this with the words "power" (*śaktiḥ*). (Verse 39) Even the power to produce effects such as sprouts is determined—through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—to belong only to existing things like seeds, not to what is non-existent. Therefore, because it contradicts observed reality, the postulation of power in a non-existent thing is improper; this is the meaning. (Verse 40)

If it were to become a cause, then even before [the effect] exists, one would have to admit that the effect already exists; for if it did not exist and yet were to arise, then oil could also arise from sand. It is precisely because the oil exists within the sesame seed that it can arise from it. Prior to roasting, names such as "soup" or "oil" do not apply to the sesame seeds, but they begin to be used after the roasting. This is what constitutes "arising."

Therefore, the reason is precisely "being" (*sat*), not "non-being" (*asat*). (38) Could it not be that the non-existent (*asat*) becomes the cause of everything through its own power? No, it cannot. [For] power belongs either to the existent (*sat*) or to the non-existent (*asat*). If it were the non-existent, then how could the non-existent ever become even a cause? If it were the existent, [then] power is observed only in seeds and the like which are existent, not in what is non-existent.

The capacity to produce a sprout resides everywhere within the seed and so forth; it does not exist in what is non-existent (*asat*). (There is no experience whatsoever of such a capacity belonging to that which "is not. As for those people who claim that this capacity exists even in the absence of gems and the like—such as the ability to burn a mine—that too is refuted.)

The capacity of fire to burn can be obstructed by a single jewel; there is such experience that as long as the jewel remains, the fire is unable to burn. Therefore, to postulate a capacity in the absence of the jewel is fallacious, unexperienced, and consequently invalid.

Now, even if one were to argue that the absence of the jewel (*maṇi*) has no efficacy whatsoever, yet there will be efficacy in that fire which exists when the jewel is absent; thus, efficacy can only belong to what is existent, not to what is non-existent. Furthermore, if the absence of an obstructor (*pratibandhakābhāva*) were included within the category of causes, then it would be impossible to have a cognition of the obstructor in its capacity as the cause of the absence of a cause.

The knowledge of the absence of the cause—which is conjoined with the obstructing factor—is dependent upon the knowledge of that obstructing factor; furthermore, that [knowledge] is dependent upon the knowledge of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) and the obstructing factor. Therefore, the knowledge of the obstructing factor is impossible. Since *sāmānyalakṣaṇā* (universal cognition) cannot be accepted, the knowledge of all obstructing factors is likewise not possible. In that case, the knowledge of the cause as qualified by the absence of those [obstructing factors] would, of course, be even more impossible. As stated previously (verse...):

94) The causality (*kāryatā*) of non-existence through destruction (*dhvaṃsābhāva*) has also been refuted. Therefore, the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika claim that just as non-existence is an effect, so too is its cause, is rendered untenable. Thus, Udayana’s view—“Just as existence [is considered], so too non-existence is held to have effects and causes; obstruction is the absence of causal conditions (*visāmagrī*), and the obstructer is the cause of that [absence]”—(Kusumāñjali 1.10) is also rejected.

In every respect, this remains unestablished. (In his commentary on the *Advaitadīpikā* and the *Pañcapādikā-prasthāna*, Mūlarasiṃha Svāmī has examined this matter through the analogy of burning a funeral pyre. Furthermore, the desire for knowledge persists.

Chapter 5, Verse 771: Is that power (śakti) existent (satī) or non-existent (asatī)? If it is existent, then how can that power reside in a barren woman’s son? For in the world, the state of being a substratum (āśrayatva) is indeed observed [only] for what exists, and not for what does not exist. If it is non-existent, how can that non-existent power be the sustainer of an array of effects? Indeed, this son of a barren woman is certainly not a sustainer of any effect; for it is precisely because of that [non-existence] that the property of being a sustainer is not observed in him.

If that power (śakti) were either existent or non-existent, then scripture would be the source [of its proof]. Therefore, by its own nature, it cannot be the cause of anything at all. (44) He refutes [the opponent's position] even by means of the unreality of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), stating: "That too... He restates the first alternative and then rejects it with: "If that... How could a power in the form of a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpā śakti*) be an attribute (*dharma*) of that which is devoid of all attributes (*nirupākhyasya*)? For we neither see nor can logically maintain the connection of such a power with things that are absolutely non-existent, such as the son of a barren woman.

Furthermore, the state of being the substratum for such a power is observed only in the case of existing things like seeds and the like, but not in the case of non-existent things like a human horn. Therefore, since it would follow that it must be of a positive (bhāva) nature—just like the seed and so forth on account of being its substratum—it is not logical to postulate that a non-existent thing possesses a power that is of a positive nature. This is the meaning. (41) He states and refutes the second alternative with the words: "If that [power] were non-existent... (sā'satī cet).

For the power that is postulated in order to establish the causality of a non-existent thing is itself non-existent; thus he says that its capacity to bring about an effect is as impossible as that of the son of a barren woman. [Objection: Let it be granted, then, that such a capacity exists for the non-existent by virtue of its own nature. To this he replies: "In the capacity of being a producer" (*nirvāhakatva*). And thus, even if a power of the nature of a non-existent is postulated, it does not [establish] the non-existent.

The meaning is that [the author] is able to establish causality. (42–43) He refutes the third [position] with the words: "Power is either existent or non-existent. Regarding the phrase "the conjunction of two defects": the meaning is that the same two defects would follow even for the positions that power is both existent and non-existent. He concludes the demonstration of the non-causality of the non-existent with the word: "Therefore" (ataḥ). (44)

If that which is non-existent (*asat*) possesses power (*sāmarthya*), would that power be existent (*sat*), non-existent, or both existent and non-existent? If it were existent, its status as non-existent could not persist. In this world, the substratum of the existent is always observed to be existent, never non-existent; therefore, if one accepts that the non-existent has an existent power as its substratum, the non-existent itself would result in being existent, which would lead to the fallacy of abandoning one's own thesis (*pratijñāhāni*). || 41 ||

If power (*śakti*) is non-existent (*asat*), how can that which is non-existent—that which does not exist—accomplish the task? Have you never seen that which is not bread perform the task of filling the stomach? Since even things like a barren woman’s son, being non-existent by their very nature, do not accomplish any task, how could the non-existent power residing within them possibly do so? Accomplishing a task is a specific characteristic [of existence].

[This] has been correctly perceived among the real entities within saṃsāra! (Therefore, since the conclusion of accepting this specific quality—either the power or its substratum—is to regard them as real, the fallacy of abandoning one's initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) is certain. || 42-43 || If one were to consider power to be of both real and unreal natures, [then first of all, it would mean that a single entity is both real and unreal].

O you who speak of the impossible! In that case, the defects of both the "existent" (sat) and "non-existent" (asat) positions would apply; therefore, one cannot accept even the existent as the cause. Thus, the view that the non-existent is the cause of everything by its own power is merely an illusion. (44) The doctrine of the non-existent cause is indeed contemptible, for it is not established upon any sound reasoning. Furthermore, O believer! Only the existent is the cause of all things, not the non-existent. (45)
Prior to creation, all this was the existent (sat) in the form of the cause; that cause was non-dual (aditīya) and without origin.

772. Therefore, this assertion that "it was non-existence" is mere prattle and lacks logical justification; hence, O believers in existence, that [Being] alone is the cause of all things. Having seen that everything was indeed Being as the cause, and knowing that this cause is both existent and devoid of specific differentiation, it was not produced by any prior effort. Through the ripening of time and karma, it has resorted to its own inherent state.

Thus, because the theory of a non-existent cause is untenable, the Śruti refutes it by means of the word "tu" (but) and concludes with the theory of an existent cause: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. He shows this [in the commentary] with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). The phrase "nāsat" (not non-existent) expresses the intended meaning of the word "tu" found in the Śruti. || 45 ||

Thus, having first asserted the thesis that by knowing one thing everything is known, and having established—by means of examples such as clay—that the effect is non-different from its cause in order to prove that [thesis], [the author] now asks: what is that single reality whose knowledge brings about this result? It is the Being (sat), which is taught as Brahman in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

For the intended meaning is that if the world is an effect of That, then by the knowledge of its cause, [the world] is known. To demonstrate that it is an effect of That, its creation from That is described in such passages as, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and so forth. Having introduced that creation, the author grasps it through the subsequent description of its nature with the words beginning with "That," etc. "Free from beginning and end": the beginning is origination and the end is destruction; it is free from both of these. (46)

Now, one might ask: how can there arise from the non-dual, existent nature (sad-rūpa), which is of a single kind, a manifold creation consisting of the world of objects (para-pañca)? To this, he says: "by the residual impressions (vāsanā) of a previous cycle. This means it is conjoined with both the latent impression produced by the experience of the world that dissolved during the past dissolution (pralaya) and the mental trace (saṃskāra) born thereof. "By the ripening of time and karma" means: by that which is brought about by time through the karma of living beings—that is, by the ripening of merit and demerit, which consists in their readiness to yield their fruits. "Resorting to the power of Being (sattva)" means: [resorting to]...

The meaning is: "delimited by that mental modification (vṛtti) which consists of a transformation of the eternal reality that serves as the material cause of the internal organ, and which has as its object the manifold of effects to be perceived externally. || 47 ||

Or rather, it is not perceived by the ignorant. || 46 || Due to the conjunction of causes and the ripening of karma, from the intense latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous actions, that Cit endowed with the power of *māyā*—residing within the *sāttvika* state of *māyā*—performed the creative play at the beginning of creation, just as a spider weaves its web.

Immediately thereafter, according to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) formed by his previous creation, he first made himself into space (*ākāśa*). Having become space, that very self made itself into air (*vāyu*). In this same manner, he created fire, water, and earth. In the present Upaniṣad, earth is referred to as "food" (*anna*). (47–49) Furthermore, that Cause-Brahman [created] those five elements...

To perform the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) of those respective portions, one should divide each portion into two equal parts. Then, each of these parts should be divided into four threads, while one part is left as it was. In this way, fifty percent [of the original] is taken; on one side, twelve percent is taken from each of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) in this manner—thus, five-fifths of the portions of the great elements are taken.

Then, by mixing each of the twelve percent portions of air and the other elements into fifty percent of space (ākāśa), one hundred percent—that is, the complete substance—is formed again; because space is predominant therein and because it is a form composed of all five elements, it is called "five-fold compounded space" (pañcīkṛtākāśa).

By combining the remaining portions of the four elements—excluding the portion of wind that was assigned to wind itself—which each consist of twelve percent, with the wind, the quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta) wind is formed. In this same manner, the quintuplicated fire, the quintuplicated water, and the quintuplicated earth are formed.

1. "Time" (*kāla*) and "fruition of karma" (*karmavipāka*); the compound of these two is [the meaning of] *tanetaya*. It should be understood that "time" is the relationship between the material cause (*mātrā*) and consciousness (*cit*), as stated in [Yogasūtra] 2.2.10. For this very reason, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) is also appropriate, since the status of time as a separate category of reality (*padārthāntara*) is not accepted. 2. Gha: *śataiḥ kāra°*. 3. Ḍa: *jñānatva*.

Thinking, "May I become the King of the gods," the powerful one resolved to create for the sake of the gods. First, he created space and wind from the thief of the sacrificial offering; then, having seen fire, and then water, and then the earth which is designated by the word *anara* (the non-moving), the gods [proceeded]. O best of gods, those three causes—Brahman, the elements, and fire—each having been made twofold, [he placed them] in their midst.

Taking that [unmanifest] and dividing it into parts for each of those [elements], the divine one takes four parts from them; having taken those four, he makes them the cause of the four elements in their proper order. According to the sequence of the elements, by means of half of one [part] at a time, he forms each one. Thus, taking these intermediate portions himself, the divine one creates each one by means of half of the interval between the elements; such is the sequence.

"I shall become many" means that, without depending on any external material cause (*upādāna*), I shall manifest the manifold world in my own essential form. But, one might object, since it is impossible for the Self—which is changeless, partless, and of the nature of pure consciousness—to become many, the Sāṃkhya doctrine of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) must be what is intended by the scriptural statement: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

If this is so, let it be. For it is impossible for that [Pradhāna] to possess the power of seeing; therefore, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa composed the Sūtra: “Because of seeing, not the one devoid of sound. How, then, is the becoming manifold of such a Brahman possible? To this he says: “Possessing power” (śaktimat). Power (śakti) is Māyā, which consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas;

it is designated by the word "power" so that its independence—like that of the *prakṛti* accepted by the Sāṃkhyas—may be avoided. And the possession of power by Paraśiva is recorded in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:

“His power is heard to be indeed manifold” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8). Although in the Chāndogya recension only the creation of fire and the other elements is recorded, and not that of ether and air, nevertheless, since their creation is recorded in the Taittirīyaka, he shows them here by incorporating them according to the principle of the "harmonization of qualities" (guṇopasaṃhāra-nyāya), stating: "Again, that... Bādarāyaṇa also determined in the section beginning with "But the ether [is not produced], because of the non-hearing [of its origin]" and "By this, air is explained," that ether and air are unproduced; yet, regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "It created fire," etc., which [mentions only these].

The creation from fire (*tejas*) is recorded in the scripture; he states that [creation] with the word "from that" (*tataḥ*). The meaning is: having first created wind (*vāyu*), which had assumed the form of fire, from that very source, he subsequently created the waters, which had assumed the form of fire. Furthermore, in this context, the ablative case in *tataḥ* is the ablative prescribed by the rule "the source (*prakṛti*) of the agent of birth" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.4.30), and not the ablative characterized by direction or proximity. This is because the case-ending of a *kāraka* (syntactic relation) is more authoritative than a case-ending used as an *upapada* (secondary word), even when the latter is supported by the ellipsis of the word "immediately after" (*anantaram*).

And there is no such contradiction regarding fire being born from Brahman in its true nature as existence (*sadrūpa*). This is because, in reality, air is non-different from Brahman. Bādarāyaṇa also set forth this very point in his Sūtras: "Fire [is born] from that, and so too [air]," and so on. Regarding the phrase "that which was denoted by the word *anna*": the meaning is that which was expressed here by the word *anna* in the Śruti passage, "They created food," namely, Earth.
