And that the word *anna* occurring in the Śruti denotes Earth has been established by Vyāsa.

It has been established [by us] from other scriptural passages concerning the nature of the earth’s authority (pṛthivy-adhikāra-rūpa-śabda). Regarding the term "the higher" (parām): it refers to the subtle state by virtue of being quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta). In the Śruti, following the creation of fire and water, the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) is recorded: "He made each of those three-fold. This indicates that quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) is implied by the inclusion of the creation of ether and air within the general creation of the elements. He demonstrates this with the words beginning "tasmāt" and so forth. Furthermore, this quintuplication is described in the tenth chapter of the *Śivamahātmyakhaṇḍa*.

This has been explained by us in detail previously. Regarding the phrase "taking four parts from each of those": when those twenty [parts] are divided into four groups, one takes four parts belonging to the ether (*viyat*), and likewise takes four half-parts belonging to the four elements beginning with air (*vāyu*). Thus, the causal Brahman joins each single part with one half-part. In this manner, having taken four parts belonging to the half-parts of the elements beginning with air, one [part] consists of a quartet of half-parts belonging to elements distinct from those respective elements.
The meaning of the syllables is that which joins together the *tāla*. (50–54)

In this manner, having rendered all beings fivefold, the causal Brahman created the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and the worlds (*bhuvana*). According to the sequence of time and in accordance with the karma of living beings, He created four types of creatures: those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*), those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*), those born from sweat (*svedaja*), and those born from sprouts (*udbhijja*). (By "living beings" here is meant the body, for it has already been stated that the conscious principle is distinct from the entered spirit, and the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) occurs [within the body]).

1. [The variant] *gha. ṇdarayosta*. 2. Here, in the *Chāndogya*, the word "this" (*etad*) refers to the earth, because the sequence of the manifestation of the elements has been set forth; because its black and white color has been stated as belonging to that very [earth] in the passage, "That which is the blackness of food is of her"; and because even the well-known traditional interpretation—namely that [the word "this"] refers to the earth from another statement, "From water, the earth"—is set aside by the context and other such factors: this is the meaning of the Sūtra.

Thus, O bulls among the gods, having quintuplicated all these elements, Brahmā, the causal source, creates the eight worlds. Through the ripening of time and by the power of the karma of living beings, he likewise creates the egg-born, the viviparous, the sweat-born, and the soil-born. Pervading everywhere in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), O virtuous ones, Brahmā assumes various names and forms according to his own will.
Therefore, although this world appears as if it were real by its own nature, it is not so; for apart from its cause, it does not exist, just like a non-entity. || 57 ||

Regarding the statement, "born from an egg, born from a womb, and born from a sprout," the meaning of "born from an egg" (*aṇḍaja*) is as follows: the inclusion of those born from sweat (*svedaja*) and so forth within the category of "egg-born" is traditionally taught in the scriptures. For this very reason, the authors of the *Āpadevī* [commentary] state: "The inclusion of those born from sweat and those born from heat/moisture (*saṃśokaja*) occurs, as far as possible, within the categories of 'egg-born' and 'sprout-born' respectively."

He states the meaning of the Vedic passage, "That divinity, having entered these beings by means of this very life-breath, differentiated names and forms," as follows: "Brahma. The meaning is that Brahma, the cause of the universe, having entered all bodies—from the body of Brahmā down to the bodies of grass—just as the sun's reflection appears in water, jars, and bubbles, and having entered them in the form of consciousness alone, differentiated names and forms according to the respective kalpas, thinking, "This is such-and-such a name, and this is such-and-such a form. (55-56)

In order to further solidify the non-difference of the effect from its cause, which was previously established through the example of clay and so forth, the Śruti provides examples such as the jar and its cause, the lump of clay, and the cloth and its cause, the threads, in the passage beginning with, "That which is the red color of fire," and so on. This entire world, which is an effect of the fivefold-compounded elements (pañcīkṛtabhūta), does not exist apart from its cause—the subtle elements—even though it appears to have a real nature. || 57 ||

55. Just as the sun enters into water and becomes waves and so forth, so too Brahman has entered everywhere; and just as in a previous kalpa, it established those same names and forms in their respective divisions.

The intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties become connected with Mahādeva, who possesses inconceivable and infinite power; consequently, the intellect itself begins to act as the possessor of consciousness (*cetana*). Just as a mirror appears radiant when in contact with the sun, so too does the intellect assume the nature of the conscious subject. Through this, one’s own true nature becomes distinct from the intellect, and becoming filled with joy and horripilation (*pulakita*), one begins to realize: "I am indeed Mahādeva alone—the one who is happy, the one who is suffering, the one who is deluded," and so forth.

Not appearing as distinct from [Śiva's] powers such as *ṛddhi*, but being perceived as one with Him—this indeed is the entry (*anupraveśa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) into Śiva. (In the term *anupraveśa*, the prefix *anu* signifies "after the connection with a limb. || 56 || Although this entire world appears as if it were real, it does not exist independently apart from Śiva, its cause.

(Alternatively, for the sake of the world: this entire universe is the effect of the five-fold compounded elements (*pañcīkṛtabhūta*). Whether in its gross form as it appears, or in its subtle causal form, there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from these great elements. || 57 || That which is red, such as mountains or fire, is the result of the uncompounded (*apañcīkṛta*) fire element. That which is white is the result of the uncompounded water element. That which is black is the result of the subtle earth element. || 58 ||

Apart from these three fires, there is no other fire that has been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*). These three fires exist by virtue of conventional usage (*vyavahāradṛṣṭyā*); any gross fire other than these is merely wind, nothing but wind.

Regarding this, there is a commentary (*bhāṣya*) serving as an explanatory restatement (*anuvādasthānīya*): "And one's own name, form, and so forth—the entire collection of modifications—is real only through the Self (*sadātmanā*); in itself, it is indeed unreal" (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, p. 238). [The term *jarāyuja* refers to those born from a womb.]

Chapter 5: 775–1 That which is red in water is always the essence of fire; that which is white belongs to water, and that which is black is indeed of the earth. There is no [quality] beyond these three; that fire is always difficult for the senses to perceive. Indeed, what is called "fire" is merely a modification of the wind and water, held together by speech. O gods, it is the truth that there are only three elements, and not fire. That which is red in fire is always the essence of heat (tejas).

That which is white is indeed the sky; that which is black is simply the earth. There is nothing beyond Being (Sat); the Sun is always [Being], of this there is no doubt. (61) Only those who lack discrimination think that the Sun alone is the end. In this same way, O best of gods, the Moon and the Fire are to be understood. (62) Whatever entities such as mountains, the elements, and the luminaries exist, they do not exist apart from Brahman; only Being (Sat) exists eternally. (63) Anticipating the question, "How is this possible? he provides the justification: "yad etat... (That which...).

In fire produced from wood, lightning, gems, and so forth, three colors—red, white, and black—are manifested. Among these, that which is red is the form of the fiery element (*tejas*); that which is white is [the form] of water (*ap*); and that which is black is [the form] of earth (*bhūmi*). (58) Now, one might ask: even if these forms belong to other things, why should fire not be the substratum (*dharmin*) possessing those properties? To this, he says: "It does not exist."

The meaning is that these three forms alone are designated by the word "fire" (agni) and so forth; there is no other reality whatsoever distinct from them. Now, one might object: how can the object denoted by the word "fire," which is experienced as being capable of burning, cooking, and so on, be denied? To this, he says: "It is merely a modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇamātra*).

The meaning is that this modification—a particular configuration denoted by words such as "small" and so forth—which exists apart from the three elements that serve as its cause, is initiated by speech alone and does not exist in reality. (Verses 59–61) Regarding the word *anyathā*: the meaning is that the empirical treatment of the effect as distinct from the cause is produced by delusion. By means of an extended application (*atideśa*), he states the meaning already explained in detail in the Śruti passage beginning with, "That which is the red color of fire," and so forth, using the word *evam* (thus).

"62. Regarding the phrase 'the jar, the cloth, and so forth': just as these [objects], such as jars and the like, do not exist apart from their constituent causes—fire, water, and earth—so too this entire world, consisting of the elements and elemental derivatives (*bhūta-bhautika*), does not exist apart from Brahman, who is its cause. The meaning is that only that which is of the nature of Being (*sad-rūpa*) exists at all times. 63.

That fire is merely a designation; in reality, it is nothing at all. In this same manner, the three colors of the sun—red, white, and black—are simply the three *sakṣama* elements in their causal form. Apart from these, the sun is also a mere name and not a substantial entity. To claim that the sun exists as a distinct effect separate from its cause is merely a delusion spoken by the ignorant, who act under such a misconception.

Furthermore, the fourteen worlds, lightning, trees, walls, and other such objects, as well as the bodies of living beings and the universe—all these are nothing whatsoever apart from their own causes. (Note: "Śabda" refers to that which has speech as its support; thus, it exists as mere name, but there are no external objects existing as substantial entities. Now, one might object: "Is this not the very position of the Kṣapaṇakas who deny external objects? To this we reply: No, because our view is that the ultimate reality is the non-dual knowledge in the form of Śiva, whereas in their doctrine such a thing is not accepted; this constitutes the distinction.
(From the *Brahmagītā*, verse 776).

By the power of that very latent impression (vāsanā), one should burn away the egoistic notion (*ahaṃmati*) regarding the body and so forth, which is as fluid as water when the fuel has been consumed. (64) States such as the heart and others are not the referent of "I," because they are insentient by nature and because they are always subject to change. (65) Just as the quality of being clay is discarded from a pot once it has been fashioned, so too are the body and other things abandoned once they have been experienced. (66) Therefore, having relinquished the notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, one should dissolve the sense of "I" into the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*). (67)

Since the individual soul (*jīva*), which will immediately be taught as being identical with Brahman through the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) in its ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), is itself the ultimate reality, the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) has that [soul] as its sole object. Yet, this notion arises as "I am a human" with respect to the body and so forth—things that are effects, unreal, and subject to dissolution. Therefore, he says: "from previous [births]" (*pūrvapūrva*). The current delusion of "I" with respect to the body and so forth is rooted in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the delusions of past births. In this way, it was also so in past births; thus, because it is beginningless (*anāditva*), there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). || 64 ||

Starting from the passage beginning with “*atramaritam*” and ending with “*dadhnaḥ saumya*,” the preceding Śruti has elaborated that because the body—composed of mind, speech, breath, flesh, blood, marrow, and bone—is insentient as an effect of the three *guṇas*, it is insentient by nature; therefore, in the ultimate sense, it cannot be the object of the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), whose sole domain is the conscious Self. He explains this in connection with that [passage]: “The body and so forth. Through delusion alone are the body and other such things the referent of the notion of “I,” but not upon critical examination.

Because the functions of the father and mother have been consumed, this [body] is characterized by the consumption of the three elements—tejas (fire), ap (water), and anna (earth)—which are the coarse, medium, and subtle [forms]. Growth occurs through the accumulation of these very elements; therefore, its manifestation also arises from them alone. To illustrate this, he says: "By earth, water, and... (Verse 66). He states the resulting purport of the scriptural passage concerning the origin [of the body]: "Therefore... (Verse 67). Because the body, senses, and mind are merely a modification of speech (vācārambhaṇamātra).

The meaning is that, since the selfhood of the body and so forth arises from their being effects of the elements such as fire and the rest, one should abandon the notion "I am this" and instead maintain that notion solely within the immutable, eternal consciousness that is the seat of the Self. || 67 ||

Since Brahman alone is the ultimate cause, all these are nothing other than Brahman. (Verses 59–63) Due to the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) accumulated from previous births, a firm delusion arises in every lifetime regarding the collection of body and senses, such as "I am this" or "this is mine. (This addresses the doubt that the knowledge of a real object can, through mental impressions, become a cause of delusion, as seen in cases such as the [illusory] snake.)

Therefore, for one who is afraid of the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), if there were no knowledge of anything more real than it, one would have to accept that some part of the phenomenal world is real; otherwise, if such a thing is not accepted, the very effort [to seek liberation] becomes untenable, and one would be forced to admit the perceived phenomenal world itself as real. The Purāṇas state that although impressions (*saṃskāra*) may indeed arise from effort, they ought to be produced by the knowledge of a real object, which is not the case here.

It is observed that even the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by a previous delusion can serve as the cause for a subsequent one; for instance, when a snake is seen in a rope due to a real perception of a snake elsewhere, the rope may at times appear as a snake again through the force of those very impressions.

No one is harmed by the fault of speaking like a madman; for instance, when someone says, "He is the Prime Minister of India," is it necessary to believe that he has actually been a prime minister at some point? Or, when one says, "This is Christ," does it mean the speaker has gained knowledge of a real Christ? Thus, neither the object appearing before one nor the mental impression produced by it is real. (64)

These objects, such as the body and so forth, are in reality not the meaning of the word "I," nor are they the Self, because they are material. Their origin, intellect, and all else arise solely from the gross elements; therefore, their material nature is well-established. Just as a wall is destroyed by water and a mud house is built up by water alone, in the same way, the body and other things are likewise nourished (developed) by the five gross elements.

1. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), certainties such as "I am superior" regarding the body, senses, and so forth, are included. 2. And how can this be true? 3. By this [it is shown that] the knowledge of a real object becomes a cause of error through the medium of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); for, both from scripture and from experience, it is known that knowledge itself is thus [the cause]. Therefore, let there be a real object of which you speak. For this very reason, the view that "previously the individual soul (*jīva*) was indeed Śiva, but then, having forgotten its own nature, it became bound, and by being awakened it is liberated," is also refuted; for if bondage were beginningless, why would this wicked one not be born again?

Chapter 5, Verse 777: Just as curds are churned by the churning-stick to produce butter, so indeed do all states of being, such as intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, emerge from the elements. (58) Then, the wise one, having again analyzed the elemental body, should direct his mind toward the Supreme Self, which is the witness within the eye of all. (59) Even when this [Self] is not perceived due to the absence of instruction, it is nonetheless present; therefore, one must certainly strive for its realization, for it is never otherwise. (70)

Therefore, O wise one, having abandoned the notion of "I" regarding this body, you who possess discerning intellect should cultivate the realization of the eternal "I" within the all-seeing form of consciousness. (79) When one abandons the notions of "I" and "mine" directed toward the collection of body and senses, and beholds one's own Self, then this person becomes absorbed [in that state]. (72) At that time, he sleeps, and no perception of suffering or the like remains. Thus is seen the supreme absorption of this embodied being into the realization of his own Self. (73) For this reason as well, the wise man, having abandoned the intellect attached to the body and so forth, should cultivate the realization of the "I" as the immediate manifestation of consciousness, which is the all-seeing form of pure awareness. (74)

If it is asked how fire, water, and earth can be the effects of the elements, the senses, and the mind, [the answer is as follows]: Just as ghee, though distinct from curds, is cited by the Śruti as being the effect of curds in the passage, "O gentle one, from curds [comes ghee]" (*dadhnaḥ saumya*), which explains that ghee arises from curds; and just as through churning, curds undergo a transformation into ghee that is distinct from them—so too, through the specific process of digestion by the internal fire, water, and earth, there occurs a specific transformation into the form of the body, the senses, and the mind. This is the meaning. 68.

By establishing through the analogy of curd that the body and so forth are composed of fear (or the elements), it is proven that the non-material existence [of the self] mentioned by Rāma is beyond reproach; thus he says: "The bodily aggregate is elemental. (69) The Vaiśeṣikas hold that while speech and breath are effects and thus elemental, the mind is eternal. With this intention—asking how the mind can be elemental—the son asked: "May the Blessed One explain this to me further."

In this regard, the father’s further [explanation] begins with “consisting of sixteen parts,” and so forth. The father’s intention—that the mind consists of food—is summarized as follows: because those who have studied the Vedas lack illumination due to the depletion [of their essence] by means of food up until the sixteenth day, whereas they possess illumination again through its replenishment by that same [food], the mind is therefore composed of food; he grasps this in the words, “It is nourished by food, not when one has not eaten. By the term “intellect” (buddhi), the mind itself is meant. || 70 ||

He states that even for the justification of a mental affliction (*aghra*) that has arisen, its result is precisely the attainment of an undesired state distinct from what was previously mentioned: "Therefore, [the result] of a wicked mind... (71–74).

From this [realization], one becomes weary of that very [world]; this fact becomes known. || 66 || Therefore, a wise person should abandon the conviction regarding the collection of the body and so forth—such as "this is I" or "that is mine"—and instead make the firm resolve: "I am the witness-consciousness. || 67 || Just as butter is extracted from curd through churning, in the same way, the objects such as the intellect (the internal organ) are produced from the great elements. || 68 ||

One should reach this certainty: "This aggregate of material elements has come into being; having abandoned it all, I am the witness, whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa), and I am eternally so. (When separate entities join together and perform a function, that collection of things is called a *saṃghāta*, and each individual thing within that collection is called *saṃhata*. For this reason, the body, the senses, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and so forth, are referred to as an aggregate. || 69 ||
What work is there for the internal organ here? For it is nourished by this [Brahman].
(1) Gha. I. Ca. *śyāyate*; (2) Ca. Jña. *bhukte*; (3) Ña. Ṇe *pañcadaśadi°*; (4) Dha. Ḍa. Ca. *pyāyite*; (5) Ha. *bhukte*.
**Brahmagītā:** Whatever is perceived by the Witness, all that is solely Brahman. That is the Truth, it is to be sought; that is the meaning of "Thou" (*tat tvam*), of this there is no doubt. (75)

Having first asserted the proposition that "this [world] was indeed one, without a second," the meaning of the first part of the passage has been explained by establishing the following: since the triad of elements characterized by fire, water, and earth, as well as the collection of material objects to be enjoyed produced from them, the bodies which are the seats of enjoyment, and the sense organs which are the instruments of enjoyment—all these exist solely for the sake of that [Brahman]—they are merely modifications of speech (*vācārambhaṇam*). Therefore, because they do not possess an independent existence separate from Him, there is no contradiction of the non-duality (*advaita*) asserted at the outset.

Nevertheless, to refute the objection that the non-duality (*advaita*) thesis would be undermined because the enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*), being eternal, possess a difference characterized by being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that [non-duality], the latter portion beginning with "Uddālaka Āruṇi" is stated.

In this regard, although the enjoyer—unlike the objects of enjoyment—is not imagined (*kalpita*) but is indeed ultimately real (*paramārtha*), nevertheless, there is no loss of the non-duality thesis due to a difference having him as its counter-correlate; for, since he is of the very nature of Brahman, there is an absence of difference. This is expressed in the passage: "This is that subtle essence; all this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu."

That which is exceedingly subtle because it transcends the range of speech and mind, yet is perceived as the "all" through superimposition upon Brahman—this entire world is, by this very [Brahman], like silver on a mother-of-pearl shell; and that very Brahman is the Self, because it is the substratum for all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*), and because it provides the existence for everything imagined. That Brahman, characterized in this way, is indeed you, O Śvetaketu; you are not different from It. And Śvetaketu is an illustration representing the entire class of enjoyers.

He explains this scriptural passage with the words "If this," and so forth. "Brahman alone" means that because [the world] is superposed upon Brahman, it has no existence apart from it. Just as when the sublation occurs—[thinking] "That which was this snake is a rope" and "That which was this silver is a piece of mother-of-pearl"—there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Regarding the phrase "Thou art That": the meaning of the word "Thou" is the individual soul (*jīva*), yet in the ultimate sense, that is indeed that very same pure consciousness-Brahman; the meaning is that one should not entertain any doubt that it is merely imagined like a horse or a cow. || 75 ||

On the day one does not eat, the covering within the belly is forgotten; therefore, there is no doubt that the function of food is for the intellect (buddhi). || 70 || Since the intellect is the form of all activities, the wise person should abandon hesitation and maintain this firm conviction: "Śiva alone is the witness of all."

Even though no one has the realization that "my intellect is wandering" and so forth, nevertheless, while the intellect and other faculties are active, everyone perceives themselves as the agent, thinking, "I am walking," "I am seeing," "I am hearing," "I am reflecting," and so on. From this, it is established by implication that we have identified the intellect with our own self.

One should abandon the confusion that arises from doubt and resolve this certainty: "I am not the one who thinks and so forth, but rather that which even knows the act of thinking. Although this too is a determination of the intellect (*buddhi-niścaya*), it is liberating, whereas other determinations are destructive; therefore, this alone is to be accepted. || 71 ||

By its very nature, when this living being abandons the state of "I" and "mine" regarding the aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth, and enters into its own self, pure consciousness—remaining as pure awareness alone, free from the transformations of ignorance and the non-cognitive—then it remains in a state of sleep, and no experience of suffering or the like occurs. It is observed that for the embodied soul in this state, there is the attainment of the bliss of its own essential nature, the Self.

72–73 || For this reason as well, the wise person should never conceive the notion of a self (*ātmadhī*) with respect to the body and so forth; rather, one should conceive the notion of a self only with respect to the Self that is the direct witness of all, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*). 74 || Whatever is an object of knowledge (*vedya*) that is characterized by the "this-ness" (*idaṃtā*) through the medium of the witness—all that is nothing but Brahman alone (for there is no effect apart from its cause, and the cause is Brahman alone).

That Brahman alone is the Truth; it alone is the Full—that is, the non-figurative Consciousness—and it is the meaning of the two words "That" and "Thou" (which denote the inner self, such as Śvetaketu), of this there is no doubt. (The Mahāvākya well-known in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is "Tattvamasi"—"That Thou Art. In this, the referent of the word "Bṛhat" (the Great) is the Supreme Self, who has fashioned this world of creation, lordship, and so forth; and the referent of the word "Thou" is—

That which we designate by the word "I" and whose experience we have through the sense of "I" is the *pratyagātman* (the inner self). The meaning of the sentence is that these two are non-different—they are one. It is evident that there is a contradiction here: how can that which is limited by the body and so forth, and subject to birth and death, be the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the universe? What doubt could there be in this matter?

In order to establish the validity of the authoritative scripture (*śruti*), it is necessary to harmonize its intended meaning (*tātparya*). When examining other Upanishadic contexts, it becomes evident that the scripture has taught that the referent of the word "thou" (*tvam*) is indeed the referent of the word "I" (*aham*), and the referent of the word "I" is indeed the referent of the word "thou.

[Chapter 5, Verse 76] That which shines as the meaning of the word "thou" is indeed the meaning of the word "I"; and that which shines as the meaning of the word "I" is indeed the meaning of the word "thou. (76)

Now, an objection is raised: "The word *tat* denotes an external object (*parāgartha*), whereas the word *tvam* denotes the internal self (*pratyagartha*); thus, like the words 'short' and 'long,' they possess contradictory meanings. Since another Vedic text declares that the internal self is Brahman in the statement 'I am Brahman' (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), how can it be said here in 'That thou art' (*tattvam asi*) that the external [object] is Brahman? To this, he replies: "The meaning of the word *tat*..."

Just as, dear one, the same Devadatta is called "son" by his son and "father" by his father, yet the identity of Devadatta denoted by those two terms—father and son—is not divided; rather, the distinction between the designations "father" and "son" is based on the difference between the speakers, not on a difference in the object to be expressed.

Thus, when the very identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman is being personally experienced as the state of "I am Brahman," it is designated by the expression *ahaṃ brahmāsmi* ("I am Brahman"). And that same unity of the individual soul and the Supreme, when being made known to another, is designated by the expression *tat tvam asi* ("That thou art"). Therefore, since the two statements have the same meaning, there is no contradiction; this is the sense. || 76 ||

"He has no duty to perform" (*na tasya kāryam*). Thus the Śruti declares that the inner Self (*pratyagātman*) is not, in reality, limited by the body and so forth: "This is your Self, which is within all" (*eṣa ta ātmā sarvāntaraḥ*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1); "He who consists of consciousness... as if meditating, as if moving" (*yo'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ... dhyāyatīva lelāyatīva*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7); "The great unborn Self, who consists of consciousness" (*mahānaja ātmā yo'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).

4.4.22) and so forth! Therefore, what is the intended meaning of "That thou art"? There is this apparent difference: one is the creator of the world (Īśvara), and the other is the bound soul (paśu). This is unreal and thus constitutes an error. To remove this, one must realize the identity: there is only one reality which is both the cause of the universe and the bound state. This very non-dual realization is the essential purport (*tātparya*) of that sentence, "He is Śiva."

Both the words *bhe* and *śiva* take the word *sa* as their object; which one do they denote? That which is neither bound nor the cause of the world. This *bhe* is indeed the intended meaning of both *sa* and *tvam*. For this very reason, it is called the indicated (*lakṣya*) meaning. The direct or expressed (*vācya*) meaning of *sa* is the cause of the world, and the direct or expressed meaning of *tvam* is the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, the two meanings are distinct.

The non-difference between these two denotata is impossible, and it is also unestablished because both of them are unreal. Even if their non-difference were somehow established, it would be useless; for if the two are unreal, their non-difference must also be unreal, and thus it is not a reality. The intended meaning of the sentence is that Reality alone is real, and it is that which is non-different.

According to the Mahāvākyas of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the referents of the terms *tat* (That) and *tvam* (Thou), and so forth, constitute the basis for linguistic usage. All Mahāvākyas consist of one word denoting Īśvara and one word denoting the Jīva; furthermore, both convey the Nirviśeṣa (the Undifferentiated Absolute) through the function of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). To clarify this, the following verse is provided. || 75 ||

That which is the meaning of the word *tvam* (you) is the meaning of the word *brahma* (in the Mahāvākya *Tat tvam asi*). That which is the meaning of the word *asi* (are) is the meaning of the word *chandojñam* (the knower of the Vedas). [This is stated in the Ārṣeya Brāhmaṇa as "this Self is other than the Ṛgveda and other than knowledge"]. || 76 || The referent (*vācya*) of the words *tvam* and *mām* (me) is that ocean of knowledge.

9 dha. ḍa. iña. duṃdata. 2 oṃ. ca. "in the state of [the Supreme]". 3 Therefore, it is a traditional saying that while "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is the sentence of instruction, "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi) is the sentence of realization. 780. But in the *Brahmagītā*, it is said: "The supreme direct perception is the meaning indicated by the words 'thou' and 'I'; and that same [perception] is the meaning indicated by the word 'that'. There is no doubt about this. (74)

Now, one might object: "In this way, let there be no mutual contradiction between the two [statements] 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*) and 'I am Brahman' (*aham brahmāsmi*). However, in the former, is not the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) denoted by the words *tvam* and *aham*, while by the word *brahma* and the word *tat* is denoted the non-transmigrating, omniscient Lord (*īśvara*)? How then can there be identity (*tādātmya*) between them? To this, he says: "By the words *tat* and *aham*... [and so forth].

The meaning is this: there is an ultimate reality that has been established as consisting of existence (*sat*), consciousness (*cit*), infinity (*ananta*), and bliss (*ānanda*); it is indivisible, non-dual, of a single essence, beginningless and endless. As for primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—which is characterized by the three qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is beginningless yet finite, and is to be removed solely by the knowledge of that [reality]—it is indeed false because it is merely a conceptual construction and thus lacks substantial reality. And that [nature] is of two kinds: one in which *sattva* alone is pure, having overcome *rajas* and *tamas*; that is called *māyā*.

Another [form] is characterized by impure *sattva* due to being overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*; this is called *avidyā*. Therein, that very [Self], reflected in the reality-level (*tattva*) of *māyā*, is called the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), omniscient and the Lord of all, having taken hold of that *māyā*. Furthermore, that same [Self], reflected in the reality-level of *avidyā*, is called the "lower lord" (*apareśvara*); being held by that [avidyā], he is the independent agent, the enjoyer, the transmigrating soul (*jīva*).

That very Supreme Self, however, being conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *prakṛti*—which has *tamas* as its dominant quality—undergoes a transformation (*vivarta*) characterized by the world of objects of enjoyment that cause fear. In this regard, the one and only Supreme Self is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe by virtue of having *prakṛti*, where *tamas* is the dominant quality, as its limiting adjunct; and it is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the universe by virtue of having *prakṛti*, where *sattva* is the dominant quality, as its limiting adjunct. Thus, it is the single, identical efficient and material cause, which is expressed by the word "Being" (*sat*) in the passage: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

For in that context, [the passage] "It thought" establishes its status as the efficient cause by virtue of its consciousness, while "May I be many" establishes its status as the material cause by virtue of its undergoing illusory transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of the effect; thus, the identity of the efficient and material causes is made clear. Therefore, here in the sentence "That thou art," it is expressed by the word *tat* (That), which refers back to the subject under discussion.

However, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is entirely conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), it is referred to by the father Uddālaka with the word "thou" (*tvam*) when Śvetaketu, who stands before him, serves merely as the occasion for that instruction. Since there is an absolute difference between those two—the meanings of the words "that" (*tat*) and "thou" (*tvam*), which are consciousness conditioned respectively by *māyā* and *avidyā*—their identity is contradictory. Therefore, the two words "that" and "thou" indicate, by abandoning their respective parts (*bhāga*), the single underlying consciousness common to both. This is likewise the case in the statement "I am Brahman. (77)

The Self (*ātman*) is that which is directly manifest (*sākṣāt*), meaning self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), and immediate (*pratyak*), meaning it can never be perceived as being distinct from itself in this manner. That very same [Self] is also the referent of words such as "That" (*Tat*), which denote the Lord (*Īśvara*); of this there is no doubt. (Although it is said that [the Lord] is omniscient...)

“Furthermore, even if the referents (*raśyārtha*) are one, one should not fall into the error of thinking that because the referents are one, the unity [of the words] is not real; consequently, *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) would become meaningless. The referent is indeed one, because it is the indicated object (*lakṣya*) of two words; therefore, the quality of duality is merely attributed (*upacāra*) to it. Even in common worldly usage, ‘that which is a jar is the same...’”

Even in such usages as “Kaṭha” and so forth, which are spoken through the distinctions of “you,” “he,” and so on, the referent—the body and so forth—is indeed one and the same; thus, this can also be reconciled. (77) In well-known Mahāvākyas such as “That thou art” (*tat tvam asi*), the referents of the words “thou” and “that”—namely, the body and so forth—are not presented as the denotative meaning of the word “that”;
nor is it said that Brahman is the body and so forth, or the possessor of the body and so forth. (Rather, they maintain that the body and so forth...)

1. And [it is said]: "The one who is reflected in Māyā... 2. That very same one who is the original object (*bimba*) of both Māyā and Avidyā is one; it is not the case that what is reflected in one place becomes a reflection in another.†

Chapter 5 78. The Śruti declares that the reality (*tattva*) of the body and other such objects—which are indeed denotable by the term "thou" (*tvam*)—is not their literal meaning; rather, it expresses that [reality] through the power of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). 79. For the Śruti, having abandoned the contradictory aspect residing in the literal meaning (*vācya*), speaks by indicating the non-contradictory aspect. 80. And with respect to that [aspect], it conveys the non-contradictory nature of the "thou" (*tvam*)-meaning, while merely indicating the causality and other qualities residing in the literal meaning.

Furthermore, the word *vid* (knowing) declares the identity of that [Self] with the meaning of *tvam* (you). For the Supreme Self, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and whose nature is established as one, its oneness is self-evident; for the believers, that indeed constitutes the meaning of the sentence. Any sentence-meaning other than this is not a true sentence-meaning at all.

[Objection: "But even if there is no contradiction regarding the identity with Consciousness (*cit*), the identity of the referents denoted by the words *tvaṃ* (you) and *ahaṃ* (I) with their respective denotata is indeed contradictory. [Reply: True, it is contradictory; however, that is not what is intended here. Thus he says: "The referents denoted by the words *tvaṃ* and *ahaṃ*... The meaning is that the state of being a transmigrating soul (*saṃsāritva*) and the state of being omniscient (*sarvajñatva*) are not intended to be expressed here as identical. || 78 ||

He states the reason for not intending to express [qualities] such as transmigratoriness when they are denoted by the word: "Because it has that as its sole purpose" (*tadarthaikatvāt*). The meaning is that the contradiction with the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of other co-occurring words is precisely the reason for not intending to express them. (79) He applies the meaning already stated regarding the referents of the words "thou" (*tvam*) and "I" (*aham*) to the referent of the word "that" (*tat*) as well: "Or, in the referent of that... (*tadarthe vā*).

The meaning is as follows: just as the transmigratory nature and so forth residing in the referent of the *tvaṃ-pada* (the "thou" term), which is contradictory with the causality of the world, omniscience, and so forth denoted by the *tat-pada* (the "that" term), are not intended [to be predicated]; likewise, the causality of the world, omniscience, and so forth residing in the referent of the *tat-pada*, which are contradictory with the transmigratory nature and so forth residing in the referent of the *tvaṃ-pada*, are not intended [to be predicated].

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having set aside the "thou" (tvaṃ) referent—which is devoid of meaning, characterized by duality, and which, apart from being the cause of the world and omniscience, is merely a form of limited consciousness—[the scripture] preserves its aspect as pure Consciousness (cidākāra) and declares that to be the true nature of the "thou" referent. Thus, when the contradictory portions of the meanings of the words "That" (tat) and "thou" (tvaṃ) have been eliminated, the meaning of the sentence is accomplished; he demonstrates this in the verse beginning with "Of the remainder of the word-meanings of 'That'... (80–89).

According to the method stated, that which is indicated by the two words *tat* and *tvam* is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of all adjuncts (*upādhi*); for that alone is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as per the scriptural text: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss. And because it is free from the three kinds of limitations, its inherent oneness and non-duality are what are propounded here by the sentence *tat tvam asi*; the meaning is not that the oneness already established through the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—like that of the ocean and its waves—is being taught. Now, [one might object]: "In reality..."

Since the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed distinct [from Brahman]—just as gold attains the state of being gold through contact with mercury—it might be asked: why would the meaning of the sentence not be the identity with that [Brahman], given that such identity is possible by virtue of the Lord’s grace? To this, he says: "Other than this... The meaning of the sentence—that the soul and Brahman are either in a state of union characterized by the absence of natural difference, or possess a distinct unity—is not, in reality, the true meaning of the sentence. This is because [the distinction between them] is real.
The meaning is that, because the non-existence of one among those two [mutually exclusive] things is not infinite, identity (tādātmya) is untenable. || 82 ||

That which is devoid [of all attributes] is Brahman. (78) The function of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) is to indicate, through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), that the essential nature of Brahman alone is non-different from the referent of the word "That" (*tat*), by setting aside those two contradictory portions which constitute the referents of the words "That" and "Thou" (*tvam*). The referent of the word "That" is the conscious Lord (*īśvara*); the referent of the word "Thou" is the conscious individual soul (*jīva*).

The contradiction in their non-difference (abheda) arises from this very fact: that one part is Īśvara—that is, the enjoyer—and the other is the jīva—that is, the sufferer. If these two parts are set aside, what remains is consciousness (caitanya), and its non-difference is free from contradiction. It is illogical for the jīva to remain as the jīva while being Īśvara; this is not the teaching of Vedānta. Their assertion, rather, is that [the Self] is Brahman itself.

Thus, the notion that identity (*tādātmya*) exists between two distinct entities qualified by difference has been established by the *Laghucandrikā*. Some modern Mādhvas, failing to understand this secret, have written that the cognition of non-difference (*abheda-dhī*) is not the meaning of the Upaniṣads, nor is it accepted even in the own-system (*svasampradāya*) of the Vedāntins. Although qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is indeed a type of relation (*saṃsarga*), nevertheless, with the intention that in the case of action it is a specific kind of relation, the statement of the Teacher (Vācaspati)—"either a relation or a qualified [entity]"—is followed here as well.

Alternatively, the meaning is that neither "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*), which is a distinct unity arising from difference, nor "non-difference" (*abheda*), which is the unity of two distinct things, is intended here. This is because non-difference is impossible between two distinct entities. Furthermore, in this context, the mention of either one [term] is intended to indicate the principle of the *avyatihāra* section (JS 3.1.24–27). Nor should it be argued that since the sentence-meaning consists of *apoha*, the sentence-meaning of "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) must be only *tat* and not *tvam*; for the impossibility of *apoha* being the sentence-meaning has been made clear by the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika* themselves, and it is not accepted [by us].

The Vedic hymn of the Brahmagītā brings about the realization of the state of being the *yṛk* (the sacrificial verse); that which possesses the splendor of the fourth state (*turya*) effects this. However, it is knowledge alone that establishes conventional ignorance.
At that time, oneness is cognized by itself and not from anything else; therefore, the statement "it is not" does not sublate ignorance. (82)
In reality, ignorance does not exist, because it is incompatible with the nature of consciousness; therefore, a statement cannot sublate ignorance in the final analysis.

[Objection: But surely, since oneness is the very nature of Brahman—which is self-luminous—that oneness is likewise self-luminous; therefore, if it were to be made known by a sentence, its status as self-luminous would be compromised. To this, he says: "the cognition of oneness. [Response: If the sentence does not produce a valid cognition (*pramiti*) whose object is oneness, then it would indeed be rendered useless. Therefore, he says: "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*). The sentence, through the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) produced by itself—which has as its object the oneness of Brahman brought forth by the ignorance (*avidyā*) [it dispels]—sublates that ignorance.

Therefore, it is not the case that [the inquiry] is purposeless (83). Now, one might argue: "The function of a sentence does not consist in the cognition of oneness; and if this [oneness] is not an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it must be non-existent, like a human horn. To this he replies: "Always cognized" (*sadā pramitam*). For it is the very fact of being an object of valid cognition that serves as the basis for declaring the non-existence of something that is illuminated by another. Oneness, however, because it is non-different from self-luminous consciousness, is itself always manifest; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

Therefore, the function of the statement is solely the removal of the obscuring ignorance (*āvaraṇajñāna*), and not the manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*); this is the meaning. (84) If [ignorance] were non-existent, its removal would be impossible; furthermore, if there were non-difference [between Brahman and ignorance], it would follow that Brahman itself is subject to destruction. Therefore, one must accept some other entity as the locus of ignorance. In that case, the consequence of [absolute] non-duality (*advaita*) would arise; to this he says: "The reality" (*vastu*). For, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), ignorance does not exist at all.

Because that ignorance is opposed to the light of consciousness which constitutes the very nature of Brahman—just as darkness is opposed to light—it is impossible for its own form to appear therein; therefore, ignorance, which is superimposed upon that true nature just like the impressions of previous delusions, is removed by knowledge (*vidyā*). When the reality is investigated, even with respect to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the sentence does not sublate ignorance; it is only from the perspective of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) that it is designated as the sublater of ignorance. || 85 ||

That which is considered the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed the *jīva*, and there is no other; if the governed *jīva* does not exist, then whose is the governing Lord (*īśvara*)? Within the indivisible pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), these conceptualizations of *jīva* and *īśvara* are imagined through ignorance (*ajñāna*). Upon the cessation of this ignorance, one becomes liberated; there is neither *jīva* nor *īśvara*, but only the one indivisible Śiva. (79–81)

That non-difference which is self-established (established independently of anything else) is alone the meaning of the Mahāvākya. If anything other than this were understood, it would not be the meaning of the sentence at all. (82) Even in the case of the Mahāvākya, it is necessary to produce a valid cognition (*pramā*) of oneness—that is, non-difference.

The resulting undivided mental modification (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*) destroys only the empirical ignorance (*vyāvahārika-ajñāna*); oneness, however, is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*). (83) Oneness always remains manifest by itself in an indubitable manner; its manifestation does not depend upon anything else. Therefore, the sentence that sublates ignorance is not the producer of the knowledge of non-difference.

[Only knowledge can destroy ignorance: This knowledge is valid (*pramā*) only when it has a real object, and only then does it truly become the sublater (*bādhaka*) of ignorance. If there were no knowledge regarding the Self, how could ignorance be sublated? The answer is that while there is indeed a mental modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*) having the Self as its object, that very modification is its own remover and is itself the sublater of ignorance.

The knowledge that constitutes the fruit is indeed self-validating knowledge (*svasaṃvedyajñāna*), which cannot be the effect of a sentence. Although on the level of empirical usage (*vyavahārabhūmi*), even self-validating knowledge might be called the effect of a sentence by virtue of being characterized by non-contradiction with ignorance (*aviyāvādhopalakṣitatvena*), in reality it is not so, because it contradicts ignorance. (Ignorance can only reside in consciousness.)

Now, since consciousness (*cetanā*) is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), how could ignorance (*avidyā*) abide in it? For elsewhere, that [consciousness] does not naturally abide in ignorance. What object could even provide a place for it to remain? Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the sentence is not even the sublator (*bādhaka*) of ignorance; consequently, it is all the more impossible for the effect of the sentence to belong to the consciousness characterized by the sublation of ignorance. || 84-85 ||

Chapter 5 783. That oneness which has been declared by the Lord Himself ought to be known by oneself; it cannot be known through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for all means of knowledge become blunted when confronted with that [Reality]. 87. Even empirical ignorance (*vyāvahārikājñāna*) is, in reality, Brahman alone. The very report that there is "ignorance" is indeed a mere flow of words. 88. For existence (*sat*) alone shines forth from that [Brahman]; therefore, in the manifestation of the meaning of the scriptures through reasoning defined by the two poles of being and non-being (*sadasatkoṭi*), nothing other than the shining Brahman alone appears.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ directed toward Brahman—which is produced by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—removes the ignorance that veils its own object; and since this [modification] is like other modifications directed toward objects such as jars and cloths, why does it lack the capacity to illuminate its own object? To this, he says: "That which is oneness... That innate oneness of Brahman and the Self which was previously mentioned is non-different from the light of consciousness that constitutes its very nature; therefore, it is capable of illuminating itself through its own self-nature alone, and not through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) are set in motion for the sake of revealing that [Reality], yet they are themselves being revealed by that very same Reality which exists as the nature of direct perception (*sākṣirūpa*), like a lamp by the light of the knower. Therefore, in that universal illumination of the conscious Self (*cidātman*), they become devoid of their own power. For this very reason, it is declared elsewhere in the scripture: "There, the eye does not go, nor speech, nor the mind. (86) [This refers to] "empirical ignorance," and so forth.

Alternatively, that which ceases through the knowledge produced by the [Vedic] statement is, in reality, upon investigation, none other than Brahman itself. This means that, just as silver superimposed on mother-of-pearl and the like is not distinct from it, so too this [ignorance], being superimposed upon Brahman, is non-different from it. Furthermore, he states "the term 'ignorance'" [in verse 87] to show that even the conventional usage of the word "ignorance" is not tenable when the true nature of the thing is investigated. Now, why not accept the existence of ignorance simply on the strength of its conventional usage? To that, he replies: "Of that which is real... [verse 88].

For the existence of an object consists precisely in its being "existent" (sat-rūpa); it does not have the preservation of that [existence] as its purpose. If it is argued, "But surely, when a cloth is existent, it is experienced as 'an existent cloth' or 'an existent wall,' and thus existence is indeed perceived," [the author] replies to this: "Because of the non-perception of the subtle. The meaning is that it is only the existence of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) that appears there through the existence belonging to the superimposed object (āropya). Now, if it is argued that "that ignorance must exist as something distinct from both the real and the unreal, because otherwise experience and sublation would be inexplicable," [the author] says regarding that: "Neither real nor unreal."

The demonstration of its being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent is intended to show that it cannot withstand an investigation into its true nature, not to establish the actual existence of such an object. Therefore, when such an object appears, even the conventional usage "it is characterized as distinct from the existent and the non-existent" does not manifest. The meaning is that since Brahman, whose nature is pure manifestation, shines forth alone and entirely free from ignorance, the manifestation of ignorance itself is impossible. || 88 ||

The non-difference spoken of in the *Uroka* can be established intrinsically (*svataḥ*) alone, and not through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because a means of valid cognition is incapable of making that [non-duality] its object. [This is because] the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are the domain of the means of valid cognition; however, Śiva—non-dual and non-distinct—is "unobjectifiable" (*aprameya*), and therefore lies entirely beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, that which is not self-luminous depends upon a luminous agent, whereas the means of valid cognition illuminate only that which is manifested by the light of consciousness.

Self-luminous [consciousness] neither requires anything else nor is it illuminated by another. (86) Even empirical ignorance (*vyāvahārikājñāna*), in reality, is Brahman itself. (Therefore, to speak of "ignorance" is also futile, because: This designation "ignorance" would be appropriate only if ignorance were some distinct entity. It is only the negation of the real (*sat*) that occurs, not of the unreal (*asat*). (Ignorance is not real because...)

[This must be refuted; therefore, how can its existence be established? As for the claim that ignorance and other such categories are said to be "distinct from both the real and the unreal" because they are perceived, that too is intended to mean that they are not any kind of entity at all. Once non-dual knowledge (*abheda-jñāna*) has arisen, ignorance does not appear even in the form of something destroyed; only Brahman remains as the sole object of manifestation. (87-88)

9. Furthermore, if that [existence] were not admitted, then since the existence [denoted by] "the pot exists" and the existence [denoted by] "the universal exists" would be identical in both cases, the distinction between them would be impossible; for there is no difference in the relation between the pot and its existence, nor between the universal and its existence. And if there were such a difference, the non-distinction of the corresponding qualified cognitions (*viśiṣṭadhi*) would be impossible; otherwise, the distinction in their relations would be rendered useless. This is also supported by the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghavatarka*). All this has been explained in detail in the first chapter of the *Siddhi* treatise. 3. The meaning of the word "only" (*kevala*) is that even the manifestation of being free from ignorance does not exist.

784. The song of Brahmā: "Manifestation" is merely a conventional term; even the notion of "manifestation" is inconsistent. (89) When the related object does not exist, the relationship itself cannot arise. When that [object] exists, there is only Brahman alone, whose nature is the relationship. (90) It is the view of the wise that it exists in an indefinable form; for that which is of an indefinable nature is indeed Brahman alone. For that very form is the supreme form, and nothing else. (91)
O best of gods, if there is even a little soup for another, then his very form shall indeed become like that of Brahmā. 92.

Now, one might object: "Granted that ignorance does not manifest by itself, it might still fail to manifest due to its lack of connection with Brahman. Anticipating this, he says: "Because of the connection with manifestation" (bhānasaṃbandhataḥ). [The reason is] "the existence of the relata" (saṃbandhisattvāt). Since a relation necessarily requires two related entities, the very nature of ignorance must be admitted, just as it is for Brahman.

And that illusory flow (sadrāva) proceeds from the very substrate, Brahman; therefore, ignorance is nothing other than that [substrate] itself, not something additional to it. Thus, because there is no distinct related entity, a relationship is difficult to establish—this is the meaning. (Verses 89–90) Now, one might object: "Granted that ignorance does not have an ultimate existence like that of Brahman, its existence as a superimposed entity (āropita-sadbhāva) does exist; why then could there not be a relationship with that very [superimposed entity]? He raises this doubt with the words "anirūpita" (unascertained). The meaning is: "in the form of being unable to withstand inquiry. He refutes this with the words "anirūpita" (unascertained).

The meaning is as follows: the very nature of Brahman alone is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon which that which is superimposed—namely, the world which is charming only so long as it is not investigated—is projected; there is nothing else, because everything other than that [Brahman], consisting of ignorance and its effects, is by its own nature devoid of essence (*niḥsvarūpa*) due to being superimposed upon Him. (91) "If there exists even another... means: if "form" (*rūpa*)—that is, a nature capable of being defined—exists even for something other than Brahman, then that form is indeed the form of Brahman itself, because there is no difference between the two insofar as they both consist of the nature of form. (92)

(Objection: It may be asked, "How is it that ignorance—which necessarily appears as connected to the Self—is not something other than the Self? For its manifestation can only occur through a connection with the Self, just as a jar [is manifested] through its connection with a lamp; therefore, why should ignorance not be accepted as a real entity? To this, the following refutation is offered: It is utterly inconsistent to claim that ignorance, which is of the nature of non-manifestation, is established through a connection with the Self, whose nature is manifestation.

(How can there be a relationship between light and darkness? Furthermore: When the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a related entity is established as existing, then a relationship becomes possible; however, the proponent of doubt (*śaṅkā-vādī*) says: "Since the existence of the relationship is already established, one should admit the existence of the related entity's own nature. Such is the argument. (First, when ignorance is latent, one must consider whether its relationship [with the self] exists or not.)

It is possible. To say "the relation is established" means that its existence as a co-inherence (*samavāyatva*) has already been accepted; however, this is not the case here. The proponent does not accept ignorance as being existent by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*); therefore, he does not accept even its relation [to consciousness].

(Regarding the verse, after the words *sambandhasadbhāve* and *sambandhirūpam*, one should supply the word *tiṣādhayiṣasi* and connect it with the phrase *vārtāpy asaṅgatā*. Thus, when ignorance is shown to be unestablished, this is the conclusion: Therefore, Brahman alone is the sole reality. || 89-90 ||

If you say that the existence of ignorance can be established through the theory of the indescribable (*anirvacanīya*), even then our position remains proven; for the true nature of the indescribable must be the Brahman itself, which serves as its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Therefore, whatever exists other than Brahman, its true form is Brahman alone and nothing else. (91) If you say that even ignorance and the like, though distinct from Brahman, can be described...

The meaning is that these two are identical in nature. Whatever is other than Brahman is "form" (rūpa) because it is subject to definition; its form is also indeed a "form" (rūpa). For this very reason, the point is that both share the same status of security and vulnerability. Just as that which is other than Brahman is Brahman itself through superimposition, so too is form.

Alternatively, since Brahman exists as form because it is the reality to be defined by such terms as "the True" (satya), if the world were identical to that [Brahman], it would be Brahman alone; if it were other than that, then that alternative is refuted in the subsequent verse.

Chapter 5 [If it is argued that] another [entity] exists in the form of Brahman, either with a difference or without a difference: (92) In that case, would there be a difference, a non-difference, or both difference and non-difference, or neither difference nor non-difference, on account of distinctions such as the sun and so forth? (94) If it were non-different from Him because of its being insubstantial (*tucchatva*), then it would be that very [Brahman] itself; however, because of the occurrence of the aforementioned defects, it cannot be both different and non-different for You. (95)

This might be so if, by means of a mere difference in form, ignorance were to possess a nature distinct from that which is the nature of Brahman; thus he raises the objection with the word "brahma" (Brahman). To refute this, he analyzes the matter through a dilemma with the words "tadā hi" (then indeed): Is that other form something distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is fit for definition, or is it non-distinct? He says "no" to the first alternative: "If it were distinct," meaning that if it were separate, it would not be a form [of Brahman] because it would lack the essential nature that is fit for definition, just like a pot or a cloth—this is the intended sense.

Regarding the second [position], he states that there is no perception of ignorance as having a distinct nature apart from Brahman: "If it were non-different" (*abhinnaṃ cet*). He rejects the third [position] with the words: "Because of the aforementioned defects" (*uktadoṣa*). This means that the two defects already mentioned regarding the positions of difference and non-difference would both result [in this case]. (Verses 93–95)

If it is argued that the ignorant one (*bāla*) is the very nature [of Brahman] (and therefore, like Brahman, is a real entity), then the question arises: is this nature of ignorance and so forth, which you describe as being incapable of definition (*nirūpaṇayogya*), identical to the nature of Brahman itself, or is it distinct from it? (That is to say: is that which is the indefinable nature of Brahman the same as that of ignorance, or is the definable nature of ignorance something separate? If it is the latter, then it is not a part of Brahman at all; if it is the former, then...)

Since ignorance and the rest are, by their very nature, of the same essence as Brahman, their existence as separate entities is not established. Thus, from the perspective of the "seer" (the subject), that is, from the standpoint of the nature that is capable of being defined; "form" (rūpa) refers to the definable qualities such as knowledge and so forth. The intended meaning is that the definable nature of Brahman is reality.

If knowledge and so forth also possess that very same nature, and if they were to grant that very nature as their own reality, then it follows that ignorance and so forth are the very essence of Brahman; thus, the proposition that ignorance and so forth are distinct entities has been refuted. (92) Furthermore, if it is argued that the definable nature of ignorance and so forth is entirely separate from the defining nature of Brahman—that too is refuted. (93)

Furthermore, it may be asked: is that [object] different from its own nature (*svarūpa*), non-different from it, or both different and non-different? If it is different from its own nature, then it is certain that the nature itself—such as ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth—is unreal; for the intention behind the position of difference is that ignorance is distinct from the nature that is capable of being defined (*nirūpaṇa-yogya-svarūpa*). And there is this pervasion (*vyāpti*): whatever is different from a nature capable of being defined is, like a rabbit's horn, [unreal].

Since it would be empty and non-existent, if one were to consider everything as distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*), it would never be established that anything possessing a nature is a real entity. Whether it be the nature itself or...

If [ignorance] were considered non-different from its own nature, then it would be impossible to say: "Ignorance and the like are real entities, because they possess their own nature. For this would mean: "Ignorance and the like are real entities; because they are ignorance and so forth, ignorance and its nature are non-different"—which is an incoherent statement. (A purely negative inference [*kevalavyatirekī*] cannot be established here, because you yourself accept that the Self is a real entity.)

If you do not accept [this], then the statement will remain inconsistent due to the lack of logical support (*tarka*). If you say that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is both different and non-different from the essence (*svarūpatva*), then both of the aforementioned defects will arise together, whereby it would become impossible. [Objection: Will these alternatives (*vikalpa*) not also arise regarding the Self (*ātman*)? [Reply: No. The essential nature of the Self is indeed non-different from the Self; the Self alone is real. We establish the reality of the Self precisely because it possesses an essential nature that is capable of being defined (*nirūpaṇārha-svarūpavattā*).

[Otherwise] no fault would arise as stated. (94-95) Therefore, this should be understood as follows: "If there were indeed no difference in form at all... [The reading] *ṇataṃ rūpaṃ na ni* [is correct]. [The reading] *pvānnaraśū* [is also acceptable]. Do not speak thus, for without Śiva there is simply an absence of knowledge. Therefore, O best of gods, my conviction is that Brahman alone is one and there is nothing else;
for the supreme Veda declares, "All this is indeed identical with That. (97–99)

Thus, he concludes that the previously asserted existence [of ignorance] in an unmanifested form is reduced to mere talk by this line of reasoning: "For this very reason" (atta eva) || 96 ||. Likewise, since ignorance lacks a separate self-nature, it is established that even empirical ignorance is in reality Brahman alone; he concludes this with: "Therefore," etc., beginning with "consisting of ignorance" (ajñānamaya).

As for this statement that "this entire world is the effect of ignorance," that too is merely words; it has no real meaning, because apart from the nature of the Supreme Śiva, who is the substratum, ignorance itself cannot be established. (97) Therefore, since it has been established that ignorance and its effects are nothing other than Brahman itself, he cites scripture to support this point: "This is the truth" (*etadātmyam*). The literal meaning of the scripture has already been explained previously. (98–99)

This is merely a statement made so that the practitioner may not fall into error; [in reality, ignorance does not exist at all]. (96) Therefore, ignorance is the eternal, self-luminous Brahman itself (there is no ignorance apart from Brahman). Such is the meaning of the sentence: "Ignorance too is Brahman alone."

In this verse, the word *api* is to be supplied [after *ajñānam*] as "even ignorance," and the particle *eva* is used for the purpose of excluding absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*). This statement—that all that is perceived is composed of ignorance—is also not tenable, because there is no such thing as ignorance existing apart from Śiva. (Therefore, it must be concluded that everything is composed of Śiva alone. || 97 ||

Therefore, my firm conviction is that ignorance and its effects are none other than Brahman alone; there is nothing else. The supreme authority, the Śruti, has indeed declared: "All this is truly the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7). Verses 98–99. This and other such non-dualistic scriptural texts are engaged in describing reality exactly as it is.

However, seeing that the minds of the listeners were incapable of comprehending this, the Śruti—overcome by compassion and constrained by its own nature—sometimes speaks of matters other than Brahman, such as the relationship between means and ends, fruits, the diversity of the world, dharma and adharma, wealth (as the objects desired by man through the means of dharma and kāma), the division of castes, the division of stages of life, their respective duties, and auspicious [rites].

Objects, impure objects, the phenomenal world of elements and their derivatives, various sounds, the separation of words from their meanings, the truth or falsity of all things other than the Self, the existence of *māyā*, the nature of *māyā*, the binding nature of *māyā*, the discourse between Guru and disciple, the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), various scriptures, diverse reasonings, a summary of other contrary arguments, the uniqueness of Brahman, and so forth—yet, regarding these matters:
What is the purport of the Śruti? (Gradually, these scriptural passages should be understood;

as it is said: "Even though these are known," etc. In the commentary on the seventy-fifth verse, the Bhāṣya explains: "The state of being this Self of all that exists is 'etadātmyam'; it explained [this] as such. The meaning is that its nature consists of this, namely, the nature of Brahman.")

Chapter 5, Verse 900: Through the manifestation of its direct objective reality, the Śruti proceeds in this manner; yet, due to the ignorance of the listeners, that very Śruti appears as if divided. (Verse 901): At times and in certain instances, it speaks of another meaning distinct from Brahman, namely, the discourse on the relationship between the means and the end, and the description of the fruit.

The description of the diversity of the world, the speaking for the sake of those desiring Dharma, the explanation of the distinctions between the castes, and likewise the teaching on liberation; the discourse on what is auspicious and inauspicious, the speaking concerning the past and the future, the definition of the distinctions between words, and the teaching on their meanings; the statement regarding the self, others, and all things—O bulls among gods, such is the speaking of falsehood, which is the speaking of the existence of illusion. (Verses 102–104)

The statement regarding illusion (*māyā*) is the discourse on the "bondage" of illusion; the discourse between teacher and disciple is the discourse on the knowledge of Brahman. (105) Even the instruction of those who are established [in truth], as well as the speech of those who are merely speculators—this web of reasoning and the speaking of various doctrines are, in brief, [mere constructs]. By means of another purpose, the Śruti speaks of Brahman; that [Brahman] is not something to be grasped by them. (106)

[Objection: But does not the Śruti also teach the distinction within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which consists of actions, agents, and fruits, in such passages as, "From the Self, space was produced," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"? How then can everything have Brahman as its essence? To this, he says: "Directly. The Śruti passage, "All this has that as its essence," is directed toward establishing the very reality that exists directly, by virtue of the nature of the object itself.

Because such a matter is difficult to comprehend for one whose mind is not refined, the scripture—following the sharpening and ripening of that mind—reiterates the distinctions established by illusory worldly convention and thereby demonstrates the diversity of the world characterized by means, ends, results, and so forth; however, this is not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is the meaning. (Verses 100–106). [As it is said: "Whatever desire he desires, that he obtains through singing" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.28); "One who desires heaven should sacrifice" (Tāṇḍya Mahābrāhmaṇa 16.15.5).

"Some say 'it exists,' and others say 'this does not exist'" (Kaṭha Up. 1.20); "Practice dharma" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.11); "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.11); "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā [iṣṭi]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.6); "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman," and so forth (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.11); "There are three branches of dharma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1); "Having completed his studentship, he should become a householder; having been a householder, he should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, he should renounce" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4).

“Self-restraint (*dama*) is the constant rule for the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*); tranquility (*śama*) for the sages in the forest,” and so forth (*Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 21). “When, in dreams, one sees a woman in connection with optional rites” (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.2.9). “This is declared for a man of little intelligence in whose house a Brāhmaṇa dwells without eating” (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 1.8). “Born from space (*ākāśa*),” and so forth (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1). “Of living beings there are only three origins: those born from an egg, those born from a living being, and those born from a sprout” (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.3.1).
