The maturity of the intellects of those whose arrows [of doubt] have been extracted—O Gods, we shall speak very gently and for your benefit, according to the sequence of the *Brahmagītā*, in accordance with the nature of the Vedas, as the supreme truth has been heard. || 107 ||

Even though they were despondent regarding the substrate (*upādhi*), those who are qualified for the mature stage [of realization] declared the supreme non-duality: "All this is indeed this Self. (108) Apart from the manifold manifestations such as the world, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Lord (*īśvara*), the Śruti is solely intent upon the identity of the Self with the Blissful Brahman. (109) "The world, the individual soul, the Lord, and so forth—all this is nothing but Brahman alone"—this is the knowledge of the state of being the thread (*ūrṇatā*), the realization of supreme non-duality. (110)
The cognition that arises other than this is ignorance; it is not yours. Through investigation, this alone is the object; through non-investigation, this alone [is so]. (119)
The knowledge that "this [self] is never subject to destruction" is extremely difficult to attain. || 112 ||

"By way of a ladder" means that, in accordance with the ripening of the listener's mind, one first teaches the dharmas such as the *agnihotra* and so forth in the earlier sections (*pūrvakāṇḍa*), and then, for those whose minds have been refined by those teachings, one imparts the meditation on the *saṃhitā* and so forth; it is not for the highest qualified aspirants who have already attained one-pointedness of mind. Thus, by this gradual process of a ladder, the Śruti makes known the non-dual, secret reality that "all this is of the nature of That. (Verses 107–108) Now, he describes the method of contemplation: "The world, the individual soul, the Lord, and so forth..."

The meaning is that non-dual realization (*advaitavedana*) is the knowledge of one’s own self as being the pure Brahman—this very form consisting of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the act of enjoyment—and the realization of one’s own essential nature as the Supreme Brahman. (Verses 109–110) "Other than this": other than this aforementioned knowledge of the Self, any knowledge such as "I am one, Brahman is another"—that is indeed ignorance (*ajñāna*). The Śruti also says thus: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know. (Verse 111)

Regarding the phrase "sudarḍabham": the meaning is that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the identity between the individual self (*jīva*) and Brahman is attainable solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord, which is evoked by the performance of the duties pertaining to the stages of life (*varṇa*) and the orders of life (*āśrama*). || 111-112 ||

According to this, the supremely compassionate Śruti, like a ladder, causes one who stands at the bottom step to ascend one step at a time; thus, every individual, regardless of whether they are lower than others, rises higher from their previous state.

In the same way, although she gradually imparts instruction on what is beneficial to people, once she finds a qualified recipient who is fit for realization, she causes them to attain the supreme non-dualistic (paramādvaita) awakening that "all this is of the nature of Śiva. || 107-108 || [She reveals] that the world, the individual soul, the Lord, and so forth, are devoid of the various and manifold distinctions that exist in diversity, and are nothing but pure consciousness.

Truth, Ānanda, is the intent of the Śruti regarding the identity of the inner self with Brahman. (108) The world, the individual soul, the Lord, and all else are nothing but Brahman—this realization of one's own perfection is the experience of supreme non-duality. (110) Beyond this, nothing whatsoever can be known; that is the state of being bodiless and equal to space.

Even through inquiry, this alone emerges as the essential truth; and upon the cessation of inquiry, this very self-luminous nature shines forth. || 111 || There is never any distinction whatsoever [between Śiva and anything else]; such a certainty is attained with great ease. || 112 || Whatever object...

And so, O gods, the Śruti [speaks] for the sake of gradual benefit. As it has been said by the Teachers: "The Śruti intends: 'Let them first remain established on the path of truth; thereafter, I shall gradually cause them to grasp even that which is the ultimate reality. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1, p.

In whatever way that which is difficult to perceive appears by its own nature, in that very way it shines forth spontaneously and without effort. (150) Whether the Vedas and other scriptures, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, or the Kalpas—I abide within that very essence. (151)

The knower (*pramātā*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and valid cognition (*pramiti*) are established in the form of the Self alone. (152) The agent (*kartā*), the action (*kriyā*), the instrument (*kāraka*), and the fruit (*phala*) are established in the form of the Self alone. (153) The enjoyer (*bhoktā*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), the means of enjoyment (*bhogasādhana*), and the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) are likewise established. (154) Merit (*puṇya*), demerit (*pāpa*), pleasure (*sukha*), and pain (*duḥkha*) are established in the form of the Self alone. (155)

1. The first word "ādi" (and so forth) is for the purpose of including *putra* and others; the second is for the sake of *pitṛ* (ancestors). 2. Here, by "ādi," the *upavedas* are meant. In the case of *smṛti* and so forth, the word "ādi" is for the purpose of including the *tantras* and other such works. In the phrase "at the beginning of the *kalpas*," that [word "ādi"] is used for the inclusion of the *vedāṅgas*.

Chapter 5: 797 I am well-established as the nature of merit, and I am well-established as the nature of sin; therefore, I am well-established. I am well-established as the nature of happiness, and I am well-established as the nature of suffering. (155) I am well-established through the distinction of Sadasiva; I am well-established through the distinction of Vishnu; I am well-established through the distinction of Brahma; I am well-established through the distinction of the gods. (156)

I am well-established through the various divisions of mortals; I am perfectly situated through the various divisions of animals; I am perfectly situated through the various divisions of birds; I am established through the various divisions of insects. || 157 ||

By the differentiation of the enclosure, I am well-established; by the differentiation of the clusters, I am firmly situated! By the differentiation of the pillars, I am firmly situated; by the differentiation of the arches, I am firmly situated. || 158 || By the differentiation of time, I am well-established; by the differentiation of the joints, I am well-established. By the differentiation of the cloths, I am well-established; by the differentiation of the walls and so forth, I am well-established. || 159 || By the differentiation of the roofs, I am established there; by the differentiation of the drinking-vessels, I am established above.

I am established by the distinction of forests; I am established by the distinction of lands. I am established by the distinction of rivers; I am established by the distinction of streams. I am established by the distinction of oceans; I am established by the distinction of lakes. I am established by the distinction of ponds; I am established by the distinction of wells. I am established by the distinction of constellations; I am well-established by the distinction of planets.

Ha || 155 || Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are established here as distinct forms of the Divine. These eleven divisions of Rudra are well known: "Anai-kapād, Ahirbudhnya, Vighnapākṣa, and Raivata; Śarva, Bhava-rūpa, Tryambaka, and Sureśvara; Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākī, and Aparājita—these are declared to be the eleven Rudras, the lords of the hosts" (Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 5).

The manifestations of Viṣṇu, such as the Fish incarnation and others, should be understood as a multitude. The manifestations of Brahmā include Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and so forth. The manifestations of the gods, such as the Vasus and others, are already well known. || 156 || Within these categories of mortals (human beings), animals (birds and beasts), and worms or insects, there are further subdivisions. || 157 || Through the distinctions of trees, shrubs, creepers, and grasses, the state of existence is likewise divided. || 158 || Time;

The distinctions of jar, bowl, lamp, and so forth, are fixed only within the child’s mind. (159) Food, drink, forest, and mountain—these distinctions exist only here [in the world]. (160) It exists through the distinctions of river, stream, ocean, and shore. (161) Lake, sky, and star—[the word *tadākāśa* refers to] the sky; for according to the *Medinīkośa*, "cloud" (*abhra*) and "sky" (*gagana*) are synonyms, and "gold" (*kāñcana*) is a distinct element. Therefore, "sky" (*nabhas*) here refers to the cloud, since the cloud will be mentioned by its own name later. (162)

798. By the division of *brahman* I am well-established; by the division of *viuṭha* I am well-established. By the division of *yata* I am well-established; by the division of *rapara* I am well-established. (162) By the division of *ganra* I am well-established; by the division of *sidpra* I am well-established. By the division of *aṣḍapa* I am well-established; by the division of *loka* I am well-established. (164) By the division of *deśa* I am well-established; by the division of *grāma* I am well-established.

I am well-established through the differentiation of the earth; I am well-established through the differentiation of water. I am situated through the differentiation of fire; I am well-established through the differentiation of the walls. I am well-situated through the differentiation of the lotus-petals; I am well-established through the differentiation of the city-gates. I am well-established through the differentiation of space and the rest; I am well-situated through the differentiation of sound and the rest. I am well-situated through the differentiation of the body; I am well-established through the differentiation of the vital breaths.

I am well-established through the distinctions of autumn and the other seasons; I am well-established through the distinctions of the feet and the other limbs. I am well-established through the various divisions of the mind; I am well-established through the distinctions of the upper [parts]. (168) [155–168]

Now, Śmaśpa-hī-ha [is situated] here; Meṣa, Vidyut, and Yatta—these two varieties of Rākṣasa—are situated here. Gaṃdharva, Siddha, Brahmāṇḍa, and Roka—in these divisions, I am well-established. Deśa, Gauva, Dhara, and Mara—I have become established in these states. Kaṭa (the rampart), Prākāra (the enclosure wall), and the vicinity of great cities.

It exists through the distinctions of earth and the other elements, sound and the other objects of sense, as well as the body and the vital breaths. (167) It exists through the distinctions of the ear, feet, mind, intellect, and so forth, as well as the celestial chariots (*vimānas*). (168) It exists through the distinctions of ego (*ahaṃkāra*), consciousness (*citta*), the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), speech, birth, and so on. (169) I am possessed of the distinctions of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state (*turiya*). (170)

The seer, the observer, and the witness are all within me; what more need be said? Everything is perfectly established within me. That which is called "this," that which is called "not this," that which is said to be known, and that which is said to be "this"—[all are within]. 171.
(Note: The phrase *śrotprabheḥ* appears to be a scribal error for *śrotraprabhṛtiḥ* [beginning with the ears], which fits the context of sensory perception.)

I am well-established through the distinction of the serpent; I am well-established through the distinction of the mind. I am well-established through the distinction of the elements; I am well-established through the distinction of birth and so forth. I am well-established through the distinction of waking; I am well-established through the distinction of dreaming. I am well-established through the distinction of deep sleep; I am well-established through the distinction of the fourth state (*turiya*). I am well-established through the distinction of the gross; I am well-established through the distinction of the subtle.

In essence, I am established as food; in essence, I am established as chaff. (171) That which is expressed by the words "it exists" or "it does not exist," and likewise that which is defined by the term "manifestation," as well as that which is defined as being devoid of manifestation—none of these are ever truly mine. (172) At that time, it exists as the object of the self because its form is devoid of the range of words; it exists as the state of "I" at all times, for even in cognition, the course is exactly thus. (173)

Since the voice of the Śruti declares that he is eternally united with the ever-yoked intellect, his state of being the truth, bliss, and pure consciousness is indeed real; of this I have no doubt. (174) Just as my own nature appears to me through myself, so too does this [world] appear to me through myself alone. Yet, at that time, it is my own conscious body that shines, and nothing else; what more need be said by me? (175)

"By the destruction of the radiance of 'I-ness'" (ahaṃkāra) means by the destruction of the blueness [of the ego]. (169–1719) "As for 'it exists' or 'it does not exist'"—the meaning is that whatever has been presented through the two states of existence and non-existence, and through manifestation and non-manifestation, all that is of the nature of impurity (mala). (172) "By being within the range of words"—whatever is made an object by verbal expression, and whatever word is unable to make an object of, all that is "I" alone. He extends this stated meaning even to the mental modification (buddhivṛtti), saying: "even in the case of the ultimate" (pratyaye 'pi). (173)

"And by the hearing" means by the sentence [of the scripture]. (174) "By the self as the 'I'": that which shines forth as the self—which is the supreme Śiva consisting of pure consciousness—both as the enjoyer through the locus of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and as the object of enjoyment through the locus of the "this-ness" (*idam-kāra*), that very pure consciousness alone is my own true nature, and nothing else; this is the meaning. (175)

No perception occurs—that is entirely my own essence; of this there is no doubt. (172) The state of being an object or a non-object of sound, as well as the state of being an object or a non-object of the modifications of the intellect—whatever stability exists within these is that very curd. (173) The words of the Śruti always and eternally describe [Me] as Pure Consciousness, Bliss, and Liberation; such is My nature of Truth, Bliss, and Awareness.
The state of fullness is the reality; there is no accumulation in this. That essential nature which is perceived as "I," and likewise... "this"... [174]

800. Regarding the *Brahmagītā*: "I am the All; there is nothing whatsoever separate from me"—this firm conviction has been established by me through the words of the Vedānta and also truthfully declared by the Grandfather (Brahmā). One whose mind is wavering in this matter is indeed fallen from the vision of the Supreme Reality; one whose mind is certain in this matter is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence, which is of the nature of suffering. (1576–1757)

Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Mahādeva, accompanied by Ambā, the liberator from the cycle of rebirth, affectionately embraced both Mahāviṣṇu and Brahmā. Beholding all the gods with a mind purified by wisdom, he spoke to those foremost of deities: "O best of gods, this delusion was yours. Then the gods honored the Lord of the lords of gods, that ocean of compassion, with offerings of water, flowers, fruits, and other gifts. Viṣṇu, the creator who has reached the state of pervading the universe, [honored] the Lord of the world, the root of the tree of progenitors.

Having placed his own head with devotion at [the feet of] Śiva, the Grandfather likewise became subject to another's will. The Grandfather, the soul of all, having placed his own head with devotion at the pair of Śiva’s lotus-feet, likewise became subject to another's will.

Since my own conviction is of such a nature, he concludes that both the Śruti which establishes that truth and Brahmā, who expounds its meaning, are speakers of truth, stating: "But by me... (vv. 176–182).

Thus it appears that this entire world is of the very nature of consciousness (caitanya-svarūpa) and is not separate from it. (175) Everything is indeed Brahman alone; there is nothing whatsoever distinct from my own nature. This truth was established by the Grandfather Brahmā through the words of the Vedānta as well as through his own instructions. (176) Whoever harbors doubt regarding this falls into misfortune.
The reason is that he remains far removed from true knowledge. He who concludes thus regarding this matter is overwhelmed by the bonds of the ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). (177)

Sūta said: Having thus completed his instruction, Mahādeva offered salutations to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and with affection toward all the gods, he said, "May it be well with you all. The gods also worshipped the Lord with parched grains, flowers, and other offerings. Viṣṇu and Brahmā rubbed the feet of Mahādeva with their own hands and became immersed in a state of ecstatic devotion.

Śiva, having danced, manifested his own Supreme Lord, whose nature is supreme bliss. (186) Then Mahādevī, the ocean of compassion, clapped her hands while watching the Supreme Lord. (184) Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and all the other gods also began to dance with joy. (185)

Chapter 5 The God of gods, Mahādeva, accompanied by Ambā, the liberator from the cycle of worldly existence, danced with intense emotion, displaying his divine power. (189) The supreme Goddess, the great goddess who is an ocean of compassion, clapped her hands with supreme delight upon beholding the Great Lord. (184) All the gods, including Viṣṇu and Brahmā, and all the people present there were delighted; they performed their respective duties according to their strength. (185)

The God of gods, Mahādeva, the ocean of great bliss, having gazed upon all of them for several days, became well-pleased and vanished right there. Having embraced Viṣṇu and beheld all the hosts of gods, the Lord of the universe departed for Vaikuṇṭha along with Lakṣmī. Brahmā too, filled with wonder upon seeing those cities, spoke out of sheer faith alone, his voice faltering.

All other sciences are directly subordinate to the science of the Self; however, the science of the Self is superior to them because it acts as their counteragent. (189) Regarding the phrase "the supreme state": he performed a dance for the purpose of manifesting that supreme state, which is the object of unsurpassed, ultimate bliss for one who has transcended all perception. Furthermore, the definition of the nature of that state has been explained in detail in the third chapter of the *Śivamahātmyakhaṇḍa*. (183–187) Regarding the phrase "being indifferent": [he remained so].

Thus, while Parameśvara and Viṣṇu remained thus exhausted, Sūta, being entirely under the sway of devotion to Śiva, spoke again out of anger regarding the meaning of the Vedic text as it had been explained by Brahmā with faith; such is the statement of Sūta. 188.

In the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the knowledge of the "Fullness" (bhūmavidyā) was taught by Sanatkumāra to Nārada. Summarizing that, [the author] states: "All these sciences," because the sciences other than the investigation of the Self lack the capacity to produce the knowledge of the true nature of reality, and instead serve merely as causes for the memorization of texts and their meanings—as recorded in the passage beginning with, "O Venerable One, I study this Ṛgveda. This he summarizes with the words: "all these sciences."

By the word "all," the meditations on the principles such as Name, Speech, and so forth—recorded in such scriptural passages as, "He who meditates on Name as Brahman"—are also included. This is because those [meditations] are understood from the respective supplementary portions of the texts to be means for attaining results pertaining to both this world and the next, as in: "As far as Name extends, he has freedom of movement therein. Furthermore, the Lord has stated that the Vedas other than those Upaniṣads have worldly results as their object: "The Vedas have the three qualities (guṇas) as their domain; be thou free from the three qualities, O Arjuna."

Thus: "For I have indeed heard from those who have seen the Blessed One that he who knows the Self crosses over the darkness of sorrow"—this is what is recorded in the scripture; its meaning is stated as "the knower of the Self. Regarding the phrase "of the darkness of saṃsāra": the meaning is "of that darkness called ignorance which is the root cause of saṃsāra. || 189 ||

Having seen everyone delighted, Mahādeva, being satisfied, vanished on the spot. (186) Viṣṇu performed the circumambulation of Brahmā and returned to Vaikuṇṭha along with Lakṣmī. (187) Overcome by devotion, Brahmā began to speak again regarding the truth, out of brotherly affection. (188) Brahmā said:
"All these deliberations set in motion the wheel of worldly existence for people; this alone is the knowledge of the Self. (189)
802. For one who is devoid of the realization of the Self, the ocean of worldly existence alone remains;

for one established in the Self, there is liberation itself—of this there is no cause for doubt. (190) Where a living being perceives something other [than the Self], hears something other, and likewise eats something other, that which is seen is merely the mortal world. (191) But where one sees nothing else, nor hears anything else, nor eats anything else... [that is the immortal]. (192)
Furthermore, he who does not perceive anything else is the Infinite (bhūman), the consumer of food. || 192 ||

Now, one might ask: why is it that other forms of knowledge do not possess the capacity to bring about the cessation of *saṃsāra*? To this, he says: "In the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). For ignorance regarding one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed the cause of *saṃsāra*. This [ignorance] cannot be removed by knowledge whose object is not the Self. Therefore, for one devoid of the knowledge of the Self, the meaning is that *saṃsāra* continues just as before. For this very reason, even though he was proficient in all branches of learning, the following statement was recorded in scripture from Nārada, who lacked knowledge of the Self: "O Venerable One, I am grieving; may the Venerable One ferry me across to the further shore of sorrow."

"Only through liberation" means that for one who possesses the knowledge of the Self, when the ignorance that veils it is removed by the knowledge of its nature, sorrow—which is devoid of any material cause and is thus impossible—cannot arise; therefore, there is no doubt here that this is indeed liberation. || 190 ||

In the Śruti, the principles beginning with Name and ending with Prāṇa—each progressively more pervasive than the last—are taught as a sequence of steps, like a staircase, as means for descending into the supreme reality beyond the intellect. Having declared that the Self, which is of the nature of unlimited bliss and all-pervasive, is what must be known in the passage, "But the Infinite (Bhūman) alone is to be sought after," the scripture then records the definition of the entity that is the Infinite in the passage beginning with, "Where one sees nothing else. This [verse] summarizes that: "Where another... and so forth.

It should be understood that the definition of the "small" (*alpa*), which was traditionally taught as being characterized by opposition to the ground (*bhū*)—namely, "Now, where there is duality"—is presented here first for the sake of ease of comprehension. This is the meaning: that entity in which the conventional distinctions of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge exist is "small," because it is delimited; for this very reason, it is mortal and perishable. That entity in which such dualistic dealings do not exist is the undelimited, denoted by the word *bhū*. (191–192)

She brings an end to ignorance, which takes the form of saṃsāra. (Since it is the effect of ignorance, saṃsāra is indeed ignorance. || 189 || For one devoid of self-knowledge, wandering in the ocean of sorrow is condemned; for one established in the Self alone, liberation follows—there is no cause for doubt in this matter. || 190 ||

In whatever state a living being perceives objects through knowledge consisting of distinctions—such as seeing, hearing, and so forth—that state is "small," meaning it pertains to the period of ignorance; therefore, it is characterized by lack of realization (avijñāna). || 191 || That reality in which no perception, hearing, or other forms of knowledge consisting of distinctions occurs is the all-pervading (vyāpaka) reality. || 192 || That which is all-pervading is itself the Good (sukha); that itself is liberation (mokṣa).

There is no happiness that is not all-pervasive; therefore, one should take firm resolve in this great non-duality (advaita). (193) For one who is established in this truth, there is neither death nor birth, neither going nor coming, neither bondage nor liberation. (194) That person becomes the very embodiment of this all-pervasive Śiva-tattva; [all] diseases...

Chapter Five That which is the Plenum (bhūman) is indeed happiness; for that is the supreme state of absolute liberation (kaivalya). There is no happiness in the finite; therefore, one should become absorbed in the Great Plenum. For one who is devoted to the Great Plenum, there is neither death nor birth. Indeed, there is no bondage for him, nor is there liberation. Right here, everything is completely dissolved by its own nature through the realization of the Self, like a dream or the appearance of a world to one who is asleep.

This supreme, absolute concealment of one's own [nature] has been spoken of by you with great severity; for there is nothing further to be told to you than this: [the attainment of] the feet of the God of gods. 196.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Single Truth from the Brahmavidyā-tāraka-nyāsa," in the latter portion of the fourth section, the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Sūta-saṃhitā.

He states the meaning of the scriptural passage, "That which is infinite is bliss" (*yo vai bhūmā tatsukham*), with the words "That which is... (*yo vā iti*). An object that is unlimited in nature is indeed bliss and is the unsurpassed liberation (*niratiśayā muktiḥ*). However, there is no such thing as bliss in that which is limited; for fear and other such states necessarily arise from the objects that cause limitation. Indeed, it is recorded in the scripture: "From duality, fear arises. Therefore, he concludes with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) that the realization of one's own nature as the unlimited bliss is precisely what must be accomplished. 193.

"Bhara-hita-para-sa" and so forth. Thus, for one who is established in the non-dual Brahman-Ātman—which is beyond all circumscription—there exists no empirical transaction whatsoever regarding birth, destruction, bondage, liberation, and the like. Rather, when all this is known in its true nature within this very ground-reality (bhūma-vastu), it is perceived as being of that very essence and does not arise again. Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "tat" (as in that). Now, ghee becomes solidified through contact with fire; yet, upon contact with that same [fire], its solidity dissolves.

In this way, one might raise the objection that even Brahmā, having previously been attached to the phenomenal world (prapañca) through his knowledge of his own sphere, later became free from defects; thus, due to being subject to modification, he would be impermanent. Anticipating this, the author states another illustration: "As in a dream" (svapna). Just as the appearance of a city in a dream occurs within the undivided and changeless reality of Brahman, so too does the appearance of the entire universe occur. Therefore, since it has manifestation alone as its body, it does not bring about any modification in its own substratum; this is the meaning. 94196. Tra.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Teaching on the Upanishads in the Brahma-gītā," in the latter part of the fourth section, the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa, of the Tātparya-dīpikā commentary on the Śrī Śiva-mahāpurāṇa. ||5||

By its own nature, it becomes the very form of the Self; just as the heat of a vessel of milk subsides upon boiling, or as the dream-world vanishes upon waking, so too does every distinction dissolve within the Rasa. || 195 || All these matters are exceedingly auspicious, pertaining to the ultimate truth and leading to liberation.

That you have bestowed this instruction upon them out of pure compassion—O Mahādeva, it is only through your grace that I have gained the capacity to speak thus; beyond this, there is nothing further worthy of being told to you. 196.

Chapter Six of the *Brahmagītā*. The Goddess said: In this city of Brahman, there is a small abode; within it is the lotus, and in the center of that is a small space (*ākāśa*). (1) Śiva, who is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), resides there. He is to be sought after by those who strive, and He is to be fully realized by the faithful, O believers, with a mind free from contraction. (2)

Thus, Brahman—non-dual, undivided by space, direction, or means of accomplishment, and consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss—is taught as being near at hand. However, because that [Brahman] cannot be directly realized by those of dull intellect, the scripture beginning with "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman" teaches the meditation upon that very same Brahman through the metaphor of a small lotus (*dahara*) and its qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāma*), for the seeker of liberation who is endowed with the perfection of means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*). This is the *Daharavidyā*.

It is gathered together in this [body], as expressed by the phrase "in this citadel," and so forth. The "city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*) refers to the body of the one qualified for meditation, which is the locus where Brahman is perceived. For it has been said: "The body of Brahman is accepted as the substratum for those who perceive [Him]; because of its uniqueness, that body becomes the city of Brahman."

And within this body, which is qualified by knowledge, there is this small lotus of limited dimension; due to the limitation [imposed] by that, the space (*ākāśa*)—though all-pervading—is taught by the Śruti as being "small" (*dahara*) in dimension, and it is that very Supreme Light, whose nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, which is to be investigated within it. For the word *ākāśa* is primarily applied to Brahman according to its etymological derivation as "that which shines forth on all sides" (*ā samantāt kāśate*). Therefore, it is declared elsewhere in the scripture: "Verily, the name 'Ākāśa' belongs to Him who is hidden within the two cavities."

In this regard, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, in the *Ākāśādhikaraṇa*, established through a Sūtra that Ākāśa is Brahman: "Ākāśa [is Brahman], on account of its being so designated" (*ākāśastalliṅgāt*). This very Ākāśa is the supreme Śiva, who is to be sought by those desiring liberation through the practice of means such as tranquility and self-control. Moreover, He is to be known through the knowledge produced by the means of hearing, reflection, and so forth. By stating this, the author explains that in the Śruti passage, "That which is within it," the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the previously mentioned lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).

For if the small ether (*daharākāśa*) were taken as the primary referent, then the earth, heaven, and so forth—which are described as being situated within it—would themselves have to be the object of meditation; and that is incorrect. Furthermore, because we understand from the text that "he who, having discovered the Self here, departs, for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds regarding these true desires," that the meditation on the Self possesses a fruit. Now, one might ask: "In that case, is Brahman to be meditated upon only in its limited aspect? No, he says: "without limitation."
The meaning is that, having abandoned the limitation produced by the adjunct (upādhi) of the lotus stalk, it is to be meditated upon in its natural, unlimited form. || 1-2 ||
The sixth chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Meditation on the Small One" (*daharopāsanā*):
although the supreme meditation has already been performed, this [meditation] is for those who are unable to grasp it [in its entirety].

One should explain the means (*sādhana*) by which this [individual] may attain equality with that [Supreme Reality]. Therefore, within the small house of the heart located in the city of Brahman (*brahmapura*), that which is the small space of ether (*ākāśa*) is Śiva, who is consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*). The seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should seek and experience that reality, which is unlimited and uncontracted. This "city of Brahman" resides within the body of the practitioner.

The lotus of the heart is the abode of Brahman; it is situated above the six sheaths (kośas), and because it is so, the city belonging to the King (Brahman) is called the "Royal City" (Rājanagara). For this very reason, the city of the body, whose dwelling-place is the heart of Brahman, is designated as the "City of Brahman" (Brahmapura). It is entirely consistent that in a small body the heart is small, and the space within it is even smaller still.

For the purpose of meditation, it is necessary to fix the one-pointedness of the mind upon a particular object. The word "ākāśa" here signifies the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Because it is bodiless, subtle, and all-pervading like space, Brahman is also called "ākāśa. [Objection: But is it not the case that the word "ākāśa" is used here not in its conventional sense (rūḍhi) for the Supreme, but rather by abandoning its conventional meaning? [Reply: Let it be so.

However, in the sūtra "And because of common usage" (1.3.17), it is stated that the word *ākāśa* refers to the Supreme Lord based on its well-established conventional meaning, according to the commentary thereon. Consequently, in this sūtra as well, the restriction of a term—such as *liṅga* and so forth—which has many established meanings to a single referent is explained by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and other criteria.

This is how it should be understood. As for those who, recollecting the rule that "it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings," have explained that the word *ākāśa* does not refer to anything other than space because it would otherwise follow that it is not the object of that [specific] reference—how can they maintain that the word *soma* refers to both the plant and the moon? Furthermore, it may be argued that words with multiple meanings are more commonly established in the field of literary aesthetics (*sāhitya*).

6.805 Due to the contraction of that which manifests it, there is the appearance of contraction in the Self; however, in its own nature, that all-pervading [Self] is never divided. 6.806 Through the aspect of being born and through the aspect of not knowing itself, everything shines to the Witness; and by virtue of its identity with that [Witness], it always shines as that very thing.

This world is indeed composed of *nāḍa* (the non-self); it appears solely through its connection with consciousness (*cit*), and not otherwise. Therefore, that Śiva, who is of the nature of that [consciousness], shines forth pervading everything. He is inherently all-pervasive and not non-pervasive, for contraction arises only from the limitation of another.

[Objection: "But surely, let there be no contraction due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*); rather, a contraction appears to be natural (*svābhāvika*) itself in bodies such as those of a seat or a horse. To this, he says: "By that which manifests its own [nature]" (*svābhivyajjakena*). The meaning is: even though the Self (*ātman*) has the nature of self-luminous consciousness (*cit*), the appearance of limitation within the Self is caused by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, which manifest [the Self] for the purpose of removing the ignorance that veils it; thus, like the reflection "the crystal is red," it is not natural. Why? To this he says: "Consciousness" (*cit*).

At all times and in every instance—during the periods of origination, persistence, and so forth—the form and essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is superimposed, is indeed Brahman, whose characteristic is consciousness. Since that which is superimposed is non-different from its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), by this [statement], the limitations caused by time and substance are refuted. (3) He now refutes even the limitation caused by space: "by way of being known," etc.

Even though the entire world appears, it shines within the witness-consciousness of the Self in the form of being "born"—that is, as an object of knowledge—and likewise in the form of being "unborn"—that is, as not an object of knowledge. The meaning is that since there is nowhere any separation from its own self-luminosity, no spatial limitation exists either. As this teacher has stated: "Every object, whether known or unknown, is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness. [The phrase] "it shines" means that very thing.

The Supreme Brahman shines by Himself at all times and on all sides; this [Brahman], being of the nature of consciousness, does not require any external means for His manifestation. (48) Now, one might ask: "Why then does the world itself not shine by its own accord? To this he replies with the word "svayam" (by Himself). The qualifying term "jaḍātmakam" (of the nature of insentience) contains a reason. (49) Thus, he concludes the established omnipresence of Paraśiva with the word "ataḥ" (therefore): having pervaded the entire world, which is characterized by ignorance and its effects, He exists as omnipresent by His very nature.
It is established, however, that its limitation [to specific locations] arises from its association with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || 6 ||

Since its usage and its etymological derivation (*nirukti*) have been made by Brahmā to such an extent that it is appropriate to accept this word as signifying the meaning "Brahman," [the author] has stated "unlimited" (*aparicchinna*) in order to show that the limitation of Brahman is not real, but rather due to the exclusion of the upper regions and so forth. (1-2)

The contraction of the Self appears due to the contraction of its own manifesting internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and other faculties; by its very nature, the Self is of the form of consciousness (cidrūpa), eternal, and all-pervading, not limited.

Even though the Self (*ātman*) is not something that can be manifested by anything else—since no manifester of the Self is possible—nevertheless, during the state of ignorance (*ajñāna*), the cognition of the Self occurs to us only through its association with some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); therefore, the limiting adjunct is designated as the "manifester. This should be understood in the same way as when, although space (*ākāśa*) is omnipresent, the conventional usage "this is space" occurs when a pot is present within it.

This designation occurs precisely according to the experience of the deluded one. [Verse 3] In the previous verse, it was shown that the Self is not limited from the perspective of time and substance; now, they show that it is likewise not limited from the perspective of space and location: everything—whether known or unknown—continues to appear to the witness, whose nature is consciousness. (Therefore, O Knower...)

9. (Ḍa-ca) ... should be understood as "evaṃ voddhavyam" (thus it should be known). 2. It is ignorance (*ajñāna*) qualified by an object that is experienced, not ignorance in itself! Since a qualified experience is not possible without an experience of the qualifier, an experience of the object must be admitted. Nor can that [experience] arise through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that would contradict its being unapprehended (*ajñātatva*). Furthermore, the experience arising from the means of valid cognition would be something with a beginning (*sādi*), whereas the state of being unapprehended is established as beginningless; thus, such an experience is not useful for the object in this context.

Furthermore, the purport of the statement of the Proponent of the Nature of Light (*Prakāśātmavādin*) is that consciousness itself must be accepted as the direct revealer of unknown objects. [Objection: "Everything shines within Consciousness" implies that [the world] is pervaded by Consciousness (*cidvyāpya*). Since Consciousness also shines, it too must be pervaded by something else; otherwise, if it did not shine, it would be non-existent. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It shines by its own nature. Thus, there is no room for the aforementioned defects—namely, that it does not shine for anything other than itself, and so forth. Nor is there a second defect, namely that it would be useless to say "it shines by itself," because [if it were not self-luminous, it would not shine at all].

806. As great as this external space is, so great is the internal space. Within it, both the earth and the sky are contained. (7) Both fire and wind, sun and moon, both stars and lightning, and whatever exists as a positive reality, (8) and that which appears as a negative non-existence—all that is contained within it. Therefore, it is all-powerful, all-pervasive, and by its very nature omnipresent. (9) This Self is the Lord, all-pervading, and forever free from all sins.
And those who are not impartial—witnesses who are wavering, lacking in discernment, or intoxicated by liquor—are not [valid] witnesses. || 10 ||
Free from sorrow, self-controlled, free from thirst, characterized by truth and other virtues, possessing true desires and true resolve—such are the bulls among the gods (O Śakras).

Having thus established the meaning, he applies the scriptural passage beginning with "As large as this space is, so large is this space within the heart," etc., with the words "As large as... and so forth. The statement "as large as that space" is intended to demonstrate the all-pervasiveness [of Brahman] through a comparison with the well-known elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*), and not to indicate its actual dimension; for Brahman pervades the entire universe, including space and everything else. Therefore, it is declared in scripture: "By Him, heaven and earth are covered."

He establishes this very all-pervasiveness with the words beginning "as far as heaven and earth," and so on. By this, the scriptural passage beginning with "Both heaven and earth are contained within Him alone" and ending with "Whatever He has here and whatever He does not have" is explained. (7–9) Now, one might object: "Let the Lord be all-pervasive; what follows for the individual soul (jīva) from that? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This [is He]. This very Lord is the Self, existing as the innermost core of all. There is no such thing as a soul distinct from Him.

One might object: "Is there not another [self] that serves as the substratum for the superimposition of *dharma* and *adharma*? To this, he says: "By sins" (*pāpmabhiḥ*). The mention of "sins" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for merit (*puṇya*) as well, since both are causes of the fruits of *saṃsāra*. Because merit and sin are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the conscious Self (*cidātmā*), which is their witness and distinct from them, is not touched by them—this is the meaning. Thus, because of its freedom from contact with merit and sin, all modifications resulting from them, such as death, old age, and so forth, do not exist for that witness; this he states with the words beginning with "immortal" (*amṛta*).

"Satyakāmaḥ satyasaṃkalpaḥ" (He whose desires are true and whose resolves are true) is the statement of the qualities to be meditated upon. The scriptural passage beginning with "This Self is free from evil, ageless... and ending with "satyasaṃkalpaḥ" is thus summarized. (10–11) 4

Since there is no absence of the self in others, the self is everything. That self shines by itself at all times; therefore, it is omnipresent in every way. (4) This world of insentient matter cannot be established on its own; the manifestation of the world occurs only on the basis of its relation to consciousness, and not without it. (5)

Therefore, having manifested and pervaded the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), Śiva—who is its manifestor—remains inherently all-pervasive; He is not non-pervasive. The perception of limitation arises only from the influence of adjuncts (*upādhi*). (6) Just as this external form is pervasive, so too is the internal space in the form of the Self (*ātman*) pervasive. Both the upper world (*uloka*) and the lower world (*pūryīloka*) are situated within this very [space]. (7)

Fire, wind, sun, moon, stars, and the directions—whatever appears in this manner, as well as that which does not appear in this manner—all that is situated within Him. Therefore, Śambhu alone is the refuge of all; by His very nature, He is all-pervasive. This all-pervasive Supreme Lord is indeed the inner self (pratyagātman).

He is eternally untouched by all merits and sins, for He is the witness of all. He is free from death, old age, grief, hunger, and thirst. Truth and the like constitute His essential nature. He is one whose desires and volitions are true (meaning that the will and resolve of Śambhu never prove futile). || 10-11 || Just as in this world, enjoyments are obtained through the cultivation of merit...

1. Ḍa. cha. jña. read *virajaḥ su*. 9. [The word "ātman" refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), because that is the well-known meaning of the word "ātman"—thus according to the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya* (p. 246, Ma.ma.saṃ.)]. Having understood this, he says: "He who has become all things. 3. dha. ḍa. ca. cha. ñña. [omit *m*]. He [attains] by this much. 4. ḍa. ca. cha. ya. read *viraja i*.

Chapter 6 Just as worlds won by action perish on earth for those who are most devoted to them, so too do worlds won by merit perish even more quickly. (92) For those who, not having known the Supreme Self, perform all ritual actions, there is no freedom of movement found in any of the worlds. (93) But for those who, having known the Supreme Self, remain established while performing actions as if they were moving, there is indeed freedom of movement in all the worlds. (94)

Just as those who are devoid of knowledge regarding what was buried there might pass over gold lying beneath them and not find it, thinking, "These are merely paths," so too, while passing into the world of Brahman during deep sleep, they do not perceive it due to great delusion; oh, the power of delusion! 95–96.

Thus, the scriptural passage beginning with "Just as here, the world won by action... summarizes the statement that knowledge of Brahman—whether devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*) or possessed of attributes (*saguṇa*)—is the cause of its imperishable fruit, and not ritual acts such as the *agnihotra*. This is because the underlying principle is that whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent. (Verse 12) He explains the meaning of the passage "But those who have not known this [world] here... (Verse 13): "Those who have not known" means those who have not understood. (Verse 13)

He states the meaning of the sentence, "But those who here, having understood the Self... with the words, "Those who, however, having known the Self characterized as described above, remain established [in it], their sacrificial acts such as the *agnihotra* and so forth do not lead them back to rebirth, O man, as if they were going; for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which possesses the nature of being an agent, an enjoyer, and so on, has been completely separated [from the Self]. He states the fruit of that knowledge with the words, "Of them," and "In all worlds."

And regarding those various worlds and specific objects of desire which have been elaborated upon in the Śruti through such passages as, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," in all of them the knower possesses the freedom of movement (*kāmacāra*). The meaning is that because the Brahman residing within the heart, when meditated upon with attributes such as having all desires fulfilled, is by its very nature unsurpassed bliss, all desires are but portions of that [bliss]. || 14 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that such Brahman is attained in deep sleep, according to the Śruti: 'Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1)? And so, why is it that the attainment of all desires does not belong to one in deep sleep just as it does to the knower? Anticipating this doubt, the author states an illustration: "Just as gold," and "the world of Brahman. The term *loka* means that which is perceived; thus, *brahmaloka* refers to Brahman itself as the world. In the state of deep sleep, Brahman—which is self-luminous—is indeed attained by all living beings, yet it remains unattained due to the presence of ignorance (*avidyā*).

For a person who does not know the meaning of the word "alms," [the goal] is like a treasure; by this, the meaning of the Vedic passage beginning with "Just as one might find a hoard of gold" is summarized. (15-16)

Even these very enjoyments obtained through merit come to an end; they do not remain inexhaustible. (19) Without knowing the Supreme Self, all actions are performed in vain; for them, freedom is never attained in any of the worlds. (13) Those who, having realized the Supreme Self, remain established in it alone—even while appearing to perform all actions—attain sovereignty in all the worlds. (54)

It is observed that gold may be buried in a field for many years; however, if one lacks the knowledge that "gold is buried in this field," people will not recognize or recover the gold even though gems continue to pass back and forth over it. In the same way, although the resplendent Brahman passes through everyone every day during the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), because they do not know Him, they are unable to attain Him.

This is the marvelous power of ignorance (which makes even one's own self unattainable! || 15-16 || Since Śambhu, who is the witness, dwells in the hearts of all without any distinction, [the text says] "going" (gacchantyaḥ). [The commentary] clarifies the meaning of the word "sthitāḥ" (situated) by stating "not, however" (na punar). The syntactical connection (anvaya) should be understood as: "having known the Supreme Support, they are situated therein."

808. This Śiva, who dwells in the heart as the witness of all without distinction, is therefore declared to be in the heart; he is the liberator from saṃsāra. He who knows this attains the heavenly world, there is no doubt. (17) O best of gods, that subtle light which has risen up from our body—that Śiva shines forth, O gods; by his own nature, he manifests himself just as one’s own reflection [appears] in water. (18–19)
This is the Self and nothing else; I have spoken the truth. This alone is the immortal, which has become manifest before you, O King. 20.

From the etymological derivation of the word *hṛdaya* as well, the residence of the all-pervading Brahman within the heart is shown by the Śruti in passages such as, "That very Self is in the heart. He summarizes this by saying, "This one resides in the heart. Regarding this knowledge of Brahman residing within the heart, he states its fruit as established by the Śruti in the passage, "Day after day, indeed, one who knows thus," with the words, "He who thus..."

By means of this direct realization of Brahman, one reaches the world of heaven; the meaning is that one attains Brahman, which is the supreme bliss, the essence of all worlds, and free from all suffering. (17) Now, he explains the manner of attaining that Brahman as shown by the scriptural passage beginning with "Now, that serene being," using the words "from this": *asmād iti*.

Having abandoned the identification with the gross and subtle bodies, and being serene—free from the distress caused by the enjoyment of objects during both the waking and dream states—one who is of the nature of the witness (*sākṣin*) should cast off even the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), which is characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*) and the lack of knowledge of the primordial Brahman. Having attained the nature of Supreme Śiva—the light-form that transcends all modifications, untouched by them, and consisting solely of the manifestation of pure consciousness—and having known it as one's own self, one abandons the limitation created by ignorance.

"One attains [it] by emerging in one's very own form. Regarding this attainment, it should be understood here as explained in the thirty-eighth chapter of the first part (*pūrvabhāga*): because it is attained through the analogy of gold already present in the throat, it is accomplished by knowledge alone (*jñāna-mātra-sādhya*), and not by action (*karma-sādhya*) like the journey from one village to another. He states the meaning of the sentence "This, indeed, is the Self," saying: "This is the Self. He emerges in this very way; this is the Self itself, and nothing else.

The meaning is that anything additional to this—characterized by the body and so forth—is not the Self because it is conditioned (*sopādhika*). He cites the scriptural passage, "This is the immortal," with the words "This very [is it]. This very undivided, essential reality is the immortal and indestructible, according to the scripture: "That which is the *bhūman* (the Infinite), that is the immortal. For this very reason it is fearless (*abhaya*), because of the absence of a second cause of fear. Precisely because of this fearlessness, this is Brahman, according to such scriptural passages as: "O Janaka, you have indeed reached the fearless," and "For Brahman is fearless. || 20 ||

Even the name "Heart" causes distress to Śiva, who liberates one from *saṃsāra*. He who thus meditates upon the Supreme Self, the witness of all, attains Brahman, whose nature is bliss. || 17 || In deep sleep (*suṣupti*), having abandoned the ego-identification with this body, that which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) becomes one with Paraśiva, who is of the nature of light; it then remains established in its own natural state.

The state of supreme bliss (*śivatā*) that one attains in deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is simply the very nature of the Self; it is not the attainment of any separate entity. To remain with innate ignorance (*naisargika-ajñāna*) is the natural condition of the Self. The superimposition of the body (*dehādhyāsa*), however, is adventitious. This very Self is that which remains in its own natural state during deep sleep; there is no other Self besides this. || 18-19 ||

This alone is the nectar, this is fearlessness, this is Brahman. || 20 || That Self which is the desireless seer is the support of all; it is the bridge, the dam. "Having become [this]," [it is said]; thus appears the reading of the commentator. 2. Chapter on Ignorance, 6. 809.

That Self which is within the small lotus-like heart, free from desire, immortal, and divine—O foremost of gods, for the non-division of these worlds, [know] this Maheśvara. (21) Day and night do not cross over it, nor does old age;
nor does sorrow, nor hunger, nor thirst, O lords. (22) Therefore, all evils turn back, O best of gods;
for this world of Brahman is free from evil and self-luminous. (23)

Therefore, one who has been pierced by the arrows of the gods becomes non-blind even while being pierced; likewise, one who was previously unpierced remains unpierced. Furthermore, one who was afflicted becomes non-afflicted. || 24 ||

Now, the Śruti—"That which is the Self is the bridge, it is not subject to affliction"—is summarized by the words beginning with "ya ātmā" (that which is the Self). "It is the bridge, the support" (*sa seturvidhṛtiḥ*). It is called a "bridge" (*setu*) because it is like a bridge, serving as a boundary. "Support" (*vidhṛti*) means the sustaining of the determinately ordered phenomenal world through the distinctions of attributes such as covering, and through the framework of action, agent, and result. If one asks for what purpose that sustaining is, he says: "for the sake of non-confusion" (*asaṃbhedāya*).

The meaning is that for the sake of the non-confusion, non-disruption, and non-destruction—meaning the non-separation—of these worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, which consist of agents, actions, and fruits, this Self is described as a "bridge" by means of the passage beginning with "day and night. Day and night, which serve to delimit every living being subject to birth, do not cross over—that is, they do not transcend—this Self which has become a bridge. Thus, like one who has crossed over, there is no delimitation by the "flood" characterized by day, night, and so forth.

The meaning is that because [the body] is superimposed upon him as having its true nature [in the Self], it is impossible for it to be the means of defining him. Likewise, old age and so forth, being attributes of the body and such, do not reach the Self, which is distinct from them and serves as their cause. (21–22) And since they do not reach him, all these things turn back, struck down by immortality. To the question "Why?", he says: "This" (eṣa). "Loka" means a world; "Brahma-loka" is the world that is Brahman itself. Because this [Self] is indeed free from evil (apahatapāpman), therefore they turn back; this is the meaning. (23)

"Therefore, indeed," and so forth. Since he is distinct from the body and other such things, therefore the wise man, having crossed—meaning having reached—this bridge-like Ātman, becomes entirely free, because the attributes of blindness and so on, along with the attributes of the gross body and so forth, have ceased to exist. This is the meaning. || 24 ||

Baudha-he! Indeed, established in this state, these obstructions do not disperse; day and night cannot delimit this Maheśvara. Birth, old age, sorrow, merit, and sin—none of these can touch him. (21-22) All evils and the like remain far removed from him. Therefore, this world of Brahman, which is self-luminous, is called "apahatapāpmā" (free from evil).

“*Apahatapāpmā* means one whose evil—consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—has been struck away; indeed, one who has destroyed all evils is called *apahatapāpmā*. (23) Therefore, he who attains this bridge does not remain blind even when blinded, nor does he remain pierced by spears and the like even when pierced, nor does he remain afflicted by diseases and other sufferings even while being afflicted. (Then:
1. Self-luminous!)

8100. *Brahmagītā*: That which has been described as this "small space" (*daharākāśa*) is the Supreme Lord. 1. Being the primordial and eternal reality, He exists prior to the body and its specific attributes. 25. That state which shines for embodied beings—neither waking, nor dreaming, nor deep sleep—even of that, Mahādeva is the witness, distinct and self-luminous. 26. Through superimposition upon that [Self], it appears and yet does not appear. 27. By means of the body, which is an object of perception, [the Self] is always [distinct] from that body. 28.

There is certainly a connection with the pleasant and the unpleasant; of this there is no doubt. But for one who exists as bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not exist. This has been spoken by me as the truth; there is no cause for doubt in this matter. O best of gods, that which is this internal space (daharākāśa) is indeed the creator of name and form; that alone is the eternal Brahman. That alone is the unmanifest, and it is the Self of all embodied beings. Beyond that, there is nothing else whatsoever, nor is there anything superior to it.
He alone shines forth through every form, yet he does not shine; oh, who indeed can know that perfection of the divine Self? 22.

Having thus taught Brahman as the object of the knowledge concerning the small [space within the heart], Prajāpati further instructed Indra regarding the realization of the Self that is liberated from states such as waking and so forth. He summarizes that knowledge—which was demonstrated by the Śruti in the passage beginning with "This person who is seen in the eye"—with the words "He who... and so on.

The meaning is that since the body and so forth, as well as states such as waking, are objects of perception for something insentient, the Self—which is their witness—must be understood as self-luminous and indeed distinct from them. (1) He establishes the objectivity of the non-Self in the verse beginning with "tasmin" (in Him). The world, which is insentient and superimposed upon that Brahman as its own nature, is sometimes perceived and sometimes not; thus, its manifestation depends on something other than itself. The point is that if the world were self-luminous like the Self, it would follow that it would be manifest at all times. (2527)

He summarizes the meaning of such scriptural passages as "For one who exists with a body... and so forth, by means of the verse beginning with "By his own agency," etc. The meaning is that for one who identifies with the body and so forth, there is transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), characterized by the experience of pleasure and pain; however, for one who knows the self alone as distinct from the body and other such things, transmigratory existence does not exist at all. || 28-29 ||

In order to strengthen the fact that the word *dahara-ākāśa* (the small ether) refers to Brahman, he cites a passage from another scripture—“That which is called ‘ether’ is the container of names and forms”—and summarizes it with the words “He who is this...”. That which is known as the ether, which abides within the heart and is the creator of names such as "pot" and "cloth," as well as of the multitude of objects denoted by those names—that indeed is Brahman, without beginning or end. [30] The term "immortal" (*amṛta*) has its meaning already explained. [31–32]

O performer of the Kārīrī sacrifice and others, grant us [the means]. We consider ourselves blind and so forth, having identified our own nature with this [condition]. One who knows the true nature of the bridge understands that he is not blind and so forth, even though from our perspective he continues to appear as if blind and so forth. || 24 || That Supreme Lord who has been described here through subtle forms is devoid of distinctions such as the body and is eternal. || 25 ||

The witness of those states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, which appear to the possessors of Śrī, is also that self-luminous Mahādeva who is distinct from them. Through the yoga of the supreme self (adhyātma-yoga), these states are sometimes perceived by Mahādeva and sometimes they are not. || 26-27 || For the person who always regards his own visible body as his true nature, [the realization] does not exist. || 28 || (Note: *ca* = "and"; *tayenāsākṣitvā* = "by means of that, due to non-witnessing").

Just as [the sun] exists pervasively through its own nature within the modifications of light, so too does the Witness of all exist everywhere, established through His own essence. (23) Or, just as water exists pervasively through its own nature within the modifications of water, so too does the Witness of all exist everywhere, established through His own love. (24) Just as fire exists pervasively through its own nature within its various modifications, so too does the Witness of all exist everywhere, established through His own form. (25)
Just as the witness of one's own transformations remains distinct from them in each case, so too does that witness abide everywhere, transcending the duality of those states.

Just as the sky exists in its own form alone, so too does the witness, who possesses all selves, exist in its capacity as a witness. (37) Though appearing divided by distinctions such as a balance, gold, and so forth, it remains undivided due to its nature as space; though appearing divided in the perception of forms, it remains undivided. (38) Mahādeva shines both through non-differentiation and through differentiation; otherwise, how could Mahādeva be Mahādeva? (39)

The example of "clay" is intended to demonstrate that Brahman persists through its own effects, such as the elements and their derivatives (bhūta-bhautika), as in [Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8]: "Just as by one lump of clay, all things made of clay are known... (32–36). Furthermore, another illustration—"the all-pervading ether"—is given to establish that even though it is pervasive, it remains untainted. (37). By the phrase "the pot, the ring, etc.," the non-difference in reality (tāttvikābheda) is established. (38). Through the name "Mahādeva," his omnipresence is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "Mahādeva is the leader of the undivided... (39).

For one who has realized the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body through the grace of the Brahman-knowers, there is no longer any connection with the pleasant or the unpleasant. (28) That which is this subtle ether is the creator of names and forms; it is the eternal Brahman. (30) It is the immortal; beyond it, there is nothing else. (31)

This very [Brahman] appears as all things, yet at times it does not appear at all; who can know this wondrous perfection of Rudra? Fire itself remains in that very form within all its own transformations, and water likewise remains in that very form within all its own transformations. 32. Fire itself remains in that very form within all its own transformations.

Just as the wind remains present within all its own various modifications, so too the Witness (sākṣī) alone is present everywhere; "uta" means that it is established through all things. (33-26) Just as the ether, though pervading everywhere, remains established in its own unchanging form, even so the Witness, despite being the essential nature [of all], remains established in its own immutable form. (37)

Just as the space within a jar and other such divisions do not in any way become distinct from space itself, even though they appear so; in the same way, although all these divisions exist, Īśāna does not in any way become divided. (38) Mahādeva alone manifests in both divided and undivided forms. If He were not thus, and something else were to manifest, then how could Mahādeva be called "Mahādeva" (the Great God)? (Mahān...)

In fact, the meaning of the term "Mahādeva" is the all-pervading God. If there were anything produced [as a separate entity], it would constitute a limitation of the reality (*vastu-pariccheda*), and thus its pervasiveness would not remain; consequently, those things would not be "great. This is the intended meaning. Indeed, Mahādeva is Mahādeva alone; He is not non-great. Likewise, Mahādeva is everything; nothing else exists apart from Him. (40)
Whatever form it may assume, that which neither exists nor shines forth, in that very same form Śiva alone manifests.

The thought that "Śiva alone exists" through whatever form He appears—let that be the supreme consciousness of Śiva; for there is no other Śiva. (42) "I am"—this [thought] is always the manifestation of Śiva, the true, solid mass of Consciousness; let it not be said that it is separate from Him. By that [realization], there is neither bondage nor liberation for the mind. (43) When all this is perceived as "Śiva," then there is neither death nor birth whatsoever. Keeping this my word in his heart, one of sharp intellect should remain forever established therein. (44)

He states that this is a designation based on its actual meaning: "Mahādeva is indeed Mahādeva. The sense is: if he were merely great (*mahān*) or if he were merely a god (*devaḥ*), how could such a name as "Mahādeva"—meaning "the Great God"—be established? (40–41) Regarding the phrase "in whatever manner" (*yathābhāsanena*): in whatever manner whatsoever anything appears, by all those very modes, that which is the consciousness and bliss constituting the substrate of all things shines forth as nothing other than the Self; the conviction that this is so is itself the supreme form of consciousness, which is none other than Śakti herself. (42)
The manifold expansion of objects, such as "I" and so forth, has been explained [in verses] 42–44.

Therefore, O Mahādeva, everything is indeed Śiva; there is no river [of existence] separate from Him. Whatever appears or does not appear through any means whatsoever, by that very means Śiva alone causes it to appear.

In whatever manner each and every object appears, within all those objects it is Śiva—whose nature is consciousness-bliss—that shines as their substrate (adhiṣṭhāna). This very certainty is also the Supreme Power in the form of consciousness, and nothing else; one should not entertain any doubt regarding this. (42) That which is to be realized through the syllable "Bha" is the auspicious, true, and dense mass of consciousness (cidghana) alone. There is never any entity whatsoever that is distinct from it.

In this way, that very same object is perceived as "this," yet bondage arises from such a perception. Liberation is never possible by relying on this perception of "this. (43) When everything is perceived as Śiva alone, then the wheel of saṃsāra, consisting of birth and death, no longer remains. One of subtle intellect should always keep these words of Bhairava in mind. (44)

O Supreme Lord, O Supreme Deity, if You are pleased, then this pure, supreme experience arises. For neither by a cart, nor a chariot, nor a palanquin, nor by a desert, nor by a mountain, nor by any other means [is one led there]. (48) O Supreme Lord, if Paramaśiva, through the knowledge of the mantra, acts upon you, then that mortal indeed attains the stainless supreme state; but if Śiva does not act, he goes to bondage. (49) For just as dense darkness is dispelled by the rays of the sun and enters the narrow channel of a stream, [so too is ignorance removed]. (50)

The darkness that lies between one state of existence and another cannot be dispelled by the sun, nor by anyone else. Hari, I, and others are all like horses blinded by the intense light of Śiva; we are obscured by his radiance. Just as the waters of rivers are driven away by the rays of the sun, so too is inauspiciousness itself spontaneously dispelled by him who is the source of awakening.

Indeed, by remembering the feet of Śiva and by worshipping them, a living being is liberated from his own darkness; for there is nothing that surpasses the remembrance of Śiva’s feet as a cause for protection from death and rebirth. (49) Paramaśiva is truly the cause of our supreme bliss; Paramaśiva is indeed our complete fulfillment. Paramaśiva is truly the support of all our burdens; Paramaśiva is truly our authority. (50)

Paramaśiva is established in all the Āgamas and other scriptures; Paramaśiva is that which is to be known through valid means of cognition; Paramaśiva is the embodiment of supreme bliss; and Paramaśiva is the bestower of supreme grace.

"Is it the *kiṃpāka*? [means: There is a species of tree named *kiṃpāka*. He concludes the matter already established with the words "The Chāndogya," etc. The primary purpose of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is the cessation of ignorance, which is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). When the obscuring ignorance has been removed, the manifestation of one's own true nature as unsurpassed bliss is the second purpose. The meaning is that the knowledge of Brahman is taught for the sake of achieving both of these.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meditation on the *Dahara*," within the *Rama-gītā Upaniṣads*, in the latter portion of the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa*, of the illustrious *Sūta-saṃhitā-tātparya-dīpikā*. The dense darkness of night is entirely dispelled by the rays of the sun alone; likewise, the cause of worldly existence—ignorance, which is denser than even physical darkness—is destroyed by the sun-like form of Śiva alone. (47) Hari, Brahmā, and all other deities appear dim in the presence of the radiance of Paramaśiva; thus, even the day becomes dim before the brilliance of the sun.

Paramaśiva alone is the one who bestows knowledge himself. (48) By remembering his feet and by worshipping them, even a living being can be liberated from its own ignorance; there is no other means for escaping birth and death. (49) He alone is the cause of both ourselves and everyone else. Whatever we possess here is Paramaśiva alone; he is our very self and he is the authority for us. (50)

The entire Āgama is the final realization (*carama-pratipatti*) of Supreme Śiva; it is realized only through that final experience (*anubhava*), for it is both that experience and its bestower. (51) Within the ocean of Supreme Śiva are Hari, all the deities, humans, animals, wild beasts, and so forth—merely as reflections. (Note)

Ha! Only those established in the Vedantic doctrine and possessing pure intellect can recognize that Śiva, who is to be realized through the heart-cave; [otherwise], they remain as if standing in the ocean. (52) Those ignorant of Śiva abandon Hari like one suffering from a chronic disease; yet they consider themselves equal to Śiva—this ignorance harms only the fool. (53) If a firefly were to weigh as much as the sun, then Hari might be equal to Śambhu; [but such is not the case, for] the *kimpāka* tree...

O Lord, if Hari were like the fierce sun or a rākṣasa, and if I were like a *kiṃpāka* fruit or a *sṛgāla* (jackal) compared to sandalwood; if ignorance were equal to true knowledge, and if people were equal to the gods—then what could I say, O Bull among Men? Therefore, only Śiva—the infinite one—can cause that darkness to subside, and no other; for by his own auspicious nature he makes all things auspicious, and by the power of Śiva, the entire universe is a variegated wonder.

Free from all desire and ever compassionate, he beheld that reality; indeed, his suffering was truly great, arising from the state of being a miserable wretch. (56) For one born of a pure nature, this world appears as "this" by its own nature, yet through the essence of stainless awakening, it is known as "the world has passed away. Indeed, for a person of a stainless mind, this is the supreme realization; by means of this supreme awakening, the human being always crosses over existence. (57)

This consciousness, which has been placed within the tip of the *endoga* [the heart] by me, the undiscriminating one, is for the complete destruction of the limbs of living beings; and out of compassion, O Lord of the Immortals, it is for the attainment of the supreme Brahman. This has been spoken according to the words of Maheśa, the sovereign lord of the gods. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meditation on the *Dahara*," within the *Brahmagītā Upaniṣads*, in the latter part of the *Sūtasaṃhitā-tātparyadīpikā*.

If sandalwood were like stone, then only could it be equal to Lord Śiva; if ignorance were like knowledge, then only could anyone be equal to Mahādeva. O gods! What mockery can I describe regarding the wickedness of delusion? (54) Therefore, all this occurs through Śiva alone and from no one else; by his own auspicious nature, Śiva brings everything under control.

This diverse world has been created solely through the power of Śiva. || 55 || The wise man always perceives everything as non-dual. A person who is utterly deluded perceives the reality [of the Self] through such things as the ground or walls, which can only be pointed out with great difficulty. Indeed, for the deluded one, that very perception is the cause of his great suffering. (Pointing out objects such as a pot is a task accomplished only with great effort.)

The operation of causal factors is not logically tenable for a jar as a cause, nor is its non-perception as something distinct from it logically tenable for a jar as an effect. (1) || 56 || For all beings, this firm conviction arises spontaneously that "this is the world. When pure knowledge becomes one's very nature, then the firm realization occurs that the world is indeed the Supreme Self.

This is the supreme wisdom that arises for one whose mind is pure; by this very realization, a human being crosses the ocean of worldly existence. (57) O excellent deities! Out of compassion for the command of Maheśa, the sovereign lord of the leaders of gods, and for the sake of the total destruction of the ignorance of the undiscerning, as well as for the attainment of the exceedingly subtle Brahman, you have all been made to hear this secret knowledge propounded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
