Chapter Seven:
815 Chapter Seven. Brahmā said: There exists that supreme reality, the manifest imperishable among perishable things; it is the substratum, incomparable, and beyond the reach of speech and mind. (9)
When that [Brahman] is well known, all this would be known;
for everything has that as its essence, and indeed, difference does not exist inherently.
Indeed, two kinds of knowledge are to be known: the higher and the lower.
Of these, the lower consists of the Rigveda and the Yajurveda. (2)
Likewise, those who know the Sāmaveda and the Atharvaveda are the preeminent among those learned in phonetics (śikṣā).

Grammar, etymology, prosody, and astronomy—these are indeed cognitions whose objects are not the Self. (4) Having thus explained that the Upaniṣads of the three Vedas have as their ultimate purport the non-duality of Brahman, [the author], desiring now to explain the same purport of the Ātharvaṇa *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, summarizes that Upaniṣad with the words "That exists" (*asti tat*) and so forth. He qualifies it as "that" (*tat*) to distinguish it from the thirty-six categories beginning with Śiva, which are merely subordinate principles (*aparatattva*). It is "that" because it is the supreme reality (*paramārthabhūta*).

Because it is beyond all categories of transformation, it is indeed the imperishable, indestructible, and truly real. For this very reason, it is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all perishable things—that is, of insentient objects. For that which is real serves as the substratum for that which is illusory. It is incomparable because there exists no other object with which it might be compared. And due to its lack of specific attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*), it is not an object of speech or mind.

In this context, because of the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not eternal," the lengthening of the vowel in the word *nāmi* is not applied. By means of the form of questions and answers beginning with, "When this is heard, O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? [the Upanishad] has shown that the knowledge of the entire world is superimposed upon the Immutable (*akṣara*), which is the foundational reality (*adhiṣṭhāna*). He summarizes that [teaching] with the words "That [is Brahman]. He states the reason for the proposition [that the world is identical to Brahman]: "Because it has that as its essence" (*tadātmakatvāt*). That foundational reality is Brahman alone, which is the Self (*ātman*).

The analysis of the compound is: "that whose own nature [is such] when the phenomenal world (prapañca) has been superimposed. The sense is that superimposed things such as silver do not, indeed, obtain a separate existence apart from their substrates such as mother-of-pearl. As for the phrase "not indeed when it is non-existent": the meaning is that the intrinsic difference of the phenomenal world from Brahman has already been repeatedly refuted by reasonings. || 2 ||

Thus, having briefly indicated the subject matter of the Upaniṣad about to be commenced, he applies the relevant portion of the Upaniṣad—beginning with "Two sciences are to be known; thus indeed say those who know Brahman"—to the present purpose: "Two sciences... and so forth. Among these, that which is the lower science (*aparavidyā*), characterized by the *Ṛgveda* and the others and enumerated as consisting of the four Vedas, does not, because its object is nameable things, establish that non-dual reality which has been proclaimed.

Likewise, the cognitions produced by those [perceptions] also have non-self as their object because they take as their domain actions such as the Agnihotra; thus, the meaning is that these too are subordinate to the higher knowledge. || 3-4 ||
The Seventh Chapter, titled "An Investigation into the True Nature of Reality" (*Vastu-svarūpa-vicāra*).

Even if conceptual constructions regarding an entity (*vastu*) are impossible—just as they are with action—if the scriptures were to describe various distinct forms of that entity, those descriptions could not be resolved. Consequently, without a definitive knowledge (*niścayātmaka-jñāna*), the cessation of suffering and the attainment of liberation would be like the mere hope of a sweetmeat. Therefore, it is necessary to observe that all scriptural contexts point toward the single, unique nature of Supreme Śiva.

It is with this very intention that the first chapter of the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā was composed. This is the reason why the Tattvadīpa states, "The definitive conclusion heard [in scripture] is that the essence of all Vedānta is Brahman alone" (verse 1001), thereby subsuming the entirety of the Vedas within the act of *śravaṇa* (hearing).

Having understood the meaning of the *Muṇḍakopaniṣad* from this very Lord, Brahmā said: "The imperishable substratum of all perishable things, incomparable, beyond the reach of speech and mind, transcending all modifications, undecaying, and the ultimate reality—this is the Absolute (*satyatattva*). (1) When that is known correctly, all this is known, for everything has that as its essence.
There is no natural difference between the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Brahman. (2) These two kinds [of knowledge] are worthy of being meditated upon."

1. Even if the conceptualization of [the world] as a real entity is impossible, someone might suspect that this [world] could still exist for the sake of aesthetic delight (*rati*). To that, it should be understood that there is no contradiction even among the scriptural texts (*śrutis*) brought forward in the section on *samanvaya* (systematic harmony). Thus, the intended meaning is that an inquiry into all the Upaniṣads must be undertaken for the sake of accomplishing the hearing (*śravaṇa*) [of the truth]. 2. [Variant reading: ...jaḍatva... 3. [Variant reading: ...na tadvāra...

816. 3. This is the Song of Brahmā (Brahmagītā). That supreme syllable (*akṣara*), which is difficult to perceive, is known by the wise through the grace of Śambhu. That which is without beginning, without end, without lineage, unmanifest, described as eternal, devoid of eyes, ears, feet, and hands; that which is constant, all-pervading, subtle, and imperishable—the wise, through their own self, realize that source of all beings.

The phrase "Now, by another [means], that Imperishable is attained" summarizes the scriptural statement. By that knowledge (*vidyā*) produced from Vedic statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which has the characteristics about to be described, that Imperishable Brahman is understood and reached; because it brings about the cessation of ignorance regarding the Self and is thus the means to liberation, it is called "higher knowledge" (*parā vidyā*). || 5 ||

The scripture beginning with "That which is invisible" is included here within the discussion of its essential nature; therefore, it will not be cited separately hereafter. It was stated that "it is the Imperishable," and now the text specifies what that is through the passage beginning with "that which... "Invisible" means incapable of being seen. The meaning is that it is inaccessible to the organs of knowledge, such as the eyes, ears, and so forth. "Without abode" means it is not an object for the organs of action, such as speech and the rest. "Without lineage" means without kinship; there is no other cause for it with which it could have a connection.

By the phrase "without color" (*avarṇam*), he states the literal meaning of the Vedic term: "well-armored" (*sūpavarmitam*). It is devoid of forms such as grossness and so forth, which are the attributes of material substances. Since it possesses consciousness—just like transmigrating beings—as indicated by the scriptural statement, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," the existence of instruments such as eyes and ears would also follow for it; therefore, he excludes this by saying "without eyes or ears" (*acakṣuḥśrotram*). By the phrase "without hands or feet" (*apāṇipadam*), he indicates its freedom from the activity of action and effort. Because it is thus devoid of the grasped and the grasper, it is eternal.

It is "all-pervading" (*vibhu*) because it exists as the various distinctions of living beings, from Brahmā down to the immobile entities; for this very reason, it is omnipresent and all-encompassing like space. Furthermore, it is most subtle: while the unevolved elements (*apañcīkṛta-bhūtāni*) are subtle, it is even more exceedingly subtle because it is their cause. Precisely because of its aforementioned nature, it is immutable (*avyaya*); for in that which is partless and devoid of qualities, decay—characterized by the loss of parts or qualities—is impossible.

The "source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*) is the source—that is, the cause—of beings such as ether and the rest. Regarding the word *dhīrāḥ*, he explains that the suffix *-mat* has the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāvārthīya*), thus [interpreting it as] "the wise ones. The connection is as follows: that which is Brahman, characterized by invisibility and so forth, which the wise perceive all around as the Self—that is, as their own true nature—that imperishable Brahman is reached by that which is the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). The fact that this passage concerning the Unseen One has Brahman as its subject matter was also determined by the venerable Vyāsa in the aphorism: "The one whose qualities are invisibility and so forth is the subject of the scripture" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.22). || 6–7 ||

Knowledge is of two kinds: the lower (aparā) and the higher (parā). Of these, the lower knowledge consists of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, as well as grammar, phonetics, etymology, prosody, and astronomy—along with the knowledge concerning non-Self derived from these branches. And the higher knowledge is this: Śiva.

The wise practitioner who is a vessel of compassion, being steadfast and supreme, remains without doubt in the Absolute Immutable; that is the *parā-vidyā*. (To describe what that Absolute Immutable is like: That which is the Absolute Immutable is beyond the reach of the ignorant and the wicked. It has no connection with anything. No quality such as grossness exists within it.

In that [Self], there is never any instrument such as the eye, ear, hand, or foot. It is eternal, yet it appears to possess various forms. The Imperishable (Akṣara) is all-pervading, exceedingly subtle, and undecaying. The wise thoroughly understand the cause of the origin of all beings through their own self-knowledge. (6-7) Just as a spider...

1. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the higher knowledge (*parā vidyā*); it is not, however, included among the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) because the term *upaniṣad*—which is a collection of words—is subsumed under [the category of] the lower knowledge in passages such as the *Taittirīya*. 2. The word "excessively" (*atyartham*) is connected with every [instance]. Since a statement of similarity might occur somewhere, at some time, or in some way—as in the case of someone like you—the qualification "this is absolutely dissimilar" is meaningful. 3. Although [the suffix *kan*] is prescribed by the rule "from *musa*, *ghrā*, and *gṛdh* [the suffix *kan* is added]" (*uṇādi-sūtra*), ...

2.25) Thus, although one who possesses *dhī* (intellect) is established as *dhīra* (wise/steadfast), the author explains the word *dhīra*—meaning one whose intellect (*dhī*) is firm (*nilaya*)—even though it has already been derived [by others] in instances such as "some are unsteady (*adhīra*)" and "the wise (*dhīrāḥ*) perceive. His intention is that in the rule *ūpasuṣimuṣkamadho raḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.107), a formal separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) must be made by reading "raḥ" as a separate rule. Consequently, even the *vārttika* beginning with "in the section on *ra*" (*raprakaraṇe*) is not strictly necessary.

Chapter 7 Just as a spider emits and withdraws [its threads], O best of gods; just as sprouts arise from a seed, and just as they emerge from it; so too, O bull among men, the hair on the body and head, as well as the nails, arise from the *akṣara* (the Imperishable). All this, which is manifold, comes into being right here, resembling a dream. (8–9)
Through austerity, Brahman is accumulated; from that, food is produced. From food arise life-breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and immortality through action.

Having stated that [Brahman] is the source of all beings, he establishes this through examples, beginning with "Just as": the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) is a silkworm. Just as it, without depending on any other cause, spreads out threads from its own body and withdraws them back into itself; and just as plants such as rice arise from the earth resembling their own causes; and just as insentient hair and body-hair arise from a living, existing person.

In this very way, from the imperishable Brahman, which is independent of any other cause, the entire world—consisting of both sentient and insentient beings and distinct from itself—is produced. Since it is not possible for the changeless Brahman to possess the nature of the world in an ultimate sense, the meaning is that the entire created world is of the nature of *māyā* and is like a dream-illusion. (8–9) He demonstrates that the world arising from Brahman is produced according to this sequence: "It heats... (10).

That cause of the world—Brahman variegated by *māyā*—is first accumulated (*cīyate*), that is, augmented, by means of knowledge in the form of an inquiry into what is to be sought, which arises from the ripening of the karma of living beings through austerity; the meaning is that it becomes slightly permeated by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), though its supreme state remains non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

And from that Brahman, accumulated by that knowledge, there arises—that which is experienced and enjoyed by those in saṃsāra, the unmanifest cause of the manifold world of objects—that [Brahman] is produced in its intended form of manifestation; the meaning is that Brahman, which was in the state of Māyā during the preliminary deliberation regarding what was to be manifested, enters the state of the desire to manifest.

Therefore, from that which is denoted by the word *ātman*—which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)—there arises, like a sprout from a seed that has swollen through contact with earth, water, wind, and fire, Hiraṇyagarbha, who is omniscient and denoted by the term "Prāṇa. He possesses as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) the aggregate body (*samaṣṭi-śarīra*) composed of the five unquintuplicated elements (*apañcīkṛta-pañcabhūta*) and their effects. For it should be understood that by the very name "Hiraṇyagarbha," the arising of the unquintuplicated elements and of the aggregate body—which consists of the transformations of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—is described.

And from that *prāṇa*, the mind (*manas*), which has the five elements as its object, arose. And from that, the "Real" (*sat*)—the five gross elements, beginning with space, denoted by the word *sat* and formed through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*)—was produced. For by the word *sat*, the triad of elements consisting of earth and the others, which are perceptible, is expressed; whereas wind and space, because they are imperceptible, are expressed by the word *tyat*, which denotes the imperceptible. Therefore, it is heard in scripture: "It became both the Real (*sat*) and the Imperceptible (*tyat*)."

The meaning is that, when these elements have thus come into being, the worlds beginning with the earth arise again through the sequence of eggs and so forth; in those [worlds], there are the actions enjoined for humans according to their castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama); and in those [actions], there is "immortality" (amṛta), because it lasts for hundreds of millions of kalpas, which is like its fruit—these have been described by him in this order. || 10 ||

The spider weaves its web and gathers it back; likewise, on this earth, rice, barley, and other crops arise. Just as hair and so forth grow from a living man, so too does the entire universe emerge from the Imperishable Supreme Lord. This world arises within this very Imperishable like a dream. (The example of the spider is indeed used for the purpose of demonstrating that [the creation] occurs without the assistance of anything else.)

The production of various effects from a single cause is illustrated by the example of the earth; the production of the insentient from the sentient is illustrated by the example of the person. In reality, the world never existed at all, because Brahman is immutable—this is the meaning of the dream illustration.

An objection may arise: if the examples provided by the Śruti do not demonstrate the falsity of the world (*saṃsāramithyātva*), how is this meaning established in the Purāṇas by employing the analogy of a dream? The resolution is that even though it was not explicitly stated there, the Śruti has indeed taught it elsewhere: "By means of *māyās*, He moves in manifold forms" (Rg Veda 6.47.18) and "He who makes the one form manifold" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.11)—thus, creation consists of *māyā*.

Therefore, it should be clarified that even here, the same conventional designation (*samaññā*) is being used; no actual creation is taking place—this is the intended meaning of the Purāṇa. Gaudapādācārya has clarified this as follows: "Like a dream, like an illusion... [and so on]. This has been established in the Śruti: "That which is other than the earth and the atmosphere—'That' is the wind and the atmosphere" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.2–3).
[This is stated in] the *Brahmagītā*, verse 818.
He who is all-knowing and all-wise, whose nature consists of knowledge.
Therefore, O Suras, this world arises preceded by name and form; its true nature is like that of a conjured illusion. || 12 ||

This is that imperishable truth; by knowing it, one is liberated. There is no liberation from karma other than through the destruction of saṃsāra. For these gods have indeed seen the sacrifices as a stone, there is no doubt.

He summarizes the very point already stated with the words "he who is omniscient" (*yaḥ sarvajña*). He is omniscient because he knows everything in a general sense; even in the state of liberation (*virotpatti*), he knows everything.

The All-Knowing One: His austerity consists of knowledge, because its very nature is wisdom, and not the kind characterized by the exertion of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances. Therefore, from that Brahman, the effect—the Brahman known as Hiraṇyagarbha—[proceeds]; and [from him] all things denoted by names such as Devadatta and Yajñadatta, the collection of substances having forms such as blue and yellow, and food characterized by rice, barley, and so forth—all these have come forth in the sequence previously described; this is the meaning. 11–12.

Thus, having presented Brahman—the object of higher knowledge (paravidyā)—through both its essential definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa) and its circumstantial definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa), he concludes that knowledge of It alone is the means to liberation with the words "This very [Brahman]" (tadetad). In the Śruti, because the presentation of the objects of lower knowledge (aparavidyā) in the passage beginning with "Rituals in the mantras... is intended to generate dispassion (vairāgya), the fact that such rituals are not means to liberation—as established by the passage beginning with "For these are rafts..."—is here summarized with the words "By ritual action" (karmaṇā). [The phrase] "unstable" (adṛḍhāḥ) [refers to those rituals].

"For a bull that is capable of reaching the far shore indeed [reaches it], but one that is weak sinks in the middle of the ocean. These sacrifices and other rites are likewise weak; thus, they do not serve as the cause for liberation in this world"—this is the meaning. (13) "Just as a city of Gandharvas is seen in a vision, so too is this entire universe seen by the wise in the Vedāntas. (2.31) Likewise: "Though unborn, he is born in many ways through *māyā*. (3.24)

The Teacher has also stated this in the Vyāsasmṛti: "Like a hole in a rope seen in the dense darkness of night, resembling a mass of clouds at twilight, [this world] is mostly unreal, devoid of happiness, and ends in destruction and non-existence. The meaning is that just as a hollow in a rope appears to be a pit or a chasm when one is enveloped in thick darkness, so too does the wise person perceive this worldly existence; this is the intended sense.

Therefore, in accordance with the unity of the Śruti, the analogy of the spider found in the Purāṇas is consistent with that [view]. (8-9) The Illusionist (Māyāvī), who is the cause of the world, being endowed with the austerity of contemplating the object to be seen, became possessed of attributes (saviśeṣa). In this state, the unmanifest condition of the world of enjoyment reached such a point that it was about to become manifest; from that, Hiraṇyagarbha arose.

Immediately thereafter, the resolve was made to solidify the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), whereby the gross elements (*mahābhūtas*) were prepared. Then, as the worlds beginning with Bhūr were being established, the karmas of humans and others were ordained, and their long-lasting fruits were fashioned. (10)

He who knows all things both generally and specifically, who is the knower of all manifest objects, and who bestows the physician’s skill—that Hiranyagarbha produces him through the prescribed ritual sequence. All names, forms, and nourishment proceed from that supreme imperishable source alone.

Even though all worldly objects appear to be real, they are nonetheless as false as the objects of a dream and are thus to be abandoned. (Although at the outset, the mind of the practitioner is gratified by showing that there are three kinds of existence, nevertheless, in the Upanishadic philosophy, there is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman.)

Therefore, having brought these three kinds [of existence] and that two-fold existence here, it is finally cast away right there; this is the connection. As it has been said by the Great Teacher: "We do not admit the existence of another entity when one is intent upon the ascertainment of the ultimate reality" (p. 251). The present context concerns superimposition (*adhyāropa*).

In order to clearly demonstrate the absence of difference whose counter-correlate is the universe, it is necessary to show that [the Self] is of the nature of the Supreme Self alone; since this is the means, it is stated that all aforementioned differences are the effect of the one Supreme Imperishable (akṣara), thereby establishing the foundation of the Imperishable. This Imperishable is indeed "Tat" (That). Only by knowing this is the attainment of liberation achieved. || 11-12 || This Imperishable is indeed "Tat. Only by knowing this is the attainment of liberation achieved.

Liberation is not obtained through the performance of ritual acts (*karma*) that belong to *saṃsāra*; these [acts] are merely raw wood, incapable of carrying one across the ocean of existence. 13. O, it is understood that from these alone we attain supreme welfare... [End of fragment]. [Notes: 1. This refers to the section beginning with "tadetad... etc. 2. In this manner. 3. Variant readings: *mokṣasā*" (for *mokṣa*). 4. Variant reading: *ṇṭhāśvaite ya*.
Chapter—7. 819.
Those people who think that [the self] is only by these [elements] and only within this [body], are indeed deluded; for they surely enter into death and old age. (914)
Established in ritual action, these wise mortals consider themselves learned, yet they are merely focused on the sound [of the Vedas]. (95)
Only the deluded do not understand; for them there is no higher word than this, just as the blind, being led by another, proceed safely.
In the same way, people devoted to ritual action fall into a blind well;
they are deluded by the thought that all who are intent on action have achieved their purpose. (10)
They conceive [false notions]. Indeed, upon the exhaustion of their karma, they inevitably fall;
for without supreme knowledge, there is no liberation for them. 18.
"Thinking that sacrifices and charitable works are the highest good, these people remain deluded; they do not attain the supreme goal, of this there is no doubt. (19)

Firmly established through the memory of many births and devoted to the essence of the Śārīraka [Upanishads], one should attain detachment from the world by realizing that it is impermanent. (20) He censures those who believe that ritual action alone is the means for attaining the supreme human goal with the words "by these very... and so on. They are fools. Their folly consists in their failure to grasp the truth: that the means to the fruit characterized as heaven and the like is actually the knowledge of Brahman, which is the cause [of liberation]. (14) He elaborates on this very point with the verse beginning "those devoted to ritual action" (karmaniṣṭhāḥ). (15–19)

Thus, having set aside the injunctions for ritual action which have as their object the lower knowledge (aparavidyā) as propounded by the Śruti, he summarizes the method of detachment (vairāgya) propounded by the Śruti in the passage, "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma... with the words "aneka... and so forth. For the root Śruti text here is: "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brāhmaṇa should attain detachment. In that context, the meaning of the word "having examined" (parīkṣya) is explained as "having understood [them] to be impermanent. (20)

O Pālagi, those two are fools who constantly fall into the clutches of disease and death. (14) Those people who consider themselves wise, thinking "We alone are intelligent," yet remain devoted solely to ritual action, are indeed fools and not the learned; for them there is no attainment of the supreme goal, which is liberation. They are like blind men walking by relying on others.

In darkness, they fall even lower than me—those people who, regarding action alone as the supreme means, remain absorbed in it, believing: "By being devoted to action, we have accomplished our purpose. Upon the exhaustion of their karma, they inevitably fall from heaven and other realms back into this world; for them, there is no possibility of liberation without supreme knowledge. (15–18)

Furthermore, those who consider the *iṣṭa* and *āpūrta* rites to be the highest fail to attain liberation due to their delusion. (*Iṣṭa* refers to sacrificial acts such as the *agnihotra*, austerity, truthfulness, Vedic study, hospitality, and offerings to ancestors and gods; *āpūrta* refers to the construction of tanks, wells, ponds, temples, gardens, and the giving of food. || 19 ||

That person who is devoted to the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis, having remained steadfast in righteousness for many births, attains the perfection known as *citta-śuddhi* (purity of mind); remembering that this entire world is impermanent, he becomes detached from it. || 20 || Only through knowledge does the destruction of *saṃsāra* occur; [not] through action.

820. "Indeed, it is through knowledge alone that one is called 'liberated from saṃsāra,' and not by ritual action. Having understood this, the foremost of the gods, desiring to attain liberation, once again approached a teacher who was learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and firmly established in Brahman. They bowed before him and spoke these supreme words of wisdom: "Just as sparks from a fire arise from the sun and, being intensely radiant, eventually merge back into it, so too do all states of being dissolve into the Imperishable Śiva."
For the divine Puruṣa is formless, both within and without, indeed bodiless; he is without breath, without mind, pure, and beyond the reach of Māyā. || 24 ||

He states the intended meaning of the statement, "There is nothing uncreated by means of the created," with the words "by means of knowledge, etc. Thus, for one who has become dispassionate through the discriminative knowledge of the eternal and the non-eternal, he says—with the words "having thus known"—that one must indeed approach a Guru who possesses the characteristics described in the scriptures. "The Guru to him": the meaning is that [the Guru] is for the sake of one who is detached from the world of transmigration, which is the object of lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*). (21–22)

Thus, it has been stated that the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman is intended for one who is endowed with the fourfold means of accomplishment (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). Regarding the statement, "This is the Truth," the restriction that only Brahman—the object of that [knowledge]—is the Truth might seem improper, since individual souls (*jīva*) are also mentioned separately. Anticipating this objection, the author establishes their non-difference through an illustration: "Like sparks from a fire" and "they arise. By the word "and" (*ca*), the dissolution (*apyaya*) into that very same source as taught in the scripture is included.

Just as sparks arising from a blazing fire dissolve back into that very same fire and are not distinct from it, so too these entities characterized as living beings (jīva), which are of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), arise from Brahman—which is of the nature of Śiva—due to the production of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as ignorance (māyā). They dissolve back into that very same Śiva-nature within the all-pervading, undivided space (nabhas), like the form of a jar dissolves into the sky; thus, they do not exceed or differ from Him. This is the meaning. || 23 ||

Now, one might object: "Why could even the individual soul (jīva) not possess beginninglessness and so forth? To this, he states its true nature as free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi): "Divine" (divya). It is "divine" because it dwells in the "sky" (divi)—that is, in its own abode characterized by self-luminous consciousness; in other words, it is established in its own majesty. And because it is "formless" (amūrta), devoid of material form, it is therefore the "Puruṣa," existing by pervading all "cities" (pura)—that is, all bodies.

"Pervading both the external and the internal" means existing together with those two, having completely permeated everything. "Without birth" (aja) means devoid of origination; this is an indicative mark for all modifications of being (*bhāva-vikāra*). One of such a nature is perceived by those with the vision of ignorance as being characterized by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva-dṛṣṭi*), it has neither vital breath nor mind. Here, by the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) which is the cause of activities such as breathing is intended; this is also an indicative mark for the organs of action (*karma-indriya*).

The mind consists of volition (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth, and it serves as the indicator for the intellect (*buddhi*), the organs of sense (*indriya*), and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Indeed, because it has no such connection with the vital breaths and the rest, it is "bright" (*śubhra*), meaning stainless. The sense is that, due to its nature of being free from the stains of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), it transcends the entire cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, [it is distinct] from the primordial matter (*upādāna*) which constitutes the manifold world of objects of experience (*bhogya-prapañca*).

The meaning is that this hope is *nirupādhika* (unconditioned). By this, the statement "the power [of knowledge] is beyond the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ śaktiḥ*) is explained. Having thus reached this certainty, one should go into the presence of a Guru who is learned in the scriptures, endowed with the experience of Śiva, and possessed of love for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Śiva. The Guru should impart the instruction of the *parā-vidyā* (supreme knowledge) to the disciple who is qualified by such devotion. (Verses 21–22). 5.

Just as sparks emerge from this fire and dissolve back into that very fire, even so all living beings emerge from the syllable named Śiva and dissolve into it in the same manner. (23) That eternally liberated Śiva abides in His own self-luminous majesty; He possesses a single form (the *karīra* body), and therefore He pervades all bodies.
Śiva remains as the underlying substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-rūpa) for everything that exists outside the body, including the body itself; no transformation such as birth or the like affects him.

1. "Out of compassion" (*dāyāt*) is the injunction; the meaning is that the Guru should instruct a worthy disciple who has approached him according to the prescribed rule. The author of the *Bhāṣya* also accepted this restriction, for the reason here is the continuity of the tradition (*sampradāya-pravṛtti*). Therefore, the exclusion of an arrogant person from the role of teacher is stated as: "for the sake of the application of knowledge" (*vidyopayoga-rtham*). "Application" (*upayoga*) means employment, which is to say, the act of transmission (*pratipatti-karaṇa*). Thus, just like the discarding of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇa-tyāga*), the depositing of the knowledge of the *Satapatha* with the Guru is also for the sake of the completion of the ritual duty (*karman-tyāga*).
2. From this, he states the meaning of the second section: "In the presence of Śiva" (*śivasamnidhau*). [Note: The manuscript variants cited are: *°viṣayatvāsasaṃ*].

Chapter 7, Verse 821: From this [Self] proceed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and all the sense-faculties (*indriyāṇi*); as well as space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe. (25) The unerring, the steadfast, the non-deceptive—the two ears, the Vedas with their various branches, the speech, the vital breath, and the heart are His; the entire earth is His foundation, for He is indeed the Truth. (26) In order to establish the state of being "without vital breath" (*aprāṇa*) as previously stated, he declares the emergence of the vital breath and the other faculties from that [Self] with the words, "From this... (*etasmāt*).

The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, as well as the five elements which are their causes, emerge from Brahman whose nature has been described. [Objection: How can Brahman, which is the cause, possess the vital breaths and so forth, given that those things do not exist prior to creation? [Response: This is like the case of fish and so forth. (25) He establishes that Virāj—the presiding deity existing within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), like Hiraṇyagarbha—also originates from Paraśiva and is non-different from Him, by stating: "From Him, indeed... (ANINARMARGHATI).

“That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire”—from this Vedic scripture, the word *dyuloka* (the heavenly world) signifies the fire. "Speech is his [the Virāj’s] covering" means that the Vedas, which have been opened up by speech, constitute his covering. "The universe is his heart" means that the entire world (*vibhvaṃ*) is the heart (*hṛdayam*), the internal organ, of this Virāj. "From his two feet, the earth"—the word "arose" (*utapadyata*) is to be supplied. "This one is Śaṅkara": the meaning is that when the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the form of Virāj and so forth are removed, this one is none other than Paraśiva, whose nature is Truth. || 26 ||

These do not exist in Him. He has no connection with the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Since they are unnecessary, the mind, intellect, and other instruments of knowledge are not present near Him. Śiva alone is stainless. Mahādeva transcends both *māyā* and the individual soul (*jīva*). || 24 || From this supreme imperishable Śambhu arise the vital breaths, the mind, all the sense organs, and all the great elements (*mahābhūta*). || 25 ||

The earthly realm is his foundation; the moon and stars are his eyes; the quarters of space are his ears; the Vedas are his speech; the wind is his breath; the entire universe is his heart; and from his feet the earth was produced—he who is Virāṭ is also but a conditioned form of Śaṅkara. (This Śruti passage is understood, according to the Sūtra *Rūpopanyāsācca* (1.2.23), as having the Supreme Self as its intended referent.)

It is entirely consistent that this "source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*) is the Imperishable (*akṣara*), as established by the context and other factors; for this description is intended to convey its nature as the Self of all, not its possession of fullness. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement that it is "formless. Some thinkers, following the *Ratnaprabhā*, do not regard this mantra as referring to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), but instead maintain that it defines the Virāṭ Puruṣa.

The author of the *Bhāmatī* has attempted, through various arguments and counter-arguments (*ūhāpoha*), to establish that the view of the "bad thinkers" (*ku-vicāraka*) is the correct one. However, according to the *Prakaṭārthavivaraṇa*, *Nyāyanirṇaya*, *Ratnaprabhā*, *Parimala*, *Brahmavidyābharaṇa*, and other such works, the view held by these bad thinkers is not the teacher’s own position (*svamata*).

Āpyaya Dīkṣita has indeed stated that whatever respect the author of the *Bhāmatī* expresses for the views of other thinkers is solely for the sake of satisfying those who hold the opinion that if the Śruti were to describe a form (*rūpa*) of the Supreme Self, that form would necessarily become ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). As for the introduction in the *Ṭīkā* [of Vācaspati] of the view of another as being the opinion of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), it is intended to show that if one does not accept the presentation of a form for the Knowable Supreme Brahman, then its possessing form [would follow].

"Be satisfied with [the view] that it might be ultimate (pāramārthika)," fearing [otherwise]. Although the *Sūrabhāṣya* considers this mantra to describe the source (*yoni*) of all beings, the Teacher has stated in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*: "Even he who is celebrated as the first-born (*prathamaja*), the supreme, the golden egg, the sovereign within the universe—that [egg] was indeed enveloped by the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). (pari-pṛ. 260)

1 ḍa. “Tā asya vā” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). In the Sūtra-bhāṣya, it is determined that this is an introductory statement concerning the Supreme Seat (*paramāsana*). As for the view held in the Bhāmatī, Bhāvaprakāśikā, and other works—that this mantra refers to Hiraṇyagarbha—that is incorrect, due to contradictions with the context and other factors; this is explained in detail in the Parimara and other texts. In the Upaniṣadic discourse, Virāj is mentioned as being superior, and it is stated that Manu spoke of the Vairāja body as being composed of that [Virāj].

The intention of the Bhāṣya is that this form [of Brahman] is due to the contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); for it is impossible for that which is devoid of adjuncts to possess a form by itself. Thus, there is a single consistent statement between the interpretation of the Śruti and the Sūtra: even when possessed of adjuncts, that which exists as "Being" is the very nature of the supreme Imperishable (*akṣara*). Here too, by stating "this is Śaṃkara," the author of the Purāṇa has accepted the very view of the Bhāṣya; such is the direction of the argument. [Note: 3. *cha*. "Great Elements"; 4. Objection: "But you are proponents of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādin*); therefore, to say 'by means of non-existent things' is inconsistent. This is not a fault.

Even if its status as an effect were admitted, it would still be incapable of being designated as such because it is not subject to linguistic usage; otherwise, the activity of the causal agents would be rendered futile. Just as Devadatta is not said to "possess a son" by virtue of a son who is merely inherent [but not yet born], so too Brahman is not designated as "possessing life-breaths" and so forth, as it is not yet manifested by them. We have already stated that this is indeed appropriate.

822. From that [Agni], the fire consumes the fuel; from Soma, the herbs and plants are produced upon the earth. Through the male seed poured into the female, many creatures are born, numerous and well-nourished. || 27 || From that [Soma] come the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, the sacrificial ladles, all sacrifices, the ritual acts, and the priestly fees. The world of the sacrificer follows in succession—wherein Soma flows and wherein the Sun shines. || 28 ||
From that very [source] were born the Sādhyas, mortals, purifiers, birds, the prāṇa and apāna breaths, rice and barley, the horse, faith, truth, celibacy, and the sacred ordinance. (29)

He explains the very creation already mentioned with the words "from that": from that Supreme Person alone, fire is born. He specifies it as "with fuel" (*samidhā*): for that fire, the sun is the fuel—that is, the cause of its kindling. The meaning is that the fire which is kindled by the sun is the one intended here.

In the Chandogya Upaniṣad, within the teaching on the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), beginning with the words, "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; its fuel is the sun," five fires are taught in the form of heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman. From the fire of the heavenly world, the moon is produced as the smoke, and from that, rain-clouds arise. From those, upon the earth, herbs such as rice and barley come into being. When these are offered as oblations into the fire of man, that man—transformed into the form of semen consisting of the essence of food—is poured into the fire of the woman in the form of the female organ.

The meaning is that all these things, though produced in this sequence, nevertheless rest upon that very Brahman. Regarding the passage beginning with "From Him" (tasmād): the meaning is that everything—including the *ṛc*, *sāman*, and other means of action (*karma-sādhana*), the actions themselves, and their results—has emerged from Him. Sacrifices such as the *agnihotra* are those devoid of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Rituals (*kratu*) such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* are those involving such posts. The year is time, which is the constituent of ritual action. The sacrificer is the constant performer. The abode (*oka*) is the result of that [action].

He is distinguished as "Soma and [the other]. The meaning is that by the ignorant and the wise, respectively, the worlds of Soma and the Sun are attained. (28. Thus, even the gods who are subject to results [of action] arise from that very source; he says, "From the Self alone [arise] the gods. The meaning is that they are of many kinds, being divided into the various groups of Vasus, Rudras, and so forth. These are specific types of deities. Breath-inhalation (*prāṇa*) and breath-exhalation (*apāna*) belong to the Maruts. The oblation consists of rice and barley. Ritual action characterized by the refinement of the person, as well as austerity (*tapas*) practiced independently, [are also from that source].

The means of attaining the fruit is well-known in the Śruti. This injunction (*vidhi*) is the prescription that "this must be done. Even though it is being characterized, it is understood from this very source as consisting of this [human effort]; for this purpose, he says: "And he explains that [injunction]: 'From this'. The Commentator’s intention is this: the Supreme Lord can only be indicated through some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); therefore, while there is a reference to that supreme adjunct, the form indicated by the adjunct is [the object].

It belongs to the Supreme Lord alone. Therefore, it is consistent as an exposition of both the Upaniṣad and the Sūtra. This very view has been confirmed by this Purāṇa through the statement: "This is the Imperishable" (26). From this supreme Imperishable Person, this fire arises in the form of the universe, whose fuel is the sun.

From that [essence], Parjanya (the rain-god) is produced; from him, the earth receives rain, and through it, the plants such as rice and barley are prepared. Having consumed them, man produces semen, and then he casts that semen into the fire of his own body, from which many offspring are born.

(In this sequence, the entire creation arises from the Supreme Imperishable alone. [This is a reference to the Pañcāgnividyā well-known in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.4.8–10), the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (6.1.12–16), and other texts. From that [Supreme Imperishable] arise the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda, sentences, the rules known as *dīkṣā*, all sacrifices—both those with sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and those without—as well as sacrificial fees such as cows, and the year. || 27 || From that [arise] the Ṛg, Sāman, Yajus, sentences, the observances called *dīkṣā*, all sacrifices together with their sacrificial posts and those without sacrificial posts, sacrificial gifts such as cows, and the year.

(That is to say, the *samaya* which is an auxiliary part of ritual action)—those worlds that constitute the fruit of the ritual for the sacrificer: "He who purifies Soma" and "He who makes the sun shine"—all these have arisen from that [Akṣara]. || 28 || From that very Akṣara, many kinds of gods, *sādhyas*, humans, cattle, birds, the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*), rice and barley, austerity, faith, truth, celibacy, and the duties of this world have been produced. || 29 || From that [same source], the seven-headed...

1. Furthermore, [the following] are possible: "Truth is the avoidance of falsehood and speaking of things as they truly are, provided it causes no distress; celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the non-practice of sexual intercourse"—this is the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Regarding the injunction "one should speak the truth," that which is known through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and is fit to be spoken is "truth"; however, even if something is known through valid means, if it is unfit to be spoken, it is not [truth]. Elsewhere it is said: "Truth is declared to be what is beneficial to living beings, not merely the speaking of things as they are. For a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), all forms of sexual activity—including seeing, remembering, playing, speaking, and forming intentions—are forbidden.

The flames of those [fires] are constant and hair-raising; their fuel consists of the seven cities of the demons. All the worlds have been previously consumed by them, yet they remain as they were, equal to themselves. || 20 ||

Therefore, all speech, all horses, and likewise all herbs and juices—everything is the Self, the Supreme Self, this ancient one who is eternal bliss and full. This entire world is the Person alone; there is nothing else, not even the slightest thing other than Him. For that is the Truth. Indeed, this is my realization, shared with the assembly of sages; it is consistent with the teachings of those who possess the sacred scriptures. 3.9–3.12.
Alas! Driven by the illusion of sense-objects, these men fall into the ocean of the misery of death; fie on them!

But by the power of the knowledge of the Supreme Śiva, they cross the ocean of birth; yet this realization of Śiva arises from the power of serving the state of Śiva. (22) The wise one who knows that the Imperishable is directly established within himself, having untied the knot of impure ignorance, shall go to eternal Śiva. (24)

"Therefore, the vital breaths," and so forth. The seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are the ears and the rest. Likewise, their seven flames are the powers of perceiving objects; the seven oblations are the cognitions of objects produced by those [powers]; the fuel is the objects that serve as the cause for kindling them; and the worlds are the physical spheres (*golaka*) for the movement of those seven vital breaths. (30) Therefore, "the oceans," and so forth, is established by the literal recitation (*nigada*). "The self of all," and so forth.

In the manner described, the Supreme Self (paramātman) is the substratum (āśrayabhūta) of all things; its own nature (svarūpa) is the unmanifested non-duality (aprapañca), and therefore, since limitation imposed by that [universe] is untenable, it is complete and eternal—this is the meaning. (31) Having thus established the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara) through both summary and detailed exposition by means of the presentation of creation, the non-difference of the created world from That is determined by the Śruti text, "This entire universe is indeed the Puruṣa. He summarizes that [point] with the words "idam" (this) and "na kiñcid aparam" (nothing else).

According to the manner stated, there is nothing beyond that which constitutes the entirety of everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. The intended meaning is that the collection of effects perceived as "other" (aparam) does not exist at all in reality, because it is superimposed upon the nature of Brahman and is therefore illusory, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. "Hidden in the cave," and so forth.

The meaning is this: he who, by his own independent power, directly realizes that imperishable Brahman—whose nature has been thus described and which resides within the heart, denoted by the word "Gah"—cuts asunder the knot of ignorance, which is the cause of his own transmigratory existence, and attains the state of Supreme Śiva, which is eternally free from all duality and consists solely of the essence of consciousness. || 34 ||

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), their capacities for desiring sense objects, and the sevenfold cognition of objects were produced; even the *golaka*s (the spheres of the senses) were formed from them. All of these arise instantaneously from Mahādeva and persist in every kalpa exactly as they were before. Thus, although established through an eternal, beginningless succession, they remain identical to themselves. [Verse 20] The oceans, mountains, rivers, medicinal herbs, and...

All these arise from Paramaśiva. He is the witness of all, the consciousness superior to all, eternally blissful, eternal, and forever complete. (9) This "what" is indeed that Puruṣa and nothing else; this "what" does not exist apart from the Puruṣa. That alone is the truth. This is the certain conclusion of myself, of the sages, of Rudra, and of Viṣṇu—all alike.

In this view of Rati, there is no room for doubt. Alas, what a tragedy! Because they lack knowledge of Supreme Śiva, these people remain fallen into the ocean of sufferings such as death, caused by the illusory power (māyā) that deludes them with sense-objects. Yet, oh, how wonderful it is to hear the news of contentment—that perhaps, by relying on the knowledge of Paraśiva, people may eventually escape from this stream of births.

This Śiva-knowledge is attainable only through the service of Śiva. (33) If a person comes to know this Imperishable One residing within the cave of the heart, then, having shattered the fortress of the multitude of ignorance, they shall attain the eternal Śiva. (34)

824. *Brahmagītā* 1. This is that Imperishable Brahman; it is the goal, and it is speech and mind. This is that Immortal Truth, which is this very thing [realized] by the wise. 25. For that Self is indeed the target to be pierced; it is called Brahman. It must be known by one who is vigilant; becoming absorbed in it, one should become like an arrow. 26. Having pierced that which is all-pervading, he immediately becomes one whose face is turned everywhere. The piercer is likewise all-pervading; the target has been pierced—of this there is no doubt. 27.
Making the self the lower fire-drill and the *araṇa* the upper fire-drill, one should obtain the God who is hidden like fire, through the practice of churning with meditation. (28)

"That which is this Imperishable" (tadetadakṣaram): that which was previously described as being situated in the sun and the moon is now described as being seated within the cave of the heart (guhā) as one's own Self. That consciousness which is Brahman is indeed the support of the entire aggregate of vital breaths, senses, and so forth, according to such scriptural passages as "the breath of the breath" (prāṇasya prāṇam). Therefore, that alone is the Immortal, free from destruction; for that very reason, it is the Truth (satya). And that should be held by the wise with a steady mind, like a balance-beam; the meaning is that the mind must be made to have that as its object. || 35 ||

He describes the method of piercing: "The enemy has been shaken off," and so forth. Just as the tip of an arrow is the cause for piercing the target, so too the syllable *om* is the bow, being the cause for penetrating the Brahman which is the object of knowledge. The Self, accompanied by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), which is the witness of all modifications, is the arrow. Indeed, through the abandonment of those adjuncts, that arrow is delivered into Brahman by its own self. And that Brahman is the target.

This must be realized by a person who is vigilant—free from the negligence of poison, thirst, and the like—and who is single-minded, using these means such as the bow and so forth. Therefore, just as the arrow becomes one with the target upon piercing it, so too the witness of the body and other elements, through the abandonment of the conceit of identity with them, becomes one with that Brahman which serves as the object of protection; the meaning is that he becomes of the very nature of that [Brahman]. (36) He states the distinction between worldly piercing and [this] piercing: "the object of protection" (*rakṣyam*). For the worldly piercing indeed results in exhaustion and limitation.

An arrow, moreover, has but a single point; and since the archer is situated only in one place, its separation from the target is possible only occasionally. But here, because of the identity [of the individual self] with That, it is said that "one becomes as if pierced"—this is the meaning. [37] Since the knowledge of Brahman through the syllable Om (praṇava) is established in another Vedic scripture, he demonstrates it by means of a summary quotation: "The Self... This is also derived from the Brahmopaniṣad.

Just as one perceives the fire hidden within the wood by rubbing together the lower and upper kindling sticks (*araṇi*), so too, by means of the *praṇava*, one who contemplates the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) seated within—that which is characterized by the states of waking and so forth—realizes its true nature through the power of that practice; such is the meaning. || 38 ||

That which is the object of the supreme knowledge (*parāvidyā*)—the Akṣara Brahman—is itself situated within the heart. It is also the vital breath (*prāṇa*), speech (*vāk*), and mind (*manas*). It is also immortality (*amṛta*) and truth (*satya*). The wise should concentrate their minds upon it. (35) The syllable *Oṃ* is the bow; the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as conditioned by adjuncts (*upādhi*), who is the witness of all knowledge, is the arrow; and Brahman is its target.

Without succumbing to negligence such as craving for sense objects, a person with a one-pointed mind should, by means of the aforementioned bow, pierce the aforementioned target with the aforementioned arrow. Then, just as the arrow becomes one with the target, so too does the practitioner become one with the Supreme Self. (The worship of *Kiva* through the *Praṇava*, as expounded in detail in the Upaniṣads, belongs to the Advaita tradition and is the supreme path.)

In numerous scriptural contexts—such as the *Kaṭha* (6.17), *Muṇḍaka* (3.2.6), *Taittirīya* (1.8), *Chāndogya* (1.1.1), *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* (5.1.1), *Mahānārāyaṇa* (24.1), *Bhaimyu Upaniṣad* (6.2), *Sasimha-Uttaratāpanīya*, *Śvetāśvatara* (1.13), and *Kaivalya* (1.11)—the injunction for the practice of *praṇava-upāsanā* is found. Therefore, one should obtain the method of *praṇava-upāsanā* appropriate to one's own qualification from one's own guru alone.

36. Since the agent of action is all-pervading and the arrow [of the mind] is likewise present everywhere, one can contemplate [the Self] in every way; for the Self is also the knower that accomplishes its own knowledge, and is therefore all-pervading. Thus, the piercing of the fruit [of the heart] is certain. 37. Then those Mahādevas appeared, who were just now manifested from this drop. (Śamī and others were made into two pieces by this stroke.)

Meditation itself is the friction; its practice characterized by long duration and so forth, performed repeatedly, is "meditation practiced thoroughly. The meaning is that one should practice meditation thus. By that [practice], it [the Self] remains as if veiled, though it has been drawn out from that very [source].

Chapter 7 Heaven, the intermediate space, the sacrificial post, the mind, the *śaṇa* grass, and the swiftest [steeds]—he who knows the truth and is composed should know that all these are indeed that One alone. (29) O most steadfast believers, one should speak speech that has the One as its sole object; any other speech is merely a waste of breath and leads to exhaustion. (40) He is the omniscient, the knower of all, whose majesty is pure. Śiva, the auspicious, dwells in the divine, vast, and infinite ether. (44)

The mind-made body, which leads the physical body, is not established within the waters of all the hearts; by the knowledge of that, the wise are completely liberated, and it proceeds from its own nature as a body of bliss.

Because its characteristics are extremely subtle, it is difficult to perceive; it is fleeting, moving about, and invisible, like a thief in the sky. This threefold world being experienced, the mind, the senses other than that [mind], and all else—that which is woven by the Imperishable Brahman—should be offered up and surrendered by the wise one whose mind is concentrated; that alone is the one thing to be known. (39) Likewise, he should speak only speech concerning That alone; he should abandon other words whose objects are not the Self.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "This [very one]. This very Self is the bridge (*setu*) for crossing over the ocean of *saṃsāra* and attaining immortality (*amṛtatva*). Therefore, the meaning is that speech should be directed toward that alone. (400) And from what source is that Self of the aforementioned kind to be perceived? To this, he says: "He who is all-knowing. "All" (*sarva*) means everything that is to be known.

He whose greatness, as previously described, is seen in this world as his manifestation (*vibhūti*), that Śiva is established in the divine city of Brahman—the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrārakamala*)—which shines as the supreme abode of all forms of knowledge; he is established there in the space (*vyoman*) situated within it. This [description of a location] is intended to be figurative (*upalakṣaṇa-prāya*), for it is impossible for that which is omnipresent like space to be situated in any one place. (41) He describes His essential nature (*svarūpa*) as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*): Śiva, who dwells in the center of the hearts of all living beings, has the form of consciousness.

It is called "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) because it is perceived there through the very functions of the mind. It is the "leader of the body of vital breaths" (*prāṇa-śarīra-netā*), meaning it is that which brings the subtle body—in the form of the vital breaths—to another gross body. Such is the Imperishable Brahman, which by its own nature, without depending on any other cause, shines by its own light as a state untouched by suffering and consisting of eternal, unsurpassed bliss; the knowledge of this is the means of liberation for the discerning. || 42 ||

It is understood that one piece of wood is placed firmly upon the ground and then struck with another piece; just as curd and other substances are churned, so too is the upper wood rubbed against it. From this friction, sparks emerge and are caught in cotton or similar material, which is then used to ignite wood and other fuel. This process is well known in the context of sacrificial rites.

This very [truth] has been given as a metaphor for the practice of *praṇava* (the sacred syllable Om). || 38 || That one alone upon which this world, the intermediate space, the earth, the mind, and all vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are dependent—upon that One alone should one meditate with one-pointed concentration. One should speak only of the eternally non-dual Brahman and abandon all talk related to the non-Self or to duality. This is the means for attaining immortality. || 39–40 ||

He who knows everything both in general and in particular—that this Self is Śiva, whose glory is manifest throughout the universe—is himself established in the space of the heart (hṛdayākāśa), which is the source of all knowledge and the locus for the realization of Brahman. This Self is composed of mind (manomaya), because it is perceived within the heart through the fluctuations of the mind.

The Self alone, having presided over the two other components—the prāṇa and the body—carries [the being] from one body to another. It resides within all hearts; it is through the true experience of that very Self that wise people attain liberation. That Supreme God, whose nature is bliss, shines by His own inherent light. Both cause and effect reside within Him.

1. That this is indeed the one Supreme Self was established in detail in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the third quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter. 2. And [He is] the witness, the breath... 3. The reading "tajjñānena" appears in some manuscripts; it seems that this very reading was also that of the author of the commentary. 826. *Brahmagītā*.

The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are resolved, and the effects of past actions fall away when He, who is both the higher and the lower, is beheld within that golden, supreme sheath—Brahman, stainless and partless, the auspicious light of lights, which those who know the Self perceive.

Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the stars, nor the lightning, nor fire shines in this world; it is when He alone is shining that all these things appear luminous. It is by following Him alone as He shines that everything shines by its own nature;
indeed, it is by His light that all this world is illumined.

He states the fruit of this knowledge of Brahman: "It is destroyed. The Supreme is the cause; the inferior is the effect. When that non-dual Brahman, which exists in the form of both those, is seen in its true nature—that is, directly realized—then the accumulation of the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*), which exists in the heart—that is, in the mind—in the form of a knot, is destroyed and utterly perishes. This is because knowledge (*vidyā*) is the remover of ignorance. For this very reason, due to the absence of their cause, the objects of the knowable are stilled.

And for this wise person whose ignorance has ceased and whose doubts have been severed—whether in this life or in another birth—the accumulated actions consisting of merit and demerit, which produce future births and whose results have not yet begun to operate, are exhausted. Accordingly, there is the aphorism of Vyāsa: “Upon the attainment of That, there is the complete destruction of both subsequent and prior [actions], because of the scriptural teaching to that effect. (43) “Golden,” etc. Golden means consisting of light.

Accompanied by the sheath of consciousness, it serves as the sheath for Brahman by being the cause of its perception; because it is the innermost of all, it is like a sheath. Such is the space within the heart (hārdākāśa) wherein [Brahman] resides—viraja, meaning free from the stains of blemish and the like.

"Niṣkalam" means that from which all "kalās"—parts or limbs—have departed; such is Brahman, which is unlimited by space or substance, the very nature of Supreme Śiva. Because it possesses the aforementioned characteristics, it is the supreme, pure light, the illuminator of all lights, such as fire and the rest, whose nature is to illuminate everything. Indeed, fire and other elements do not shine apart from the illumination of consciousness. The meaning is that those who know the Self through discernment realize it to be of the nature described. (44)

He explains how it is that [Brahman] is "the light of lights" with the words: "Not there... (IV.3.9). Regarding the reason why the sun and other luminaries do not shine there, he states: "Him alone... (IV.3.10). For the manifestation of the object of cognition (*cetya*) is preceded by the manifestation of consciousness (*caitanya*). Therefore, that which appears subsequently is not capable of illuminating the consciousness that exists prior to it; this is the meaning. Furthermore, he states that its shining is not inherent to it: "By His light... (IV.3.11).

By means of the *akāra* of consciousness, which is the very nature of that Supreme Śiva, all this manifold diversity is superimposed there and appears; however, it does not dissolve [into Him], such is the meaning. 46.

Upon correctly knowing that non-dual Brahman, ignorance is brought to an end. Consequently, the dense consciousness within the heart and the failure to discriminate between the sentient and the insentient are easily removed. All bonds are severed; even the accumulated karmas of the knower are destroyed by his realization. (43) "I am situated within the body," such is the light of self-awareness.

While one remains in the body, Śiva is established within that lotus of the heart, which serves as the locus for attaining grace (rahma). Śiva is free from the impurities of ignorance and the like, partless, pure, and brilliantly radiant with the light of fire and other luminaries. That very reality which the wise who know the Self discern through discrimination is indeed this Śiva of the aforementioned nature. 44.

Regarding him, neither the sun, the moon, the stars, lightning, fire, nor any other light can shine. Since Śambhu is of the nature of knowledge, he shines by himself through his own form. On account of his natural luminosity, everything else shines; indeed, it is only through his manifestation that this entire universe appears.

For this reason, even the sun does not make those objects visible; the wind also cannot blow toward them. All the gods do not make Paramaśiva an object of their perception. Mahādeva is the one who brings about the welfare of all living beings. Regarding this, it was determined by Pārāśarya [Vyāsa] in the passage beginning with *tasyeti prājña ālocyate* (1.3.22) and *tasya ca* (1.3.22). Here, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Everything shines only after Him, who shines by His own nature. It is not [the case that everything shines by its own power].

Chapter 7 || 827 And there, neither the form of the sun shines, nor do the winds blow; the deities and their steeds have departed. This god, the creator of all beings, having pierced his own self, shines forth in his nakedness. 47 Brahman is infinite and supreme in the east; Brahman is infinite and supreme in the south; and Brahman is infinite and supreme in the north. 48

In the beginning, the two—Hiraṇyagarbha and Īśvara—were situated within our bodies as the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). Maheśvara does not fear the fruit of karma; rather, Maheśvara shines forth by himself as a mere witness, without [undergoing] experience. The distinction between those two is imagined through Māyā. Just as space is imagined through the distinctions of the space within a jar or the space within a pot, so too the supreme consciousness is imagined and conceived in the form of Śiva.

Thus, having cited the scriptural text, "The sun does not shine there," he reveals its meaning, which is beyond fear and incomprehensible: "There they do not shine. (47) Thus, he concludes that very essence of Brahman—which, as the cause of the entire universe, has been established as self-luminous: "This is that. (48)

Now, one might object: "Since the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) possess distinct attributes such as being subject to transmigratory existence and so forth, their natures are as different as shadow and sunlight; how then can there be identity between them? Anticipating this objection, the author refutes it with the verse beginning, "Two birds... (*dau suparṇā*). "Suparṇau" means those with beautiful flight. "Jīvaḥ phalam" means the individual soul is the fruit. Because the soul has fallen into identification with its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it experiences pleasure and pain—the fruits of merit and demerit that have ripened. The Lord, however, due to the absence of agency resulting from the lack of contact with limiting adjuncts, does not experience those fruits.

Therefore, having abandoned the state of being an enjoyer, [the Self] manifests by itself as pure consciousness alone, entirely free from forms such as objects of enjoyment. Thus, the distinction that appears between these two—characterized by the attributes of being an enjoyer and not being an enjoyer—is imagined through *māyā* and is not real. [49-50] It shines forth by its own pure and stainless nature. [46-47] Brahman alone is immortal; it is that which is present before us, infinite, supreme, and behind all. Though it is infinite and beyond measure, it is also manifest within itself. [48]

(If this infinite Brahman is the only one reality, then who are we who experience pleasure and pain? To clarify this, it is said that we are non-entities distinct from Brahman; therefore, experiences such as enjoyment are also non-entities. To establish this, they say: Within this body, two birds named Jīva and Īśvara dwell together.

Among these, it is the bird called the *jīva* that experiences the fruit of its actions, not the Lord (*īśvara*). Maheśvara remains self-luminous solely in the form of a witness and does not experience enjoyment. The distinction between these two is imagined through *māyā*. (49–50) Just as space is imagined to have divisions such as the pot-space and the great space (*mahākāśa*), so too the one Brahman, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is imagined in the forms of both the *jīva* and the Lord. (51)

In reality, both Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) are consciousness (cit) alone; and consciousness is non-different from the nature of consciousness—it is not distinct. If consciousness were different from the nature of consciousness, it would necessarily follow that it is insentient (acit); therefore, in its essential form, consciousness is not different from consciousness. If [you object]: "But..."
