828. Śiva, who is the reality of all things, is then [perceived] as if distinct from consciousness; yet he is not different from the form of consciousness, because that would entail the loss of his nature as consciousness.

If the nature of consciousness is perceived as inert, it is indeed always divided by the notion of duality. (52) He establishes the stated proposition through an illustration: "Just as," etc. Just as the single nature of space is conceived as distinct—such as the space within a jar or the space within a pot—due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

In this way, the one and only Brahman, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is conceptualized as distinct as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) due to its association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—namely, impurity and purity respectively. However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), when the distinctions created by the adjuncts are abandoned, both are identical; the meaning is that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of both is beginningless and endless consciousness alone. Now, one might ask: "Since the consciousness of the Lord has all things as its object, whereas the consciousness of the individual soul has only limited objects, how can there be oneness between these two? To this, he says: "Because their form is consciousness."

That which is the limitedness of the object of consciousness is produced by the impurity residing in its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and not produced by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, in the form of consciousness (*cidākāra*), it exists as one and the same in both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*); it is not divided. Furthermore, the proponent who asserts that it is divided must be questioned: "Is it divided in the form of consciousness, or in the form of the insentient (*jaḍa*)? Regarding the first alternative, he says: "Because it is of the nature of consciousness."

The meaning is that consciousness does not become differentiated because it lacks the nature of being a wall [an insentient substrate]; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of its very nature as consciousness. Regarding the second case, however, he states—“because it is of the nature of the insentient”—that such differentiation belongs only to the insentient, not to consciousness. (51–53)

To some extent, a difference may appear due to ignorance; thus, a certain kind of difference arises regarding the insentient (*jaḍa*), while consciousness (*cit*) remains eternally one. (Some scholars, such as Śaṅkara Upādhyāya and others, maintain that a thing can be negated in such a way that, once negated, that thing appears as possessing a specific distinction which never existed in it before.)

The technical definition of *anyonyābhāva* (mutual absence) is an absence whose counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by a property that resides exclusively in the counter-positive and nowhere else. For example, it is said of someone: "It is useless for him to have wealth, because he does not associate with the virtuous. In this case, the mutual absence is of wealth, and its counter-positiveness is delimited by the property of being associated with the virtuous—a property that resides only in the virtuous and not in the wealthy person.

Regarding the line "The peacock feather does not become a companion in times of distress": although it is being said that it does not become a companion, its failure to become a companion is not being stated from the perspective of *sāthī* (companion); for from the perspective of *sāthī*, it certainly becomes a companion. However, it is being stated that it does not become a companion from the perspective of *dosta* (friend). Friendship does not remain in the highest [state], but resides elsewhere.

And thus, the property that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence of "being a knower" (*sādhīka*)—namely, "friendship"—is *vyadhikaraṇa* (residing in a different locus) because it exists elsewhere than in that speaker; therefore, this is a statement of an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a *vyadhikaraṇa* property. In the same way, when the difference of a conscious being from the form of a corpse (*nauśūpa*) is being stated, upon reflection, it appears that the aforementioned example is indeed appropriate.

It is merely being said that such a person does not become a friend; it is not being said that he does not become a companion. Thus, in all instances, the negation results in the negation of a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*), while the existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) itself remains intact.

For this very reason, Gaṅgeśopādhyāya and others maintain that "a property residing in the locus of the counter-positive does not become the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of counter-positiveness. In other words, a property that does not reside in the counter-positive cannot serve as the delimitor of counter-positiveness. Consequently, from their perspective, there can be no absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a property residing in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇa-dharmāvacchinna-pratiyogitāka-abhāva).

Accepting this established conclusion, it is stated in the Purāṇa that the meaning of asserting such a difference is the assertion of a difference in insentient matter (*jaḍa*), and not in the sentient (*cetana*). This does not imply that an absence having the aforementioned counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is unacceptable; for in cognitions such as "that dog does not exist" and "that dog is not with the cat," difference is indeed experienced.
Nevertheless, the intended sense is that in the final analysis, there is only the negation of a property (*dharmaniṣedha*). || 53 ||
1 cha. *artaśvacra* | 2 jña. *thametayo* | Chapter 7: 829.
Since the oneness of consciousness (*cidekatva*) is established by your own authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [the following applies].

When the intellect has attained the state of *guṇa* and yet remains contrary [to it], that is the intellect of the Great-Souled One who has manifested the supreme reality of the body. Indeed, for one whose intellect is fixed in the oneness of consciousness (*cidekatva*), there is no falling away and no delusion; through the thorough knowledge of the oneness of consciousness, he attains that which is beyond the three qualities, the supreme bliss, the auspicious, and the absolute.

Even while situated in this body, which is the abode of Śiva, one remains immersed in the ocean of suffering and the like through the power of one’s own māyā, and being tormented, one grieves. || 57 ||
That which appears as other than itself, yet is enjoyed by itself alone, is the substratum of the entire universe and the treasury of consciousness. (58)
Having resolved "I am this," he becomes free from sorrow regarding this [Self], which is pure consciousness, his own, the witness of all. (59)
When one knows the greatness that has this characteristic as its highest limit, then, having directly realized that very [reality], one becomes this world. 60.

And through reasoning, one transcends the vital breath (*prāṇa*). From the aforementioned scriptural authority, such as "All this is Consciousness (*cit*); it acts and it causes to act," the meaning is that Consciousness is one. [5455] Regarding the phrase "from the thorough knowledge of the oneness of Consciousness":

The meaning is this: when one abandons the distinction created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) between the eater and the eaten—the two entities existing within the body—and realizes their unity in the form of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), that very knowledge is the cause of liberation for the emancipated, as it secures the attainment of supreme bliss by removing the fear of saṃsāra, such as grief and delusion. (56) Thus, by means of this commentary on the *Ṛgveda* mantra "Two birds of beautiful wings," which dispels the view of duality, the aforementioned truth is directly established.

He explains the mantra "samāne vṛkṣe" with the words "in the abode of Śiva. Regarding the phrase "by one's own *māyā*": the meaning is that [the individual soul] is made dual by that *māyā* which, consisting primarily of impure *sattva*, serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the self, the living being (*jīva*). (57) Regarding the phrase "as distinct from oneself": [it means as something other than one's own nature].

When some individuals, through the means of hearing, reflection, and so forth, come to know by their own self that very nature of Paraśiva—which appears as distinct from and different in character from their own transmigratory state, and which is free from the entire multitude of worldly sufferings—they then directly perceive the majesty characterized by the supreme state described above. In the phrase "of one's own" (*svasya*) and "of all" (*sarvasya*), the two genitive cases are in apposition. By the word *sva* (one's own), the causal Brahman is referred to;
the meaning is: "of everything belonging to oneself, including one's own world-cycle, up to the imperishable."

At that very moment, by means of the knowledge (*vidyā*) which has as its object the nature of one's own self as Brahman, one becomes liberated from the bonds of *saṃsāra*; this is the meaning. (58–60) Furthermore, even when the unity of Consciousness (*cit*) is established through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), sinful people arrive at a contrary conviction. (54) Only for a Great Soul (*mahātman*) whose mind is purified by the constant practice of both scriptural (*śrauta*) and traditional (*smārta*) conduct can the realization of the unity of Consciousness arise through the grace of Śiva. (55)

Through the knowledge of the uniqueness of consciousness (*cetanā*), sorrow and delusion no longer arise; there is only the attainment of Śiva, the supreme, undivided bliss. || 56 || Even while residing in this body, which is the abode of Śiva, one who remains ignorant of his own [true nature], even slightly, wallows in an ocean of sufferings such as worldly existence and attains delusion; thus, he utters this verse: || 57 ||

That very Lord who appears as distinct from oneself and whom we conceive of as separate is the Truth, the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), and the substratum of the entire universe; by resolving that He alone exists, this individual soul (*jīva*) becomes devoid of its [illusory] form. When the soul realizes the supreme, incomprehensible majesty of this pure Consciousness, which is the witness of all—then [it attains liberation].

Then the Brahmagītā [proclaims] the Great Lord Maheśvara, who is the source of Brahman, complete, and of the color of the sky (skmavarṇa). He is perceived as the limit, manifested through the state of Kaṭha. Through many millions of kalpas, by means of meritorious deeds, through logic and authoritative testimony, and from the Supreme Lord Īśvara, when the best of sages hear and know Him, they become liberated from the accumulation of merit and sin along with all causes. He attains the state of being all forms, characterized by supreme non-duality;
there is no doubt to be entertained here by the wise.

One might object: "How can there be liberation for the individual soul (jīva) through the higher knowledge (paravidyā), given that merit and demerit—which bring about future births—still exist? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "The source of Brahman" (brahmayoni). This refers to the source or cause of the lower Brahman, Hiraṇyagarbha. The word "full" (pūrṇam) is an explanation of the term "Person" (puruṣa) found in the Śruti. Regarding the phrase "not being perceived elsewhere": it means that while [the soul] is not perceived as an agent of action, it is manifested in its true nature; that is to say, it is manifested as the agent of the act of knowing.

When one perceives Paraśiva in such a form as being identical with oneself, then that knower, having shaken off the accumulated merit and demerit that cause rebirth, and being entirely dissociated from the body, senses, and so forth which were previously conditioned by those [karmas], attains in every respect equality with Śiva—that is, oneness with Him. This is the meaning. (61–64)

When accompanied by knowledge, that which was born of time becomes dissolved. (In this way, the question "Who are we? has been resolved: we ourselves are Śiva, though unaware of our own nature as Śiva. Because of that ignorance, we think there will be some other Śiva whom we must worship and so forth. There are not two Śivas—one who is ignorant and another who knows; Śiva is one alone.)

In that state, there is not even a trace of ignorance or its effect, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). The distinctions between the individual soul (*jīva*), Śiva, and the universe are all established merely through appearance (*pratītimātra*). To dismiss appearance by claiming it does not exist is futile. Therefore, accepting appearance as it is, the scriptures and other teachings provide instructions on the means that brings this sense of duality to an end. There is neither the reality of duality nor any means for its removal.

Truth alone is Śiva. || 58-60 || When the practitioner, through the assistance of merit accumulated over many millions of kalpas, by means of reasoning, valid cognition, and the grace of the Supreme Lord, perceives with faith the Supreme Lord—who is the cause even of Hiraṇyagarbha, eternally perfect, whose form is the light of consciousness, who sees even while being unseen, and who shines as the "Agent"—then...

This dispassionate person, having no connection whatsoever with merit or demerit and their causes—the body and so forth—attains from Śiva a state of equality in every respect, that is, the form of supreme non-duality. The wise should have no doubt about this. (61-64) The essential nature of both the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva is indeed pure consciousness alone.

How can there be similarity in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is devoid of differentiation when it is the essence (*rasa*)? (Only non-difference remains; similarity occurs only between distinct things, for there is no self-similarity within a single entity itself). Therefore, in the section [of the Brahma Sūtras] beginning with "Because of being seen as non-distinct" (4.4.4), it was established that the liberated soul is indeed non-distinct from the Supreme Self. Furthermore, since "supreme equality" is specified here as a qualification, it should be understood that this very non-distinction is what constitutes supreme equality here, and not things such as servitude (*sāṣṭrya*) as held by others.
Chapter 7, Verse 831:
For at that time, pure consciousness alone belongs to both Śiva and Nivṛtti.
This being so, how can there be equality [between them] when consciousness alone is devoid of differentiation? (65)
Even if their similarity were as described above, even then there could never be equality between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 66 ||

The state of equality with Mahākāla and the others is entirely like that of Kaṭākṣa; just as it does not exist [independently] for them, so too it does not exist for the individual soul (jīva) apart from Śiva. 67.

Or let there be equality with the Lord; even then, that equality must be through action or through attributes, and not otherwise. (68) Now, is the equality between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) in their nature as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), or when they possess limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*)? It is not the first case; thus he says: "For [the difference] consists in consciousness. It has been stated previously that there is no difference between the two in their aspect as pure consciousness. Furthermore, since equality presupposes difference, it is not tenable in that case. (65) He refutes the second alternative: "In the state of being joined with limiting adjuncts. There can be no equality at all.

The meaning is that because those with adjuncts (*sopādhika*) are connected respectively with limited knowledge and omniscience, they possess absolute dissimilarity; therefore, there can be no equality between them. (66) He establishes the impossibility of equality between those with adjuncts by means of an illustration: "Like the great space... (67). Having thus raised an objection against equality by examining the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), he raises it again by examining their cause (*kāraṇa*): "Or let it be... and so forth. (68)

For form (*rūpa*) is a substance (*dravya*), and no equality can exist between these [two]. (65) Even if there were equality regarding their connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that would be inconsistent; for these forms are indeed utterly distinct. Just as the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) cannot be identical to the great space (*mahākāśa*), so too, when considered in relation to their limiting adjuncts, there is no equality between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva.

Just as in the example, there is only identity between the sky and the pot, not similarity; for the sky is one, and thus there is identity through its nature as consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). (It is not that similarity is untenable, nor is there any reason for it—this is what is being established: Even if one were to admit similarity between the individual soul and the Lord, it would have to be due to either action (*karman*) or knowledge (*jñāna*); no other cause is possible. (66–68)
If it were claimed that similarity is the cause of [the cognition], then it would follow that [the cognition] occurs even without [the object].

One must state what this similarity is: is it eternal or non-eternal? If it were eternal, the futility of the means of proof (*sādhana*) would be an obvious flaw. Nor should you say, "The flaw is equal for you as well," because I do not accept the means of proof for the sake of attaining similarity; rather, it is my view that its utility lies precisely in the removal of ignorance.

If it is argued that liberation is something to be accomplished through practice and is therefore impermanent—being merely a state of equality—then one must choose between its attainment being through action (*karman*) or through knowledge (*jñāna*). It cannot be through action, because that would contradict the Śruti and other authorities. Furthermore, if it were attainable through action, there would be the further defect of it being non-eternal. Thus he says: "And if [it were] by action... (Verse 69). In my view, however, the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), having arisen as a positive entity (*bhāva*), is destroyed; from that, supreme equality (*sāmya*) arises, and that is indeed a non-entity (*abhāva*). The meaning is that for a produced entity (*janya-bhāva*), destruction is inevitable.

Now, if it is objected that "equality is produced by knowledge," [the author] anticipates this and says "no" with the words "by knowledge. To this it is replied: Is it produced by knowledge directly or indirectly? It cannot be the first, because it is not observed; for knowledge is never seen to be the direct producer of anything. Thus he says: "as will be shown later. Furthermore, it must be stated of what [knowledge] is the cause. If it is said to be of equality, he replies: "as will be shown later. For the object is the cause of knowledge; therefore, [if knowledge were the cause of equality], there would be a confusion of causes and effects.

If you accept [the Self] as the cause while asserting that it is to be accomplished through knowledge, you will surely become an object of ridicule. If you say "of the Self," even then, one must state whether it refers to both selves—the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—or to one of them; for there is no experience of equality between the two. And is this equality intended to be described in terms of similarity or in terms of difference? In the first case, there would be the constant existence of equality. In the second case, there is no experience of equality. If you argue that the production of equality is what matters and not the experience of it, we have already stated that such production does not occur directly through knowledge.

He said: "It is most excellent. For it is observed that knowledge is the cause of desire. To this we reply: Knowledge is not the cause of desire, because even when knowledge exists, the absence of desire is observed; for example, a wise man, though knowing of a crow's flesh, does not desire it. Indeed, invariable concomitance is what makes the relationship between cause and effect intelligible. Knowledge is a cause that is otherwise established [as being dependent on something else] by desire. Desire is dependent upon an object already known, and the known object is dependent upon knowledge."

Knowledge is the cause of that worldly transaction [of desire] only through the observation of desire; thus, knowledge is its cause. What then is the cause of desire? Are you asking for its material cause (*upādāna*) or its instrumental cause (*nimitta*)? If the former, it is either *māyā* or the mind (*manas*). As for the instrumental cause, it is the superimposition of beauty (*śobhanādhyāsa*) for the desire of the individual soul (*jīva*), whereas for the desire of Śiva, it is the actions of the vital breaths (*prāṇakarmāṇi*). Therefore, knowledge is not directly the cause of anything at all. [Objection: Let it be, then, indirectly, through a flawless succession? [Reply: No, for it is said: "it never acts."

The meaning of this *paraṃparā* (succession) is that there exists some factor between Vidyā and Sāmya that produces *sāmya*. Is that [factor] knowledge (*jñāna*) or action (*karman*)? It cannot be the first, because [knowledge and action] are equal [in being incapable of producing it]. Nor can it be the second, because it would entail the consequence of the destruction of *sāmya*; such is the sense.

832 | Through action, O Cedi, destruction occurs; for that which is accomplished by action is perishable. Just as a thief devours his own prey even before [the victim's] eyes, so too does knowledge destroy ignorance even before one's very eyes. Furthermore, false knowledge never produces a real result. This being the case, they say there is equality between those two through their essential nature alone; for both the thief and the teacher of truth act even before [the fact is realized]. Thus it is with Śiva and Nīla. 69–71.
Beyond that, liberation exists as a single defining characteristic; thus Śiva, though non-different, appears divided by ignorance.

Regarding the question of what the cause of that equilibrium is—whether it be karma or knowledge—the first alternative is refuted by the words "If [it were] by karma. This means that because action is invariably pervaded by impermanence. As for the second alternative, he states the uselessness of knowledge with the words "But by knowledge alone. For knowledge is the indicator of an equilibrium already existing previously, not its producer. Thus, since that equilibrium exists for both of them even before [the rise of knowledge], it does not become the fruit of knowledge; this is the meaning. || 69 ||

He shows that it is well-established in other contexts that knowledge possesses only the quality of making [an object] known (*bodhakatva*) and not the quality of being a causal agent (*kārakatva*), by saying "as previously stated" (*purastādeva*). (70) When thus challenged, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) states his own intended position of equality, beginning with "In that case, thus... (*tatraivam*). The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the opponent's position.

For that which is equal to everything in every respect—such equality characterized by non-duality and independent of distinctions—is what is intended here; the meaning is that it is not a kind of equality where, due to the absence of distinction, equality would be untenable. As for the attainment of equality through knowledge mentioned previously, he accepts that very point as being desired, stating: "previously... and "it is established by the nature of protection."

Because the Witness, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, is the cause of the manifestation of all objects, it exists eternally as their ultimate substratum; and because it is of the nature of bliss, its essence consists solely of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (*satya-jñāna-ānanda-ekarasa*). This very same nature belongs to Paraśiva, as established by the scriptural text: "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite. Thus, there is non-difference in characteristics between the two.

Therefore, the meaning is that because they possess identical characteristics, their oneness is established at all times. [Regarding the phrase] "not being overcome by non-discrimination" (aviyayānabhibhūta): for non-discrimination, being inherently false, does not bring about an ultimate duality in the nature of Paraśiva; such is the meaning of the Śruti. (71–72)

Whatever arises from karma is necessarily transitory. If equanimity (*sāmya*) occurs by reason of knowledge (*jñāna*), then it must follow that equanimity exists only within the veil (*paṭala*); for knowledge brings about the cognition of an object as it existed previously, and knowledge cannot produce a thing that did not exist before.

Therefore, the intention behind asserting equality on the basis of knowledge is that the absolute identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva has existed from all eternity. This very equality is liberation (*mokṣa*), for as the Śruti declares, "he attains supreme equality" (*sāmyam paramam upaiti*). Consequently, it follows that liberation is also eternal. Indeed, eternal liberation (*nityamuktatva*) is the very nature of Śiva.

If the individual soul (*jīva*) is understood in this manner, then by the principle of "the identity of the one" (*ekasyatā-honeḥ*), the non-difference (*abheda*) of both is established. (Therefore, even if one considers them equal, upon reflection, the conclusion leads only to non-difference! Thus, the intention of the Śruti is that Śiva is eternally non-dual; due to ignorance (*avidyā*), it is as if He is deluded and appears separate from the individual souls and so forth. When, through knowledge (*vidyā*), ignorance ceases to exist, [non-duality is realized].

One becomes established in that supreme equality which consists of non-difference and is one's own essential nature (*svarūpabhūta*). No other process is possible beyond this. Therefore, the equality spoken of in the Vedas is indeed non-difference (*abheda*), and nothing else. (Verses 69–73). Thus, when the individual soul (*jīva*) attains firm knowledge of its own Śiva-nature—[as it is said]: "Then [he attains] that [equality]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3)—it is supreme equality, according to the scriptural statement: "Supreme equality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). *Notes:* 1. *jja. tu tatsā*" | 2. *ḍa. nāsyeva |* 3. "'paraṃ sāmyam‌'" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3) iti śrutau |*

Chapter 7 Knowledge attains identity with Him through the destruction of ignorance, and not otherwise. Therefore, when there is equality between the two, there is indeed oneness, and nothing else. (73) Thus, the individual soul (*jīva*) beholds its own Śiva-nature as taught by the Veda; it always performs delight, play, and other activities within its very self. (74) Even external activity occurs within itself, in Śiva, whose nature is pure consciousness (*sattva*); thus, he perceives everything as expanding from his own self alone. (75)

When one recites everything fearlessly by means of one's own self alone, then one is united [with the Absolute], for there is no liberation for one who is bound. (76) Thus, through such fruit-bearing knowledge, as well as by austerity and by the observances of celibacy and so forth, according to the path declared in the Vedas, when ignorance is removed by wisdom, the identity of the individual soul and the Lord—which is established by its very nature—remains; that indeed is what is intended by the term "equality. He concludes with the word "therefore" (ataḥ). (77)

"He is this very breath"—thus he summarizes the meaning of the sentence according to its purport with the word "evam" (in this way). The meaning is that if, by the method described, one directly perceives without doubt the nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) as being non-different [from Brahman], then, due to the absence of any other entity, play and so forth belong to that knower only within his own self. The phrase "anything else" means meditation, worship, and so on. He explains the scriptural term "one who performs actions" (*kriyāvān*) with the word "bahis" (externally).

The meaning is that for one who knows that even the activity of driving [a chariot], which consists of the movement of the hands, feet, and so forth, is not distinct from the Self, there will be nothing further to be done. (75) "Then he is neither bound nor liberated. Since bondage consists of ignorance (*avidyā*), liberation is likewise of that same nature; thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), he possesses no state of being liberated either. For this very reason, the Teacher said: "There is no cessation and no arising; there is no bound soul and no seeker of liberation."

"One who is not liberated is indeed not liberated; this is the ultimate truth. (76) Now, regarding the production of supreme [knowledge], he summarizes the *Manu-smṛti* verse which establishes the means for the auxiliary causes: "By truth, by austerity... and so forth. Truth (*satya*) is the abandonment of false speech. Austerity (*tapas*) is one-pointedness of mind, which is conducive to the vision of that [Self]; it does not refer to the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Smṛti: "The one-pointedness of mind, speech, and senses is called austerity (tapas). By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "by celibacy and so forth," there is the inclusion of non-violence, truthfulness, and other such yogic practices. "In the manner prescribed by the Vedas" means by way of the injunction: "It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. In this regard, that which is the essence and the supreme love is my very Self; whatever else he does, such as sitting and so forth, he does all within the Self.

(That is to say, his love does not abide in anything other than the Self, nor does he engage in play or other activities with that which is other than the Self. The reason is clear: nothing whatsoever remains for him apart from the Self. || 74 || He knows that "all activity appearing in an external form belongs only to the essence of true bliss," and he continues to perceive [everything] solely as the essence of the Self. || 75 ||

When one perceives that everything is one's own true nature, the living being (*jīva*) becomes fearless—for fear always arises from another. This state of fearlessness is itself liberation (*mokṣa*). Even while residing [in the body], he does not become bound; had he been bound, he would have become liberated. Since he was never bound at all, what occasion is there for liberation? This is the ultimate truth. (76)

In this manner—that is, through the practice of *parā vidyā* (higher knowledge), which is characterized by liberation and is devoid of causal agency—the observance of truth, austerity (*tapas*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and so forth [leads to the goal]. [Notes:
1. ḍa. reads *sato*; 2. śaṣa. reads *bandho na*; 3. This verse is found in the *Sāhasrī* reading (17.25), as well as in the *Mokṣadharma* (250.4) and the *Vanaparvan* (260.25).]

834. Within the body, [the wise] perceive their own light, their own path, and their own sovereign power. Those whose divine nature is diminished behold it, while others, veiled by *māyā*, do not. (58) He who possesses such thorough knowledge is a supreme yogin. For him, who is complete in all respects, there is no wandering anywhere. (59) Just as the one sky appears to move due to the movement of clouds, so too he who knows the omnipresence of the Self moves nowhere at all. (60)

Neither by sight, nor by speech, nor by the austerity of another deity, nor by ritual action is He perceived; rather, one whose being is purified by the clarity of knowledge beholds Him, who is partless and beyond comparison. (81) Through meditation upon the Supreme Lord in His form as Śiva with Ambā, the thorough knowledge of one’s own partless nature arises, and not through any other cause. (82)

“Within the body” means situated in the center of the heart-lotus (*hasuṣḍarīka*). “Whose defects are destroyed” means those whose defects—such as desire, anger, and so forth, which cause mental agitation—are diminished or abandoned; they are thus described. He states the meaning of the sentence “Truth alone conquers, not untruth” with the words “not others. For others are of an unreal nature due to *māyā*; therefore, being deluded by it, they are unable to perceive the true nature of their own self. || 78 ||

He explains the purport of the mantra, “And that is great and divine,” as follows: “Of such a nature. Since the self is of the nature of the independent, unlimited Supreme Śiva, movement and the like are not possible for it, because those are attributes belonging to limited entities. (79) He establishes this very point by means of an illustration: “Like space. (80)

That which is this state of being Śiva—who is self-luminous and completely full—has been taught as having such means as truth (*satya*) and so forth as auxiliary instruments for its realization. Now, however, he teaches the extraordinary cause [of realization] with the words: "not by the eye" (*na cakṣuṣā*). Because it is devoid of form and other qualities, it is not an object of the senses such as the eye. "Not by speech" (*na vācā*): the meaning is that it cannot be grasped by the organs of action, such as the mouth, which are distinct from the sense organs. "By austerity" (*tapasā*): by means of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth. "By ritual action" (*karmaṇā*): by means of rituals such as the *agnihotra*.

If it is argued that the eye and other organs are not perceived [as such], how then can there be knowledge of them? To this he replies: "By the clarity of knowledge" (*jñānaprasādena*). A person whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is purified—that is, one possessing a pure continuum—when the turbidity caused by impurities such as passion born from contact with objects has been removed through the clarity of knowledge, which is the transparency and lucidity of cognition, directly perceives his own supreme form of the Lord, which is free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). || 81 ||
He states that even the virtuous meditation of a pure being is a cause for the non-existence of the uncaused—thus: "by meditation," etc. (82).

This can be achieved through the practices prescribed in the Vedas. || 77 || Only those whose attachment and other afflictions have been exhausted are able to perceive the Supreme Self, which is self-luminous and resides within the body; no others can. || 78 || For the supreme yogi who possesses such knowledge as described, there is no need for eating or sleeping; he is of a complete nature and all-pervading. || 79 ||

Since this one Ātman is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), it neither comes nor goes; for that very reason, even the knower of its pervasiveness neither comes nor goes. (80) This nature of the Self as being "complete" (*pūrṇa-svabhāva*) cannot be made an object by the eyes, speech, other senses, or by action.

When the knowledge of a person with a pure mind is no longer defiled by association with any other object, only then does that partless (niṣkāraka), supreme (Śivābhinnapada) state become accessible to a person whose mind is otherwise distracted. || 81 || Even through meditation on the Supreme One, whose body consists of half-Umā, the knowledge of one's own partlessness (nirviśeṣatā) can be attained; there is no other means for its realization. || 82 ||

This extremely subtle Self can be attained through one-pointed intellect. It is the refuge of all; even the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are established within it. (From the passage beginning, "He withdraws all the breaths" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.3], the *prāṇas* are understood to be the support of everything; by stating that their support is Śiva, His status as the support of all becomes clear. || 83 ||

The meaning is that, having attained the form of the *sūraṇa* (the root tuber), it is like the state of being free from all bonds. When the mind is brought under control through the practice of the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahma*), that very [Brahman] becomes directly perceived, stripped of the fabrication of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is to be understood in accordance with the statement of the teacher Kalpa-ruma: "When the mind is mastered, through the meditation on the Brahman with qualities, that [Brahman] itself is realized directly, with the conceptualization of adjuncts removed. (Note: The text contains several scribal errors and fragments; the translation above interprets the core philosophical intent regarding the attainment of the Brahman's nature through the mastery of the mind and the removal of adjuncts.)

Chapter 7, Verse 835. One should know that the Self is indeed most pure; it is established in the supreme state, wherein the gods abide for the sake of all prosperity. (832) Whatever world a wise man perceives through his own mind, he desires that very thing and consequently conquers it without effort. (84) Therefore, one should seek out a knower of the Self—the best among men, a deliverer from the ocean of existence—who, by means of his own body, [leads others] to the goal through the practice of yoga. (85)

"This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellectual power, nor by much hearing. Only he whom this [Self] chooses, by him is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3) This [verse] summarizes the statement "This [Self] is atomic" by saying "this Self."

In that supreme support (paramālambana), which is the locus of the conceptualization of the entire world and resides in the middle of the heart, the vital breath (prāṇa) has entered by means of its fivefold modifications, such as prāṇa, apāna, and so forth. The meaning is that this Self, although appearing small due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is to be known as the nature of the non-dual Śiva—unlimited in its prior and subsequent forms—by means of a one-pointed mind that serves as the cause through the clarity of knowledge (jñānaprasāda). || 83 ||

He states the fruit characterized by the attainment of everything for one who has realized that which is defined as above through the complete absorption of all objects of desire: "He manifests... (saṃvibhāti). The meaning is this: when one whose intellect is thus purified speaks, as established in another Vedic text beginning with "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," then whatever world he contemplates with his mind and whatever enjoyments he desires therein, he attains all of that—everything without exception—by his own will alone. || 84 ||

Since all desires are thus of the very nature of the one who possesses knowledge, the meaning is that for one devoted to its service, the attainment of the fruit of enjoyment is accomplished. (85) He shows that the taught truth of the Self cannot be known by any means other than the aforementioned method—by saying "not this": not by *pravacana*, which is the recitation of the Vedas and scriptures; nor by *medhā*, which is the capacity to retain the meaning of what has been learned; nor by *bahuśruta*, which is hearing [the teachings] many times.

By these conditions, He is not obtained—that is, He cannot be reached. By what, then, is He obtained? It is said: he who desires this very Supreme Self as described above—desires to attain it—for that reason, the Supreme Self is obtained by him and not by any other means. For that wise one who seeks His attainment through hearing, reflection, and so forth, this Self rends asunder—that is, reveals—the covering of ignorance that envelops Him.

The meaning is that when that ignorance is removed by the knowledge produced through the means of hearing and so forth, one's true nature manifests. (86) Whatever desire one has, one attains it without effort. (84) Therefore, the knower of the Self is the manifest Lord himself; he alone can deliver one from saṃsāra. One should worship the knower of the Self with one's own body, wealth, and other possessions. (85)

The study of the Vedic scriptures does not by itself lead to the attainment of the Self; even by memorizing a great deal, one does not achieve self-realization. Repeated hearing (*śravaṇa*) is also not the cause for attaining the Self. The Self is attained only through an extremely intense longing to find it. In reality, the Self reveals its own nature by itself; no external means is the cause for its perception.

The praise of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) should be understood as follows: without an extremely intense longing, the practice of spiritual means cannot take place; therefore, this alone is declared to be the primary qualification. As stated in the *Cūḍāmaṇi*: "When fully developed, it brings forth the fruit" (verse 29). When dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) are not intense, even qualities such as forbearance (*kṣamā*) are useless. Consequently, the desire for liberation is the principal distinguishing characteristic of the qualified seeker.

He himself will remain engaged in the remaining means [of realization] (vha.-ho gyāṃ to bākī sādhanoṃ ko svayaṃ juṭā rakhegā). || 86 || One who is not overcome by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)—that is, one in whom there is no such [defect]—cannot attain the Self. This Self is not attained by one who is devoid of strength, nor through negligence, nor through austerity that bears another mark. But for the wise man who indeed practices these [means], this eternal abode is revealed. (85) The sages, whose minds are perfected, who are free from sorrow, self-controlled, and tranquil, having reached all things and being steadfast with disciplined souls, they illuminate everything. (86) Those who know the Vedānta, who have ascertained the meaning of the Upaniṣads, who have renounced the fire-sacrifices and their observances, and who are pure—they all, at the time of the final end, attain the supreme liberation in the world of Brahman. (87)

He says, "Not this," [meaning] that those things which serve as companions for the striking and the pulling must be prepared; for a man devoid of that vigor (vīrya) or strength (bala) produced by the completion of the striking (ālaniṣṭhā), [it is not possible].

He is not to be attained [merely] through lack of exertion, nor through negligence, nor through lack of attention caused by attachment to objects such as sons and cattle; nor through austerity devoid of the marks of the various stages of life (*āśrama*)—here, "austerity" means knowledge—for even from such knowledge, He cannot be known. Thus, the meaning is that effort, heedfulness, and austerity, when conjoined with the specific stages of life, are the internal means for His realization. This summarizes the scriptural statement: "By these one is purified. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).

The meaning is: "by means of these, such as *bala* (strength) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "this [Self] of him": for that knower who strives by means of *bala* and the rest, this Self—which is directly perceived, free from all impurity, and whose nature is splendor (*tejas*)—attains the unconditioned Brahman; such is the meaning. (87) He describes the manner in which the knower attains that state with the words "having attained" (*saṃprāpya*). Having attained—that is, having reached through perfect knowledge—this immortal state, the seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*), being possessors of vision, are satisfied by that very knowledge. They are "perfected in self" (*kṛtātmānaḥ*), meaning they have achieved certainty.

Those who have cast off sorrow and are free from the worldly sufferings of grief, delusion, and the like; those who have reached the end and whose senses are stilled—they are the knowers of the Self (*ātman*). Being wise, discerning, and disciplined in soul with minds eternally composed, they perceive Brahman—the all-pervading which is like space—as devoid of limitation, even at the time of the body's fall. Having abandoned the limitation of adjuncts (*upādhi*) created by ignorance, such as the distinction between "I" and "not-I," they enter into the undivided, limitless Brahman which is present in all things. (88) Thus says the Vedāntin.

Those for whom the aforementioned object is firmly established by that distinguished knowledge—which has as its content the non-duality of Brahman and the self (*brahmātma-advaita*)—and which is produced by the great Vedāntic mahāvākyas such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*); who, through the renunciation of all actions characteristic of the stage of *saṃnyāsa*, have attained the state of being devoted solely to Brahman; and who, through yoga and other means, are diligent in their practice; and therefore possess purified internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

All those who have become thus, at the time of the final end through the dissolution of the body composed of the elements and their derivatives, are liberated when that supreme cause—ignorance—is destroyed. Because they have attained the knowledge born from the practice of the most excellent nectar-like immortality (*amṛta*), they are absorbed into Brahman; "the world" (*loka*) here refers to Brahman itself as the object of absorption (*rokyate*). When Brahman is being absorbed into its own true nature, they are completely released—that is, they are freed from all bonds of *saṃsāra* beyond all possibility of return.

The meaning is that while remaining right here, through knowledge, when the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are dissolved, they attain the state of the undivided Brahman, just like the space within a jar and so forth. (89) O friend! Through inquiry, one should firmly establish this: that which appears does not exist at all. By asserting this very point, statements such as "neither existence nor non-existence" become possible. Even while there is negligence in the form of attachment toward sense objects, proximity [to the goal] is difficult to obstruct.

Even through knowledge, it is difficult to attain the state beyond the *ālamba* (support) for one who is devoid of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). (For that bliss indeed arises only when there is renunciation; therefore, the word "king" (*rājya*) has been used here in the sense of renunciation.)

Since renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is a means for the realization of the Self (*ātman*) and its true purpose, it is indeed [necessary]. Alternatively, since renunciation is accomplished when knowledge (*jñāna*) arises, renunciation is said to be a limb (*aṅga*) of knowledge. In any case, knowledge does not exist without renunciation; as it has been stated, only knowledge conjoined with renunciation is the cause of liberation (*mokṣa*). Although knowledge does not depend on anything else for the sake of liberation, it nevertheless depends upon itself.

The sense is that this renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is much more internal than one's own *siddhi* (perfection). It is called renunciation because it is the abandonment of action along with its means, based on the realization of the self as a non-doer. If, however, knowledge is attained through austerity (*tapas*), then there is hardship.

In the *Paramṛta Upaniṣad*: "Those who have become the Supreme Immortal (*paramamṛta*)—that is, Brahman, which is by nature deathless—are the *parāmṛta*; they are those who, while still living, have become Brahman and are thus the Supreme Immortals. This is the commentary on that [term]. According to the commentary, the meaning of the mantra is: "While still living, they attain absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) upon the abandonment of the body. They are *yatayaḥ* (ascetics) because of the effort (*yatna*) by which all efforts are ceased for them. 2. "What is the stake? 3. [Variant readings: *gha*, *jña*: *°bandhānyu°*. 7.

The fifteen parts that have gone forth—the foundations, all the gods, and their respective deities—as well as actions, consciousness, and the great self, all become one in the supreme, imperishable One. (7.837) 90.

He explains how the constituent parts (*kalā*s), such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, belong to that liberated one with the words, "The parts have gone. These are introduced in the *Praśna Upaniṣad* with the statement, "Sixteen parts come into being," and are then recorded as follows: "He created the vital breath; from the vital breath, space, air, light, water, earth, the senses, the mind, thought, deliberation, faith, austerity, sacred formulas, action, the worlds, and names within those worlds. These parts, beginning with the vital breath, are the causes for the transmigrating soul's commencement of another body.

But for the wise, at the time of liberation, those fifteen *kalās*—the term “pratisthāḥ” being in the second case plural—having gone to their respective causes, become merged therein; this is the meaning. And as for the deities such as Āditya who abide in the sense organs like the eyes as their sustainers—as per the Vedic text, “Āditya, having become the eye, entered the two eyes”—they too go to their own respective divine bodies; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, those karmas whose fruits have not yet begun to manifest, as well as the agent-self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), predominantly characterized by consciousness, and distinguished by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—all these become one with the immutable, indestructible, non-dual Brahman, which transcends the entire collection of modifications. The meaning is that it is just like the reflections of the sun in vessels of water [merging] into the sun itself when those vessels, their supports, are removed. || 90 ||

The following connection should be understood: "Not by austerity, nor by progeny, nor by wealth is the Self attained" (*tapasā na labhyo nānyena karmādinā na labhyaḥ*). The Self is not attained through the performance of austerities, nor by assuming the marks and so forth of others, nor through the worship of symbols (*pratīkopāsana*) and the like. For the wise person who strives by means of these [proper] methods, the Self in its manifest form attains the abode that is the true nature of Brahman. || 87 ||

Having attained this, the sage, satisfied through knowledge, becomes one who has accomplished his purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*), free from sorrow, and devoid of desire. He realizes the all-pervading Self as his own very self. With a mind always absorbed in meditation, he remains established in the Brahman that is everything. (88) Through the specific knowledge regarding the identity of Śiva and the Self, born from hearing the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) and other means, the aforementioned supreme reality—

What is the certainty? It is this: when, through the practice of yoga consisting solely of devotion to Brahman preceded by the renunciation of all actions, that pure and great-souled one—who is the cause of the world—attains the supreme state at the time of the cessation of primal ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), he becomes liberated from all the bonds of transmigratory existence by means of that knowledge which removes ignorance and serves as the instrument for attaining unsurpassed immortality; thus, he becomes his own self-luminous nature.

It stands as the support for Brahman. (One should understand that the commentator has provided an alternative interpretation of this verse by following the words of its root mantra and by applying the context of the word *oṃ*). || 84- || The subtle parts of the liberated soul, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), etc., become merged into their respective causes.

While bestowing grace upon others through powers such as *ṛddhi*, the deities who remain present abandon that act of bestowing grace and stay within their own respective spheres. The agent—the *cidābhāsa* (the reflection of consciousness)—which possesses adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the *saṃyita* functions and the intellect (*buddhi*), becomes dissolved into the supreme, immutable Brahman. (This refers precisely to the occasion of the death of the liberated one; the dissolution of the vital breaths and other elements is described in the *Praśnopaniṣad* 6.4).

Although that boar possesses fifteen digits (*kalā*), nevertheless, he has brought together his vital breath (*prāṇa*) and mind (*manas*) and placed them upon his feet. Alternatively, the final digit remains as the name "Nāmaḥ. People remember [this] by saying, "Śuka was liberated," and so forth; therefore, it is said to be fifteen. (90)

Just as rivers, having become full, reach the ocean and cast off their respective names and forms, even so the knower of the Śiva-principle, transcending name and form, attains the Supreme Person, the Brahman who is beyond the *para*. (Because *māyā* is the cause, it is called *para*; because it is beyond even that, Brahman is called *parātpara*). Even when the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) is destroyed, the soul is not destroyed, just as—

1. "When threefold knowledge is maintained [in the body], why does it not leave it? "Because of Name," says Artabhāga, following the words of Paraśu (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.12). The mention of "Name" as something distinct from the two numbers, sixteen and fifteen, is for the sake of reconciling the difference in enumeration. In reality, however, the statement that "only its name remains" means that nothing at all remains; this is clear from the commentary of the author of the Bhāṣya on the cited Śruti. The discrepancy in the number should be reconciled by the hypothesis of its inclusion within another category. 2. gha. oṃ.
cha. ka. śtyā de". (Note: The final string of characters appears to be a scribal or typographical artifact.)

838. As rivers flowing toward the ocean lose their names and forms upon reaching it, even so the wise man, liberated from name and form, goes to the Supreme Puruṣa, the Brahman beyond the beyond. O bulls among sages, he who indeed knows that Supreme Brahman [attains liberation].

Through knowledge one becomes Brahman itself; there is no cause for doubt. (92) If one knows Brahman with absolute certainty through one's own direct experience, then in his lineage there shall be no one who does not know Brahman. (93) He crosses over sorrow, he destroys the evil, and the knot in the heart is rent asunder. The wise man stands at the forefront; this which I have spoken is indeed the truth. (94)

This entire [work] is most excellent, capable of shattering the thicket of grief and delusion; it shines for one devoted to the Veda, having been imparted by me as a means for attaining the realization of reality. Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Investigation into the Nature of Reality," within the Brahma-gītā Upaniṣad, in the latter part of the fourth section, the Yajña-vaibhava-khaṇḍa, of the Sūta-saṃhitā in the Śrī-skanda Purāṇa.

He establishes the aforementioned state of oneness by means of an illustration: "Just as [in the case of] water... and so forth. Regarding "from name and form": "name" refers to Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and so on; "form" (rūpa) refers to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) characterized by the body, limbs, and so forth, which is called "food" (*sūpa*) because it is consumed. From that cause of differentiation, he becomes distinct. Being "supreme" (*para*) because he pervades his own effects, he attains the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), who is beyond *māyā*, who is auspicious (*puṣya*), complete (*pūrṇa*), and whose very nature is Brahman. || 99 ||

Since the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is based solely on one's own ignorance (*avidyā*), and since upon its cessation no means other than knowledge is required—just as the attainment of gold already present around one's neck is accomplished by mere awareness—he shows this with the words: "He who indeed... (92). He explains the meaning of the passage, "For him there is no doubt regarding Brahman," with the word "well-settled": the sense is that whatever is born to one who knows Brahman, all that becomes nothing but the knower of Brahman itself. (93)

"He crosses over sorrow," and so forth. He crosses over—meaning he lives beyond—sorrow (*śoka*), which is mental anguish caused by the loss of many desired things. He also crosses over evil (*pāpmānaṃ*), consisting of both merit and demerit, which is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Even that which is bound by the impressions of non-discrimination residing in the cave of the heart (*guhā-nadarda-dayastha-aviyā-vāsanā-granthaḥ*) is destroyed. Thus, the wise man, being free from desire and having attained clarity, attains immortality through knowledge; this is the meaning. (94) He concludes the subject matter of the Upaniṣad that has been expounded: "Thus it is said" (*samuktam*). (95)
Thus ends [the section] in the fourth Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa of the Śrīsūtasaṃhitā-tātparyadīpikā.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Investigation into the Form of the Dweller," in the *Brahmagītā Upaniṣads*. [Commentary: Even though the Gaṅgā ceases to exist as a separate entity upon merging into the ocean, the Gaṅgā is not destroyed; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that [liberation] would not be a human goal (*apuruṣārthatā*). Whoever knows the Supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself on the basis of that knowledge; of this there is no doubt.

(For since he is eternally Brahman, once the ignorance regarding this has ceased, the conventional usage arises that "he has become Brahman. || 92 || He who has experienced even a slight realization of the Supreme Brahman has no fear whatsoever that he might not attain Brahman. || 93 || He becomes liberated from sorrow and sin.

The knots of his mind are loosened; he becomes completely filled with the mutual contemplation of Śrī Rādhā and others. This state is known as the complete cessation of all worldly existence (nirvāṇa). He himself becomes the immortal Brahman—this is the truth. (94) Thus, everything that bestows auspiciousness has been explained. The total destruction of the entire mass of worldly delusion occurs through this knowledge alone.

This is the very means for the extremely swift attainment of the reality whose nature is Sat-Cit-Ānanda. O practitioner, he who maintains faith in the authority of the Vedas and persists in hearing [the scriptures] and other practices attains the certain realization of this experience. || 95 ||

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). Alternatively, the meaning is that even one who is a dog becomes a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) because the knower of Brahman is all-pervasive. Or rather, the construction is: "even a dog becomes a knower of Brahman. Here, the result is to be understood as follows: whether in this life or in another birth, one born in that lineage becomes a knower of Brahman. Or it should be understood that he becomes a knower of the Vedas, or that he becomes one who has attained the Lord. If he becomes even a dog in some way, he becomes a knower of Brahman; otherwise, he does not become so at all. This is the sense.

Chapter Eight Brahmī said: There exists that supreme reality, directly worshipped by Śiva, Sadāśiva, and the others. That lower [form] is to be attained with great effort by the wise. (1) This very [reality], which is exceedingly beautiful and hidden, should be meditated upon by ascetics; it destroys all sins without exception and bestows the state of a *patra* (a worthy recipient). Bow down to it! (2) O best of gods, she is attained through faith, through great devotion, through meditation, and through yoga—indeed, O gods, she is attained through knowledge and not through ritual action (*karman*), nor through progeny, nor through wealth, nor even through renunciation alone. (3)

Now, wishing to demonstrate that the *Kavalyopaniṣad* is devoted solely to the non-dual reality (*advaita*), the author summarizes it with the words beginning "There is that Reality" (*asti tattvam*). [The phrase] "concentrated as Śiva, Śakti, Sūdra, and so forth" means that because its nature is unsurpassed bliss, it is called *Śiva*; and because it causes the drying up (*drāvaṇa*) of the suffering of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), it is called *Rudra*—the meaning is that it has attained such a name. Having thus stated the subject matter of the knowledge (*vidyā*), he proceeds to show the qualified seeker and the purpose of that knowledge in sequence, starting with "That must necessarily... and so forth.

For it is heard thus: "Then Āśvalāyana, having approached the Blessed One Parameṣṭhin, said: 'Teach me, O Blessed One, that most excellent ignorance which is always being practiced, though hidden; by which, having quickly cast off all evil, the knower goes to the Puruṣa who is higher than the high. Thus, in all the matters about to be explained, the root scripture is to be inferred. (1) (2)

He points out the favorable means for the arising of that higher knowledge (paravidyā) with the word "śraddhayā" (by faith). Faith is conviction in the matter taught by the guru. Devotion is constant absorption in that [matter]. Meditation (dhyāna) is a continuous flow of similar cognitions regarding that taught matter. Yoga is of the nature to be described hereafter, as stated in the Śruti: "Seated in a comfortable posture in a secluded place. All of this is the means for the arising of higher knowledge.

It is shown that for one endowed with such means, the renunciation of the threefold desire alone is the means to liberation and nothing else, by the words "That indeed is not... [sā neva]. By "action" (karman) is meant sacrifice, charity, and so forth; by "offspring" (prajā) is meant sons, daughters, and so forth; by "wealth" (artha) is meant riches. For these—action and the rest—are means for impermanent results, whereas the supreme knowledge is of a different nature; thus, the meaning is that it is attained only through the abandonment of action and the other two. || 3 ||

Now begins the chapter titled "The Method for Knowing That Reality" (based on the *Kaivalyopaniṣad* to demonstrate that the Śruti has elsewhere also provided a description of Śiva preceded by the instruction on the means [of realization]):
Brahmā said: "The reality is self-established; Śiva, *Sat*, and so forth are its names. Having exerted every effort, the wise should know it as non-dual. (1)

A renunciant must certainly practice this secret knowledge (*vidyā*) which takes the reality of *usra* as its object; it swiftly destroys the sins of people and brings about the attainment of the Supreme Brahman. (2) This supreme knowledge is obtained through faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga, but not through ritual action. It is not attained even by means of vehicles, boats, or wealth.

Rather, it is through the renunciation of karma and the like that this [ignorance] is destroyed. (Through meditation [dhyāna], one should contemplate the "destined" [diṣṭam] which will be explained here [from verse 7 onwards] as nididhyāsana and yoga. || 3 || By means of the knowledge arising from hearing the great Vedāntic Mahāvākyas, those whose hearts are purified by supreme wisdom have reached a firm certainty regarding the ultimate reality (paramārtha). While still dwelling in this body—which is merely a reflection of the Self—the root cause known as ignorance is destroyed.

1. [The author] refutes the previous [view] (3.46) by establishing the existence of the Supreme, stating: "It exists. Some have stated the existence of the Supreme through such passages as, "Neither by breath nor by the out-breath" (*na prāṇena nāpānena*). With his neck, head, and body perfectly composed, and veiled by a white garment; having extinguished all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the sons of the gods bowed with devotion to their own teacher and meditated upon him within the lake of the heart—[upon] that Lord who is like lightning, stainless, infinite, pure, unmanifest, and inconceivable by all living beings.

Now, preceded by the statement of the uncommon causes for the commencement of the inquiry into the supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*), he describes the qualified seeker and the fruit to be attained: "Those who [know] the Vedāntas... This has been explained in the previous chapter. (4–5) Thus, the nature of knowledge has been taught along with its subject matter, purpose, means, and qualified seeker. The connection [of the terms] is as follows: because it is free from the turbidity produced by the enjoyment of sense objects through dispassion toward them, it is "rare" (uninterrupted) and stainless; therefore, it is "pure," being the water of the heart-lake. He shows the object to be contemplated within that lotus of the heart: "clear" (*viśada*). "Clear" means stainless. It is "space" (*ambaram*) due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Māyā, which is primarily composed of pure *sattva*. It is "infinite" (*anantam*), meaning devoid of end (*anta*) or destruction; for this very reason, it is "pure."

It is unmanifest due to the absence of the causes of manifestation, such as sound, touch, and so forth; for this very reason, it is inconceivable even by the mind, because it is absolutely free from conceptual construction. || 9 ||

Upon its attainment, all these become liberated and become established in a state of supreme purity. (4-5) Having attained this, the wise seeker of liberation should, having purified himself, sit comfortably in a very pure and solitary place with his head, neck, and torso held straight; he should also apply a smear of white ash.

Restraining the outward movement of the senses, one should offer salutations to one’s own guru and focus the mind one-pointedly within the lotus of the heart. (6–8) The heart of this practitioner (at least during the period of meditation) should be free from desire for sense objects and recollection of enjoyments. One should meditate upon the pure Lord. Beyond purity and lordship, there is another quality of the object of meditation: infinity, which means being devoid of destruction.

Purity (*śuddhi*) means being free from defects such as suffering and the like. Unmanifestness (*avyaktatā*) means being devoid of all specific qualities such as sound and so forth. Inconceivability (*acintyatā*) means being beyond the reach of mind and speech. Auspiciousness (*śivatā*) means being of the nature of well-being due to the perception of supreme bliss. Tranquility (*praśānti*) means being free from agitation. Immortality (*amṛtatā*) means being unrelated to time.

The state of having the Vedas as its source means, by implication, being the cause of all things; from this, one should also understand its causality with respect to everything. Being devoid of beginning, middle, and end means being free from modifications such as birth and so forth. Unity means being non-dual. Manifestly means being non-distinct from itself. Omnipresence means pervasiveness. Formlessness means being devoid of shape. Being consciousness-bliss means *sac-cid-ānanda*. Transcendence means being beyond the world. Supreme sovereignty.
Accompaniment by Umā means being accompanied by one's own power (*śakti*).

Therefore, O gods, you must go for refuge to Him, the source of all that is heard, the witness of everything; what I have spoken is the truth, and it cannot be otherwise. (1) By virtue of his nature as supreme bliss, he is the bestower of auspiciousness; he is the nectar, the means to immortality, who causes the cessation of the waves of suffering in the ocean of transmigratory existence.

This is the explanation of the word *brahman* found in the Śruti, which has the Vedas as its source. It is free from beginning, middle, and end; it is defined by being devoid of internal division, remaining as it is in the beginning, the middle, and the end. It is one and without a second. It is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), meaning it extends everywhere. (10) It is formless, meaning it is devoid of worldly forms. Thus, having been established through its general characteristics, its specific nature is set forth as *sac-cid-ānanda* (Being-Consciousness-Bliss). It is accompanied by its own power, meaning it is endowed with its own inherent energy.

It has been established through reasoning that she (Śakti) is non-different from the essential nature of Paraśiva. For this very reason, the meaning of "Om" is being presented. Since the syllables *sa* and *ha* of the supreme mantra *so'ham*, which denotes Śiva and Śakti, are elided when forming the Praṇava, it has been stated by the Teachers: "Having elided the letter *sa* and the letter *ha*, one should apply the sandhi known as *pūrvarūpa*; thereupon, it becomes the Praṇava. Having thus described the formless aspect (*niṣkala-rūpa*), he teaches the playful form (*līlā-vigraha*) for the purpose of meditation: "three-eyed" (verse 11). Regarding the phrase "thus intent on meditation" (verse 12): meditating upon the aforementioned state of Supreme Śiva within the lotus of one's own heart, through the direct realization of that very nature, one attains the Supreme Śiva-nature—such as this—which is the cause of the entire world consisting of the elements and elemental derivatives beginning with space, the witness of all that, and which transcends darkness, that is, Māyā. (Verses 12–13)

He establishes for all people the aforementioned non-duality of that Supreme Śiva (Paraśiva), whose nature has been taught as the object to be known, with the words "This which... Supreme Śiva alone is designated by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of deities such as Brahmā and others. Therefore, these [deities] are not separate from Him. Such a Supreme Śiva is imperishable (*akṣara*), meaning devoid of decay; He is the cause even of Brahmā and the others.
He is *svarāṭ*, shining by Himself, independent; others, however, are not self-ruling (*asvarājaḥ*) because they depend upon Him. || 54 ||

"Omarthatā" means "the state of being the referent of the *praṇava*. (This is indeed meditation on the formless (*niṣkala*). For those who are unable [to practice this], he now describes meditation on the formed (*sakala*) nearby: One should meditate with full awareness upon Mahādeva, who possesses three eyes, a blue throat, and is established in a state of supreme tranquility. The sage who is devoted to that meditation attains the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that Brahman through self-knowledge—that which is the cause of all beings, the witness of all, and beyond ignorance. These very things—the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*)—which sever the bonds of worldly existence, are indeed Śiva; they are "this" (*idam*), they are without vowels (*anasvara*), they are beyond all, and they are entirely independent.
Viṣṇu, Prāṇa, Kāla, Agni, and Earth—who else could there be? What more need be said? Whatever has been and whatever will be among these beings, all that is indeed Mahādeva alone.

Making the self the lower friction-stick and the intellect the upper friction-stick, the wise man burns away the bonds of the vital breaths simply through the churning of meditation. What more need be said? The entire world is twofold: that which was delimited by past time and that which will be delimited by future time; both of these are not distinct from His own nature. (15) Thus, since there is nothing whatsoever existing apart from the nature of the Supreme Self, He shows that the knowledge of one's own identity with Him is indeed the means to liberation in the verse beginning with "jñātvā" (having known). Even during the state of appearance, one perceives oneself as established within that [Self], which is free from the proliferation of fear regarding the elements; and one will see all beings as resting within the Self as its effects. Thus, by the very attainment of this knowledge of omnipresence, the meaning is that one realizes that non-dual, supreme Brahman. || 17 ||
