For in the state of dream, even though the external senses have ceased their activity, there exists the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which undergoes transformation into the forms of those various dream-objects; yet that too is dissolved during the stage of deep sleep (suṣupti). Therefore, when the entire collection of instruments has dissolved, being enveloped by darkness in the form of positive ignorance (bhāvarūpājñāna), one experiences and realizes the bliss that is one's own essential nature. For this very reason, one who has awakened from sleep possesses the retrospective reflection: "I slept happily. || 23 || 24 ||

O Prince, [princes] generally engage in play without any specific purpose. During the waking state, they obtain satisfaction through enjoyments such as food, drink, women, and so forth. (19–21) In this manner, Śambhu, appearing in the form of the individual soul during the dream state, experiences all the enjoyments—such as divine pleasures and sorrows—ordained by Himself. (22)

During the time of deep sleep, the mind dissolves along with everything else; there remains only a single, raw state of ignorance. In that state, Śiva enjoys the great bliss that is his own essential nature, free from all objective objects. (23) Then, when the fruits of previously performed actions begin to manifest as pleasure, those very same living beings awaken again to the states known as waking or dreaming. (24)

The three cities (states)—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—are created by the Māyā of the Lord solely for the enjoyment of the Self. Furthermore, the enjoyment of this Self is merely play; it never becomes a cause of suffering. (The Self does not experience suffering; suffering belongs to the *ātmābhāsa*.)

Just as there is no trembling in the actual sun, but trembling occurs in the reflection of the sun (sūryābhāsa), so too, according to the maxim "the particular exceeds the general," although the reflection of the Self (ātmābhāsa) is considered non-different from the Self due to its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it can nevertheless be said to be distinct from the Self, just as the reflection of the sun is said to be distinct from the sun. In that reflection of the Self, suffering occurs, but not in the Self.

The Self’s experience is indeed its state of being a witness; for one whose construction of the three cities has been destroyed, suffering and the like do not affect the witness. It is argued that experience is the fruit of karma; however, karma belongs not to the witness, but to the reflection of the Self (ātmābhāsa). Therefore—

1. The meaning is that one has completely accepted the conceit (abhimāna) such as "I am a human being" and so forth. 2. This portion [of the conceit] persists even during the waking state; however, because the superimposition of the body alone was mentioned there, it was not stated in that way here. It should be understood that although the superimposition of the body is unmanifest during sleep, the term "living being" (jīva) is used for the sleeping person because the maintenance of the vital breaths (prāṇa) is manifest.

3. Regarding the doctrine of the dissolution of all things (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭinaya*), it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa* that in another theory, there is only the dissolution of the aspect of cognition (*jñānāṃśa*). [It says: "For those who maintain [the existence of] a causal agent (*kalayatām*), there is the dissolution of the aspect of the power of cognition (*vijñānaśakti*), while leaving aside the aspect of the powers of vital breath (*prāṇa*), momentary action (*kṣaṇakriyā*), and agency (*śakti*); because the instrument (*karaṇa*) possesses a substrate (*sāśatvāt*), as in the case of dreams and so forth. Alternatively, by observing the creation and dissolution [of objects], or by means of the perspective of a person in deep sleep (*supuptapuruṣadṛṣṭi*), the dissolution of everything therein is demonstrated.

[This is] because the perception of another person whose vital breaths and body have entered deep sleep is an error" (p. 329, Kula). 4. Because the mind dissolves during deep sleep, and since the mind is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), the scriptural statement regarding "attainment of Being" (*satsampatti*) implies that the state of being an individual soul persists here in deep sleep.

Nor should it be said that this results in the collapse of the doctrine that the conscious individual soul (*jīva*) is the enjoyer of the three states; for it is established that the *jīva* itself exists as Brahman at that time, since its persistence is dependent upon the non-abandonment of its essential nature. Furthermore, this method should be understood to have been adopted in the commentary on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (p. 252), which begins with the words, "Even though Brahman is understood to be subject to hunger, thirst, and so forth," and concludes by following the unity of the *jīva* and other principles. Alternatively, the *jīva* remains even in deep sleep.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) itself constitutes the body of the individual soul (*jīva*), for that [ignorance] exists there as its very nature. Precisely for this reason, it is said: "He is of the form of bliss. He does not experience bliss as something distinct from himself; rather, he experiences bliss through differentiation. For this very reason, in the *Māṇḍūkya*, the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) does not mean that he is bliss itself, but rather that he is "full of bliss," because of the absence of the suffering of exertion. Regarding this, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "This state is experienced as being of the nature of the non-existence of sorrow; therefore, he is called 'the enjoyer of bliss' (*ānandabhuk*).

Likewise, in the passage "What did he become then?", the word "became" (*abhūt*) indicates only the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) who was previously denoted by the word "he" (*sa*); such is the direction of the argument.

This triple world was created solely for the enjoyment of the Pure One; its enjoyment is constant play and never leads to suffering. (25) Supreme bliss, independent, free from all defects, and unattached to all things—how could such a one ever be miserable? (29) That living being is not other than Śiva who [seeks] the fruit of actions; because there is no duality, consciousness does not deserve the fruit of action. (27)

"Regarding 'these three cities,' etc.: the meaning is that these three stations—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—are brought forth by the Māyā of the Supreme Lord solely for the enjoyment of the Person (puruṣa). Now, an objection is raised: if the Lord Himself indeed exists in the form of the individual soul (jīva), then his experiencing enjoyment is not logical, because of the scriptural text: 'Without eating, he shines forth. To this, he says: 'And his enjoyment... Even the experience of various pleasures and pains, such as those of heaven and hell, is his sport; it is not a cause of suffering for him. (25)

Why is this so? To this he says: "He who is superior to the universe" (*viśvādhika*). Since He is superior even to the entire world (*jagat*), because He abides as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the limit (*avadhi*) for both its superimposition and its sublation, therefore His unreal experience is not a cause of suffering. Furthermore, He is Great Bliss (*mahānanda*); other pleasures are merely fragments of His bliss. For this reason also, the enjoyment of worldly pleasure is a mere play (*līlāmātra*). He is independent (*svatantra*) and free from exhaustion (*nirupadrava*); for dependence is indeed the cause of suffering.

In the absence of that [object], he would become miserable; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Let it be so for the Lord (Īśvara); but as for the individual soul (jīva), since he is distinct from Him, his experience must be real. Why should it not be so? To this, he says: "He is not the jīva. There is no real difference between the jīva and the Lord, because it has already been established that there is no difference in the nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra) which resides in both. Furthermore, the object of cognition is indeed the fruit of karma.

Furthermore, because that [object] is superimposed upon the nature of consciousness, it is false. Therefore, how could the enjoyment of that object be real for the Self, whose nature is like the sky? This is the meaning. 27.7

How could creation be for the sake of the enjoyment of a witness? This and other such positions have been extensively refuted. Based on these very arguments, the great teacher [Śaṅkara] established that the views that creation is for the sake of enjoyment or for the sake of sport (*krīḍā*) are flawed. Ignorance alone is the motive for creation. On this subject, one should consult the *Bhāṣyavākya-kārikā* (1.8.9) and the commentary (*bhāṣya*) by Ānandagiri.

If the playful nature (*līlātmakatā*) of creation were to be discarded, its purpose would necessarily be the absence of any motive; however, that is not the case, as play or the cessation of boredom can indeed serve as a motive. This is clearly explained in the commentary on *lokavat tu līlākaivalyam* (2.1.33).

The venerable Ācārya has said: "Even if some slight purpose were to be found in the world's activities, still, no purpose whatsoever can be asserted here, because of the scriptural teaching that [the Lord] has all desires fulfilled. This entire intention should also be understood from the present Purāṇa: "When the capacity for action has been attained for the sake of the person's enjoyment, it is for the purpose of negating that very thing that 'enjoyment is play' is stated."

The *yāsyā* of this [verse] is as follows: “*na duḥkhāya*,” which means: “Indeed, you play; what is the purpose? It is not for the sake of any objective characterized by suffering. If there is a desire to know the reason for this lack of purpose, then the two words “*na kadācana*” should be understood as being uttered together in a single compound (*tantra*). For these three cities never existed at all; therefore, their creation was for the sake of purposeless play.

From this, it follows as a matter of course that [the world] is composed of *māyā*. || 25 || That which transcends the universe (*viśva*), whose nature is great bliss (*mahānanda*), which is independent, unassailable by afflictions such as disease, and is not connected with any defects—how could such a being suffer? || 26 || The individual soul (*jīva*) who experiences the fruits of karma is none other than Śiva; for [it is Śiva himself who appears as the enjoyer]. || 27 ||

Chapter 8 Therefore, the Supreme Lord, the witness of all, is impartial; He alone is worthy of being honored with compassion by those who seek the Great Bliss. (28) This triad of abodes of Śambhu never leads to suffering; it shines as His playground, and the Great Lord does not waver from it. (29) This triad of abodes of Śambhu does not exist through division; He does not bestow [the fruits] in such a way that He is dependent on another. (30)

Through the sequence of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, that [Self] appears to you; may that All-knowing One, who is beyond all sin, be your refuge. For the Viśva (the waking state) is always the enjoyer of the gross; the Taijasa (the dreaming state) is the enjoyer of the subtle; but the Prājña (the state of deep sleep) is the enjoyer of bliss, the witness, absolute, and characterized by pure consciousness.

Since it is impossible for the Supreme Self, which has entered into the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, to experience objects that are external to It, all those various conditions and diseases are merely *māyā*. This is established by the statement, "It plays" (krīḍati). That is to say, the three states beginning with waking are merely a garden for the purpose of play for Him who is eternally free; because there is no other motive for Him whose desires are fulfilled, there is no possibility of His being subject to worldly enjoyment. Thus, [it is concluded that He is not bound].

The meaning of the objection is as follows: [Objection] "But in this way, since there is a threefold state [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], and because [the Self] exists as a playground or a pleasure-garden, does this not lead to the contingency of duality? To this he says: "This... (Verse 30). The meaning is: that Self—whose nature is pure consciousness alone, which is distinct from the various states such as waking and so forth that are superimposed upon It—successively assumes the designations of Viśva, Taijasa, and so on, due to its dependence on those differentiated forms. (Verse 31). He states their slight difference: "For Viśva... (Verse 32).

Viśva alone is the presiding deity of the waking state. He is the "gross-eater" (*sthūlabhuk*), for his object is gross—the fivefold elements of sound, touch, and so forth. Alternatively, he is the enjoyer of that "gross" world of objects which is created by the Māyā of the Lord as common to all enjoyers. Taijasa, however, is the witness of the dreaming state and the "eater of the subtle" (*praviviktabhuk*). He experiences the "subtle"—that is, the collection of objects that are distinct from the inner self, uncommon, and imagined solely through one's own ignorance.

The King, as the witness of the state of deep sleep, together with the group of cognitions and their objects—which have ceased due to the absence of the activity of the instruments—enjoys his own essential nature, which is pure bliss, within the ignorance that constitutes its own cause, by virtue of the absence of desire and aversion. Thus, his experience is produced solely through connection with these states; however, in its true nature, it is of the form of supreme bliss, absolute, the witness, and pure consciousness alone. || 32 ||

Since there is no difference [between the Self and the individual], one cannot conceive of the *jīva* as anything other than the auspicious (*śiva*). (Why, then, would the experience of results not be the cause of such difference? The answer is: In reality, the object of cognition (*cetya*), the visible (*dṛśya*), and the fruit of action (*karmaphala*) cannot be connected to the conscious *jīva*. (Therefore, the *jīva* is not the enjoyer of the fruit of action, nor does a difference caused by that exist; only a false enjoyment can give rise to a false difference.)

There is not even a trace of difference; indeed, there is no difference at all. || 27 || Thus, the witness of the entire world, the conscious Self, the non-dual Supreme Bliss, the True One—the Supreme Lord—He alone is capable of experiencing [the fruits of action through] Māyā. || 28 || Even the three states, such as waking and the rest, which constitute the entirety of worldly existence, are never afflicted by suffering; from the perspective of inquiry, those states are like a garden of flowers. || 29 ||

These things are already well-known; therefore, one cannot ask why the Lord fashioned this world full of suffering, why He ordained the continuous succession of death and so forth, or why He created the hierarchy of high and low, and so on. (In a game, someone is designated as a "thief. He runs about in fear; if he is touched by anyone else, that person becomes the "thief.")

"Is there anyone for whom this entire world is not a dream? Can one find fault with anyone? Regarding the creation of the body, [the author] states the nine-fold Māṇḍūkya-activity, beginning with "jāgrad" (waking). [The waking state is] the unobstructed state of consciousness. In deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because of the absence of pain—which is the obstacle to the manifestation of the portion of bliss—the blissful aspect remains unobstructed; therefore, it is said that there is the enjoyment of bliss at that time. [This is] the *prājña* (the wise one) in its own nature. "Ālam" means for the purpose of support.

846. That which is proclaimed as the threefold path worthy of the Brahman-songs, and that which is celebrated as devotion—O Brahman, he who knows both of these in the Veda is not defiled even while enjoying the three worlds. || 23 || Even if one were to perform hundreds of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Brahma-sacrifices, one is not liberated unless one proclaims the state of oneness. || 24 || He who, standing like a spectator, sports within the city of the body—he is not a living soul (jīva); he is the Supreme Self (Svayambhū), the Truth itself, and not the individual self (sāya). || 25 ||

Then, having perceived that entire manifold world as it arose, they likewise perceived the bliss of consciousness (*cit-sukha*) through its nature as the witness and its nature as the pervader. Because it is the ground of all valid cognition, it is non-dual; because there is an absence of differentiation, it is the eternal sun. Therefore, these three cities (the body, senses, and mind) dissolve into that very [consciousness]. The individual soul does not appear as a living being; it is directly nothing but absolute Brahman. Due to ignorance, it appears in the form of a living being, but not by its own inherent nature.

"In the three abodes" (triṣu dhāmasu): because the phenomenal world of objects of enjoyment is superimposed upon the nature of the supreme Śiva, which is free from all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), it is illusory even within the three states beginning with waking; and since the enjoyer, upon the removal of his limiting adjuncts, is non-different from that [Śiva], both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment are Brahman alone. Thus, for one who knows this, there is no taint arising from merit or demerit produced by enjoyment. This is the meaning. (33) He explains this very point in the verse beginning with "aśvamedha. (34)

Having thus stated the fruit of the knowledge of oneness, he establishes that very oneness with the words "as if in the form of a living being" (*jīvarūpa iva*). It is the Lord alone who, by means of his playful power (*līlā-śakti*), has remained in the form of a living being; the living being is not something other than him. He proves the point already asserted with the words "from that it was born. From that very non-dual Brahman, this entire manifold world—consisting of enjoyers and objects of enjoyment—has arisen like an illusion (*māyāvat*); it appears as if real, but is not real in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

In order to declare the oneness of his own self with Brahman—whose nature is characterized by the absence of shame—he establishes its nature as the all-pervading reality, stating: "He is Truth. Since everything that is unreal is perceived as having the nature of an object, the witness of all that is necessarily to be regarded as Truth itself. For this very reason, because he is the witness of the inert phenomenal world, he is of the nature of Consciousness (*cit*). Because he is the locus of the experience of bliss, he is of the nature of Bliss (*ānanda*). And because, according to the method previously stated, difference cannot be established anywhere and thus there is no absence of the manifestation of one's own essential nature, he is Non-dual (*advaita*).

Thus, that Witness whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss alone undergoes the three states of waking and so forth. Since He is the witness of the three states as their very essence, He is not a transmigrating being (saṃsārī); rather, appearing like a living being due to adjuncts (upādhi), He is in reality Brahman itself, because all adjuncts have been cast off. If it is asked, "What then is the adjunct that makes Him appear like a living being? he says: "From ignorance" (ajñānāt). (Verses 36–38)

There is no question, nor is there any possibility of fault. (29) Even in these three states, there is nothing at all separate from Śambhu; it is Śiva alone who appears within these forms. There is never anything other than the Supreme Lord. (30) Those forms possessing the states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are respectively called Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña. (31) Viśva is gross.

The *viśva* experiences objects consisting of gross elements; the *taijasa* experiences objects consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); the *prājña* experiences bliss. However, by its own nature, Śiva is merely the witness whose essence is pure happiness. (32) That Brahman which is the common substrate (*sāmānya*) for both the object of experience and the experiencer—well-known in all three states—is not tainted by merit or demerit arising from that experience, even while experiencing. (33)

If the vision of non-duality (*advaita*) has been attained, then one must certainly act otherwise; for whether one commits the sin of killing a Brahmin or performs some meritorious deed, neither merit nor sin remains. That which is conceived as the individual soul (*jīva*), which plays through the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], that indeed is the *jīva*; yet even while appearing to play eternally, it is Śambhu.

Another [scriptural passage] also declares: “This is the abode and the greatness of the Brāhmaṇa; it does not increase by action, nor does it become smaller” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23). The term “of the Brāhmaṇa” refers to one who has abandoned the pursuit of those [three] goals [of life], meaning one who knows Brahman. [The word *brāhmaṇa* here is derived from the root *brh* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, meaning] that which causes to grow (*bṛṃhayati*). [The commentary notes various readings: 3. *dha. ḍa. ca* read “*sya tvāt*” and 4. *dha. ṇ* read “*duḥkha*.”

Chapter 847 From Brahman is born the mind of Śrāṇu, the support of all intellects. Space, wind, light, and water are the sustainers of this world. (1) That which is the essence of Brahman is the great abode of the universe; it is the most subtle, the most ancient, and indeed the eternal meaning of the word *tattva*. (2) Whatever is the meaning of the word *tat* (That), that indeed is the meaning of the word *tattva*. The two words *tat* and *tva* ultimately rest upon the self-established Pure Consciousness alone. (3)

Thus, having established the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being non-different from pure consciousness and bliss through its defining characteristic (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), [the text] now establishes that same nature for Brahman through its indirect characteristic (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) by means of the passage beginning with "From [Brahman] the mind is born," and so forth. (39) Regarding the phrase "subtler than the subtle": the subtle refers to the elements such as space (*viyat*) which have been withdrawn into their causal state; subtler than that is the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*); and subtler even than that is the Cause of the World, which is Brahman. That very Brahman is the referent of the word *sva* (Self), which here denotes the individual soul (*jīva*). (40)

In the fifth chapter, it was questioned how the word *tat*, which denotes the ocean of the world, and the word *tvam*, which denotes the body as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), can both abandon their respective specific meanings and become intent on establishing the oneness of the consciousness (*cit*) that underlies both; this was addressed by the passage beginning with "of the very meaning denoted by the words 'thou' and 'I'" (*tvamahaṃśabdavācyārthasyaiva*). This very point is stated here for the sake of confirmation: "it remains as pure consciousness alone" (*cinmātre paryavasyati*). Indeed, this is so; there is no doubt about it. (35)

Furthermore, that which appears as if it were entirely real is the manifestation of Śambhu, who is the source of all auspiciousness and wondrous power. Since Śambhu is the witness of mere unreality (*asatyamātra*), He is distinct—that is, real—and since He is the witness, He is conscious (for only consciousness can be a direct witness). Thus, because He is the object of unsurpassed love, He is of the nature of bliss.

The absence of the threefold division therein is what constitutes non-duality (*advaita*). If the witness (*sākṣin*) were false, then the distinction between witnesses would also be false; since that does not exist for the Self-possessor (*ātmavat*), there is no loss of non-duality. All three states merge into that very Śambhu.

(Since the processes of *anugata* [pervasion], *vyāvṛtta* [exclusion], *antarbhāva* [inclusion], and *vilaya* [dissolution] are well-established, the Witness of the states can be understood as tolerating dissolution. Because the Self has the nature of being pervasive (*vibhu*), it is not the individual soul (*jīva*). It is Brahman itself that appears in the form of the individual soul; through ignorance, the Supreme Self alone appears in the form of the individual soul.

Its own essential nature is immutability. || 36-28 || Prāṇa, mind, all the sense organs, and all the great elements (mahābhūtas) arise from Brahman alone. || 39 || It is the Self of all, the ultimate support of all; subtler than the subtlest of the great elements, even subtler than the unmanifest (avyakta), eternal—it is that which is the meaning of the word "That" (tat) in the Great Saying (Mahāvākya), "Thou art That. || 40 ||

Whatever is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of the word *tvam*, that very same is the indicated meaning of the word *saḥ*. By means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), both the words *tvam* and *saḥ* point toward self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśa-caitanya*). Upon hearing "Thou art That," the initial cognition arises: "That which is being spoken of is this [Self]. Immediately, a doubt arises: "But by the word 'That,' something characterized by remoteness and so forth is expressed."

In order to justify the two words "this" (*eṣa*) and "that" (*saḥ*), the listener expects that something must necessarily be indicated which is both "this" and "that. Since the body (*peśī*) cannot possibly be "that," and since "this" and "that" are [ordinarily] distinct, it follows that the meaning of "that" is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
(Brahmagītā 8.48)

The non-difference that is conceptualized regarding the meaning of the two words [“That” and “Thou”] is established solely through the distinctions of Māyā, ignorance, and the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and not in reality. (42) For those who do not know the self-established unity, the Upaniṣads, out of compassion, teach the unity that is established by its very nature to those who are qualified. (42) Having realized that Brahman—which shines as the manifold expansion of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth—is "I," one is liberated from all bonds. (44)
When a man understands the Brahman through his own self, his direct experience follows its own nature. || 45 ||

Regarding the phrase "the meaning residing in the two words": by means of the two words *tat* and *tvam*, having abandoned the contradictory portions such as transmigratoriness (*saṃsāritva*) inherent in the literal meanings, that very meaning which is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as being of the nature of pure consciousness is the ultimate reality. Through that [realization], the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who are distinguished by their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is established. The limiting adjunct of the Lord is *māyā*, which consists primarily of pure *sattva* and does not cause delusion to its own substratum. The limiting adjunct of the individual soul is *avidyā*, which consists primarily of impure *sattva* and causes delusion to its own substratum.

Therefore, the meaning is that the difference between those two is not real, but exists only from that [ignorance]. —42— Regarding "the ignorance of oneness": the meaning is that ignorance is that which veils the oneness which is inherently eternal. Regarding "the scripture with reverence": this scripture is as follows: "O Knower of the Self, you are eternally That; You alone are That. He restates the established meaning of this scriptural statement [with the verse] beginning with "jāgrat" (waking).

The meaning of the sentence is this: that very Brahman which appears as the distant (parokṣa) in the form of the states of waking and so forth, and in the form of the manifold expansion consisting of the vital breath, mind, and the rest—that same [Brahman], appearing as the immediate (aparokṣa) and manifesting as the inner witness-consciousness (pratyak-cit), is what is indicated by the words "thou" (tvam) and "I" (aham). || 43 || 44 || 45 || Thus, one cannot apprehend any object whatsoever [as separate from it].

Therefore, that very thing which is the intended meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is indeed the meaning of the suffix *-tya*. However, when the two meanings of "this" (*idam*) and "that" (*tat*) are brought together, a contradiction appears; these two meanings are called the "contrary meanings" (*viruddhārtha*). In this context, the *Śārīraka-saṃkṣepābhidhāna* (1.196) should be remembered. 41.

The very same single reality that constitutes both [Brahman and the individual soul] is conceived as differentiated in every way. Due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of *māyā*—which is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*)—this entire differentiation is imagined. (Alternatively, due to the distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā*, this differentiation between Īśvara and the individual soul (*jīva*) is imagined.)

In this regard, it should be kept in mind that although the Vedānta mentions a distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā*, nowhere is it intended to suggest that these are two different principles (*tattvāntara*). Rather, they are simply two distinct states or different powers of the same single ignorance (*ajñāna*)—namely, its pervasive and limited aspects. This is just as one considers both the sword and its sheath to be the same substance. Thus, both [are one].

The very meaning of *mithyā* (falsehood) is to consider two things as non-different when they are actually different; therefore, even one who asserts the doctrine of the non-difference between Māyā and Brahman is refuted for considering them as one. Nevertheless, that [non-difference] does not cease to exist because of such a consideration. || 42 || The ignorance of unity is beginningless and innate.

When one is intent upon the Śruti, that very [scripture], through its own power, brings about for the qualified seeker the realization of the eternally established oneness. || 43 || Having known that whatever appears—whether in the waking, dreaming, or deep sleep states—is indeed this [Brahman], the individual is liberated from all duality. || 44 || He who knows Brahman as being of the nature of the non-dual is... [liberated]. || 45 ||

This natural experience remains constant: the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the enjoyment of all three states, as well as the witness distinct from them—all exist within the entirety of consciousness. I alone am everything; I have arisen, I am the state of bliss, and I dissolve back into myself. That non-dual Brahman is I; I am both the smallest atom and the greatest mountain. I am all-pervading and pure.

9. Māyā itself is ignorance (*avidyā*); that which has these as its means is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā-avidyā*. The distinction based on that [adjunct] is a distinction imagined in that form; the meaning is that it is a distinction consisting of limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*). Alternatively, the single limiting adjunct is twofold because two kinds of effects are observed. In any case, one should not accept a distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā*; such is the direction. 2. "In order to know [it] by setting aside [the notion of difference]"—this is the fault. Having set aside [the idea] that "that is indeed this reality," he makes [the disciple] understand "you yourself are that. The meaningfulness of these various statements is elaborated upon in the *Vyatihārādhikaraṇa* (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.23–37).

Chapter 8 That which is the knower (*kṣetrajña*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and likewise enjoyment (*bhoga*)—I am distinct from all those, the witness, pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), existing eternally. (46) Everything is measured by me alone; everything is established in me. Everything goes to dissolution in me; therefore, I am that Brahman, the beginningless one. (47) I alone am subtler than the subtlest; I am that Great One; I am the universe; I am Viṣṇu. (48)

I am the ancient one, I am the Puruṣa, I am the Lord; I am golden, I am the form of Śiva. (48) Without hands I grasp, without feet I walk; without eyes I see, without ears I hear. Abiding in solitude, I discern; the Knower does not eat, for I am eternally consciousness. (49) Through many Vedas I alone am known; I am the Vedas and the knower of the Vedas. There is no death for me, nor fear, nor birth, nor dependence on a body, mind, intellect, or ego. (50)

Thus, with the verse beginning "tariṣu" (46–48), he describes the manner of contemplation for one who is free from the impurities of the *brahmāla* state and is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). He is the Ancient One, the Person (*puruṣa*) who carries away all sins; He is the Golden One (*hiraṇmaya*), the Self (*ātman*) situated within all, who is the essence of all causes and effects and is full of knowledge; and He is Brahman, whose nature is auspiciousness. Though devoid of hands and feet, He possesses inconceivable power; though without eyes and ears, He sees and hears.

I know this entire phenomenal world as distinct in form from the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties. There is no knower other than me; I am eternally conscious. No one other than me can create all the various Vedas; I alone am the expounder of the Vedānta scriptures and the one who dissolves even all the Vedas at the time of dissolution. Merit and demerit do not attach to me; my non-existence is impossible.

Birth, body, senses, and growth—none of these have any connection with me. I am unconnected with the great elements (mahābhūtas) such as earth and the rest; I am eternally the same. Thus it continues to manifest, and through my own innate ignorance, I continue to appear as "this" or "that."

The undiscriminating person, failing to distinguish between these two, experiences them as a single cognition: "This is Devadatta," "This is standing," or "This is the ear," and so forth. That very [cognition] is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). In this regard, "I" is the manifestation of the Self as the Self, while Devadatta and the rest are the manifestation of the Self as "this. Even though both manifestations belong to that same [ego-sense], one should practice regarding them in this way: "This is I," and "This is not I."

Elsewhere it is said: "I am the Self," "This is the Self," and "I am this Self. I appear only within the fourfold states of the unknown (*ajñāta*), the known (*jñāta*), consciousness (*jñāna*), and unconsciousness (*ajñāna*). Therefore, I alone am the ancient God. (45–52) Having thus realized the nature of the partless, non-dual Supreme Self residing within the cave of my own heart, I have attained equanimity.

One's own nature becomes free from the pairs of opposites (dvandvas), and the attainment of the state of the pure Supreme Self occurs. || 53 || Therefore, for the sake of liberation, one should daily [reflect upon] the words of Vedānta through the grace of Mahādeva, the leader of all, by means of the scriptures and logical arguments.
[Note: 1. *Dha. chaṭa. vicitram* refers to a specific textual variant. 2. The meaning is that I am Vyāsa, the author of the Vedānta Śāstra. 3. *Brahmagītā*.]

I am neither earth nor water, nor fire, nor wind, nor am I space. I am always "I" alone; by my very nature, I shine as this [universe]. (51) In the form of non-manifestation and likewise in the form of manifestation, through the state of being luminous and through the state of non-luminosity, I remain all-pervading. Therefore, I am the ancient God. (52) Having thus known the supreme Self, which dwells in the cave of the heart, which is partless and without a second—

Devoid of that which is not [the Self], he who has destroyed the darkness of ignorance attains the supreme state, which is the true nature of the Supreme Self. || 52 || The Lord Śiva, who is eternally free from all impurities, should be contemplated through the words of the Vedānta, through the teachings of the Guru, and likewise through reasoning, as He is devoid of all differentiation. || 54 ||

The Kevalyopaniṣad, swift and joined with the supreme velocity, spoke clearly; it was also received with reverence by Śarabha, Itihāsa, and others. O you who have transcended the state of being a mere knower of the Vedas, O you who are devoted to the Supreme Brahman beyond the three worlds—this doctrine has been understood through intense devotion by those qualified aspirants. 55.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Method for Knowing Reality," within the section on the Kaivalya Upanishad, in the Brahmagītā Upanishads, in the latter part of the fourth section, the Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. **The Ninth Chapter** Brahmā said: Śiva is the one whose nature is free from all defects; he is characterized by bliss and the absence of sorrow. Because he is perceived as the supreme among the supreme, he is the foremost of sages. He is the bliss of the state beyond the subtle (paśyantī); indeed, he is the bliss of the highest state.

It does not move, it does not perceive; there can be no other knower than I. I alone am always the one who flows [through all], the knower of everything in its true nature. (vv. 49–52) He states the fruit of such contemplation: "Thus" (v. 52). He concludes the matter thus established: "Therefore" (v. 54). Regarding the phrase "with intense devotion": "O gods, you must know—understand—the meaning that has been explained by me, which is to be grasped through the purport of the Kaivalya Upaniṣad. (v. 59)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Method for Realizing the Truth," in the *Rama-tapaniya Upanishad*, within the second part of the fourth section on the majesty of sacrifice (*yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Sūta Saṃhitā-tātparya-dīpikā*. Now, the fact that the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* is devoted to the non-duality of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*) is established through two chapters.

In this regard, since the first chapter consists of an instruction for the sake of attaining liberation—by means of demonstrating the means for obtaining even a single drop of nectar, namely the vision of the Supreme Reality, as well as the means for that [vision] such as hearing and so forth—he first summarizes its subject matter with the words "ratirūpa" and so on. That Supreme Śiva, who appears as the "I" through self-awareness and has assumed the state of the individual soul (jīva), is directly of the nature of supreme bliss. He states the reason for this with the word "parā"; he then dispels the charge that this reason is irrelevant by using the word "parama."

Although the bliss born from objects such as having a son—which serves as a basis for higher and lower [levels]—is not the primary bliss because it is subordinate to something else, nevertheless, that bliss which is the locus of unsurpassed bliss is indeed bliss itself due to its primacy; thus, the meaning is that even a fragment of the nature of bliss, when it is the supreme object of experience, is an indicator [of that state]. || 1 || Together with this, [it] tears apart [ignorance]. || 54 ||

O Lord! You are supremely compassionate; having thoroughly and clearly revealed the nature of liberation through the Upaniṣads, You have taught the supreme Brahman—which is attained by those such as Hari and Brahmā—through the medium of the Vedas and other scriptures to all qualified seekers, so that they may realize it through direct, immediate perception. It is my desire that You may know all this. 55.

The commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the ninth chapter [concludes]. [In this chapter,] liberation as the attainment of the true nature of Paramaśiva is established. Almost everyone has the experience that happiness arises from the acquisition of objects. And according to the Smṛti: "That which is not known by the mind, nor expressed by speech... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.3.45), the meaning should be understood accordingly. Having established through his own declaration that the Supreme State is the ultimate goal, [the author] now speaks these secret words in order to reinforce it with both reasoning and scripture.
He is dear to his wife; such is this husband, possessing the splendor of a god. 2. (Verse 9, Adhyāya 851)

A husband is not dear for the sake of his own desire; rather, he is dear in every way for the sake of his own self, and therefore he is himself most dear. (2) A wife is not dear for the sake of her own desire; indeed, a wife is not considered dear [for her own sake]; rather, she is dear for the sake of one's own self, and therefore he is himself most dear. (4) And sons are not dear for the sake of their own desire; nor do sons become dear for their own sake.

However, [the text asks]: "Is it for the sake of the self that everything is dear? and thus concludes that the self is itself most dear (5). Anticipating the objection that this might be established through mere reasoning, the Śruti establishes its status as the dearest of all by presenting a series of many passages, such as: "Verily, O Maitreyī, a husband is not dear for the sake of the husband; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that a husband is dear. By demonstrating that the husband, wife, children, wealth, and so forth are dear only as subservient to the Self, the Śruti proves that the Self is the dearest of all. This is what is expressed in the passage beginning with "He becomes dear," and so on.

The fact that a husband is dear to his wife is not for the sake of the husband’s desire; rather, it is solely for the sake of the wife’s own happiness. Likewise, whatever one regards as one's own, there arises a special affection even toward the defects of that very thing—just as one feels toward the defects of one's son or wife. Thus, because she regards her husband as her own, the husband is dear to the wife, but her own self (ātman) is even more exceedingly dear to her. [Ra. 3] "Of the wife... and so forth.

The statement "the wife is dearer than the foot" refers to the mouth of the wife; however, the foot is dearer still because it is one's own seat, as previously explained. Furthermore, the husband is even more beloved than that. Thus, the application [of this principle] should also be understood in other contexts, such as "one does not desire sons," and so forth. || 4 || 5 ||

Indeed, this river has liberation as its object of attainment; consequently, since the happiness of liberation does not exist [in worldly life], it is a river of human goals (*puruṣārtha*). No one desires a river that consists solely of suffering; rather, for the sake of even a small amount of pleasure, they endure considerable suffering.

Considering that no one would engage in the pursuit of liberation unless the blissful nature of the Self were established, Brahmā, reflecting upon the dialogue between Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī which demonstrates the blissful nature of the Self, said: "The inner Self, which is Śiva, is self-luminous and possesses the nature of supreme bliss; for this reason, its manifestation is entirely dear."

That which becomes the object of supreme, unconditional love is, in reality, bliss itself. Whatever we desire—whether it be health or anything else—is ultimately desired for the sake of our own happiness. This is true, however selfish it may seem; we also desire happiness for ourselves. When the choice is presented, "Either this happiness shall be yours, or you shall suffer from disease," we invariably choose the former.

Even when suffering from the agony of suicide, one strives only for self-purification; therefore, it is established that we possess an excessive and causeless love for ourselves. We also regard our own nature as equal to others, and we maintain a degree of love toward them exactly proportional to how much or how little we regard their nature as equal to our own. This is the very essence of happiness: to have causeless love for oneself.

In this way, the notion that "the self is happiness" burns intensely; otherwise, no pleasure would arise from it. Nevertheless, due to ignorance, we are incapable of knowing this truth, and through delusion, we consider sense-objects to be happiness, whereby our minds remain intent only upon worldly activity (*pravṛtti*). Consequently, since the attainment of unsurpassed happiness is possible through the cessation of ignorance, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

And for that [realization], he states that the means is precisely the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the great Vedāntic statements (*mahāvākya*), which has been refined by the two processes of reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—thus he says: "and hearing. Therein, "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) is the investigation of the meaning of the words through the analysis of their semantic power (*śabdaśakti-tātparya*). "Reflection" (*manana*) is the investigation of the reasoning that establishes the reality of the meaning as presented by the semantic power, by way of removing doubts regarding its impossibility and so forth.

Thus, reflection (*vicintana*), which is another synonym for *nididhyāsana*, is a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions, uninterrupted by heterogeneous impressions, intended to produce direct realization of the object already attained through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*).

And thus it is declared in the sacred tradition: "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. By the phrase "through hearing and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) as enjoined by scripture. The Self (*ātman*) is indeed of the nature of bliss (*sukha-rūpa*), because as many forms of bliss as exist are preserved within the Self. Whatever is called "this" or "that," as well as all other distinctions such as *māyā*, *avidyā*, *tamas*, and *moha*, are all the Self alone and nothing apart from it. There is no cause for the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) other than the Self.

[Specifically,] *prakṛti* characterized by the predominance of the quality of purity (*sattva*) is *māyā*; that same *prakṛti* characterized by the predominance of the quality of impurity (*rajas*) is *avidyā*; and *prakṛti* characterized by the predominance of the quality of darkness (*tamas*), which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the gross elements such as space (*ākāśa*), is *tamas*; while the error regarding mother-of-pearl and similar objects is *moha*.
