However, because it is a transparent substance (being composed of the *sāttvika* transformation of the subtle elements), there is this distinction regarding its functions (*vṛtti*): when the true nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*) is not distinguished from it, that [Self-nature] appears within those functions, just as the capacity for reflection exists in objects such as a pot. Thus, the Self is [reflected].

Once it has become undifferentiated from them, it causes the reality of the self to be perceived within itself. That by which knowledge is perceived when it becomes undifferentiated from its own modifications (*vṛtti*) is the Self; it is that which shines forth equally whether those modifications exist or do not exist. Only the "Seer"—that is, the conscious one—can be so called, and not inert objects such as a jar.

However, generally speaking, it is only when vision exists that an object is said to exist, and not otherwise. Even in the absence of vision, consciousness itself appears; and while that [consciousness] is manifesting, the non-existence of vision is established.

If the Seer were not present, from what would the arising of the seen arise? How could there be a cognition of the "unseparated" (avivikta) object? That which arises through seeing is indeed the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). Even when seeing ceases, there remains the ego-sense which is sometimes with seeing and sometimes without seeing; that which is both the state of having seeing and being agitated by it—both of which are conceptual constructs—is intended here as the "Seer of the Seer."

When the night has passed, that which remains as pure vision (*dṛṣṭi*)—and not as the functioning of knowledge (*vṛttijñāna*)—is the Seer (*draṣṭṛ*). (One should consult the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya*, p. 93, and pp. 247–249. || 6 || Everything other than this Self is "other" (*anya*); upon investigation, all of that is found to be unreal. Only the Self alone is perceived in every respect as the ultimate reality. || 7 ||
Just as all earthly objects are woven across and through the earth, so too [is this] the definition [of Brahman], together with its two states of manifestation. 7.1.7.

Chapter 190 865. O gods, just as everything on earth is woven warp and woof, so too, O deities, is everything woven warp and woof in the waters. 9. And the wind blows, O gods; likewise, it is woven warp and woof within the intermediate spaces (antarikṣa) and throughout the worlds, O leaders of the gods. 10. Within the intermediate spaces and the worlds, as well as among the Gandharvas—those known as Gandharvas who reside in the world of the Ādityas—are established in these worlds.

Having thus taught the inner self's state of being the warp and woof (*sūtra*) with respect to the individual soul (*pratyagātman*), he now takes up the great example in order to teach that same state with respect to the objective world (*adhibhūta*)—beginning with the words "As on the earth," and so forth.

For there, in order to demonstrate the unsurpassed subtlety and all-pervasiveness of the Self which is within all, the sequence from the earth up to the world of Brahmā is recorded in the scripture as being successively woven as warp and woof, characterized by increasing subtlety and pervasiveness, and existing in a relationship of relative gradation, according to the passage beginning: "Whatever exists here is woven across and woven lengthwise."

Just as a cloth exists upon its warp and woof threads through the relationship of being woven lengthwise and crosswise, so too does the entire earthly world exist within the earth-element—which is the cause of all—that pervading *samā* (the equalizing power), through the relationship of being woven lengthwise and crosswise. Just as this is so, in that same way, the principle of earth (*pṛthivītattva*) exists within the waters, which constitute its cause, through the relationship of being woven lengthwise and crosswise. This should be applied in the same manner for what follows. 8.

The entire earth is woven through and through with water. (The verbal root *ve* [bhū, ubhayapada] means "to weave. By adding the suffix *kta*, the word *uta* is formed; *uta* means "woven. When the prefix *ā-* is attached, it becomes the word *ota*, meaning "well-woven. This is also the meaning of the word *prota*.)

When both [the cause and the effect] are employed together, there is the sense of identity (*tādātmya*). That which is being woven is not distinct from that [cause], just as cloth is not distinct from its threads. And thus, every effect is not distinct from its own cause.

Therefore, O King, since the substance "earth" is not distinct from its cause, water, it is said to be woven warp and woof within water; that is to say, if one considers earth to be a cloth, its length is woven from water and its width as well, for there is no part of it that is not composed of water. (The same should be understood for the other elements). || 8 || Water is woven warp and woof within fire.

(Since fire is found only in other elements such as wood and lightning, and this [text] intends to demonstrate that it is woven warp and woof within some independent principle, it is stated that water is woven warp and woof within air, which is the cause of fire: Air is woven warp and woof within the worlds of the atmosphere. (Because they consist of the five elements, these worlds are indicated by a plural ending; this plurality arises from the multiplicity of their constituent elements.)

One should understand that each successive world is subtler and more pervasive than the preceding one. (9) The Antariksha-loka is within the Gandharva-lokas; the Gandharva-loka is within the Aditya-lokas; the Aditya-loka is within the Candra-lokas; the Candra-loka is within the Nakshatra-lokas; the Nakshatra-loka is within the Deva-lokas; the Deva-loka is within the Indra-lokas; the Indra-loka is within the Prajapatya-lokas (Prajapati meaning Virat, the collective gross body-consciousness);
and the Prajapatya-loka is within the Brahma-lokas (Brahma-loka meaning the subtle five elements).

1. Let this be understood as the conclusion. 2. [This applies] to the *Nalayu* recensions. 3. The meaning is that the explanation regarding the purpose of the Brāhmaṇa for the *Kahoḷa* [recension] is indeed applied to the *Upabrāhmaṇa*; thus it is established. Nor should it be questioned how there can be two Brāhmaṇas in the Śruti, because it is intended to demonstrate therein the process of purifying the meaning of the words (*padārtha*). 4. In the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*, in this sixth Brāhmaṇa, the nature of Brahman is investigated.

"O good one, the all-pervasiveness of Brahman is established through the determination of all things," so it has been said. (17.188) It has been stated that it is "woven lengthwise like the threads of a long cloth and woven crosswise like the woof, or vice versa. Its own clarification is shown by the statement: "pervading both within and without. (Brahma-gītā 8.66): "The lunar worlds are woven in the solar worlds, and likewise the solar worlds [are woven] in the lunar worlds; and the foremost of the gods [are woven] in the worlds of the stars. (8.69)

"In the worlds of the Devas—the Nakatra-lokas are likewise merged; and the Deva-lokas, O gods, are situated within the Indra-lokas. (12) In the Prajāpati-lokas are situated the gods, the bulls among the Suras; and the Prajāpati-lokas are likewise situated within the Brahma-lokas. (13) Those gods, the Brahma-lokas, are well-established in the Viṣṇu-loka; and the Viṣṇu-lokas are likewise merged within the Candra-lokas, O wise one. (14) The Candra-lokas, O bulls among the Suras, are situated in the worlds of Īśvara."

O best of gods, by their mercies the worlds of Sadāśiva are sustained; those worlds are woven like warp and woof within the supreme, auspicious Brahman. Thus, all are eternally situated within the Self that is consciousness, whose nature is that of the witness.

"And waters in air. Now, one might object: "Fire is the cause of water, according to the Vedic revelation, 'From fire, water [arose]'; therefore, it should be said that 'waters are in fire'? This is not a fault. Since fire does not exist as a dominant presence apart from its constituent elements—namely, the earthly and the airy—its causal state within the air is designated by way of its being woven warp and woof therein. "And air in the intermediate spaces," and so forth; this refers to air in relation to the worlds of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

Because it is the locus of movement, [the world] exists there in a state of being woven lengthwise and crosswise. The five elements themselves, having become integrated and transformed into forms that serve as increasingly superior bases for experience through a sequence of degrees of subtlety, are designated by their respective specific locations as various worlds (*loka*). For this very reason, even though each individual world—such as all the worlds of the atmosphere, the worlds of the Gandharvas, and so forth—is singular, the plural form is employed. [This applies to] "among those belonging to Prajāpati," etc. (9–12). 1.

Prajāpati is Virāṭ, the one who identifies with the gross body. The meaning is: "in those" refers to the five elements that originate that body and serve as the means for the enjoyment of the state of Virāṭ; these are the worlds belonging to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyā lokāḥ*). Regarding the phrase "belonging to Prajāpati": those very same elements, beginning with ether (*viyat*), which were made "fivefold" (*pañcīkṛta*) by Brahmā when he attained the state of Hiraṇyagarbha and which constitute the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), are designated by the term "the world of Brahmā" (*brahmaloka*). The meaning is that within those [elements], which exist as causes, the worlds of Prajāpati—which are their effects—exist in a state of being woven like warp and woof (*otaprotabhāva*). 13 || 14 || 15 || 16 || 1 ka $ ^
The originators are the five unevolved great elements (*apañcīkṛta-mahābhūta*): the world of fire (meaning the unevolved earth), the world of Viṣṇu (meaning the unevolved subtle water), and so forth.

In the world of Viṣṇu is the world of Rudra (I am the subtle fire); in the world of Rudra is the world of Īśvara (I am the subtle air); in the world of Īśvara is the world of Sadāśiva (I am the subtle ether); likewise, in the world of Sadāśiva is the Supreme Śiva named Brahman (I am the causal Brahman); and all these are woven warp and woof within the inner Self, which is the nature of the Witness.

(Although this Upanishad concludes its discussion of the *Gārgī Brāhmaṇa* with the pervasiveness of the five gross elements (*pañcamahābhūta*)—the products of *pañcīkaraṇa*—which is designated by the term "Brahmaloka," it is stated in the Upanishad that [the inquiry] extends only as far as the Brahmaloka. [Note:
1. In the Upanishad, it is stated only up to the Brahmaloka. 2. Variant readings *gha* and *ca*: "of the gross phenomenal world."]

Chapter 90 867. In the All-pervading One (Sarvatratama), the hearers and those who have merged [into Him] abide as presiding over all. || 17 || O best of gods, that Self which is self-luminous, possessing its own substratum and free from the notion of "otherness," does not exist as something established by another; it is of the nature of pure Being. || 18 || Since everything remains eternally within Him in a state of non-destruction, He alone is all this and nothing else—such is the description of His form. || 19 || This very Self shines by itself through its own existence, devoid of anything else; He alone is the innermost essence of all things, and no other. || 20 ||

"They exist through superimposition. Just as all these worlds exist only by being superimposed upon their respective pervaders and are therefore not real, even so, at all times, all those worlds ending with the world of Brahmā exist in the state of being woven like warp and woof—by the power of Māyā—within the Inner Self (pratyagātman), who is the ultimate reality (sat) and consciousness (cit) and the substratum of their own manifestation. The Inner Self, which is the substratum of all, does not exist in a state of being woven like warp and woof within anything else distinct from itself; rather, [it is the reverse].

He is established in His own majesty. For those things whose manifestation is dependent on another and which are distinct from pure existence (*sat*), there must be a state of being woven warp and woof within that [substratum] in order for their existence and manifestation to be established. But this [Brahman] is self-luminous, manifesting by Himself, and is the very nature of existence; therefore, how could He abide in another as something woven warp and woof? This is the meaning. (Verses 17–18)

Having thus established that everything from the earth up to the world of Brahmā is perceived as superimposed upon the innermost Self, he states its non-difference from the substratum in reality with the words "In which... (verse 19). Having thus demonstrated the all-pervasiveness of the Self by virtue of being the locus for the conceptualization of the entire universe, he now introduces the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa with the words "This Self who... in order to demonstrate its all-pervasiveness also by way of being the inner controller.

This very Self, who was previously described as being within all and whose nature is existence (sat), is indeed the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) because he dwells within the hearts of all and exercises control over them; the meaning is that he is not some other entity distinct from the innermost Self (pratyagātman). || 20 ||

Nevertheless, since Āruṇi has already described the individual soul (*sūtātmā*) as being within the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), it should also be included here in the Purāṇa; therefore, the gradual pervasiveness of the subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūta*) has been stated. Regarding the inclusion of the earth and other elements under the term "the worlds beginning with Brahmā" (*brahmādi-loka-rāśi*), one should rely on the basis provided in the fifth chapter (*pañcamadhyāya*, 4.94 of the *Purva*).

Just as space is naturally woven across and through everything because it is the cause of all things like the Avīci hell and Brahman, so too, pure consciousness—being the substratum even for ignorance—is "woven across and through" that which possesses ignorance. Hereafter, however, there is nothing through which the Pure is woven; the Witness alone exists within itself (meaning, everything is woven across and through Him, but He is not woven through anything). Upon that very [Witness], all things exist through superimposition.

The essential nature of everything is the self-luminous inner Self (*pratyagātman*). It does not reside within anything; it is the very essence of existence (*sattāsvarūpa*). (10–18) When one reflects upon reality, everything exists as a superimposition (*adhyasta*). Just as a rope is mistaken for a snake, all that appears to be real is nothing other than that [Self]. (19)

1 dha. ca. paṇam‌ || 19 || 2 ḍa. svarūpavyati” | 3 Udāraka says that the Sūtra is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin). Regarding this, the answer is "Vāyu. That very Vāyu who was previously mentioned in relation to Bhujyu is here also called the Sūtra. "The Sūtra is declared to be the effect of the un-pañcīkṛta elements; the elements that originate the cosmic egg are woven lengthwise and crosswise therein. That which is distinct from the Sūtra is called the Antaryāmin."

"This causal relationship is fully established in our teaching" (17.210-11). This is a summary of the manner of experience. The inner controller (*antaryāmī*) is the Lord named Nārāyaṇa, not *pradhāna* or other [principles]. Therefore, it should be understood that the nature of the Saguna Brahman is revealed here. There is an extensive discussion in the *Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa* (1.2.5.18).

That which is within the earth, yet is always other than the earth; whom the earth does not know, yet whose body the earth is—He who, dwelling within, governs this earth from its very foundation; He indeed is our manifest Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), standing beyond the highest. In the waters, O gods, there is one who dwells within, whom you do not know; whose body these waters are, and who, dwelling within, governs the waters—He indeed is our manifest Inner Controller, standing beyond the highest.

In the Śruti, He is described as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*)—the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*) who, while abiding within as the material cause of that which pertains to the deities (*adhidevata*), the elements (*adhibhūta*), and the self (*adhyātma*), is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—by virtue of His activity of governing each of those. This is stated in passages such as, "He who dwells in the earth... and so forth. He explains that [passage] with the words, "In the earth": "He who is the causal Self, dwelling within the earth, governs it."

Intending that one situated outside the earth is unable to control it, he specifies "within the earth. Because it exists pervasively even within the earth by virtue of being its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), it is "within the earth. Thus, the deity of the earth does not know that which exists within her, thinking, "There is yet another controller of me as well."

And for whom this earth is the body—that is, the covering like a body—for him there is no body other than that. He who is such, the Supreme Lord, dwelling within this earth, governs it; he alone is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). Now, one might object that because of his engagement in the activity characterized by inner governance, there would follow the consequence of his being subject to modification (*vikriyā*); to this, he says: "without parts" (*niṣkriya*).

The meaning is that, without abandoning His ultimate, essential nature (*pāramārthika-niṣaya-rūpa*), He appears as if delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Now, one might raise the objection: "Since He possesses limiting adjuncts, is He not merely a *jīva* like ourselves? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "He is the Supreme Immortal" (*parāmṛta*). Because He does not identify with the internal ruler (*antaryāmin*) due to the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts, He is directly the Supreme Immortal. He is beyond all categories of modification (*vikāra-jāti*) and untouched by the miseries of worldly existence; such is the meaning of "the Supreme Immortal. This same principle should be applied to the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the waters" (*apsu tiṣṭhan*). || 21 ||

22 || 23 || That Self which shines by itself and exists in its own form is the non-dual (aditīya). It alone is the immediate inner controller (avyavahita-antaryāmī) of all; there is no other. (The author of the Brahmavidyābharaṇa has clarified this in the Antaryāmī-adhikaraṇa: "Its status as the cause of existence for all worlds consists in its being the bestower of the fruits of actions and so forth. The inner controller is indeed the Supreme Lord. Māyā...)

Indeed, that is the means for their regulation, as stated in the *Nyāyaratnākara*: "And because it is possible for the Supreme Lord—who is established by other Śrutis as the cause of the world and possesses all powers—to possess the power of regulating everything by His own nature" (p. 128). It is also stated that the Witness (*sākṣin*) alone is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), for the *Nyāyaratnākara* clarifies this in the commentary on the Sūtra "He who in the self" (*ya ātmani*) and "He who in the intellect" (*yo vijñāne*) (Śārīraka Sūtra 1.2.20).

The speaker is not the knower (*pramātā*), but rather the witness (*sākṣin*) is being grasped. [As stated: "And this one, denoted by the word 'Self-knowledge,' is indeed the witness of the individual soul (*jīva-sākṣin*), and not the witness of the universal Self (*tat-tvam-ātmaka-sākṣin*), because of the indication in the singular number. Thus, the Lord (*īśvara*) who has the cosmic illusion (*māyā*) as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*)—has been described; whereas the knower (*pramātā*) has already been excluded from all beings. Although the witness is one, it possesses both concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*), whereas the Inner Controller is devoid of these. This has been made clear [in verses] 17.217–18.

Chapter 10, Verse 869: In this very way, he who is the leader of the intermediate space, the doorkeeper of the wind-prefaced *sarasvat*—of both the conscious and the unconscious—is indeed our manifest inner controller (*antaryāmī*) from the perspective of the Supreme. He is unseen yet seeing; likewise, he is unheard yet hearing; he is unthought yet thinking; and he alone is the swift knower.

Having thus composed the section on the variations (*paryāya*) according to the scriptural text, he summarizes the variations beginning with "He who dwells in fire" and "He who dwells in the intermediate space" by means of extended application (*atideśa*), because their wording is identical, using the word "thus" (*evam*). Regarding the phrase "of that which has *du* as its predecessor": having pointed out [the section] "He who dwells in wind," that which has "wind" (*vāyu*) as its predecessor—namely, that which is pointed out by the subsequent passage beginning with "He who dwells in the quarters" (*diśi tiṣṭhan*)—is referred to as such.

The meaning is this: he who is the leader of all this manifold phenomenal world (kāryaprapañca), which is characterized by both sentience and insentience, and who impels it toward its respective functions with necessity—he alone, being the innermost Self (pratyagātman), becomes the "Inner Controller" (antaryāmī) through his connection with the act of internal governing. Now, one might ask: why do the deities of the earth and other elements not perceive this Inner Controller residing within their own selves, just as we and others do? To this, the text says: "He is unseen."

Because it is devoid of form (*rūpa*), it is not an object for anyone’s sight and is therefore unseen; yet, because it is itself present within the eye, it is the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) as the very nature of seeing. Likewise, because it is devoid of sound (*śabda*), it does not fall within the range of anyone’s hearing and is therefore unheard; yet, by being present within all other [senses], its power of hearing is unimpaired, and thus it is the hearer (*śrotṛ*). Since the mind (*manas*), which consists of volition and conceptualization, has been rendered non-existent [by it], it is unthought (*amata*); being itself possessed of unimpaired power of thought, it is the thinker (*mantṛ*) everywhere.

Because of its presence within the minds, the Self is the "thinker" (*mantṛ*); because of its presence there, it is the "cognition" (*vijñāna*) consisting of the nature of determination (*niścaya*). The meaning is that it is merely the cognizer (*vijñātṛ*), but it is not made an object by that cognition. By this, the meaning of the scriptural text, "The unseen seer, the unheard hearer," is summarized. Thus, by establishing that the Inner Controller alone possesses the forms of being the seer, the hearer, and the thinker, the delusion of difference—that the controller is one thing and the objects to be controlled, such as the seer and so forth, are another—is dispelled.
For this very reason, it is heard in scripture: "There is no other seer than this; there is no other hearer than this," and so forth. || 26 ||

The fool says it is a distraction. However, it is stated in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*: "The reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), which consists of the determination of its own effects, is the ultimate reality according to the conclusion of scripture. This very thing, as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is declared to be the Supreme Controller, but not so by itself. He is omniscient, omnipotent, the self of all, all-pervading, and eternal; this supreme Lord is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world. (17.221-22)

O dull-witted one, why this doubt? Since a Lord distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) has been taught as its controller, how can the oneness of the *jīva* and the Lord be refuted? The answer to this is given in the *Sūtrabhāṣya*: "The designation of difference between the embodied soul and the inner controller is caused by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the body and organs presented through non-investigative [empirical] cognition; it is not ultimate" (1.2.20).

Now, therefore, that one Supreme Immutable, through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), becomes the individual soul (*jīva*) and its inner controller (*antaryāmī*); in reality, it is not the case that these two are separate. (20)

He who dwells even within the earth, whom the earth-deity herself does not know, whose very body is the earth, and who, remaining inactive, governs the earth from within—He alone is our immediate inner witness, the Supreme Self, the Immortal. || 2122 || He who dwells within the waters...

Ha! Even the deities of fire and water do not know Him; even water is His body, for He who rules over water is our manifest Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), the Supreme, the Formless. 23. Likewise, He who is the ruler of all moving and non-moving beings—fire, the intermediate space, wind, and so forth—is our manifest Inner Controller, the Supreme, the Immortal. 24–25.
This seer is not seen; he is never perceived.

[As stated in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa* (17.330–31): "The state of being a seer belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) which is established in common worldly experience; if the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) were also a seer, he would appear within the body. To exclude this possibility, it is said that 'there is no other. In the world, the inner controller is perceived as the individual soul by the ignorant. 1 "Of the soul established in common worldly experience, the state of being a seer likewise exists; if the inner controller were also a seer, he would appear within the body. To exclude this possibility, it is said that 'there is no other. In the world, the inner controller is perceived as the individual soul by the ignorant. (Anubhūtiprakāśa 17.330–31).

O best of gods, for eighty-seven thousand, sixty hundred, and sixty years, the sun and moon existed; yet the mind shines as its own witness solely by its own light. O bulls among the gods, the mind knows the absence of its own mental activity through its own light, and it perceives even that state of deep sleep.

One might indeed suspect that there are distinct transmigrating individual souls (*jīvas*) who experience pleasure and pain during the states of waking, dreaming, and so forth, who are different from the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). Anticipating this, the author summarizes the section on "Light" (*jyotiḥ*) found in the sixth chapter in order to demonstrate their non-difference, beginning with the words "The sun, the moon," and so on. For in the *Jyotirbrāhmaṇa*, it is stated that throughout the various states such as waking and dreaming, despite the engagement in the activities of those respective states, there is no following after any of the aforementioned attributes—such as sitting, standing, or the accumulation of merit and demerit—and thus [the Self] is established as being free from attachment.

The self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*) and other attributes—namely, the nature of unsurpassed bliss (*aniratiśayānanda-svābhāvya*) and non-duality (*advitīyatva*)—have thus been established. In that regard, for the purpose of establishing the self-luminosity of the Self which is the witness of the three states (*avasthā-traya-sākṣin*), the following is recorded in the scripture: "O Yājñavalkya, when the sun has set, when the moon has set, when the fire has gone out, and when speech has ceased, what light does this person have? The Self alone becomes his light," and so forth. This [scriptural passage] is summarized as: "the sun, the moon," etc.

The meaning is this: even when external lights such as the sun have ceased, the Self continues to shine at all times through its own mode of manifestation as the witness (*sākṣin*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), by means of the light of consciousness (*caitanya*) which constitutes its own essential nature; it does not, however, depend upon an external light for its own manifestation. By this, the waking state (*jāgrad-avasthā*) has been described. [Verse 27] "By the cessation of consciousness," etc.

But when, in the state of dream, because the eyes and other sense organs have ceased their activity, the mind also ceases its engagement with external objects and persists merely through a transformation into the forms of dream-objects, then that very mind knows the dream-state by means of its own intrinsic luminosity alone, independent of any other light. It perceives [the dream] even in deep sleep.

But when that ignorance which constitutes the cause—even though it is most deeply enveloped by other faculties—dissolves, then there is the state of deep sleep; at that time, this Self knows even that state consisting solely of ignorance through the light of its own essential nature. || 28 ||

Indeed, this hearer is never heard; it is the unthought thinker and the unknown knower. (The meaning is that the Self never becomes an object in any way whatsoever, but because its nature is consciousness, it remains the subject of objects; however, there is no reality in such subjectivity. For otherwise, even ignorance, *pradhāna*, and so forth could be considered subjects).

The intention behind mentioning the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), the hearer (*śrotṛ*), and so forth is merely to show that [the Self] cannot be identified with any one of them. As stated in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*: "The states of being unseen, unheard, and so on, may also occur in the case of the inner darkness [of ignorance]; therefore, to exclude that, the scripture speaks of 'the hearer' (*śrotr*). (17.228). Furthermore, by this, its non-difference from the Self is made clear. Since the seer and others are things to be governed, once even the Governor (*niyantṛ*) is called a seer and so forth, there remains no suspicion whatsoever of a difference between the two. || 26 || 5 ||

When all modifications such as fire and the rest have ceased, this very Self shines by its own self-luminous nature through the medium of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-citta*). [27] When the mind has no connection with external objects and assumes only the forms of dream-objects...

That very same Self becomes established in its own nature without any other assistance; being of the nature of self-luminous consciousness (*caitanyātmaka*), it perceives the absence of external activity and knows itself. In the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), that same Self knows that state—which consists solely of primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)—through its own consciousness (*cit*). (In this manner, the Self is proven to be distinct from the three states, which are subject to appearance and disappearance. || 28 ||

This very Self, which is self-luminous, eternally cognizes all things—whether manifest or unmanifest, and whether in the form of existence or non-existence—and is itself the reality devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 29 || Existence.

1. In the section on fulfillment (papūraṇa): 2. According to the sequence of the *Upaniṣad-krama*, the fourth chapter is stated; according to the sequence of the *Brāhmaṇa*, it is called the sixth. Therein, the third is the *Jyotir-brāhmaṇa*. It was understood from tradition in the *Gāyatrī-brāhmaṇa*; it was directly proclaimed in the *Sāmaveda-saṃhitā-brāhmaṇa*; it was known from the *Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa* as being beyond hunger and thirst; and it was shown there as the Imperishable Person (*akṣara-puruṣa*) within, whose nature is consciousness and bliss. That very same [Reality] is now made known by this other [text] for the sake of attaining fearlessness.

As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "[This chapter] is commenced with the thought that 'one must realize His distinctness, purity, selfhood, luminosity, the nature of unimpaired power, the state of being unsurpassed bliss by nature, and non-duality. Chapter 10, Verse 871: But You, whose nature is devoid of manifestation and disappearance, and who are beyond existence and non-existence—that Absolute (Kevala), You alone know this [reality]. (29) O best of sages, this entire universe is known through the nature of existence and non-existence; yet He alone knows it, and nothing else—this is the perfect definition. (20)

Thus, through investigation by means of one’s own self, one should know you; that yogi never wavers, even when amidst the highest duality. There is no such thing as "this" or "that"; this alone is the distinction. One does not consume the fierce duality, but remains merely the witness.

Therefore, throughout the three states, this Self is self-luminous consciousness, devoid of the attributes of manifestation and disappearance. For this very reason, this Self—eternally and at all times, free from all adjuncts (*upādhi*), consisting solely of self-luminous pure consciousness—knows its own world, which is twofold by way of being known and unknown, and consists of both existence and non-existence. (29) The phrase "consisting of existence and non-existence" means "in the form of the known and the unknown."

The author states the reason for this: "All things, whether known or unknown, are indeed objects of the consciousness that is the substrate. Thus, because it does not depend on the light provided by external sources such as the sun or the moon, and because it is itself the illuminator of everything during states such as waking, its nature as one's own light is established; and since it persists even when those [external] states cease, its distinction from them is proven. He concludes with the words "etenaiva" (by this very [reason]).

The meaning is that only the perceived object (*vedya*) is perceived as such, and there is no duality; for that [duality] is a mere mental construction (*parikalpita*) and is therefore false. (30) He explains the Vedic scripture beginning with, "When one sees the manifold, then one sees duality," and so forth, with the words "In this way, duality... and so on.

Thus, by the aforementioned reasoning, the yogi who knows that very Self—which is the witness of the three states, distinct from them, and self-luminous by nature—as being independent, does not perceive the sleeping state even while sleeping in all conditions at all times; this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). This is the meaning: because for the knower, the objective world, the senses, and their effects—which are distinct from himself—have been sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*), he does not perceive the sleeping world through the specific cognitions produced by the eyes and other senses.

Moreover, it is indeed manifested by the knowledge of its own nature. Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*). There is no destruction of that vision which consists in the manifestation of the Seer's own Self. Just as heat belongs to fire as long as the fire exists, so too, for the indestructible Seer, vision is indestructible and coextensive with his existence. Therefore, there is neither loss nor gain for him. By this, the scriptural passage, "For there is no defilement of the Seer, because of his imperishability," is explained.

[Objection: "If that very [consciousness] which was seen before exists at all times, why is there not a constant disappearance of the appearance of the visible world? To this, he says: "The visible alone... For, because one does not see the visible world—the object of sight—due to the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the world becomes sublated within the perceived limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); therefore, the appearance of the defect is caused solely by the absence of the object, and not by a loss of the essential nature of consciousness. This is the meaning.

Therefore, at that time, there is no manifestation of the knower, nor is there anything manifested; this occurs in states such as meditative absorption (samādhi) or deep sleep (suṣupti). Only pure consciousness remains.

By this, scriptural passages such as "But there is no second" become meaningful. (32) Since the non-existence [of everything else] is established in Him, He alone is the knower of all that is to be known; there is nothing other than Him who could be the knower. (30) [The commentary-based meaning of "in the form of existence and non-existence," etc., is: "He knows all this precisely in the form of the known and the unknown."]

The yogi is he who, through this kind of inquiry, perceives that which appears as duality as being solely the nature of the Self. Although that duality appears to be seen, he does not see it. (Or, from the perspective of conventional usage, although he sees it, he does not see it from the perspective of ultimate reality. || 31 || There is no name for the object of vision (*dṛśya*) which is the very nature of the Seer, the Self; it perishes at that very moment.

That which is perishable and the visible world is not, in reality, distinct from the Self; it is only the Self that exists. (32) The total cessation of all that is visible and remaining established in one's own nature is the supreme state of the yogi.

1. In the editions ḍa, ca, cha, and ña, it is *daitavi*. 2. This investigation has been shown in detail in the Śruti (4.3.1–22); here, however, it is not stated along with its impurities (*sakaṣāya*). 3. In the edition gha, ca, and cha, it is *va hi na*. 4. The word "explanation" (*vivaraṇa*) is to be supplied [to the preceding term] (p. 99, line 6). 5. Regarding the non-difference of the genitive case: because of the statement in the Bhāṣya (Vṛ.bhā.p. 335), "The state of being self-luminous (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) consists in having consciousness as one's own nature (*caitanyasvasvabhāvatā*)."

This is his Brahman-nature; this is his supreme essence, which is indeed beyond all else. This is his highest world, for this is the supreme bliss. (39) Just as a snake, having cast off its slough, remains free from it by its own nature, so too the wise man should have no notion of "I" regarding the body. (40) In that which is self-supported, self-luminous, unborn, pure, consisting of delight, and the supreme bliss—therein nothing whatsoever exists as manifold. (41)

In this way, the unsurpassability of those who are established in the knowledge of the second [Brahman], such as Vāmadeva and others, is recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) through such passages as, "This is his supreme goal" (*eṣā'sya paramā gatiḥ*). This is summarized by the phrase "this is his. "That wherein one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else"—this is the supreme attainment (*paramā saṃpat*) of one established in Brahman. Since other attainments are impermanent due to being produced (*kṛtakatvena*), they are inferior; thus, the meaning is that this attainment alone is distinguished. Likewise, this alone is the supreme goal (*gati*) for this wise person.

The meaning is that the various states of existence, from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, are "inferior" because they are imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*). Likewise, for this knower, this alone is the supreme world (*loka*). Those worlds which are based on the fruits of action are inferior; however, this state of abiding in the aforementioned Brahman is "supreme" because it is innate and is not produced by any action whatsoever. Thus, due to its unsurpassed nature and its being the object of vision, it is called the supreme world.

For this alone is the supreme happiness, namely, abiding in the state of Brahman which is unsurpassed bliss; indeed, that is supreme because it is eternal, whereas sensual pleasure is inferior because it is non-eternal; the meaning is that the latter should be disregarded here because it is transient. || 33 ||

Thus, a person who has become Brahman no longer identifies the aggregate of cause and effect as "I"; this is established by the Śruti with an illustration beginning with, "Just as a snake has cast off its slough which lies dead in an anthill," and so forth. He summarizes that [passage] with the words, "the slough cast off by a snake. "Ahinirvayanī" means the skin of a serpent.

Just as a snake, having cast off its slough from its dwelling such as an anthill, no longer perceives it as itself due to its own true nature; even so, the knower of Brahman never identifies the body and other such things—which are distinct from him—as the Self. This is the meaning. Furthermore, intending to show that the identification with the body and so forth depends upon the notion of difference and that such a difference cannot be established, he cites the scriptural text refuting it: "There is no diversity here. (34)

Regarding this, he explains that which was indicated by the locative form *atra* (here) as the locus for the negation by stating "the support of all" (*sarvādhāra*). Since Brahman, as described, is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the appearance of the world of duality, it alone is the limit (*avadhi*) of that negation. To ward off the suspicion that even this [Brahman] might be superimposed (*adhyasta*), like the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), he states "self-established" (*svataḥsiddha*). This means it is established by itself alone; that is to say, its existence does not depend on anything else through being superimposed upon another substratum.

"Stainless" (*nirmala*) signifies the removal of *māyā*. The meaning is that when such a state called Śiva is established as the supreme reality, there exists no object whatsoever that is separate from it in the ultimate sense. || 35 ||
It bestows prosperity, it bestows the supreme goal, the supreme world, and supreme happiness. || 33 ||

Just as a leech, having left its own slough, no longer perceives it as "this is my body," so too for one established in Brahman, there never arises the notion of "I" or "this is mine" regarding the body and other such things. || 34 || In the Self—named Śiva—which is the support of all, self-evident, stainless, the nature of the innermost consciousness (pratyagātman), and supreme bliss—there is in reality no object whatsoever that exists as separate from It. || 35 ||

A person who, despite reality being as it is, falsely imagines that the individual self is one thing, the Supreme Self is another, and the world is yet another, falls repeatedly into the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, one should diligently perceive the superimposed ignorance and its effects as being of the very nature of the single essence of the Self alone. This Self is not an object of knowledge (*prameya*), nor is it characterized by attributes such as *dharma* and *adharma*.

Chapter 10 The mortal who possesses this knowledge attains immortality; he no longer perceives diversity here. Therefore, ignorance and its effects are superimposed upon the Self. (36) Indeed, those desiring liberation should behold the One alone as the Great Abode—the Self that is immeasurable, stainless, and free from duality. (37) Having realized that very [Self], the wise man should perform his duties for Brahman; he should not pursue many words through discursive inquiry, for that is merely a weariness of speech. (38) He...
Or rather, this Great Self is described as being beyond the reach of speech and the mind; He is the controller of the entire world and the sovereign lord of all. (29)

He provides an example of the sublation [of the opposite view] with the words "from death" (*mṛtyoḥ*). The meaning is this: he who perceives difference in Brahman—which abides as our very self—thinking "I am one, and the other is the world, the Lord, and so forth," being thus characterized by ignorance, undergoes repeated death, which is the departure from life; that is, being born again and again, he continues to die. Therefore, he concludes that the aforementioned vision of non-duality alone is the truth, with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since there is thus no ultimate difference, therefore ignorance, its effects, and the entire world consisting of the elements and elemental objects beginning with space, are superimposed upon the non-dual Brahman. Consequently, all this must be viewed as being of one single nature, namely, the form of the substrate-self; for it has been stated elsewhere that "it is indeed one-fold. Thus it is declared: "This immeasurable, unborn, and eternal [Brahman] is to be perceived as one alone. This is the meaning of it all.

This Self must be seen as one alone—that is, in a single manner characterized by being a mass of consciousness (vijñānaghana) of a uniform essence—by means of great effort. Having attained the cessation of that very effort produced by the performance of the entire collection of means characterized by tranquility, self-control, and so forth, a direct realization (sākṣātkāra) is to be accomplished. The ablative case in "mahāyāsāt" (from great effort) is used in the sense of the object (karma), with the elision of the suffix -lyap. [Objection: If the Self is indeed the seer, then since it is the object of seeing, it would follow that it is an object of perception (dṛśyatva), like a jar; therefore, [the author] says: "of the immeasurable" (aprameyasya).

That which is produced would be cognized by something other [than itself]. How could one's own non-dual Self be an object of cognition for another? Therefore, when the direct realization of its own object has arisen, it shines forth solely through its own nature; thus, it is "incognizable" (aprameya). Regarding the phrase "free from passion" (*viraja*): "passion" (*rajas*) refers to the impurities such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and delusion (*moha*); He is devoid of that. "Great" (*mahān*) means all-pervasive due to being the cause of all. "Firm" (*dhruva*) means immutable (*kūṭastha*). He summarizes the aforementioned thought with the words "the wise man... Him alone" (*tameva dhīraḥ*): "Him alone," etc.

The wise and intelligent person, having understood the Self as it truly is through instruction, subsequently performs supreme knowledge (*parajñā*) which consists of direct perception regarding that very object. The sense is that an error concerning something not directly perceived cannot indeed be removed by a cognition that is itself not directly perceived. Thus, the knower of the Self, being free from objects other than the Self, meditates upon the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*. The suffix *laṭ* (present tense) takes the augment *āṭ*. To the question "Why?", he says: "Of speech... (*vācaḥ*).

For this reason—that is, because the contemplation of that seer and his words causes the exhaustion of speech, specifically bringing about the weariness of the organ of speech—this is the meaning. [38] Now, he summarizes this section beginning with "He, indeed, is this great unborn Self," which was recited as being intent on demonstrating the means for attaining the aforementioned cessation; he summarizes it with the words "He, indeed, is this. In that context, first the nature of the two is set forth.

This aforementioned one, who is the cause of the world and who dwells within this very heart—He who is the Great, the Unconditioned Self (ātman), free from all worldly modifications such as birth and destruction—is indeed the Controller (*vaśī*) of all, including Brahmā and the rest; for everything exists under His control. Indeed, it is declared in scripture: "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear of Him the sun rises," and so forth. He is not only the Controller, but He is also the Ruler (*īśitā*) over all, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. || 39 ||

It is uncreated by *mala*, all-pervasive, and eternal. || 36-327 || Having known that very Self through knowledge (*jñāna*), one should realize it directly. A Brahmin should not contemplate words that denote the non-Self (*anātman*); they are merely causes for the acquisition of speech and the like, but not for the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). || 38 || That indeed is this Great Self, unborn and undecaying; it is seen in the Upaniṣad as "immeasurable and fixed" (*apramayaṃ dhruvam*). [Note: 1. From birth to death; 2. Ja. This is the meaning; 3. Jña. "characterized by knowledge"].

874. The Brahmagītā: He is the sovereign lord of all, pure, and not diminished by the performance of burdensome rituals; nor indeed is he made lesser by unrighteous action, O you of great speech. (40) Thus he is the Lord of All, the source of the beautiful world, and the protector of beings for the sake of the non-confusion of the worlds, O friends. (41) This is that difficult-to-sustain [state] which the best of Brāhmaṇas seek through the recitation of the Vedas, through sacrifice in its entirety, through charity, through austerity, through divine worship, and likewise through the fire-oblation—seeking it as those sages who know it do. (42)

Regarding that, he says "the sovereign of all" to explain the state of being free from decay (*ahānatva*). "Sovereign" (*adhipati*) means one who presides over and protects; the meaning is that he is independent. For he who presides and protects rules, and he who is the ruler necessarily becomes the controller (*vaśī*). In this way, the superiority of each subsequent one over the preceding among these three qualities should be understood.

Since this Self is pure and its nature is such that no excellence can be added to it, it does not become greater through good action prescribed by the scriptures, such as the Agnihotra sacrifice; the meaning is that it does not become augmented by any quality whatsoever from its prior state. Likewise, it does not become smaller—that is, even slightly less—through evil action prohibited by the scriptures, such as the killing of a Brahmin; the meaning is that it does not diminish from its prior state.

For a body modified by karma can indeed possess excellence or deficiency produced by good or evil actions; however, this Self is without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), the Lord of all, whose nature is to rule over the entire world together with its karma. Therefore, the meaning is that good and evil karma are not capable of producing any modification characterized by increase or decrease in Him. (40) Likewise, this very inner Self is the sovereign lord of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

Likewise, he is the "Protector of Beings" (bhūtapāla) because he protects those beings. This is for the sake of the non-confusion—that is, the non-transgression—of the boundaries of the worlds, beginning with the earth and ending with the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), so that there may be no intermingling or overstepping of their respective limits. He is this very Self, the "Supporter" (vidharaṇa); being the ordainer of the established order of the castes (varṇas), stages of life (āśramas), and so forth, he becomes the bridge. The meaning is that, just as a worldly bridge is a cause for non-confusion, so too does he become such a cause.

The meaning is this: he who follows the path declared in the Śrutis and Smṛtis composed by Him is carried across the ocean of saṃsāra by the merit produced thereby; thus, He is a "bridge" (setu). Having thus established the nature of the Veda, [the author] summarizes that very point regarding the fact that the study of the Vedas and other such acts are prescribed as means for its realization in passages such as, "Him [one seeks to know] by the study of the Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), with the words: "Him alone... (tameva).

By the recitation (*anuvacana*) characterized by the constant study of the Veda composed by Manu and others; likewise, by sacrifice (*yajña*) in the form of obligatory and occasional rites such as the *agnihotra* and so forth; by giving (*dana*) such as that prescribed by the *śruti*, *smṛti*, and *purāṇas*, including the *tulāpuruṣa* and other offerings; and by austerity (*tapas*) in the form of fasting—not by the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and similar penances—[one attains the goal]. Here, by the word "fasting" (*anaśana*), the non-granting of desired objects is intended, not the mere cessation of eating.

If that were so, it would follow that knowledge would cease to exist due to the resulting loss of life. Thus, one who desires—meaning wishes to know, perceive, or understand—that Ātman of the aforementioned nature by means of these [acts] such as the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*), etc., has here established, through the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), that the recitation of the Vedas and so forth serve as the means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by way of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Furthermore, that seeker of knowledge (*vividiṣu*) must subsequently attain that Ātman of the described form through the knowledge arising from hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other practices, such as tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and the rest, which will be mentioned later.

One who possesses the yoga of the mind characterized by the direct realization of the Self becomes a true sage (*muni*), but not any other person who lacks knowledge of the Self. For even though such a person possesses the mental faculty, because their mind is connected to ritual action (*karman*) within the sphere of the unknown, they remain merely an agent (*karmin*) and not a sage. However, one who knows the Self is a sage alone, because he has accomplished all that was to be done. By this, the Vedic restriction—"Only by knowing this very [Self] does one become a sage"—is explained. || 43 ||

He exists. He holds all the worlds within His thunderbolt; He is the Lord of all. (39) He alone is the sovereign ruler (the independent protector) of all, and He is eternally pure. He does not suffer any diminution through good deeds, nor does He undergo any deficiency through evil deeds. (40) He alone is the Lord of all. While remaining as the inner self (pratyagātman), He is the supreme master of all living beings. 9. *iṣmadhipaḥ* 1. *ta*.

Chapter 90, Verse 875: He who is designated by "not this, not this" (neti neti) is indeed the accomplisher of all; he is the eternal knower of the Self, for he is never grasped as an object. Likewise, O gods, do not entertain the notion that he is "this" or "that," for the Blessed One is never defined by such attributes.

Lest there be a misconception that the reality of the Self—taught through the method of affirmation in passages such as "the knower of all, the lord of all"—is something conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the scripture now teaches its true nature, which is beyond the reach of speech and mind, through the method of negation, in the Śruti passage beginning with "This Self is 'not this, not this'. This is summarized here by the phrase "not this, not this. By the word "this" (idam), which signifies "this [world]," the heart (the internal organ) is referred to; and by the repetition [of "not"], there is the negation of all that.

The meaning of this is as follows: having dissolved all this world of duality—this "dyad" that has arisen—by means of "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), there remains this very Self (*ātman*) which is the ultimate limit of all negation, extracted and free from all adjuncts (*upādhi*). This alone is the accomplisher of all; it is the producer of all worldly transactions, such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and karma. There is no other agent or enjoyer besides this, who exists in the ultimate sense. Regarding that Self, which is the limit of all negation, he states its natural form: "This is that."

This [Self], whose nature has been described as being proximate and always ungraspable by the hands, feet, and other specific organs—indeed, it is not grasped by any sense organ, because the senses have as their objects things possessing form and the like (rūpādimat)—likewise, this Self does not possess the nature of a forest of illusions in which the phenomenal world is superimposed; for it certainly does not decay.

Because it is partless, it is impossible for it to be disintegrated; therefore, the meaning is that this reality, which serves as the limit for the negation of the visible, is at all times a nature free from sublation (*bādhaviśuddhasvarūpa*). Now, one might object: "Could there not be a modification of the Self, which is the substratum of that [visible world], due to contact with the visible—which possesses the properties of coming and going? To this, he says: "of the unattached" (*asaṅgasya*). Its nature is like that of a lotus leaf in water; for it is not attached anywhere, because there is no sense of "mine-ness" or identification with anything whatsoever.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for that which is non-existent—being merely an appearance—and is false by nature, to be perceived as having ultimate reality; for the desert ground is not made real by the water of a mirage—this is the sense. || 45 || He is the teacher. He protects all beings. For the sake of ensuring that all worlds, beginning with the earth, do not transgress their respective boundaries, he acts as a bridge (setu) to restrain them.

(Meda: That which is called a *setu* (bridge/dam) is that which restrains water; likewise, all things remain restrained by it. The cause of this is the Supreme Lord alone; therefore, He is the *setu*. For the sake of desiring to know that very Self, the best of Brahmins engage in the study of the Vedas, all sacrificial rites and other rituals, charity, austerity, and the renunciation of desire. The best of Brahmins perform the study of the Vedas, all sacrificial acts and other rites, charity, austerity, and the renunciation of desires, solely for the purpose of seeking to know that very Self.

Just as one who has already eaten the most delicious food might take powdered medicines and the like out of a desire for further eating, so too are the study of the Vedas and other such practices performed as means to attain the inquiry into the Self.

Nevertheless, even though they produce the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), study and other such acts are beneficial until the attainment of knowledge; however, apart from that which produces the desire to know, there is no necessity for acts such as study for the sake of the descent of knowledge. Once the desire to know has arisen, it is only by performing *śravaṇa* and so forth—preceded by the cessation of all ritual actions and the practice of tranquility (*śama*) and the like—that knowledge is attained. One who knows this Self is indeed a sage (*muni*).

[This] is the perfection of both childhood and wisdom; there is no other sage [like this]. (41-43) Having stated that whatever can be perceived in this manner [as an object] is not the Self, the Śruti has drawn out the conclusion regarding the Self: that very Self is the one who bestows eternal bliss upon all. Its essential nature is such that it can never be made an object of perception. (44)

In this same way, by its very nature, it is not subject to destruction; and because its nature is non-manifest, it is not an object of perception—this is the section [ending with] *agrāhyasvarūpa*. Furthermore, [the text reads]: "Whether in the body or elsewhere... [variant readings: *gha* and *cha*: *ṇsarvamiti neti vi*; *ca* and *cha*: *pasarvamiti neti neti vi*; *ḍa*, *ṇka*, *ca*: *ṣkaḥ kaści*; *gha*: *ṣdāśrotrādi*; *jña*: *taṃ kṛtvā sa?*].

4. The Brahman-meditation. 876. This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa: it does not diminish through action, nor is it increased by inaction. Having realized that very [Self] which is spread beyond [the world], one is not stained by evil action. 46. One who knows the Self as being like a fire that has consumed its fuel—tranquil, self-controlled, truthful in speech, and noble; having abandoned action and attained success through the cessation of all worldly ties—should constantly approach such a person for instruction. 45.

One who is devoted to the worship of Śaṅkara should always practice the offering of water from three vessels, the best of honey, and curd; one should mutter the word "Śiva" and other such names without anger, and with vigor, one should offer the fourfold oblation to Hara. 48.

This is corroborated by the scriptural statement, "This has been declared by the Ṛgveda verse," which cites the following mantra to confirm the meaning already established: "This is his eternal greatness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23). By means of the negation of all other attributes through the formula "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*), that state which was described as his own nature during deep sleep is shown to be the eternal majesty (*mahiman*) of the Brāhmaṇa who knows Brahman. Other forms of majesty, however, are impermanent because they are produced by action (*karma*); this [majesty], on the other hand, is eternal because it is innate (*svābhāvika*). To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "It does not age. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23)

By means of the two kinds of action, namely merit and demerit, it does not undergo modification characterized by increase or decrease, because its separation from attachment to the causes of change has been established. Therefore, due to this very absence of modification, it is eternal; such is the meaning of "this greatness. And thus, one would become a knower of that greatness. "Pada" (foot/abode) means that which is reached, attained, or known—namely, its own nature. The meaning is that one would become a knower of that *pada*. Having directly realized that Self which is eternally of the nature of light, the knower is not smeared by evil action. Here, by the word "evil" (pāpa), both [evil and merit] are intended, because even meritorious action is a cause of saṃsāra. Therefore, the meaning is that for the knower, all duality consisting of the two kinds of action—merit and evil—which are causes of saṃsāra, is brought to cessation. In this regard, the external means for knowledge, such as the recitation of the Vedas and so forth, have been previously demonstrated.

Now, he shows the internal means of realization taught in such passages as "Therefore, one who knows thus, being calm and self-controlled," by the words "Therefore": "Therefore... Because this fruit is of such a nature—consisting in the non-dual consciousness free from the body and so forth—one should possess qualities such as calmness in order to attain it. In that context, "calm" (śānta) means one who has desisted from external activities; "self-controlled" (dānta) means one who has turned away from the thirst for mental objects. Regarding "truthful in speech": this speaking of truth is an indicator of the absence of passion.

The term *karmatyāgī* (one who has abandoned action) is an explanation of the word *uparata* found in the scripture. Its meaning is: one who has abandoned those actions which are the means for attaining other worlds and which are antagonistic to knowledge (*vidyā*). "Established in all Vedāntas" means that one should constantly pursue the causes of knowledge—such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and so forth—as set forth in the Vedāntic texts beginning with "He is to be heard, He is to be reflected upon. — 47 —

Likewise, he states that even practices such as the *tripuṇḍra* and *dhāraṇā*, which are taught in the *Jābālopaniṣad* and other texts, are internal means for attaining the supreme reality because they cause pleasure to Śiva: "The triple mark," etc. (Verse 48).

He does not take up those [bonds]. || 45 || This very supreme Śiva is the eternal majesty of the knower of Brahman; He neither increases nor decreases through action. (The meaning of "knowing that which is not an object" is to remain without knowing anything other than Him. || 46 ||

Others, desiring the knowledge of the Supreme, should control their intellect, mind, and senses; they should remain truthful, renounce action along with its means, and practice the methods that are the source of wisdom, as taught in all the Upanishads. For it is heard thus: "Indeed, these two do not cross over this [Self], thinking 'I have done evil' and 'I have done good'; he indeed crosses over both of these; neither what has been done nor what has not been done afflicts him. Having explained the Śruti passage, "Evil does not overcome him," he also cites the Śruti that demonstrates how evil does not torment him: "na enam" (it does not torment him). "Indeed, it does not burn him [with remorse], thinking: 'Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is evil? "Why did this happen? Why did that not happen?"—in this way, no remorse arises; for only those who possess knowledge experience remorse for their actions. O gods, everything that has been proclaimed by me out of compassion for others must be performed; indeed, nothing at all remains to be done for one who is established in the Self, which is Brahman. For this reason, knowing that the action performed by this Guru—which is like a soup consisting of the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman, the means to attain immortality—one should never commit any injury toward him out of gratitude. The commentary on the *Kaṭhavallī* and the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, consisting of eleven chapters [states]:

"Truth is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and devoid of differentiation (*avikalpa*). Therefore, all the Upaniṣads describe the Supreme Lord in one and the same way. The refutation (*pratiṣedha*) is also identical in the Upaniṣads for the same reason that they cannot be challenged in any way. Thus, in order to connect the general principle regarding the relationship of extended application (*atideśa*) with the nature of non-duality (*advaitasvarūpa*), the subject matter of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* is also being summarized here.

Previously, while explaining the meaning of the *Kaṭhopaniṣad*, Brahmā said: "The Śiva-tattva is immediate yet difficult to perceive, hidden, most subtle, concealed everywhere, situated within the intellect, beyond all existence, and more minute than the minute. This [soul] does not cease to exist; some maintain that it is merely dust, while others hold that it is something else, or according to another view, that although it remains after death, one cannot know it. Yamarāja has explained the nature of that Self, stating that it is the Self and that its very essence is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is not the one who undergoes birth and death who is the deceiver; for if it were never perceived that the one undergoing birth and death deceives anyone at all, then to say that he does not undergo birth and death would be considered inconsistent. This is the point.

Having observed the point of doubt in the preceding text—that because only one who possesses the final [knowledge] is fit for the state of being a knower (*vijñātṛ*), the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) cannot be non-existent—the author explains the Kaṭha Upaniṣad in order to show that it is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*) who is the seer, and that he is none other than the one described previously, by means of the reply beginning with "Just as a man, my dear... and continuing with "Other than dharma, etc. Therein, from the second Vallī onwards, he states the meaning of the supreme Self (*para-ātman*).

This very syllable (akṣara), characterized by Hiraṇyagarbha and so forth, is the lower Brahman. This same syllable, when all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) have been cast off, is the higher Brahman, whose sole essence is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). Because the Praṇava is a symbol (pratīka) for both of these, it is designated as identical with them. Therefore, this very syllable, the lower Brahman, is to be meditated upon through yoga; and the higher Brahman is to be realized. Thus, it is taught that the very knowledge of the perceiver of dreams and so forth is the fruit of liberation (4.4), while the vision of duality is censured (4.10); from this, non-duality is once again established. Now, by means of that *praṇava*, he points out the Supreme Brahman as it is in its essential nature with the words, "It is not born. Furthermore, this Self is not produced from any other cause, because no such distinct entity exists. [Objection: But surely entities such as space (viyat) and so forth do exist? Therefore, due to the absence of any other cause, this Self is devoid of birth; for this very reason, it is eternal (*nitya*) and stable (*dhruva*). It is unchanging, being free from decay. In the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), one becomes adorned with majesty (*mahimāmaṇḍita*). (From the worship of the lower [Brahman], the fruit for the living being is the attainment of the world of Brahman and a highly praised state; from the experience of the higher [Brahman], the fruit is the realization of non-difference from Brahman. Kuṭha, though bad by its very nature (svarūpataḥ), becomes good from the perspective of the goal (upeyadṛṣṭyā). That Self neither dies nor is ever born; its essential nature is such that it never undergoes destruction.

The self (ātman) has no cause, nor is it the cause of anything else. (It is not produced by anyone, nor does it produce anything. That unborn self is eternal, indestructible, and always one in nature. Even when the body is slain, the self is not slain. 6.

That which is called equanimity (*samatā*)—the one who kills or nourishes the self—is false equanimity; for it neither kills nor can it be killed. (7) From here and there, from all sides, this very Self remains established as the form of the Self within the cave of the heart of every living being. "Smaller than the small," and so forth: smaller (*aṇīyān*) than the small (*aṇoḥ*), that is, more exceedingly subtle than even that which is of minute dimension; likewise, greater (*mahīyān*) than the great (*mahataḥ*), that is, larger than even that which possesses great dimension. Whatever exists in the world, whether subtle or great, all of that derives its existence from this very Self as its cause; thus, because He pervades both, the Self is designated as "smaller than the small" and so on. That Self is hidden in the cave—the heart—of this living being, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; the meaning is that He abides there in the form of the inner Self.

A person who is free from desire, having become dispassionate toward objects seen and unseen, beholds—that is, directly realizes—that aforementioned tethering post. Through the clarity (*prasāda*) of the elements—the sense organs such as the mind and so forth being called "elements" because they sustain the body—due to the absence of the harshness born from the enjoyment of objects, he perceives through direct vision the "greatness" of this inner self, characterized by its nature as the undivided Brahman. At that time, his sorrow having departed, he is liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra.

The meaning is that he exists [thus]. || 8 || Regarding the passage beginning with "moving far away" (*dūraṃ vrajati*): while seated—that is, remaining motionless—he moves; likewise, while sleeping, he goes everywhere, he travels. The meaning is that since the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is omnipresent, there is no contradiction in the simultaneous appearance of these mutually contradictory states—such as sitting, moving, and lying down—within it. Furthermore, because such a conjunction of contradictory attributes is impossible for that which is limited, this Great God, the Self, is unlimited (*aparicchinna*).

By this, the phrase "I have attained, I have attained" (*madāmadami*) found in the Śruti is explained.
