Regarding the phrase "without a body" (*anaṅga*): by its own essential nature, it is unembodied, resembling the ether. It dwells through its presence in the transient bodies—devoid of stability and lacking permanence—of gods, ancestors, humans, and so forth; yet it is itself eternal and great.

Lest its greatness be considered merely relative—like that of an atom or the like—he qualifies it with the word "all-pervading" (vibhum): having understood through reflection and ascertained by means of meditation that the Self is all-pervasive, omnipresent, and unlimited, and that it is the "I-sense" (ahamati) which animates all living beings, one no longer undergoes the sorrow of saṃsāra. || 10 ||

Who is the maker of conventional designations? [It is] the one who has transcended sorrow; for the world is indeed like a pit. This very self, though remaining right here, appears as if far away; while sleeping, it wanders everywhere.

Furthermore, who other than Mahādeva himself could know this? By calling the Self "the one who breathes through the Rudras" (*virudra-dhmātā*), its quality-less nature (*nirdharmakatva*) is made clear; it becomes evident that all things are conceived within it in an identical manner. The meaning of the phrase "he who knows it by turning inward" (*antarmukhatvena vijñā*) is that only one who is inward-turned attains the realization of this; therefore, only an inward-turned person can comprehend it.

Furthermore, I have stated the manner of my own experience: "I perceive myself as having my roots within; what other person, whose intellect is directed toward the external, could possibly know that [Self] which shines forth as a contradictory nature? (11.31). 9.1. When this unstable body perishes, what wise person would grieve for that Great Self, who is distinct from the body and all-pervading?

1. Some construe [the term] as "one whose sorrow has been taken away" (*dhīta-śokaḥ*). Others explain it as "one who is devoid of recollection of what is disagreeable. 2. According to the *Medinī* lexicon, *dhātu* means "a mountain" (*adri*) or "a vein" (*śirā*). Here, however, *dhātu* signifies the elements (*dhātavaḥ*) which are the causes of the body's stability; their serenity is its lack of agitation. Therefore, the Commentary states: "The instruments, such as the mind and so forth, are the *dhātavaḥ*. Others, however, maintain that the *dhātavaḥ* are specifically the seven constituents of the body, beginning with semen (*śukra*), which serve as the causes for the sustenance of the body.

They also connect [the verse] with the phrase, "The birth of the knowledge of the Self is not for one who is heedless" (1.3). For the meaning is this: "Only one who possesses subtle intelligence, and likewise only one whose intellect is subtle, would know this, and no other. The word *asmat* (from us) is capable of referring here even to that other Brahman mentioned in the Upaniṣads; however, when instruction is given through the vision of the scriptures, the meaning is: "Who else but the inner self (*pratyagātman*) could know Him? This is consistent with the statement, "There is no other seer than He," and here it is said that the inner self would behold Him.

Therefore, the sense is that there is non-difference between the two. (4) "The all-pervading" (*vibhum*) means one who assumes manifoldness (*vaividhyam*). Thus, it is said in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa* (11.37): "Having realized that the Self is the substratum of all states of existence, one does not grieve. [From the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 1.2.22–23]: "He is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellectual power, nor by much hearing. Only he whom this [Self] chooses is able to attain Him; to him this Self reveals His own nature. (19) Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one whose mind is not composed, nor even one who possesses excessive pride, can attain Him through knowledge. (12)

"This Self cannot be attained by instruction"—that is, it cannot be grasped through the study of various Vedas; nor by intelligence—that is, by the capacity for retaining texts; nor by much hearing—that is, by listening to many scriptures. By what means, then, is this Self to be attained? It is said: "Whomever this aspirant chooses, by that very person is this Self to be attained. That is, it is to be grasped by the aspirant through whom he seeks refuge.

And therein, for the sake of the seeker, this very Self reveals—that is, makes manifest—its own form, which is entirely free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi). "Nor one who has not turned away from evil conduct," etc. One who has not turned away from, or desisted from, evil conduct—meaning sinful behavior—cannot attain this aforementioned Self. Nor can one who is not tranquil, meaning one who has not desisted from the restlessness of the senses. Likewise, even one who is undisciplined, lacking one-pointedness of mind, is unable to attain it. Similarly, one whose mind is not peaceful.

Even one whose mind is restless and not withdrawn from sense objects does not attain this. But he who, being devoted to good conduct and the like, is tranquil through the power of his intellect, whose mind is concentrated and whose inner self is fully subdued—he alone attains this Self by means of the supreme knowledge produced by the grace of the teacher; that is, by means of excellent, unshakeable, direct realization—this is the meaning. || 12 ||

He does not act. (By calling Him "the Great Pervader," His omnipresence in every respect is indicated; alternatively, the meaning of *vibhu* is "possessing various forms," that is, the substratum of all. || 10 || This Self is not attained through the study of many Vedas, nor by engaging in much debate, nor by hearing much.

This practitioner can attain the goal only by maintaining desire for his own true Self alone; the Self then reveals its own nature to him. By choosing the Self as the sole objective, one may subsequently perform the practice of all the means for its attainment. The Self manifests its own nature of its own accord; no effort is required for the sake of self-knowledge.

Elsewhere, the Teacher has stated: "Only the cessation of the superimposition of name-and-form upon the Self is to be accomplished, not the production of the knowledge of the consciousness of the Self... [Gītābhāṣya, p. 507]. Therefore, regarding Brahman, one must merely perform the removal of the superimposition caused by ignorance; no effort is required for the knowledge of Brahman itself. || 11 ||

He who has not abandoned sinful conduct, who has not brought his senses under discipline, who has not concentrated his mind, and whose mind is not turned away from sense objects—he cannot attain this [Self] through lack of wisdom (for it is through lack of wisdom that one fails to attain it). (Righteous conduct is the initial and indispensable step for spiritual practice.)

How can acting according to one's own whims grant liberation, and how can devotion to Brahman grant it? Although all these various practices have been imagined as a single path by everyone, nevertheless, before all of them, one must first abandon wrong efforts. In reality, the renunciation of efforts impelled solely by desire is primary. These efforts may be impelled by desire, yet they can also be considered impelled by the Self.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), all activity is indeed impelled by desire; however, this much can be admitted: a person of discrimination (*vivekī*) does not perform scriptural activities merely out of desire, but rather performs them because they are scriptural.

It is true that the acceptance of the scriptures and so forth is possible only as long as desires exist; however, since all obligatory (*nitya*) and other types of rites are indeed *kāmya* (performed for a specific desire), the objection that one might act according to one's whims even when a desire exists—thereby disregarding the scriptures—is countered by the fact that a person is not motivated solely by desire. Although the desire to avoid hell and so forth is certainly present, it is nevertheless accepted as a concession (*abhyupagama*).

1. Ḍa. śdhaina nā5. 2. "By him"—that is, by the choosing [of the Lord]; this is the meaning according to the *Muṇḍaka-bhāṣya*. Alternatively, as stated in Ānandagiri’s commentary: "Whomever the Supreme Self, who is the subject of this section, chooses—that is, favors—by that very one favored by the Supreme Lord, He is attained. Therefore, the *Anubhūtiprakāśa* states: "He whom the Lord favors within, by him He is attained" (1.39).

884. *Brahmagītā*: "For whom both Brahman and Kṣattra are the boiled rice—what god knows him thus, or what other mortal man, where he is? 2. "Drinking the Truth (*ṛta*) in the world of good deeds, entered into the cave of the heart, seated in the highest supreme goal—the knowers of Brahman speak of those two as shadow and light, inseparable and joined together."

"Of whom *brahman*..."—of that Self, both *brahman* and *kṣatra* are the *odana*, the food. This is an elliptical expression; the entire world, including the *brahman* and *kṣatra*, being withdrawn into itself, becomes its own supreme food, with this [world] standing in the place of the *odana*. It is heard [in scripture]: "Death is the sauce for the *odana*" (*mṛtyur asyopasecanam*), and death is said to stand in the place of the condiment (*upadaṃśa*).

And as for that Supreme Self, who among gods or humans could possibly know its true nature—that which is characterized by such a form? (13) In order to clarify the aforementioned point through the metaphor of a chariot, by way of the relationship between the attainer and the attainable, [the author] restates the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), which is based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is well-known in the world, with the words "drinking the truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*). To reveal the intention behind that [verse], he recites it: "Drinking the truth... and so forth.

In this world, which is the fruit of well-performed action—action performed by oneself and brought to completion—they have entered the cave, namely the intellect (*buddhi*) which is a transformation of *sattva*, within our own physical body; and they have entered that supreme space within the heart, which is more excellent than the external elemental ether because it is the locus for the realization of the Supreme. Thus, they have entered into the state of the *sattva* of the intellect situated within the space of the heart.

And those two—the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*)—are said to be "drinking," that is, experiencing the fruit of karma which has been manifested. In this context, it is the individual soul alone that partakes of the fruit of karma, and not the supreme self, according to the Vedic scripture: "The other, not eating, looks on" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 4.6). Therefore, by the principle of the "eating and non-eating" (the *acchati-nyāya*), the word "drinking" is applied to the collective pair consisting of the one who drinks and the one who does not drink. Furthermore, these two are distinct from each other like shade and sunlight; they demonstrate the difference between Brahman through the distinction of being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) and being free from it (*asaṃsāritva*).

And those who have performed the five fires (*pañcāgni*)—as described in the section on the five fires—and who have kindled the *Nāciketa* fire three times are the *triṇāciketas*. These also establish [the meaning] in this very way. Furthermore, the fact that this mantra refers to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) has been affirmed by the venerable Vyāsa as well: "The two who have entered the cave, for they eat that [fruit]" (Brahma Sūtra 1.2.11). || 14 ||

It may be that there are two motivators for this matter: one is desire (*kāmanā*) and the other is scriptural injunction (*śāsana*). It is evident that the motivation of the scripture consists of its informative nature (*jñāpakatva-svarūpa*). Nevertheless, it is desired that one should act in complete conformity with the scripture. Elsewhere also it has been said: "The end of action... and so forth (*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 3.2.10).

"Austerity, self-control, and ritual action" (Kena Upaniṣad 4.8), and so forth; furthermore, in the Gītā as well, there are many injunctions regarding the conduct of virtuous people. || 12 || For him, the entire world—characterized by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others—is like food (he does not destroy everyone in the same way that ordinary people consume their meal). Who can know that Supreme Śiva who abides within his own essential nature?

But [it may be argued]: "Śiva's nature can indeed be manifested at dawn; that is to say, it cannot become the object of any conceptual knowledge. Some teachers have also interpreted this Vedic scripture (*śruti*), "He is not known by these means," as follows: "One who lacks those aforementioned means of realization cannot know Him. || 13 ||

The teachers state that in the supreme state of Brahman, knowledge and action are said to exist; the sense is that even those two have their locus therein. In the section on *anarthakaraṇa* (1.2.2.9), the deliberations regarding the verbal root should be examined. He states the meaning of the third case ending from this point.
Chapter 99, 885.

Within the body, in the excellent abode of the space within the heart—the cave of the intellect—two beings reside, experiencing the fruits of their own actions: Śaṅkara and the embodied soul. Their natures are distinct, like darkness and light. This secret—that they are indeed Brahman—is taught by the wise. (Previously, the consideration of the Inner Controller has already been discussed.)

Śaṅkara is the inner controller (antaryāmī) who resides within the cave of the intellect while experiencing the fruits [of karma], whereas the individual soul (jīva) resides there while experiencing [the fruits] itself. Although the literal meaning of every syllable of the Śruti and its corresponding Purāṇas states only this much—that "two persons, drinking the truth (ṛta) of their good deeds (sukṛta), have entered the cave in the most excellent place"—nevertheless, the word *sukṛta* here does not refer merely to merit (*puṇya*), but to all actions performed by oneself.

What is its essential meaning? The word *ṛta* denotes "truth" (*satya*). As evidenced by such citations as "ṛtaṃ satyaṃ samīcīnaṃ samyak tathyaṃ yathātatham" (Halāyudha) and "ṛtamucyate śīle satye" (Nirukta), this is established. However, since this [truth] is necessarily inherent, the word *ṛta* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for the fruit of action (*karmaphala*), which is the truth.

First, there are two [entities] who experience—that is, the literal meaning of the words—but it must be considered who these two are. Generally, one might say that both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the living being (*jīva*) are the experiencers of the fruits of karma; however, this position is untenable. For one must necessarily accept the living being as the experiencer of the fruits of karma, and not anyone else. When [the intellect] is joined with the conscious living being...

If it is said that there is a second, it is logical that this too must be sentient, not insentient; therefore, the second is the sentient Supreme Self (paramātman). Furthermore, the fact that the Lord resides in the "cave" and so forth is well-known from other sources. Now, it is shown that the Supreme Lord is neither one who performs meritorious deeds nor one who does not; He drinks the *ṛta* (the Truth), for He is described as "one who looks on without eating" (*anaśnann abhicākaśīti*).

In this way, if the second [entity] were the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other were the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there would be a contradiction in the gender (*liṅga-virodha*) on both sides. For instance, the drinking of *ṛta* (the "Right") is impossible for the Supreme Lord, and the entering into the cave (*guhā-praviṣṭatva*) is inconsistent with the intellect; furthermore, the mention of dwelling together with the individual soul (*jīva*) is incompatible with the intellect. Therefore, for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion, one must rely upon the remainder of the passage (*vākya-śeṣa*). If there are passages that clarify this particular statement, then the determination shall be made from them.

If this very sentence has come for the purpose of supporting some other matter, then the intended meaning of this [sentence] will be established through the meaning of those [other] sentences. Its own independent meaning, however, is not understood; moreover, merely pointing out two drinking vessels does not accomplish any human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Consequently, this [sentence] has come for the sake of some other purpose. That purpose is determined by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

In the preceding section, the means and the fruit of knowing Brahman have been explained; furthermore, it has been stated in the subsequent mantra that we can know the Imperishable Supreme Brahman, which serves as the bridge. Then, through the Ratharapaka, the description of the enjoyer who attains the Self has been given, and the fruit consisting of the attainment of the supreme state has been shown. This too has been stated.

(3.12) Is the Supreme Self hidden within all beings? Because He is subtle and difficult to perceive, one attains Him through one-pointed concentration. The difficulty of the path to His attainment serves as an incentive for the exertion of great effort. Furthermore, the nature of the Supreme Self has been described as being like that of a thief. Thus, the preceding and subsequent contexts concern the unity of the Supreme Self alone; and this mantra follows as the means for realizing that.

Reflecting upon the means [of liberation], the following self-reflection (*ātma-dhṛti*) has been made: "The objects of the senses are beyond the senses; the mind is beyond the objects; the intellect (*buddhi*) is beyond the mind; the Great One (*mahat*) is beyond the intellect; the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is beyond the Great One; and the Person (*puruṣa*) is beyond the Unmanifest" (3.10–11). Thus, it is stated that the Person is indeed beyond the intellect. That alone is the subject to be known in this context. Consequently, it is appropriate to state in the present mantra that He alone is situated within the purification of the intellect (*buddhi-śuddhi*).

The meaning is that because it is such, one should perceive it as pure, possessed of a focused mind, and endowed with discernment (3.8), using a subtle and higher intellect (3.12). If it were not such, it would not be clear how or by what means it could be perceived. On the other hand, if a different intellect were assumed in this present mantra, no result would be obtained within the context.
Furthermore, it has been stated: "It exists in the supreme *parārdha*. The meaning of *parārdha* is...

886. *Brahmagītā*: "O Supreme One, what is the highest station?"—"The station of the Supreme (*para*)"; [the Lord] abandoned the "Supreme" (*para*). It is said that the Supreme Person is the "Person within" (*puruṣaḥ praḥ*), and His supremacy is stated in its primary sense: "There is nothing higher than the Person" (2.11). Therefore, by the scriptural authority of this statement, "entered into men," this very Lord is to be accepted. Now, on the other hand, there is only one proof for the side of the intellect (*buddhi*), whereas for the side of the Lord...

The three means of proof—*liṅga*, *vākya*, and *prakaraṇa*—belong to the former [the individual soul], while the latter [the Supreme Lord] will be established by other means. As for the matter of "drinking the *ṛta*," that can somehow be reconciled. For a master does not personally make shoes; rather, he causes them to be made by his servants, yet this very fact leads to the common designation: "So-and-so the merchant makes shoes," and so forth.

In this same way, although the Supreme Lord does not experience enjoyment Himself, He certainly causes enjoyment to take place. For this reason, it is stated that He "enjoys. Alternatively, just as one who accompanies those carrying umbrellas is also called "one with an umbrella," even though he himself does not have one—this can be understood accordingly—it is determined that this statement refers exclusively to the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara).

Therefore, it has been clarified in the Purāṇa that [the two] are designated as "the embodied one" and "the Lord. Vyāsajī reached this very conclusion in the Guhādhikaraṇa (1.2.11). Now, a single doubt may arise: how can the Śrutis, which establish non-difference, speak of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara) as two? The Ācārya has provided a prompt and decisive resolution to this.

The precise meaning of this statement becomes intelligible only after determining its underlying purport (*tātparya*). From the aforementioned reconciliation (*samālocanā*), it is understood that for the sake of the knowledge of Paramaśiva, the statement is intended as a means of negation (*apavāda*) regarding the nature of the self. In this manner, what does the statement intend to convey? It is this: that the Self is by nature devoid of sound and other qualities, and is neither an agent nor an enjoyer.

That is to say, the purpose of this statement is not to establish difference. Why, then, was difference mentioned? It is clear that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of indicating [the Self's] non-enjoyership and so forth. We have now reached two positions: one is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and the other is the witness (*sākṣin*). Upon examination, these two are distinguished like shadow and sunlight. The enjoyer is like a shadow—unilluminated; the witness is like sunlight—self-illuminating.

Therefore, one should know that very self-luminous reality as one's own true nature; it is this which stands as a bridge, and only by means of it can one cross beyond fear—this is the intended meaning. Thus, the number "two" is stated not with a desire to express numerical duality, but with a desire to convey the essential nature of the entities. Just as when two sticks are placed upright and leaning against each other, it appears from a distance as if the two sticks are standing supported by one another.

Upon examining it from another perspective, it becomes clear that this is indeed *nīṃ* (the syllable *om*). Those who explain this are called *samavāyinaḥ*. When one fault is attached, two faults arise; when two are attached, seven faults are said to occur—but these are merely restatements (*anuvāda*). In the same manner, *prakṛti* and the other [categories] should be understood as being equal in their application. Furthermore, the doubt regarding the distinction between the regulated (*niyamya*) and the regulator (*niyāmaka*) has already been refuted in the commentary on the *Antaryāmī-brāhmaṇa*. || 14 ||

Chapter 11, Verse 887: Śiva, the knower of Yoga, considers the fruit of actions to be dependent on the body. From the perspective of common perception, these two appear contradictory; however, the difference between them is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Verse 96: One should know the Self as the rider, and the body as the chariot. Know the intellect (*buddhi*) as the charioteer, and the mind (*manas*) as the reins. Verse 97: Know the senses as the horses, and the objects of the senses as the paths. Those who know the truth declare that the Self, when joined with the intellect and the mind, is the enjoyer.

But when one is devoid of knowledge, those very senses then become ungoverned by that unrighteous person, like vicious horses for a charioteer. (18) Nor is there a real difference between these two; thus he shows that the mind has as its object an improper meaning—namely, "the bearer of the body. The difference between those two, the soul and the intellect, is adventitious (*aupādhika*). That difference, belonging to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), is perceived within the undivided Brahman, just as the reflection of the moon appears divided in a bowl of water.

Therefore, the meaning is that the non-difference between these two is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*) and not real (*vāstava*). In this regard, he explains—through the metaphor of a chariot—the two-fold process of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*): namely, its wandering in *saṃsāra* due to ignorance and its attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*) through knowledge (*vidyā*)—in the verse beginning with "the Self" (*ātmānam*). One should know the transmigrating Self, the enjoyer of the fruits of action, as the "charioteer," the master of the chariot.

One should know that the body presided over by that [Self] is the chariot. For that chariot is drawn by the horses, which are the sense organs. One should know the intellect (*buddhi*)—which consists of the transformations of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) such as determination and moments of resolve—to be the charioteer; for it is by means of the intellect that one directs the senses and so forth. One should know the mind (*manas*), characterized by volition and the like, to be the reins. (16) The eyes and other sense organs are the horses.

Just as the movement of the feet is directed toward objects such as soup and other foods, so too is the movement of the body and its parts conceived of as being like a chariot and its components; and their nature as a chariot and so forth is likewise imagined. In this context, it is shown that the Self, which is distinct from the body and the rest, is the enjoyer and not the mere collection of them. Here, the word "Self" (ātman) refers to the body; for one might otherwise understand the enjoyer to be the Self merely as conjoined with the body, senses, and mind.

But one who is devoid of that [desire] has the nature of pure *māyā* alone and is a non-enjoyer, according to the scriptural texts: "He meditates as it were, he moves as it were," and "The other, not eating, looks on. (17) By the verse beginning with "He who," the author establishes that for the non-discriminating person, the state of being subject to the chariot and its path is like that of a dependent, whereas for the discriminating person, there is mastery over the chariot and the exhaustion of the path of the intellect. He who is a mortal wandering in *saṃsāra*, lacking the knowledge that discriminates between what is to be done and what is not to be done, becomes joined with a mind that is uncollected and seized by the aforementioned [desires].

Therefore, for the ignorant, the senses such as the ears and so forth must necessarily be regarded as defects; that is to say, they are impossible to master and difficult to restrain. Thus, while the individual soul (*jīva*) experiences the fruits of karma and Śiva makes them possible, these two—according to the perspective of the Supreme Reality (*paratīti*)—appear to possess distinct natures, yet in truth they do not.

Their difference is merely conditional (*aupādhika-mātra*). (The conditional difference culminates in the difference of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi-bheda*), which does not affect the difference of the substratum (*upadheya-bheda*); this is observed everywhere in the case of space and so forth. Therefore, Śiva is not different from the individual soul (*jīva*). Only the limiting adjuncts of the one [Reality] are different. Whether these be called *māyā* and *avidyā*, or *ajñāna* and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they may be understood by any name; it makes no difference to the non-duality. || 15 ||

(Through the metaphor of the chariot, it is understood that from ignorance comes saṃsāra and from knowledge liberation is attained. The Self, which is the enjoyer of the fruits of karma, should be regarded as the rider; the body is the chariot; the intellect is the charioteer, and the mind is the reins.

The horse of the senses indeed carries one to such objects; these horses cause the self, together with the body, senses, mind, and so forth, to experience [objects] (it does not experience alone or without limiting adjuncts). For one who is undiscriminating and possesses an uncontrolled mind, even the horse of the intellect does not remain steady in the chest, like a wild elephant. Whoever...

One who possesses discernment and a controlled mind has senses that are like well-trained horses under the control of the whip. However, one who lacks discernment and has an uncontrolled mind is always impure due to the fault of desire; such a person never attains that supreme state (liberation), but remains wandering in the cycle of rebirth.

One whose mind is restrained and who possesses discernment (*viveka*) is not afflicted by desire; it is such a person alone who attains that supreme state from which there is never again a fall, and thus one does not have to enter the cycle of birth and so forth. Only the seeker who makes discernment his charioteer and the restrained mind his reins crosses over the course of worldly existence, even while still longing for sense objects.

The very indivisible nature of the all-pervading Brahman—consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss—is the supreme goal to be attained. In reality, the body of the all-pervading Śiva is indeed the true nature of all embodied beings. Śiva alone, who is the supreme object of attainment and non-dual, is the Lord.

1. The meaning is "that which causes falling away. It is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the living self (*jīva*), which serves as the charioteer for the manifestation of experience. 2. "By means of the intellect, the mind, and the senses"—this is the meaning. For the commentary states: "The instruments, such as the sense of hearing and so forth, proceed when grasped by the mind, just as horses [proceed] by means of a bridle. 3. For this very reason, it is designated as the "abode of enjoyment" (*bhogāyatana*). The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is intended to include the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) and the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*).

As it is stated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*: "And while all these exist, the status of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtva*) cannot be attributed to the Self, which is by nature unattached (*asaṅga*). 4. And [it is] "form" (*rūpa*).

888. But he who possesses knowledge, O Mṛtyu, with a disciplined mind, his senses are then under control like well-trained horses following a charioteer. However, he who lacks knowledge, O Mṛtyu, being without a disciplined mind, is always impure.

He does not attain that state, and he enters the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). But the mortal who possesses discernment (vijñāna), whose mind is composed, who is self-controlled and pure—he attains that state; having gone there, he is not born again. He for whom discernment is the charioteer and the mind is the bridle of the reins—he reaches the end of the journey, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which belongs to the embodied beings beginning with the gods.

That supreme, unsurpassed state is Śiva, whose form is with Ambā. O Mother, for those who have ascended the path of Viṣṇu and for other embodied beings as well, what else could there be except the supreme state belonging to Mahādeva? || 22-24 ||

Furthermore, for that person who possesses discriminative knowledge and is endowed with a mind that is concentrated by means of the opposite of repetition, his senses can be brought under his own control; that is to say, they can be directed or withdrawn like well-trained horses. || 19 ||

He states that these two are, respectively, the qualified candidates for transmigratory existence and liberation—beginning with the words "But he who... He who is devoid of knowledge as previously described, whose mind is uncontrolled, and who is therefore impure and lacking in taste for the truth, being led astray by desire even toward what should not be done—that ignorant person does not attain this supreme Brahman, known as the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which is to be reached and is symbolized by the *praṇava*. Not only does he fail to attain That, but he also attains the cycle of transmigratory existence characterized by birth, death, and so forth, along with its dissolution. || 20 ||

But he who is the opposite of that—one possessing discriminative knowledge, whose mind is concentrated, and for that very reason who is always and at all times pure and clean—he attains the Brahman that is to be reached there. He specifies that which is to be reached by saying "from which": because from that attained state, having fallen away, he is not born again; he does not enter the cycle of worldly existence. The meaning is that he attains the nature of Brahman, characterized by non-return. 21.

Furthermore, it explains the destruction of the sixfold path with the words "by means of discernment" (*vijñāna*). Discernment is the knowledge that distinguishes the Self from the non-Self through the removal of doubt. The mind is characterized by conceptualization and discursive thought. Thus, being led by the charioteer whose nature is discernment, and having restrained the mind, the wise man reaches the further shore of the course of saṃsāra. Through the knowledge of the true nature of one's own self, he is liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra and so forth. And that further shore belongs to Brahman, which is beyond the reach of speech and mind.

The "supreme" (*parama*) means most excellent; the "state" (*pada*) refers to that which is to be reached or attained—namely, one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), whose sole flavor is existence-consciousness-bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda*). (22) [He himself explains the Vedic statement, "That is the supreme state," with the words: "That which is the state..."

"That wherein one knows nothing else and hears nothing else"—this non-dual reality, which is the destruction of the triad [of knower, known, and knowing], is indeed the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*) for all embodied beings, including gods and humans. Because it consists of unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*), it is the very goal desired by all. It is this very supreme state that has become Śiva, who assumes the form of Ardhanārīśvara through his power of grace (*līlayā*). || 23 ||

The meaning is that this very form of Paraśiva—whose sole essence is consciousness and bliss—is the supreme state for Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the others who possess bodies through the influence of the *guṇas*, as well as for Indra and the rest. || 24 || Who else could be the supreme goal to be attained by Śiva, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and all other embodied beings, apart from Mahādeva, who assumes the form of Ardhanārīśvara? || 23–24 ||

(To explain the subtlety and transcendence of Śarabha Maheśvara, it is said: The senses are directed toward objects. (The objects themselves reside within bodies by means of the instruments—the senses—and through the subtle body). There is no entity whatsoever that is entirely distinct from the senses and their objects.

The commentary clearly states: "The supreme, excellent station (*pada*) of Viṣṇu, who is the Supreme Brahman, is his true nature (*satattva*). Here, *satattva* means his essential form (*svarūpa*). The genitive case (*viṣṇoḥ*) is used figuratively (*aupacārikī*). However, others interpret it thus: "He protects" and so forth refers to the meaning of "thou" (*tvam-artha*); "of Viṣṇu" refers to that which is denoted by the word "he" (*tat-pada-vācya*); and "the supreme station" is the meaning indicated by secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā-artha*). If this were the case, the meaning would come to be that the supreme station is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Viṣṇu as possessing attributes (*saviśeṣa*). 5. 1–5.

Chapter 19, Verse 889: The objects of the senses are superior to the senses; the mind is superior to these objects; the intellect is superior to the mind; and the Great Self (Mahat) is superior to the intellect. (25) The Unmanifest (Avyakta) is superior to the Great Self; the Puruṣa is superior to the Unmanifest. There is nothing superior to the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal. (26)

By means of the verse beginning with "Beyond the senses" (*indriyebhyaḥ*), [the text] demonstrates the unsurpassed subtlety and so forth of the Supreme Reality, which is to be reached through the progressive sequence of increasing subtlety, pervasiveness, and perceptibility among the senses and the rest. First, the senses, being products of the elements, are gross; and those objects—namely the sense-objects such as sound and the rest—by which they are impelled toward their respective activities, are "beyond" (*parāḥ*) the senses, which are their own effects, being more subtle and greater in magnitude.

Beyond those objects, the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*) that constitutes the mind and is denoted by the word "mind" (*manas*) is superior. Beyond even that mind is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is subtler, greater, and the source of the self. That which constitutes the subtle element initiating determination (*adhyavasāya*) is denoted by the word "intellect. Beyond even that intellect is the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*), which is its collective totality (*samaṣṭi*); it is the intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha, which transcends the individual intellects.

Because it is the cause of all intellects (*buddhi*), it is subtler than them, all-pervasive, and inward-facing. Therefore, even beyond the Great One (*mahat*), the Unmanifest (*avyakta*)—which is correctly described as being more subtle, inward-facing, greater than all else, unevolved, consisting of name and form, the seed of the entire world, and synonymous with terms such as *māyā* and *prakṛti*—is superior. Even beyond that Unmanifest, the Self (*ātman*) is more subtle and is the cause of everything.

For this very reason, the Puruṣa is the fulfiller of the entire manifold of effects by means of his own nature; or rather, he is called Puruṣa because he lies within (śete) all things as the "Full" (pūrum). Because he is the innermost self of all, the author says "from the Puruṣa" in order to preclude the possibility of anything else subtler than him. There is indeed no entity whatsoever superior to the Puruṣa, who is the innermost self and whose nature is pure consciousness. This is because the qualities of subtlety, greatness, and being the innermost self find their ultimate limit in him alone.

That alone is the supreme pinnacle, the ultimate ground; that alone is the supreme, most excellent goal (mati)—the object to be reached and attained—by those travelers who wander in saṃsāra. Other goals, however, are inferior because they involve return; but the goal described above is supreme because it is free from return. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "That which, once gone, they do not return from—that is my supreme abode. And since this consists in the attainment of one's own essential nature through the realization of the inner Self, it is also the supreme state of pure knowledge.
Or rather, the meaning is that its impermanence should not be suspected, because it is established by the necessity of there being no other possible course of action. || 2526 ||

No. In the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*, it was stated: "The instrument (*karaṇa*) is merely another configuration (*saṃsthānāntara*) of the object itself, acting as its grasper" (2.4.11). This has also been made clear in the commentary on the relevant passage. For a cause must indeed be distinct from its own effect. Therefore, the mind (*manas*) is distinct [from the body]. (By the word *manas*, the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) that constitute the mind are intended.)

Alternatively, one should accept the interpretation that this is determined by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*). Since it is the cause of the elements, it is beyond the elements; beyond the mind is the intellect (*buddhi*)—whether the intellect is understood as the originator of the elements or as the meaning of the word "intellect" in the Lord's resolve, such as "May I become many. Beyond the intellect is the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*)—the Great Self being Hiraṇyagarbha.

Alternatively, the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is indeed the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*). From the Great One comes the Unmanifest (*avyakta*)—that which is well-known by names such as *māyā* and so forth. It is appropriate to understand that even beyond *māyā* is the Illuder (*māyin*). Beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa-Self; there is nothing higher than the Puruṣa. In Him alone everything is contained (He is the ultimate limit of transcendence), and He is the most excellent object to be attained. (25–26)

The Puruṣa is Śiva himself, whose nature consists of Truth and the rest; because he is *pūrṇa* (complete/perfect) here, he is called *Puruṣa*. [The root] *pṛ* (to fill/complete) is explained as *pūrī āpyāyane* (Dhātupāṭha 1.869). By resorting to the *bāhulaka* rule, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Alternatively, there is also a *curādika* root *pūrī* in the sense of "to heap together" (*saṃghāte*), from which the suffix *pacādyac* is added.

1. "For the sake of perfect knowledge, the Person is established here as superior to all; the teachers have indeed concluded in the *Ādhyāna-adhikaraṇa* (3.3.7.14) that what is intended here is not the mutual superiority of other [entities]. 2. Or rather: "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot; the Self alone, when joined, is the enjoyer, the master, and is called the Great One.

3. In the *Ānumānika-adhikaraṇa*, it was established with great effort that the body is denoted by the word *avyakta*; since the body also possesses the nature of being illusory (*māyika*), the interpretation here as *māyā* is entirely appropriate. 4. [The reading] *svarūpa* is found in the Dha. and Ca. manuscripts.

890. The Brahmagītā states: "The Puruṣa is indeed the fourth [state], Śiva; he is characterized by truth and other qualities. At the time of the cosmic dissolution, he is either Viṣṇu or the unborn Brahmā. (27)

This Self, though hidden within all beings, does not shine forth; it is perceived by those who possess keen vision through a refined and subtle intellect. The wise man should restrain speech within the mind; he should restrain the mind within the intellect; and he should restrain the intellect within the Great Self. || 29 ||

He himself explains the word *puruṣa* found in the scripture: "The one named *puruṣa*" refers to that which is free from the three kinds of limitation (*pariccheda*), characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, and is the very Supreme Lord directly denoted by the term *puruṣa*. It is He alone who, in order to manifest His own nature as the embodiment of Śiva-Śakti, assumes a form consisting of half-man and half-woman (*ardhanārīśvara*). The meaning is that even the forms of the qualities (*guṇamūrti*) such as Brahmā and the others are not distinct from Him. [Verse 27] "This [Self] in all... and so forth.

This Puruṣa, whose nature has been described, is concealed by the ignorance of obscuration within all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; though he dwells as their very support, he is not manifest because his distinction from the intellect and other faculties is obscured by delusion.

Even so, that person is able to see—that is, he is capable of perceiving—the reality of the Self, which is exceedingly subtle and difficult to perceive, by means of an intellect that is tranquil, restrained, withdrawn from external objects, focused on a single point, and therefore steady. (28) He states the means for that perception: "One should restrain," etc. One should restrain—that is, one should withdraw—the entire collection of external sense organs, indicated here by the word "all" (*sarva*), into the mind.
By reading *avratamanasi* with the locative ending, [the author] refers to the Vedic textual reading *yached vāṅmanasī*.

(3.1.134) By adding *ha*, the word *pūraṇam* is formed. The person who brings about the completion of all things is the Puruṣa. In reality, however, from the root *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" and "filling" (*juhoty-ādi*, *parasmaipada*), by taking the *uṇādi* suffix *kuṣan* (4.75), the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *u* according to *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (7.1.102); since it is certain that this [substitute] is followed by *r* (*rapara*), the word *puruṣa* is thus formed. Its meaning is: "that by which [all things] are filled."

Therefore, the *Nirukta* states: "From the root *pṛ*, [the suffix] *vāḥ*" (*2.1.4*). Although the word *puruṣa* is derived from the root *pṛ* in the sense of "to go forward" (*pura agragamane*; Dhatupatha 590), as explained under the *Uṇādi* sūtra "from *pṛ*, *kuṣan*" (*Si. Kau.* 4718)—meaning "one who goes forward"—nevertheless, in the commentary on the aforementioned *Nirukta* passage by Durga, the suffix *kuṣan* is accepted after the root *pṛ*. Yāska Muni [states]: "By that, this [world] was filled with *puruṣa*" (*Bhava.*).
3.9) This scripture is cited as the basis for the aforementioned etymological definition. They alone manifest as Ardhanārīśvara; neither Rudra, Viṣṇu, nor Brahmā exists apart from them. || 27 ||

This Supreme Person alone is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all living beings; therefore, although He exists, He does not appear distinct from the body, the senses, and so forth. He is perceived only by those whose intellect is subtle and one-pointed. [The state of being] endowed with the means [of realization] is *saukṣmya-darśitā*. The author of the *Bhāmatī* has clarified the meaning of this perfection (*pauṣkalya*) as follows: "It refers to the state of being fully developed."

The intellect (*buddhi*) is the root; one must correctly perform hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), and possess one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), having already accomplished the practice of *nididhyāsana*. || 28 || A person of discrimination (*vivekī*) should withdraw all the channels of expression, such as speech and the rest, into the mind (*manas*), and withdraw the mind into the intellect (*buddhi*). Then, his...

The teachers, however, say: "One should experience [the Self] through meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*) in this sequence: first, 'I am indeed distinguished by the mind,' which is superior to the senses; then, 'I am distinguished by the intellect (*buddhi*); then, 'I am the individual soul (*jīva*'); and finally, 'I am the Self devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*). In this regard, an investigation into the sheaths (*kośa*) described in the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad* may also be helpful. 2. *ḍa* and *ca* read *śasya śa*.

Chapter 11 That which is beginningless, without touch, formless, undecaying, likewise without taste, eternal, and without smell; that which is infinite and beyond the Great (Mahat)—having perceived that which is heard [in scripture] as such, one is liberated from the mouth of death. The Great Lord (Maheśa) indeed taught this to Aruṇi, but he did not teach it to anyone else, for he knew that it would not endure among others. However, a certain wise man, seeking immortality, received this self-knowledge through faith.

The phrase "dagdhvā chāndasam" (having burnt the Vedic [form]) is thus explained. One should withdraw the mind—which has its organs of action withdrawn—into the self of the intellect (*buddhyātman*), which consists of the nature of light. Then, one should restrain that intellect-self, which is of the nature of determinative knowledge, within the Great Self (*mahadātman*), which is its collective totality, more subtle, and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Hiraṇyagarbha.

And one should restrain that principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), known as the Great Self (mahadātman) or the state of Hiraṇyagarbha, within the primary Self—which is tranquil, devoid of all specific forms, changeless, the innermost of all, and whose nature is pure consciousness alone. The meaning is that, having thus dissolved everything from the ego (ahaṃkāra) down to the causal source, one should become intent upon the contemplation of the supreme, perfect, self-luminous, and conscious Self. || 29 ||

Since it is observed that among the elements beginning with earth, there is a gradation of subtlety due to the successive reduction of one quality at each stage, what need is there to mention the unsurpassed subtlety of that which is devoid of all qualities such as sound? Intending this very point, he characterizes its true nature by negating those qualities, saying "without sound. The term "unborn" (*aja*) has already been explained.

"Imperishable" (*avyaya*) means that whatever possesses sound and other qualities is subject to the nature of decay; however, this very essence of Paraśiva, being devoid of sound and the like, does not perish nor diminish, and is thus imperishable and indestructible. "Without taste" (*arasa*) is the exclusion of taste, which is a quality of fluidity. Because it is imperishable, it is eternal; such is the nature of this reality. "Beginningless" (*anādi*): "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to a cause, and it is devoid of that. "Endless" (*ananta*): "end" (*anta*) refers to an effect, and it is devoid of that.

Since transformation into the form of an effect is the cause of impermanence for that which possesses a cause, both of these are excluded by this [description]. From the Great One (*mahat*), known as the principle of *mahat-tattva*, there arises the intellect (*buddhi*), which is of a different nature—meaning it has the nature of eternal consciousness. It is firm, immovable, eternal, and changeless. Having perceived—that is, having ascertained—Brahman to be of such a kind, one is liberated from the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), characterized by ignorance, desire, and action, which leads to both the age of truth (*satyayuga*) and the age of untruth (*anṛtayuga*). || 30 ||

The collective intellect (*samaṣṭi-buddhi*) is likewise Hiraṇyagarbha; its dissolution should also be understood as occurring within the non-dual Self (*nirviśeṣātman*). (The withdrawal of the senses while the mind remains awake is indeed their dissolution into the mind). Therefore, at the very outset, it is necessary to withdraw from the perception of "I" and "mine" regarding the body, as well as from bodily movements.

Furthermore, the mind (*mana*) consists of volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*); it does not remain fixed on a single point. When the intellect (*buddhi*) awakens—remaining as a single, firm determination—and the mind becomes motionless such that volitional constructs and the like no longer arise, this is the "binding" of the mind, which is its withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*). There is no separate intellect apart from the all-pervading Hiraṇyagarbha; to ascertain this is the supreme withdrawal of the intellect. And so forth.

The determination of one's own non-differentiation (*nirviśeṣatā*)—the certainty that there is not even a hair’s breadth or a mountain’s height of difference [between oneself and Brahman]—is the final dissolution. This has been described as one stage of *nididhyāsana*. The dissolution of the intellect (*buddhi*) can also be understood as occurring within the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).

In the section concerning those who rely on inference (1.4.1), while explaining the meaning of the relevant scriptural passage, the Commentator has presented this alternative: "Even in that case, one should restrain the intellect within the Great Self, the experiencer, by bringing about its refinement. In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad] as well, the experiencer is indeed situated within the agent. This succession is clearly elucidated in the famous verse from the Pañcadaśī (3.2): "Water... [and so forth].

One who knows [the Self] alone is truly wise; one who acts is not—such is the intended thought. || 29 || The Self is devoid of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; in it, no deficiency ever arises. It is neither cause nor effect; it stands beyond both the individual and the collective intellect (*buddhi*). Being eternally immutable (*kūṭastha*), it is only through the certain realization of that very Self that liberation can be attained.
No doubt can be raised regarding this instruction from Yama, for he knows correctly the means to escape from death. || 30 ||

1. From this, he summarizes the fourth verse: "Having created others [the senses], He has cast us aside"—this should be supplied as the ellipsis to complete the sense. For the senses do not perish because they are directed outward; rather, it is we who would perish in such a state.

892. The *Brahmagītā* says further: "Fools pursue desires; they go toward what is contrary [to their true nature] due to their own delusion. But the wise, having known the reality of the Self, go to that very reality, unattached to desires. (22) "By this alone one attains the essence of the Self, which is beyond sound and beyond form. What more could be desired here? (32)

To the question, "Why is this Self, described as such, not perceived? he states the reason: "Parāñci" (turned away). The Great Lord, the Supreme Ruler and creator of the world, having created the "khāni"—the sense organs such as the ear, characterized by their respective forms—and having made them "parāñci," meaning turned outward by nature toward the manifestation of external objects like sound, He "uttered" (*utṛdirat*) them. The verbal root *utṛdir* signifies "to injure" or "to disregard. (Note: The term *khāni* refers to the apertures or cavities of the senses; *parāñci* indicates that these senses are oriented toward external objects; *utṛdirat* implies that the Lord withdrew or disregarded those senses from the Self so that they would not perceive it.)

Since this is so, therefore a person looks outward through the senses such as sight and hearing; he perceives only external objects through speech and the other senses, and does not know the nature of the Self. Nevertheless, some wise man, desiring immortality—liberation—having turned back the senses such as sight and hearing, which are the means for perceiving external objects, having withdrawn them from their respective domains, beholds the inner Self characterized by the previously described marks, whose nature is beyond the cycle of transmigratory existence.
[The use of the present tense here is according to the rule: "In Vedic usage (chandas), the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *laṭ* [tenses may be used interchangeably]. || 31 ||

"Turning away," it is said: fools and ignorant people pursue their desires—the objects of desire such as sound and other external sense-objects. Those seekers of pleasure go toward the extended burden of fetters, which is the collection of ignorance, desire, and action that constitutes death. He states the reason for this: "By their own," meaning by the power of the delusion of the self, which is the obscuration of ignorance.

When there is the reversal of fearlessness and egoism, wise and discerning people—having known and directly realized immortality, which is characterized by abiding in the true nature of the Self—being unattached and unbound, go to and attain that eternal, supreme reality, the Brahman-bridge. (32) He states the means for attaining that [Brahman] with the words "by which": By which, having crossed over the torrent of the world, one does not grieve; by that very same path, O son of Pr̥thā, cross over [the world]. (33) By which means, having crossed over the torrent of the world consisting of the cycle of birth and death, one does not grieve; by that very same path, O son of Pr̥thā, cross over this world. (33) What is that? He says: Knowledge and non-knowledge are said to be distinct. I shall tell you what knowledge is, and what non-knowledge is. Knowledge is said to be that by which one knows the One Imperishable; non-knowledge is said to be what is otherwise. (34) Knowledge and non-knowledge are said to be distinct from each other. I shall tell you what knowledge is, and what non-knowledge is. Knowledge is said to be that by which one knows the One Imperishable, the Supreme Reality; non-knowledge is said to be what is otherwise, that which is different from it. (34) What is that knowledge? He says: Those who perceive diversity here go from death to death. Those who perceive the manifoldness of the One Imperishable enter into darkness. (35) Those who perceive diversity—that is, those who see various separate entities here in this world—go from death to death; they do not escape the cycle of rebirth. But those who perceive the manifoldness of the One Imperishable—the manyfold manifestations of the single, undivided Reality—enter into darkness, meaning they fall into ignorance. (35) Furthermore: But those who perceive the One in the diverse, and the diverse in the One, they, being wise, proceed from death to immortality. (36) But those who perceive the One, the Supreme Reality, within the diverse multitude of beings, and perceive the diverse manifestations within the One Reality—they, being wise, proceed from death to immortality, that is, they attain liberation. (36) What is that One? He says: Light and darkness are said to be distinct, as are pleasure and pain. Know that non-knowledge is darkness, and knowledge is said to be light. (37) Light and darkness are said to be distinct from each other, as are pleasure and pain. Know that non-knowledge is darkness, because it obscures the true nature of things; and knowledge is said to be light, because it reveals the truth. (37) How does one transcend these two? He says: One reaches the end of non-knowledge through knowledge; thereafter, one attains the immortal state. When knowledge has arisen, one sees the One through the mind's eye even while in this world. (38) One reaches the end of non-knowledge through knowledge; thereafter, one attains the immortal state. When knowledge has arisen, one sees the One, the Supreme Reality, through the mind's eye even while in this world. (38) What is that One? He says: The sun does not illuminate That, nor the moon, nor fire. Having gone there, one does not return—that is My supreme abode. (39) The sun does not illuminate That, nor the moon, nor fire. Having gone there, one does not return—that is My supreme abode. (39) What is the nature of that supreme abode? He says: A portion of Mine, having become the individual soul (jīva), draws the five senses and the mind, which is the sixth, toward the objects of the senses. (40) A portion of Mine, having become the individual soul, draws the five senses and the mind, which is the sixth, toward the objects of the senses. (40) How does it draw them? He says: When the sovereign presides over the ear, the eye, the organs of touch, taste, and smell, and the mind, then it enjoys the objects of the senses. (41) When the sovereign presides over the ear, the eye, the organs of touch, taste, and smell, and the mind, then it enjoys the objects of the senses. (41) What is the nature of that sovereign? He says: Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect. Higher than the intellect is the Great Soul (Mahat); higher than the Great

By means of that consciousness (*vijñāna*) which, while moving through the various objects of the senses, clearly perceives—that is, knows with distinct clarity—the connections between pairs of opposites (*mithuna*), such as pleasure and pain; by this very [consciousness], which is distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth, he perceives those [objects] through the mode of pure consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*). The meaning is this: that which is the witness of all cognitions of forms and so forth is alone the Self (*ātman*); however, the aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth is not the Self, because, being possessed of form and other qualities, it lacks selfhood (*anātmatva*), like a jar or similar objects. What remains to be known in this world? Nothing at all.
The meaning is that everything whatsoever is to be known as nothing other than the Self in the form of pure consciousness; not even the slightest thing remains apart from it. || 33 ||

I have driven away from me those who were my own kin; indeed, they have acted as enemies toward me. It is as if they have killed them by turning them outward. (If they had not been so, they would have been helpful in attaining immortality; by turning them outward, their capacity was not allowed to remain—this is the meaning. For this reason, *hari* (the one who takes away) takes away power (*śakti*) only when it is directed toward external objects of knowledge.

He, one's own Self, is never seen by anyone. Only a rare, steadfast person becomes capable of it—one who, desiring the attainment of immortality, turns the senses away from their objects and beholds the inner Self (pratyagātmā). [3-31] Ignorant people continue to run after external objects that serve as the targets of desire. They become ensnared in the coils of the serpent of death, which is their own delusion (moha). Those who are the opposite of these...

The person of discrimination, having completely renounced all desires, realizes the immortality of the inner self (pratyagātman) and attains the immutable, eternal Supreme Śiva. || 32 || [Through the knowledge of the Self, one transcends the external.]

1. First, let us examine the meaning of "discrimination" (*viveka*). By what means is there the non-arrival at objects? Is it through the presence (*āsā*) or the absence (*anāsā*) [of discrimination]? It cannot be the second [alternative], because that is impossible. Regarding the first, let it be analyzed: what is its nature? If one suggests it consists of the forms of waking and so forth, that too is not correct; for even waking and the other states are seen to be permeated by that [discrimination], and it is illogical for that which is pervasive to be distinct from those excluded [from it]. Furthermore, it is established that these [states] are merely conceptual constructs (*kalpita*). This was indicated in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa* (11.68). 2. [Variant reading]: ...deveva | 4.
