The manner of inference, however, is as follows: from observing the coming and going of the senses, one realizes that they are not the Self; then, through happiness, one awakens to the state of being Brahman within oneself, who is the witness of those [senses]. If [the Self] is dull, then by means of a subtle intellect, one perceives its own nature after gradually discriminating it from the aggregate of the senses, the intellect, and the agent—[which is] the unmanifest form. (11.101-2) Common usage intends by "Sattva" and "Ahaṅkāra" [the ego-sense]; following that convention, even in scripture, the intellect (*buddhi*) or indeed the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) may be [meant]. [This refers to] the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

900. He who stands firm in the Song of Brahman (brahmagītā) does not falter; no one can lead him away by means of sacrifice or ritual. When the Self is thoroughly prepared by the heart, by wisdom, and by the mind, then that Self can be known through the grace [of the teacher]. 55.

Now, one might ask: "How can this unconditioned Self be known? Anticipating this doubt, the text says: "It is not within the range of sight" (*na saṃdṛśe*). The true nature (*svarūpa*) of the inner Self does not abide within the sphere of perception (*saṃdarśana-viṣaya*). Therefore, it cannot be reached by the eye; this is merely an illustration, meaning it cannot be perceived by any sense organ whatsoever, such as the eyes and so forth. If that is so, how then is it to be seen? It is said: "By the heart, by thought, and by meditation" (*hṛdā matvā manīṣā*). Here, "heart" refers to the intellect (*manas*), and "thought" (*manīṣā*) refers to its function in the form of volition and the like.
Thus, by such an intellect—that is, by the mind characterized by subtle reflection—and by being thoroughly disciplined through right meditation, this Self can be directly perceived. || 55 ||

Once this has become one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*), the practitioner becomes endowed with supreme intelligence and transcends all sorrow. (51-52) The mind is superior to these [senses]; from the mind, its causal constituent, *sattva*, is superior; superior even to that is the collective intelligence (*samasthi-buddhi*) of Hiraṇyagarbha; and superior to that is its cause, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Beyond the unmanifest (avyakta) is Śiva himself, all-pervading and beyond the reach of the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties; by knowing Him, a person attains immortality for himself. (53-54) The inner self (pratyagātman) never becomes an object of perception for itself; no one sees it with the eyes. It is perceived through the certainty (*smya*) produced by the intellect (*buddhi*) which governs the mind (*manaḥ*) within the heart. (55)

The Self, manifested on all sides, can be realized exactly as it is. (It should be remembered that whatever the eyes and other senses perceive is a visible object, and therefore illusory. If one were to see even the Supreme Self, that too would be subject to the status of being illusory. Although the forms of the Supreme Self appear in that same way, these forms are merely products of *māyā*; they are indeed illusory.)

We can perceive [the world] only as an object, and that perception is indeed false. As for the vision that occurs when it is not an object—that is, through direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*)—that alone is the vision of Śiva. Regardless of which person, driven by the intensity of their spiritual longing, may have regarded what was perceived as an object to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it is certain that what he saw was actually false. This is another matter: the body, the forms, and so forth, which were the objects of appearance, are real; however, that which appeared [as the self] is indeed unreal.

The direct, immediate, and truly realized vision (*sākṣāt-aparokṣa-vastava-darśana*) is the very nature of the Supreme Lord. While the means to attain this may include the vision of His *rūpa* (form) and so forth, to consider that alone as the ultimate goal is erroneous. By this, questions such as "Who has seen the Supreme Self? are answered. What is the meaning of "seen"? If you mean seeing with the eyes and other senses, then the answer is: "No one."

If your intent is this, O Anubhava, then your own experience is the authority for all those who know Brahman! Furthermore, what does it matter to the seeker whether someone has given it or not? What is the use of the appearance of another's seeing? Is that the truth? This is the truly appropriate question: "How indeed might one know That? (Śloka).

43) The *upaniṣad* clearly states: "But how may I know that? How can I comprehend it? It is in response to this very inquiry that it is said: "With the heart (*hṛdā*), with wisdom (*manīṣā*)," and so forth. Through *hṛdā*, one may understand *śravaṇa* (hearing); through *manīṣā*, *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation); and through *manasā*, *manana* (reflection). According to the commentary, *hṛdā* and *manīṣā* are to be understood as being in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

One should contemplate through *manīṣā* (insight) by means of the illumination of the *śruti*, and through *manas* (the mind) by means of the method of reasoning (*nyāya*). Alternatively, the meaning of *hṛdā* (with the heart) is through the negation of everything by means of passages such as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*); from that, *manīṣā* arises as the knowledge of the Self, and consequently, everything appears as Brahman alone through the *manas*. Or else, *hṛdā* means with love, and *manīṣā* means with discriminative intellect (*vivekabuddhi*), while *manasā* means with undivided knowledge (*akhaṇḍajñāna*).

Those who seek the means [to liberation] should study in detail that very extensive exposition which the Teacher has provided elsewhere in his commentaries (3.13, 4.17, 4.20). || 55 || Chapter on Being and Non-being—91. Thus, by means of this reasoning, mortals come to know Brahman as the direct cause of the world, which consists of being and non-being; through knowledge and yoga alone, they become liberated. || 56 ||

He summarizes the meaning of the Vedic statement, "That which is here," along with the remaining portion of the text and the purport of the entire context, by saying "Thus" (evam). Thus ends the commentary on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.

The Śruti declares that the Supreme Brahman is the direct witness of the entire world, consisting of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). Those who realize Him through scripture and reasoning by means of this aforementioned method, attain liberation through the power of that realization. || 56 ||

(Now, in this *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, Brahmā speaks as follows, summarizing its essence: That which is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) proclaimed by the Vedas—the aforementioned Supreme Reality—possesses an inconceivable and inexhaustible power; for the Knowable Brahman created the beginningless universe, and only that which possesses power can effect such a feat. That non-dual Brahman is of the nature of Truth (*satya*), Bliss (*ānanda*), Non-attachment (*asaṅga*), and Pure Consciousness (*jñānamātra*). It is...

That very Śakti becomes the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the enjoyed (*bhogya*), and the instrument (*itara*)—thus possessing these three distinct aspects. (This was stated precisely to dispel any doubt regarding the reality of Śakti: "While remaining non-dual, true, and without a second, just as one who is truly one appears as two, so too has Brahman become three. For this duality or triad...)

Indeed, while being unreal, the capacity for being one, two, or three is real. Being is natural; it is for the sake of producing these various states that the *Upaniṣad* introduces "the yoga of power" (4.1) and then calls it *māyā* (4.10). Furthermore, its independent existence is denied by the statement, "There is no other than Him capable of ruling" (6.17).

By saying, “My nature” (7.4), the Blessed Lord has also negated its independence. There are two primary distinctions between *māyā* and the *prakṛti* favored by the Sāṃkhyas: they regard *prakṛti* as real and independent, whereas *māyā* is illusory and dependent.

The description in the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad] is difficult to understand; having become confused by it, one might mistakenly accept *prakṛti* as being intended there. However, this is merely the result of failing to analyze that context. Beginning with the passage "without sound" (1.1.5), the great sage Pārāśarya has established at great length that *prakṛti* is not accepted by the Śruti. This is true for almost every instance where...

The view that my own nature (*prakṛti*) is the supporter [of the soul] has arisen; however, that very [view] has already been examined. Therefore, it is solely due to a deficiency in hearing (*śravaṇa*) that the delusion regarding *prakṛti-śrotṛtva* (the state of being the hearer of nature) occurs. Since this summary of the meaning of the Upaniṣad is now being commenced from the very beginning, the possibility of such a delusion is natural.

Therefore, one should remove the possibility of that delusion by attaining a thorough understanding of the Upaniṣad. Earlier, it was stated, "That very power of the Self" (1.3). By saying "the power of the Self" (*devātmabhakti*) instead of "the power of the gods" (*devabhakti*), the meaning is that this power is not separate from or independent of the Divine. Through the statement, "Thinking [it] as such, one wanders in delusion" (1.6), the fact that worldly existence (*saṃsaraṇa*) is rooted in ignorance and is the product of the perception of duality (*bhedadṛṣṭi*) has been made clear.

By stating that liberation comes from knowledge in the verse, “Having known [the Self], they are freed from the womb” (1.7), the denial of bondage as something distinct from ignorance is being established. In the verse, “The perishable is primary matter” (1.10), the eternally accepted *pradhāna* of the Sāṃkhya is explicitly called the "perishable"; this is never acceptable to the Sāṃkhya. The second chapter primarily teaches the means (*sādhana*). The third chapter begins with the verse, “He rules by means of the ruling powers” (3.47).

When the distinction of the *iḍā* [vital breath] was being established, it was stated in the second mantra: "They did not stand for a second. Furthermore, by the words "one encompassing all" (*ekaṃ pariveṣṭāram*, 3.7), the existence of any other all-pervading reality was negated. Then, by the statement "The Person alone is all this" (*puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam*, 3.15), the possibility of any other principle was blocked. At the beginning of the *Cūḍālā* [dialogue], it is said: "Brahman is indeed that which is beyond this; it possesses some inconceivable power."
When pierced by power, that reality becomes non-dual; it is the oneness of bliss, non-attachment, and pure consciousness. || 57 ||

Thus, the supreme unity of the single essence of consciousness, bliss, and the one *brahman* has been shown according to the Kaṭha and Śākha Upaniṣads. Now, he demonstrates that same supreme reality even according to the Śvetāśvatara Śākha Upaniṣad, by means of the entire first chapter beginning with "Having thus... and so forth.

For therein, in order to lead one to understand that Brahman which is the cause of the world, the text first raises as prima facie views (pūrvapakṣa) that time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, and so forth are the causes of the world—beginning with the words "Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance"—and then describes the causality of Brahman, who is accompanied by the power of Māyā, who is self-luminous, whose essence is consciousness, and who is concealed by his own qualities, in the verse: "Those who have attained the yoga of meditation perceived that Power, which is difficult to perceive and hidden by its own qualities. Thus, the causality of Brahman is described.

It demonstrates His possession of such power with the words "this [Vidyā]": that Vidyā which was previously enumerated—by means of that, the Brahman which is to be known and is well-known in the Kaṭha, Vedānta, and other texts—is such that it is "inconceivable" (acintyavidhā), meaning there exists in Him a certain power indeed that is inconceivable and capable of accomplishing all that is difficult to achieve. For otherwise, in one devoid of that power, the causality described in passages such as "He created fire" would be untenable; this is the meaning.

In this context, a threefold division—consisting of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), and the bestower of enjoyment (*bhogaprada*)—is intended to be established. Anticipating the objection as to how this can be possible within the non-dual Brahman, he says "by its power" (*śakyā*): that non-dual Brahman, characterized by existence (*sat*) and so forth, becomes possessed of distinctions through its power—that is, through *māyā*, which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—just as space is divided by limiting adjuncts such as jars and the like. (57)

It has been stated: "In the beginning, He alone existed. However, within that very mantra, Māyāvāda is clarified in two ways: "He withdraws [it] back into Himself at the end" (*vi ceti cānte*), meaning "at the end, He causes it to go away into Himself"; and "in the beginning, He was all this" (*ādau sa viśvam*). Thus, in the beginning everything was of the nature of Śiva alone, and at the end, Śiva again dissolves everything back into Himself.

This activity is possible only through *māyā-śakti*, and not otherwise. That which is called "unborn" (*ajā*) in verse 4.5 is referred to as "ignorant" (*anīśā*) in verse 4.7; that is, it is "without mastery" (*anīśa*), meaning it is not independent. Therefore, it cannot be the *pradhāna-prakṛti*. Furthermore, by the phrase "obstructed by *māyā*" (*māyayā saṃniruddhaḥ*) in verse 4.9, *māyā* is explicitly stated to be the cause of bondage. Moreover, in that same context, *māyā* itself is [identified as] *prakṛti*.

It has been clearly established that there is no other [nature] than this; therefore, it is sheer folly to attempt to prove from the verse *ajāmekām* (4.5) in that same chapter that there exists a *prakṛti* other than Māyā. Indeed, at the very beginning of the fifth chapter, ignorance (*avidyā*) residing within Brahman is declared to be the cause of the world, and not some independent *prakṛti*: "The wise ones call it Ignorance, which is difficult to cross, consisting of the three qualities."

In the sixth [chapter], ignorance (*avidyā*) is called "the majesty" (6.1), yet this is also a delusion, by which this wheel of Brahman is made to revolve (6.1). Later, the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) is described (6.8), and that power always acts in dependence upon the possessor of power (*śaktimān*). Furthermore, Paramaśiva is called the "Lord of the field-knower" (*adhānakaṣetrajñapatiḥ*) (6.16).

In this manner, even the *Śvetāśvatara* does not accept an independent reality as *prakṛti*. Therefore, the Vārtikācārya has refuted [this view], stating: "For in the Vedānta, no other cause is established—unlike the Sāṅkhya school—as something distinct from the unborn Knower (*aja-jñātṛ*)" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka-vārtika 4.4.179). || 57 || The one form of Brahman is that of the individual soul (*jīvātma*), and its other form is that of the object of experience (*bhogya*). Beyond these, the form of the Lord (*īśvara*) who bestows experience is also Brahman; whereas the supreme Self (*paramātman*) is its pure form (*śuddha-rūpa*).

1. The two [texts], the *Asmadguravaḥ* and the *Gītāśaveta*, demonstrate a great degree of similarity (Sve. p. 7). Therefore, it should be understood that after stating the correspondence regarding *rati* (pleasure), Brahmā speaks in order to also show the correspondence regarding *smṛti* (memory). 2. And: *ṇanāṃ tatkā°*.

Chapter 19 The one *brahman* is the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the object of experience; the manifold universe (*viśva*) is another form of *brahman*. Beyond this, the *brahman* is the source of all, consisting solely of consciousness, the subtle form of the Supreme. (58) When the sacrifice is completed and everything has been offered into that *brahman*, the individual soul shines forth within the wheel of *brahman*. Having realized through reasoning that the Self and the Impeller are one, the mortal attains immortality. (59)

Through scripture, logic, reasoning, and one's own direct experience, one should know that the living being and the Lord are indeed non-different. Māyā is the cause of enjoyment for the enjoyer; the Supreme Self, by means of these [factors], appears in universal form as the non-agent.

In this context, that form of Brahman which is delimited by *māyā* dominated by *sattva* receives the designation "individual soul" (*jīva*). That which is delimited by *māyā* dominated by *tamas*, however, becomes the world of objects of experience (*bhogya*). Furthermore, another form known as "Lord" (*īśvara*), which has as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) *māyā* dominated by pure *sattva*, provides those experiences. This is what is meant by "another form."

The meaning is that the pure form of that Brahman—which transcends *māyā* and is the sole essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*)—as established by all the Vedāntas, is distinct and different from its conditioned (*sopādhika*) forms. For he will indeed say: "The enjoyer and the object of enjoyment" (Śloka 63). Regarding what is declared in the Śruti by the mantra "the life of all" (1.6)—namely, the soul's wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra through ignorance and its identity with the Self when freed from ignorance—he says: "the life of all."

*Ājīva* is livelihood from all sides; that in which there is the livelihood of all is *sarvājīva*, and in that *sarvājīva*. *Saṃstha* is the end, death, or the final state of all; that in which there is the end of all is *sarvasaṃstha*, and in that *sarvasaṃstha*. Regarding the word *bṛhante*, it should be understood that the suffix *ghan* prescribed by the rule "the roots *jṛ*, *viśi*, and *bhā*" applies here as well.

In that vast and expansive wheel of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāracakra*), the individual soul (*jīva*) is made to wander by its own ignorance (*svāvidyā*) through the power of the enjoyment of objects. However, that soul—by virtue of the merit it has earned, through the grace of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), and by performing the means such as hearing and reflection (*śravaṇa-manana*)—learns of the Lord who is the self of all through hearing the scriptures taught by a guru. Having realized Him as the one without a second through reasoning and intellect, he attains immortality, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). This is the meaning. || 59 ||

Having supplemented another mantra that clearly establishes this identity between the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśvara-tādātmya*), [the author] explains it at 1.9 with the words: "The Knower and the Unknower. The "Knower" is Paraśiva, the referent of the word *tat*, whose nature is undivided consciousness. The "Unknower" is the agent, the enjoyer, whose knowledge is veiled; he is the referent of the word *tvam*. These two, though appearing distinct through conventional perception, are in reality the individual soul and the Lord.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, those two are non-different according to such scriptural statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), as well as by the reasoning that follows them and by the experience of the wise. The meaning is that their difference is caused solely by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); it is not real at all. He shows the limiting adjunct that brings about their difference with the word "Mayā": for the *jīva*, who is the experiencer and the transmigrating self, is made an agent and an enjoyer when he is conditioned by *māyā*—the source of enjoyment consisting primarily of the unreal—which is the material cause of the world.

The Supreme Self, however, is the enjoyer of all objects of experience—whether imagined through the various states such as waking and so forth that are dependent on itself—and is the creator of manifold worlds; yet it is devoid of all the attributes of transmigratory existence, such as being an agent and the like. Therefore, the intended meaning is that their identity is to be firmly resolved upon by abandoning those limiting adjuncts (upādhis). || 60 ||

O Mother! You are the one celebrated in all the Upaniṣads. (58) It is in you that all living beings sustain their livelihood and reside; yet, within this wheel of worldly existence (*saṃsāracakra*) set in motion by Brahman, the individual soul (*jīva*) continues to wander, perceiving itself as separate from Śiva. [You are] the Supreme Brahman, the Self, and the Impeller.

O Śaśaka, by logically regarding Īśvara as non-different [from himself], even he attains immortality. (The reading "Īśvara is made to wander by Śramaṇa" is preferred over "Śramaṇa wanders," according to the commentary. || 59 ||

The nature of indeterminate consciousness is Paraśiva, while the ignorant individual soul (jīva) is perceived as distinct from Him; however, through scripture, reasoning, and the self-experience of the wise, these two are established as non-different. Māyā is the instrumental cause for the experience of the enjoying soul (bhoktā). Although the Supreme Self sustains all things, He remains the non-doer (akartā); such matters as His sustaining them are not [attributable to Him] in that sense. || 60 ||

Māyā is perishable (*kṣara*), whereas the individual soul (*jīva*)—that is, the one to be slain—is imperishable (*akṣara*) and indestructible; for the one self-luminous Lord appears in these two forms as the perishable and the individual soul. That Supreme Śiva...
[1] Ca. and Evam. [2] Jaña. *sthitiśvāpyasmi*. [3] *Yadā pṛthagātmānaṃ preritāraṃ ca matvā juṣṭaḥ*—the meaning is that he rejoices; the Ātmanepada ending is an archaic usage.

904 | The Imperishable (akṣara) is the syllable *Mā*, and the Imperishable is the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). By means of the Self, the one God manifests. Through meditation upon Him, through His nature, and through His state of being, there occurs at the end of the upward breath the cessation of universal illusion (*viśvamāyā*). Having known Him thus, there is the destruction of all bonds; the knot of the heart is untied, and the supreme state is attained. Through the dissolution of the distinction between His sound and His inner form, one attains universal sovereignty, which is the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). || 61-62 ||

For this purpose, one should always remain established in the Self; indeed, there is nothing further to be known. Having understood that the enjoyer, the objects of enjoyment, and the body are the threefold Brahman, one transcends sorrow. (63)

He states the meaning of the mantra, “The perishable is *pradhāna*; the immortal-perishable is *Hara*,” as follows: “The perishable is *māyā*. The perishable (*kṣara*) is that which is subject to decay and destruction; because it is composed of the various categories of limited knowledge (*vidyā*), it is the principle of *māyā*. The imperishable (*akṣara*) is the non-decaying form of Brahman that has attained the state of the individual soul (*jīva*). Both of these, being essentially one, appear as distinct from the self-luminous Supreme Śiva. The meaning is that because the distinction between *māyā* and its effects is superimposed upon Him, they are not separate from Him.

Since immediate liberation is not observed from mere knowledge [of the scriptures], it might be mistakenly thought that [the realization of Brahman] is not the means for that [liberation] because it contradicts direct perception; therefore, to dispel this delusion, he cites the hundredth [sūtra]: "From meditation on That... (tasya). From meditation on That—that is, on Brahman, which is devoid of all distinctions and whose sole essence is consciousness and bliss—arises the knowledge "All this, indeed, is Brahman. This knowledge, born of hearing [the scriptures], is a direct perception whose object is non-duality; from this, the cessation of the phenomenal world of difference occurs.

Thus, by the unification through the application of the identity "I am indeed that Brahman," the notions of "I" and "mine"—which arise from verbal knowledge and the resulting reflection (*manana*)—are removed from the non-returning seeker. Furthermore, through the cultivation of the absence of those [notions] and the realization of one's own nature as being that [Brahman], which is synonymous with *nididhyāsana*, there arises direct, immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) regarding that object. And by that [direct knowledge], the desire for that [worldly existence] is dispelled.

Even when that [avidyā] has been removed, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by it persists until the exhaustion of the fruits of the *prārabdha* karma; therefore, it is not contradictory that the embodied one continues to engage in worldly activity for a limited time even after becoming a knower (*vidvān*). Furthermore, at the end—meaning at the conclusion of the experience of the fruits of the *prārabdha* karma—in the state of *videha-kaivalya*, there occurs the cessation of all *māyā* along with one's own latent impressions. This is the meaning. (61) He cites the scripture that establishes the result of what was stated: "Having known," etc.

By knowing the God—who is luminous, self-manifesting, and the supreme support—in the manner described, there is the removal of all ignorance. 1. The meaning is that one attains the complete destruction of all bonds, such as *māyā* and *karman*, as well as all afflictions (*kleśas*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), and so forth. He explains the scriptural passage, "From the contemplation of Him, after the dissolution of the body, [comes the third state]," with the words beginning with "of Him" (*tasya*).

When the fundamental ignorance has been removed through the direct realization of Brahman as the second [principle], the soul attains the state of liberation, characterized by abiding in absolute consciousness—an independent lordship consisting of all-pervasive sovereignty. || 62 ||

Because its desires are fulfilled and by virtue of its power over *māyā*, it has abandoned this apparent diversity—which exists in the form of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and so forth—and that which has been described as the real, non-dual state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*): this alone is to be known, realized, and directly perceived as the eternal, ever-present Self, abiding as the innermost essence (*pratyagātman*). One might object: "Could there not be something else to be known beyond this? To this he says: "There is nothing beyond this."

Therefore, there exists no other reality whatsoever to be known apart from this Brahman, which is characterized by unsurpassed bliss, according to the Śruti: "Other than this is wretchedness" (*ato'nyad ārtam*). He cites and explains the mantra that establishes the meaning that even this threefold world—which appears through the distinctions of enjoyer, objects of enjoyment, and so forth—does not differ from Brahman when investigated, because it has no existence apart from Brahman, which transcends Māyā; thus he says: "The enjoyer... and "This is Brahman. The form *ambhaḥ* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) usage. || 63 ||

Through meditation, application, and realizing the true nature of reality (if one maintains this vigil, ignorance is dispelled even in this very life), then upon the completion of the fruits of past actions (*prārabdha*), all *māyā* comes to an end.

In the Śruti, *abhidhyāna* is mentioned, the meaning of which has been explained by Śaṅkarācārya as "I am Śiva" with respect to one's own self, and "Śiva is all" with respect to all objects of experience; thus, the meaning of the term *abhidhyāna* is the vision of non-duality (*advaita-darśana*). Likewise, when, through such *abhidhyāna*, the distinction between the meditator (*dhyātṛ*) and the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) vanishes, and the perception of the non-self (*anātma-māyā*) [ceases]...

Chapter 11, Verse 905: "Just as the form of fire situated within its source is not seen, nor indeed is there a destruction of its subtle mark (*liṅga*), yet it exists as fire itself, being held within the source of fuel; even so, O Bhārata, [the Self] is indeed [held] in the body by means of the *praṇava*. (64)

In order to explain the means of knowledge for such a Brahman, [the author] summarizes that which has been traditionally taught in the passage beginning with "As fire... by saying "by friction" (*vahnaiḥ*). The nature (*svarūpa*) of fire residing in its source—that is, fire produced from the source which is its cause, the fire-drill—is not seen by the eye, nor is it perceived by touch; nevertheless, it is certainly not devoid of an inferential mark (*liṅga*). Even when the fire-drill is being rubbed, there exists no visible mark whatsoever that indicates the presence of fire.

That fire, being produced from fuel—meaning from wood in the form of a fire-drill (*araṇi*) by means of a method such as friction—is perceivable by the sense of sight. Just as this is the illustration, so too Brahman, though entered into the aggregate of cause and effect and thus not perceived through discrimination, can nevertheless be grasped by means of a specific method. He shows that method with the words "Then... The word "vā" has the sense of "ca" (and).

And that *brahman* is of two kinds: the moving (*sara*) and the other [the non-moving]. It exists within the body—the physical frame—in the center of the heart-lotus, as the object of meditation and as the object of knowledge, being grasped by means of the *praṇava*, the syllable *oṃ*. This is the meaning. || 64 ||

The objective at that time is the attainment of *sāyujya* (union) with Him, from whom one has completely withdrawn [from all else]. Furthermore, the meaning of *tattvabhāva* is this: through the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of Vedāntic statements, may there occur the descent of unsurpassed bliss—which had been obscured by dualistic delusion (*dvaitabhrama*) and *avidyā*—such that both the intervening dualistic delusion and the root *avidyā* are consumed by the fire of knowledge.

"Therefore, you must understand that the true nature of the oneness of all things is Śiva himself; this is the state of being, the state of reality. (Pañcārthabhāṣya 71–72). This is made clear by the *Anubhūtiprakāśa* (12.28–29). Alternatively, the direct meaning is that hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) constitute meditation (*dhyāna*) because they are to be performed as a single unit.

The logical establishment of the meaning (*artha*) through reasoning is *manana* (reflection), which serves as the broth; the contemplation of the sharp and indivisible Truth is *nididhyāsana* (meditative absorption), which is of the nature of *dhyāna*. *Nididhyāsana* results in the fruit of the cessation of all illusion (*māyā*). Alternatively, within the causal agent, *nididhyāsana* takes the form of the fruit consisting of consciousness and knowledge, resulting in the cessation of universal illusion and the liberation of the body (*videha-kaivalya*). Having known the Supreme Self, all bonds are severed. || 61 ||

With the cessation of *kleśa*, there is no longer birth and death. Upon the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Śiva, when the primal ignorance (*ajñāna*) that is the root of *saṃsāra* is removed, the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) is attained for all those who possess excellence. [The fivefold impurities consist of: external factors such as son, wealth, and so forth; internal factors such as egoism (*ahaṃtā*), possessiveness (*mamatā*), and the like; the six sheaths (*kośa*) such as attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), merit (*puṇya*), demerit (*pāpa*), and so on; or alternatively, the five impurities (*mala*) well-known from the *Kaula Āgamas*, beginning with *avidyā*.

O you who have attained perfection through Yoga, Haṃ! || 62 || This Śiva alone, abiding as the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is the object of knowledge; there is nothing other than Him. If you determine the conclusion by reflecting upon the enjoyer (*bhoktā*), which is the individual soul (*jīva*); the enjoyed (*bhogya*), which is the world (*jagat*); and the impeller (*preraka*), which is the Lord (*īśvara*), you will come to know that Brahman alone—of whom no other exists—is manifesting in these three forms. || 63 ||

The flame and other manifestations of fire, which reside within its own causes such as the *araṇi* wood and so forth, are not perceived; however, one cannot say that their non-existence (*nāśa*) occurs there along with the qualities [of the fuel], because that very fire is indeed perceived in that same fuel and *araṇi* (following the process of friction and so on). (If it were entirely non-existent, it would not appear even in sand.)

Just as oil is never absent from sesame seeds, so too both types of Brahman—the higher and the lower—reside within this body and are attained through the *praṇava*. (64) By making one's own body the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) and the *oṃkāra* the upper fire-drill, and through the constant practice of whirling [the drill] in the form of meditation, [one attains the goal].

906. *Brahmagītā*, Chapter 6: Making one’s own body the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) and the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) the upper fire-drill, one produces [the Self] through the friction of meditation, like fire hidden within wood. (65) As butter is produced from curds, as water is drawn from moist sands, and as oil is extracted from sesame seeds, so is this Self perceived within the self by one who knows it through truth and austerity. (66) The all-pervading Self is contained within the body like clarified butter in milk; its root is the knowledge of the Self and austerity, and it is the supreme goal of those desiring liberation. (67)

He explains how the *praṇava* serves as the means for perceiving That [the Supreme Reality] with the words: "One's own body... Having made the heart—characterized by one’s own body—the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*), and having made the syllable *Oṃ* the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*), the friction produced by the effort of meditation consists of the contemplation of either the higher or the lower Brahman, whether as that which is denoted by the *praṇava* or as its support; that itself is the "rubbing. The repeated practice of this, performed with the persistence of the syllable *dhauk*, is said to be the means for attaining the goal. (9.5)

Until one realizes—that is, perceives directly—the self-nature which is luminous, self-manifesting, and free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), it remains as if hidden. The meaning is that it is just like fire hidden and dissolved within wood, which is brought forth by the churning and friction of the lower and upper kindling sticks. (65) Establishing the realization of the Self through various methods, he teaches the means such as truthfulness and so forth, beginning with the words "Just as...": Just as oil exists pervading sesame seeds, or as...

Clarified butter exists within curd as its essence; water exists pervading rivers that abound with sand; fire exists within the two kindling sticks and their shavings. Just as these substances—oil and the like—though not perceived separately from sesame seeds and so forth, are nevertheless apprehended by one who discriminates through pressing, churning, digging, and friction, even so this Self, which is free from limiting adjuncts and whose sole essence is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, resides hidden within the heart of the self; it is realized through the mind purified by repeated practice such as hearing and reflection.

The connection is as follows: by that person who, possessing means such as truthfulness and austerity—consisting of fasting for specific periods, *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth, as well as one’s own duty (*svadharma*) prescribed according to caste and stage of life—is a seeker who pursues and attains Him; by that person endowed with such means as truthfulness and the rest, He is grasped. For this very reason, it is declared in the Atharvaṇa Upaniṣads: "By truth and by austerity, this Self is to be sought. (1.66)

He demonstrates that the Self, which exists as all-pervasive—like oil in sesame seeds and so forth—is not metaphorical but rather direct and real, by stating: "all-pervading" (*sarvavyāpinam*). Just as milk, when boiled, remains situated within its cause and thereby pervades it, so too does the Cause pervade the entire world as its effect; thus, He is "all-pervading. To establish His identity with the nature of Brahman, he provides a direct proof, saying: "the Self" (*ātmeti*).

The term *ālāna* refers to that which is of the nature of the single essence of consciousness-bliss (*cit-ānanda-ekarasa*). That knowledge (*vidyā*) which consists of direct realization and is produced by means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), as well as that austerity (*tapas*) consisting of the duties prescribed for the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*)—namely, rituals such as sacrifice (*yajña*) and charity (*dāna*)—both of these are the causes for the attainment of the Self; he is thus described [as having them]. He who, being wise, perceives the Self as being of such a nature—that very thing is the Supreme Brahman. It is qualified as "Upaniṣad. Regarding the word *upaniṣad*, there are three meanings characterized by the roots *sad* preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *ni*: [the sense of] dissolving, [the sense of] reaching, and [the sense of] destroying ignorance.

The *upaniṣad* is so called because the non-dual Brahman, having entered into the state of being the inner self (*ālambhāva*) within all living beings and manifesting in its unconditioned form (*nirupādhika-rūpa*), utterly dissolves (*vijṛṇāti*)—that is, destroys—their worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Alternatively, it is the Supreme Brahman as the *upaniṣad*, because the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), abiding in the state of the individual soul (*jīvabhāva*), brings about the attainment of oneness by leading [the soul] to its own true nature, and thereby causes that ignorance (*avidyā*) to perish—that is, renders it slack.

Since it is recited as "sad-om" in the Upaniṣad scripture, it should likewise be recited here. Thus, by the word "Upaniṣad," the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is meant; the meaning is that [Brahman] is to be reached or attained by means of that [knowledge]. || 67 ||

One should behold the Supreme Lord, who is utterly free from all attributes. (This was also established previously [in 7.38 and 8.18]. || 65 || Just as there is oil in sesame seeds, ghee in curd, water in a stream, and fire in the fire-sticks, so is this Self within the intellect. He who strives to perceive Him through truth and austerity attains direct realization of Him. (This is to be understood through the traditional lineage.)

Regarding the means (*upāya*), the first is the practice of yoga (*yogābhyāsa*), the second is devotion (*bhakti*) and detachment (*vairāgya*), and the third is the absence of causal agency (*akartṛkatva*); these four examples have been explained in detail by the Teacher (pp. 87–89). [The fourth is] the efficacy of truth (*satya*) and austerity (*tapas*).

Endowed with devotion to Śiva and having prostrated at the feet of the Guru, and likewise by hearing the great sayings (mahāvākya) of the Vedāntas, as well as by reflection and meditation upon the Supreme Self, one attains the knowledge of the oneness of the individual self and Brahman and goes to the supreme Śiva. Having gone there, he immediately attains his own perfection in the form of Śiva right here.

And that Self, which is traditionally taught in the *Sāra* and *Upaniṣads*, is the very essence of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). Thus he says: "It exists"—that indeed is the Self. Although consciousness, as distinguished from the aggregate of cause and effect, appears as the Self by virtue of being denoted by the word "I," [the true Self] is not the body, senses, and so forth, because these are objects of perception like a jar and thus lack selfhood. Therefore, the innermost witness, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, is the Self indicated by the word "I," and not the body and such; this is the meaning. The meaning is that by this [ignorance], there is the concealment of one's own nature as Brahman, which is beyond saṃsāra. "Even though he is Śiva" means that although Śiva is omnipresent, he alone appears within all living beings as the individual soul (jīva), delimited by various respective adjuncts (upādhis), according to the Vedic text: "Having entered with this living self, let me evolve names and forms. || 2 || 3 ||

Thus, since the state of being a transmigratory being (*saṃsāritva*) is caused solely by the ignorance of one's own true nature, its cessation does not depend on anything other than knowledge; and that knowledge is established by this method. This is a useful summary of the subject matter. Listen with faith to this exposition of the supreme reality. O Devas! That which is the object of these words and experiences is the Supreme Knowledge alone; it is the Self of us all. (It is not an object for the self-consciousness.)

The Self, characterized by the nature of being an agent and so forth, becomes an object [of cognition]; this and more should be seen in detail in the commentaries on superimposition (*adhyāsa*). This *Brahmagītā* is hereby concluded.
